title: IMMS (Intelligent Material Management System) for the entire library collection.
source_description: Helsinki City Library introduced the Intelligent Material Management System during its transition from separate library-specific collections towards one shared collection serving the whole city network. The operational problem was that materials needed to move more flexibly between branches, while library staff required better visibility over where items were located, how they circulated and how available space could be used. The objective was to support a “floating” collection model, in which books and other materials are no longer tied permanently to a single branch but can circulate according to user demand and operational needs. Implemented in May 2019, IMMS complements the existing library management infrastructure by adding a more detailed layer of collection, space and logistics management. The system uses data collection tools to track materials at granular locations, including shelves, shelving carts, transport bins and storage areas, thereby creating greater transparency across the material flow. It supports decision-making on stock distribution, item movement, collection balance and physical space use across the library network. As a result, Helsinki City Library has been able to move towards a model in which most of the collection floats between libraries. The main benefits include more efficient use of the overall collection, improved staff control over logistics, better alignment between material availability and user demand, and a more scalable approach to managing public library resources across multiple branches.

title: NeRo Chatbot - Chatbot for clients of maternity services
source_description: The City of Helsinki developed NeRo to support parents, expectant parents and carers who need reliable information about pregnancy, infant health and the early development of children. Maternity and child-health services often receive recurring questions on topics such as growth, nutrition, dental care, speech development and everyday health concerns, and users may need guidance outside normal service hours. NeRo responds to this need by offering an around-the-clock digital support channel in Finnish, giving families an accessible source of basic information before they contact health professionals or attend appointments. The chatbot is designed to answer questions related to pregnancy and the health care of babies and small children, covering both preventive guidance and common development-related issues. Technically, it applies conversational technology and language understanding to interpret user questions and match them with curated information from municipal health-service content. The system provides automated responses within a defined service scope and can guide users towards relevant topics without replacing professional medical assessment where individual care is required. Its impact is primarily qualitative: it improves the availability of trusted municipal guidance, helps families obtain answers at any time of day, reduces the burden of repetitive enquiries on maternity and child-health staff, and strengthens the digital service offer of Helsinki’s public health system.

organization: Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment
title: Job Market Finland - Matching employees with right jobs
source_description: Job Market Finland was developed by the KEHA Centre and the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment to improve how jobseekers, employers and service providers interact within the Finnish labour market. The service addresses a core policy and operational challenge: matching people to suitable vacancies in a context where skills, occupations, training services and employment opportunities are distributed across multiple public and private platforms. Its objective is to create a shared digital environment where jobseekers can present their profiles, employers can identify relevant candidates, and different labour-market services can be connected more coherently. The emerging technology component is centred on an AI-based matching solution that compares jobseeker profiles with vacancies using both structured data, such as skills and occupations, and unstructured natural-language information contained in descriptions. The system scores the degree of fit between candidates and roles and presents matches to both jobseekers and employers. It also assists users in describing the skills they offer or require, helping to improve the quality of profile and vacancy information. The expected impact is a more efficient matching process, better visibility of opportunities, reduced friction in recruitment, and stronger alignment between labour supply and employer demand. By combining public employment services with data-driven matching, the platform supports a more transparent, scalable and user-oriented labour-market infrastructure.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI assisted chat service - Chatbot for tax purposes
source_description: OmaVero is a chatbot service that provides the Finnish Tax Administration with a digital channel for answering common tax-related questions from individual taxpayers. The service responds to the recurring need for quick, accessible and low-threshold guidance on tax matters, particularly when users are looking for general clarification rather than case-specific decisions. It allows customers to receive assistance without calling the administration, paying telephone costs or completing identification steps for basic enquiries. During office hours, the interaction can be escalated to a human agent when the automated response is not sufficient, ensuring that more complex issues can still be handled by staff. The technological implementation combines a virtual agent with natural language processing, which converts customer messages into a form that the system can interpret and route towards relevant tax content. The underlying AI-assisted chat solution was developed by a commercial provider, while the Finnish Tax Administration remains responsible for governance, including training, monitoring and content creation through its chat-product team. This arrangement allows the administration to retain control over service quality and accuracy while using external technology to support delivery. The main benefits are faster replies to routine questions, broader service availability regardless of time, reduced demand on telephone and front-office channels, and a more efficient allocation of human agents to cases requiring judgement or personalised assistance.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: MLOps platform for classification purposes - Developing classification models
source_description: Statistics Finland’s MLOps platform is designed to make the development, deployment and maintenance of machine-learning classification models more robust within official statistics production. The operational problem is that statistical organisations increasingly use models in internal workflows, but each project can otherwise require separate decisions on architecture, security, deployment, monitoring and maintenance. This creates duplication and weakens consistency across statistical processes. The platform supports expert users working with internal data or statistical production pipelines, where classification models may operate either in batch mode or as online prediction services. Its implementation defines common architecture and security policies for model development, reducing the need to redesign governance and technical arrangements case by case. Conceptually, the system covers the machine-learning lifecycle, from model construction and deployment to monitoring and operational maintenance, while ensuring that outputs remain internal intermediate products before aggregation and publication as official statistics. The expected impact is improved reliability, easier model reuse, stronger governance, reduced operational risk and more efficient development of classification models. By standardising MLOps practices, Statistics Finland can scale machine-learning use while preserving statistical quality and confidentiality requirements.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Anomaly detection in e-government administration
source_description: Hungary’s anomaly-detection initiative focuses on protecting the reliability and availability of critical digital public services. The operational challenge is that modern e-government systems generate large volumes of technical and usage data, while service disruptions or misuse can affect citizens’ ability to complete administrative procedures. IdomSoft, a state-owned company responsible for a wide range of Hungarian digital government services, is introducing machine-learning techniques to predict future system loads and identify abnormal use of public-service systems. The implementation applies anomaly-detection algorithms to data generated by administrative digital services, enabling the authority to analyse usage patterns and detect possible service corruption, overload or misuse. Conceptually, the system combines monitoring data, predictive modelling, anomaly detection and operational alerting to support service continuity. The expected impact is improved resilience of e-government platforms, lower risk of disruption, better targeting of technical interventions and reduced operational costs. By moving from reactive maintenance to predictive monitoring, the initiative can strengthen the dependability of digital administration and improve the user experience for citizens relying on online public services.

title: Prediction supply of trucks - Machine Learning to predict truck scheduling
source_description: La Poste’s truck-scheduling use case addresses the difficulty of managing loading operations when incoming trucks arrive early, on time or late because of congestion and other disruptions. The operational problem is that uncertain arrival times reduce loading-bay utilisation and force logistics operators to make costly rescheduling decisions. The solution combines a machine-learning classifier with an optimisation model: the classifier estimates the probability that each truck will arrive early, on time or late, and these probabilities are then used to proactively adjust loading slots. At a conceptual level, the system links real-time truck-location information, historical traffic data, predictive classification and mathematical rescheduling. The expected impact is more efficient loading-bay management, lower disruption costs and better transport-flow optimisation. Research on the case reported that the combined predictive and proactive approach reduced rescheduling costs by around 42% compared with a baseline schedule without real-time arrival predictions. This indicates that predictive information can materially improve operational planning when integrated with optimisation rather than used only as a passive forecast.

title: a-z.lu to digitise text documents for Luxembourg's National Library
source_description: The Bibliothèque nationale de Luxembourg implemented this use case to improve the accessibility, usability and long-term management of textual documents held in its collections. National libraries are responsible not only for preserving documentary heritage, but also for making it discoverable and usable for researchers, public institutions and citizens. The operational challenge addressed here concerns the conversion of scanned or image-based materials into structured, searchable and better-organised digital resources. The objective is to enhance the quality of digitised content by correcting errors, identifying meaningful information within texts and improving the organisation of associated image content. The implementation uses optical character recognition as a foundation for transforming scanned documents into machine-readable text, followed by correction processes to improve the reliability of the extracted content. Entity extraction is then applied to identify relevant names, places, organisations or other significant references within the material, while image-content organisation supports better structuring and retrieval of visual components. Together, these techniques make the digitised collections easier to search, classify and reuse. The impact is a stronger digital library service, improved discoverability of national documentary resources, higher-quality metadata and text outputs, and better support for research and public access. Over time, the approach contributes to more scalable digitisation workflows and strengthens the National Library’s capacity to preserve and disseminate Luxembourg’s cultural and documentary heritage.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Kranj Digital Twin - Representation of the city digitally
source_description: The City Municipality of Kranj launched this use case in 2021 to explore how a residential district could be managed through more integrated, data-informed urban services. The pilot focused on Mlaka pri Kranju and was carried out with a consortium of local companies, including RIKO d.o.o., 3fs d.o.o., Iskraemeco d.d., Komunala Kranj d.o.o., Domplan d.o.o., Elektro Gorenjska d.d. and Vigred d.o.o. The main operational need was to obtain a clearer, more timely picture of how neighbourhood infrastructure performs, particularly in relation to utilities, environmental conditions, traffic and connectivity. Rather than managing these domains separately, the municipality aimed to create a smart-neighbourhood model that could later be extended to other parts of the city. The technological implementation centres on a digital twin approach, combining data from smart electricity, gas and water meters with environmental and traffic sensors, supported by a telecommunications backbone. These inputs are collected, visualised and analysed to create a digital representation of selected neighbourhood functions and infrastructure conditions. The resulting model can support monitoring, planning and service coordination at local level. Its value lies in giving the municipality and service providers a more coherent operational view, improving evidence for infrastructure decisions, enabling future scalability across Kranj, and establishing a practical foundation for broader smart-city development.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AuroraAI - Ministry of Finance
source_description: AuroraAI was launched in Finland as a national service model intended to support more human-centric public services and more informed public-sector management. The underlying challenge was that services were often organised in silos, making it harder for citizens and businesses to receive timely support aligned with real-life situations and harder for authorities to allocate services in a coordinated way. AuroraAI sought to respond to this by creating a “well-being snapshot” and linking it to service provision across different life events, with the objective of improving relevance, timing and coordination in public support. The stakeholders included citizens, companies, responsible authorities and public-service organisations, with the broader aim of reshaping how government worked across institutional boundaries. The solution was implemented through a decentralised network architecture designed to connect service providers and allocate services more effectively based on identified needs. At a conceptual level, the model combined distributed data use, service-matching logic and ethical-governance principles, with responsible organisations coordinating the application of the model to selected life events. This was intended to enable knowledge-based management as well as more timely support for end users. The anticipated impact included better cross-service coordination, less fragmented service supply and stronger conditions for ethically functioning digital support in government. Although the service model is no longer in use, AuroraAI remains significant as an ambitious attempt to redesign public services around life events, wellbeing and coordinated digital governance.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: DBA - Intelligent Control Platform
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: The Danish Business Authority developed the Intelligent Control Platform to strengthen how public-sector control, supervision and decision-support processes are carried out in areas where large volumes of administrative and operational data must be continuously assessed. The research unit behind the initiative was established in 2017, when the Authority put its first two models into production and integrated them directly with internal control systems. The purpose was to move beyond static checks and enable more dynamic monitoring, where changes in data could be evaluated quickly against defined thresholds and used to support operational decisions. The platform has since evolved through several generations and now includes around 30 models in production. Technically, it combines machine-learning models with internal control-system data, allowing new information to be assessed as it becomes available. The Authority is also working with real-time graph machine learning and fraud-detection methods, supported by a data-platform architecture designed to handle continuous analysis and model deployment. The system therefore functions as an intelligent layer over existing control processes, identifying patterns, risks or threshold breaches that may require attention. Its impact is a more scalable and data-driven approach to supervision, improved capacity to detect irregularities, faster interpretation of changing datasets, and better support for staff responsible for control activities and fraud prevention.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Civocracy - Online Platform
source_description: Civocracy provides public authorities with an online participation environment designed to improve dialogue between citizens, businesses, civil-society organisations and governments. The use case addresses a recurring challenge in public consultation: traditional participation processes can be fragmented, limited in reach and difficult to analyse systematically once large volumes of feedback are collected. By offering a structured digital space for discussion, debate and idea generation, the platform aims to make consultation more transparent, inclusive and continuous. It has been used by cities in Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, supporting local authorities that want to involve communities in policy development, urban planning or service improvement. Its implementation combines online discussion-board functionality with tools for crowdsourcing ideas, tracking participation, producing statistics and monitoring the impact of engagement activities in real time. Data analytics and machine-learning capabilities support the analysis of group sentiment and help public bodies understand how participants respond to proposals or policy themes. This makes consultation outputs easier to interpret and compare, particularly where feedback is broad or diverse. The platform’s main benefits include wider participation, clearer evidence from citizen input, more transparent follow-up on public discussions and stronger trust-building between institutions and communities. For administrations, it also creates a reusable and scalable channel for managing participatory processes across multiple policy areas.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Chaos - Analysis of multiple data sources to forecast property market performance
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: CHAOS provides AI-driven location intelligence for the real-estate sector by analysing multiple data sources to forecast property-market performance and generate actionable insights. The business problem is that investors, property developers, cities and retail operators need to understand how neighbourhood dynamics, service accessibility, demographics, mobility and local amenities affect real-estate value and urban development potential. Traditional property analysis can be fragmented, slow and insufficiently sensitive to changes in urban environments. CHAOS addresses this by combining data analytics, AI and built-environment expertise to support more informed decision-making. Conceptually, the platform integrates heterogeneous urban and market datasets, models location attractiveness and produces insights that can guide investment, development and planning choices. The expected impact is faster property analysis, more evidence-based investment decisions, improved understanding of local demand and support for more liveable urban development. Recent company information indicates that CHAOS has moved beyond an experimental phase and is scaling its AI-driven location-intelligence platform across the Nordics and DACH region.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Prediction of heart failure from exacerbations in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) patients
source_description: This use case focuses on reducing avoidable deterioration and hospital admissions among patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and heart failure by identifying warning signs early enough for preventive treatment to begin. In routine care, exacerbations can escalate quickly, and delayed intervention may result in emergency admission, worsening health status and higher pressure on clinical services. The use case therefore involves patients, clinicians and remote-monitoring teams, with the objective of detecting elevated risk before a serious event occurs and enabling earlier, more targeted clinical action. The solution is implemented through a predictive algorithm that analyses patient-reported measurements such as blood pressure, oxygen saturation and heart rate. At a conceptual level, these physiological data are captured through monitoring processes, assessed for risk patterns associated with exacerbation or heart failure, and translated into alerts that notify healthcare professionals when a patient’s condition appears to be deteriorating. This allows preventive treatment to be initiated before the event fully develops and integrates monitoring with clinical decision support. The expected impact is fewer admissions, better prevention of deterioration and a more proactive model of care for vulnerable patients. More broadly, the use case improves service responsiveness, enhances patient safety and experience, and creates business value through more efficient use of healthcare resources and better continuity of care.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Artificial Intelligence for faster and better diagnosis of emergency patients
source_description: In emergency departments, clinicians must decide quickly whether a patient can be safely discharged or needs immediate admission, often while facing incomplete information, time pressure and high patient volumes. This use case addresses the operational need for faster, more reliable early assessment of emergency patients, particularly in distinguishing non-critical cases from those requiring urgent hospital care. The stakeholders include emergency physicians, nurses, laboratory services and hospital managers, all of whom need better decision support to improve triage, reduce delays and allocate beds and clinical attention more effectively. The objective is to strengthen the initial diagnostic process so that patients receive the right level of care sooner and hospital resources are directed where they are most needed. The solution is implemented through a diagnostic-support tool that analyses blood and urine samples and applies predictive models to identify the 15 most common acute illnesses and infections seen in emergency settings. At a conceptual level, the system combines laboratory data, probabilistic ranking methods and workflow integration to produce a prioritised list of likely diagnoses within 60 minutes of the patient’s arrival. This enables clinicians to incorporate rapid analytical insight into admission and treatment decisions. The expected impact is quicker diagnosis, more accurate triage and improved use of emergency capacity. In practice, the tool supports better patient flow, a more consistent clinical response and greater value through safer, more efficient acute-care delivery.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Artificial Intelligence in general practice
source_description: General practitioners routinely receive large volumes of clinical information, including laboratory results, many of which do not require immediate medical action but still demand time and attention to review. This creates an administrative burden that can reduce the time available for direct patient care and increase the risk that urgent findings are not prioritised as quickly as they should be. The use case therefore focuses on supporting physicians in general practice by improving the handling of incoming test results and helping surgeries manage clinical information more efficiently. The stakeholders include GPs, practice staff and patients, with the objective of reducing routine workload, sharpening clinical prioritisation and freeing up professional capacity for treatment and patient interaction. The solution is implemented through algorithms that automatically process selected test results, sort blood-test outputs and flag results requiring immediate physician attention. At a conceptual level, the system uses classification and prioritisation techniques applied to structured clinical data, embedded within the practice’s existing information flows so that incoming results can be routed, filtered and escalated appropriately. This means routine or low-risk results can be handled more efficiently, while urgent cases are surfaced promptly for review. The impact is expected to include lower administrative effort, quicker response to clinically significant findings and better use of time in primary care. More broadly, the approach improves reliability, enhances workflow efficiency and strengthens the overall quality and responsiveness of general-practice services.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Real-time predictions and essential information for clinicians
source_description: Hospitals need timely and accurate information on ward occupancy, discharges and likely patient returns in order to plan staffing, organise patient pathways and make the best possible use of available beds. Without a current picture of capacity, operational decisions can become reactive, leading to bottlenecks, inefficient resource allocation and pressure on both patients and staff. This use case addresses that challenge by equipping health professionals with real-time insight into hospital capacity and expected patient movement. The stakeholders include ward managers, clinicians, discharge planners and hospital operations teams, with the objective of improving day-to-day planning and supporting smoother patient flow across the organisation. The solution is implemented through predictive models that estimate bed-occupancy rates, the expected number of discharges and the risk of patient readmission. At a conceptual level, the system combines hospital activity data with forecasting techniques to generate a live operational view of capacity, which can be integrated into existing planning and coordination processes. This allows staff to anticipate pressure points rather than simply react to them once they occur. The expected impact is better use of hospital capacity, more efficient organisation of patient pathways and improved staff planning. In operational and business terms, the approach increases scalability, supports more reliable decision-making and enhances the patient experience by reducing avoidable delays and improving the coordination of care delivery.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Better diagnosis of prostate cancer
source_description: Prostate cancer is frequently identified at an early stage, when the disease has not yet spread beyond the prostate, yet many patients still undergo surgery that may later prove unnecessary and can cause complications or long-term discomfort. This use case addresses the clinical and operational challenge of determining which patients genuinely need intervention and which can be managed more conservatively without compromising outcomes. The stakeholders include urologists, oncologists, multidisciplinary cancer teams and patients, with the objective of improving treatment decisions, reducing overtreatment and ensuring that surgery is reserved for cases where the risk of progression is sufficiently high. The solution is implemented through a risk-assessment model trained on historical disease patterns and clinical outcome data to estimate the likelihood that the cancer will spread from the prostate. At a conceptual level, the system analyses patterns in previous patient trajectories and produces an individualised risk estimate that can be incorporated into medical assessment and treatment planning. This supports clinicians in distinguishing patients who may require surgery to prevent metastases from those who may safely avoid surgical treatment. The expected impact is more precise diagnosis-related decision-making, fewer unnecessary operations and a better balance between clinical benefit and treatment burden. In practical terms, the use case improves patient experience, supports more efficient use of surgical resources and creates value through more personalised and proportionate cancer care.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Artificial Intelligence for better planning of cancer treatments
source_description: Cancer services must balance clinical complexity, finite resources and the need to tailor treatment to the individual patient’s likely trajectory. A major operational challenge is to identify which patients are at greater risk and therefore need more intensive treatment or closer monitoring, and which may be managed through less demanding pathways without compromising outcomes. This use case focuses on stratifying cancer patients into meaningful risk groups so that care plans can be better aligned with individual needs and clinical resources can be deployed more effectively. The stakeholders include oncologists, cancer-care teams, hospital planners and patients, with the objective of supporting more personalised treatment planning and improving the overall efficiency of care delivery. The solution is implemented through predictive models that divide patients into high-risk and low-risk groups on the basis of relevant clinical data and disease characteristics. At a conceptual level, the system combines risk stratification, pattern recognition and decision-support integration so that treatment pathways can be adapted according to the patient’s expected level of need. This enables clinicians to supplement their judgement with structured analytical insight when planning therapies and follow-up. The expected impact is better adaptation of treatment plans, improved use of healthcare resources and more consistent targeting of intensive care to those most likely to benefit. More broadly, the approach supports scalability, strengthens clinical precision and enhances patient value through more individualised cancer treatment.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Artificial Intelligence to prevent complications after bowel cancer surgery
source_description: Bowel cancer surgery carries substantial risk: around one in four patients develops complications after the operation, and roughly one in three experiences relapse. This creates a pressing need for earlier identification of patients who are most vulnerable to poor outcomes so that treatment plans can be adjusted before surgery and postoperative care can be better targeted. The use case therefore addresses the challenge of improving risk assessment in bowel cancer pathways, with the aim of reducing complications, mortality and recurrence. The stakeholders include surgeons, oncologists, perioperative teams and patients, all of whom benefit from more precise information when deciding how treatment and follow-up should be organised. The solution is implemented through a predictive model trained on health-registry data relating to bowel cancer patients and embedded in a software module for clinical use. At a conceptual level, the system analyses individual patient data to estimate the risk of death, complications, readmission, re-operation and relapse, providing structured support for preoperative and postoperative planning. This allows clinicians to identify higher-risk cases earlier and adapt treatment plans accordingly. The expected impact is more proactive care, fewer preventable adverse outcomes and stronger support for personalised surgical pathways. In practical and economic terms, the approach can improve patient safety, reduce avoidable readmissions and complications, and generate business value through better resource use and more efficient management of complex cancer care.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Reduction of radiation dose in relation to scans used in cancer treatment
source_description: PET imaging is an important tool in cancer diagnosis and treatment planning, but it requires the injection of a radioactive tracer, and higher tracer doses generally produce clearer images. The operational challenge is therefore to maintain diagnostic image quality while reducing the radiation exposure faced by patients, particularly when repeated scans may be required over time. The stakeholders include radiologists, nuclear-medicine specialists, oncology teams and patients, with the objective of making imaging safer and more cost-effective without undermining its clinical usefulness. The solution is implemented through image-processing models that work on scans acquired using a reduced radiation dose. At a conceptual level, the system addresses the increased noise created by lower-dose imaging by applying denoising and reconstruction techniques that enhance image clarity sufficiently for diagnostic use. This allows the scan to retain its practical value while lowering the quantity of tracer administered. The expected impact is a reduction in radiation exposure and, consequently, a lower long-term risk associated with imaging, alongside savings linked to reduced use of radioactive tracer. In broader terms, the use case improves patient safety, supports more sustainable imaging practice and enhances service efficiency by preserving diagnostic quality while lowering both clinical risk and material cost.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI-Rehabilitering (AIR) - Intelligent rehabilitation and targeted healthcare services for citizens
source_description: In municipal rehabilitation services, one recurring challenge is that citizens who could benefit from physical exercise or preventive support are not always identified or referred at the most appropriate time. This can delay intervention, reduce the likelihood of successful outcomes and limit the efficient use of rehabilitation resources, assistive aids and fall-prevention measures. The AIR use case, anchored in the Municipality of Aalborg, addresses this problem by supporting case workers who must decide which rehabilitation pathway best matches an individual citizen’s needs and prospects. Its objective is to improve the consistency and timing of referrals, strengthen professional judgement and ensure that citizens are directed towards the course of action most likely to deliver benefit. The solution is implemented as a decision-support tool built on statistical modelling and predictive analytics. At a conceptual level, it analyses citizen-level data to estimate current eligibility for a rehabilitation course, the likelihood of completing it successfully and the expected level of benefit from participation. These outputs are designed to complement, rather than replace, the case worker’s assessment and can also support decisions on specific interventions, assistive-device use and fall prevention. The expected impact is more targeted rehabilitation, earlier and better-informed intervention and improved allocation of municipal care resources. In practice, this can enhance service quality, increase consistency in decision-making and create value through more efficient and personalised support for citizens.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Faster case processing when granting cleaning services using new technology
source_description: Assessing whether a citizen should receive municipal cleaning assistance can vary considerably in complexity, as case workers must evaluate individual need on the basis of health, living conditions and household circumstances. This variation creates uneven workloads and can slow down decision-making, particularly where straightforward cases consume time that could otherwise be devoted to more complex assessments. The purpose of this use case is therefore to improve the quality and speed of case processing for citizens while releasing capacity for staff to focus on cases requiring greater professional attention. The stakeholders include municipal case workers, social-care administrators and citizens applying for support, all of whom benefit from a more consistent and efficient assessment process. The solution is implemented through a decision-support tool that uses structured data on the citizen’s condition, housing situation and possible cohabitants to inform recommendations on eligibility for cleaning services. At a conceptual level, the system applies classification and pattern-recognition techniques to comparable historical cases and integrates the resulting output into the case worker’s existing workflow. This allows routine applications to be assessed more efficiently while preserving human oversight in the final decision. The expected impact is shorter processing times, improved consistency in eligibility assessments and better use of staff resources. More broadly, the approach strengthens service quality, improves the citizen experience and supports a more scalable model for handling municipal care applications.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Intelligent sorting and filing of mail to provide citizens with faster case processing
source_description: Norddjurs Municipality receives substantial volumes of digital mail and emails every day through a central inbox, and each message must be sorted, routed to the correct case worker and filed appropriately before any substantive action can begin. These are routine but resource-intensive administrative tasks that consume staff time and can delay the start of case processing for citizens. This use case addresses that operational bottleneck by aiming to streamline intake management and reduce the manual burden associated with handling incoming correspondence. The stakeholders include administrative staff, case workers and citizens, with the objective of accelerating distribution, improving filing accuracy and ensuring that enquiries reach the right destination more quickly. The solution is implemented through an automated mail-handling system that classifies incoming digital mail and email, distributes it to the relevant recipients and files it in the appropriate location. At a conceptual level, the system combines text classification, routing logic and document-management integration to interpret message content and connect it with the municipality’s internal case-processing structure. This enables intake tasks to be handled with greater speed and consistency than purely manual processing. The expected impact is reduced administrative workload, quicker initiation of citizen cases and improved reliability in document handling. In practical terms, the use case supports faster case processing, better internal efficiency and a more scalable way to manage growing communication volumes in municipal administration.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Shorter response time to construction applications and help submitting correct documents
source_description: Municipal construction applications often take a long time to process, not only because of the complexity of planning and compliance checks, but also because many submissions are incomplete or incorrectly prepared from the outset. This creates delays for applicants and additional workload for case workers, who must spend time identifying errors, requesting further documentation and comparing the case with similar precedents. The use case therefore focuses on improving the efficiency and consistency of construction-application handling, with the objective of reducing response times and supporting better-quality submissions. The stakeholders include applicants, municipal planning officers and case workers, all of whom benefit when straightforward errors can be identified early and previous comparable decisions are easier to consult. The solution is implemented as a decision-support tool that screens applications for likely errors and retrieves relevant decisions from earlier similar cases. At a conceptual level, the system uses document analysis and case-comparison techniques to highlight missing or problematic elements and present precedent information within the case worker’s assessment process. This helps staff make more informed and consistent decisions while also improving the quality of the material under review. The expected impact is shorter case-processing times, fewer avoidable delays caused by incorrect documentation and greater consistency in planning decisions. More broadly, the approach improves the applicant experience, reduces administrative effort and creates value through more efficient municipal permitting processes.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Correct and uniform case management when sanctioning unemployed citizens
source_description: Deciding whether an unemployed citizen should be subject to an economic sanction is a difficult and sensitive task, as case workers must consider not only the triggering event, such as absence from an interview or activation offer, but also whether a sanction is likely to have the intended effect on the person’s availability for work. In practice, these judgements are not always applied uniformly, which can lead to inconsistency in case handling and uncertainty for both staff and citizens. This use case addresses the need for more consistent and evidence-informed decision-making in employment services. The stakeholders include case workers, employment-service managers and unemployed citizens, with the objective of supporting fairer and more uniform assessments while helping staff distinguish between cases in which sanctions may be effective and those in which they may not. The solution is implemented through a decision-support tool that analyses factors associated with positive or negative effects on a citizen’s likelihood of becoming more available for employment. At a conceptual level, the system evaluates adverse events and broader citizen characteristics to support judgements on whether a sanction should be triggered. These analytical outputs are integrated into the case worker’s decision process rather than replacing professional discretion. The expected impact is more consistent case management, better-targeted use of sanctions and improved transparency in decision-making. In operational terms, the approach enhances fairness, reliability and resource efficiency across municipal employment services.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Targeted employment programmes for unemployed citizens
source_description: Employment services often need to decide which programme or activity is most likely to help a job-ready unemployed citizen return to work quickly, yet this is difficult to do consistently without clear evidence on what interventions deliver the strongest results for different profiles. The challenge is not simply to offer support, but to direct each individual towards the activities most likely to shorten unemployment and improve outcomes. This use case responds to that need by helping case workers design more targeted employment programmes for unemployed citizens. The stakeholders include employment advisers, case workers, programme managers and citizens seeking work, with the objective of reducing unemployment duration and improving the relevance and benefit of employment services. The solution is implemented as a decision-support tool that uses individual citizen information to propose specific activities expected to reduce the likely period of unemployment. At a conceptual level, the system combines predictive modelling with recommendation logic, drawing on patterns from previous programme outcomes and citizen characteristics to identify interventions with the greatest expected effect. These suggestions are then incorporated into the case worker’s planning process. The expected impact is more personalised employment support, faster transitions back into work and better use of programme resources. More broadly, the approach strengthens the effectiveness of labour-market services, improves the citizen experience and creates value by aligning support measures more closely with individual needs and likely outcomes.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Better match between unemployed citizens and companies
source_description: Even where employers are actively seeking staff, matching unemployed citizens to suitable vacancies can remain difficult because the fit between a person’s experience, transferable skills and available roles is not always obvious from standard job titles or sector boundaries. As a result, case workers may struggle to guide citizens towards realistic opportunities, especially where alternative occupations or industries could offer a viable route back into employment. This use case addresses that challenge by improving how unemployed citizens are matched with company demand and by supporting more targeted job-search strategies. The stakeholders include case workers, job-ready unemployed citizens and employers, with the objective of increasing the effectiveness of employment programmes and improving the connection between labour supply and labour demand. The solution is implemented through a matching tool that compares the professional and personal capabilities described in citizens’ CVs with the requirements listed in current job openings. At a conceptual level, the system uses skills-matching and recommendation techniques to identify suitable vacancies, including alternatives in other industries or job types that may not have been considered initially. These results support the case worker in guiding the citizen towards a broader and more realistic search strategy. The expected impact is better job matching, a more focused job-search process and improved employment outcomes. In practical terms, the approach enhances service quality, increases the utility of available vacancy data and creates value through more efficient and responsive labour-market intermediation.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: NER-based extraction of contract data
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Public bodies that handle large volumes of incoming correspondence and forms often face a difficult administrative problem: important information is buried in siloed documents and must be extracted manually before it can be reused in central systems. Smals, as an ICT provider for government, explored this challenge with public-sector partners such as the RSZ/ONSS, where the broader aim was to support data centralisation and reduce the effort required to process incoming material. The use case focused on extracting structured information from emails and forms, including names, roles and telephone numbers, so that staff could move faster from unstructured documents to usable records. The stakeholders include administrative teams, ICT specialists and the government bodies seeking to consolidate data sources, with the objective of improving efficiency while retaining sufficient control over data quality. The solution was implemented through named-entity recognition and related natural-language-processing techniques applied to scanned documents and digital correspondence. At a conceptual level, the system first converts paper-based material into machine-readable text through scanning and OCR, then applies entity-extraction models to identify specific data fields. The proof-of-concept work showed that highly structured information can be captured with reasonable effectiveness, while context-dependent elements such as job functions remain more difficult to interpret reliably. The impact lies in reduced manual effort and better support for mailroom and intake automation, but also in a clearer understanding of the limits of current extraction tools, including the need for human validation where full accuracy cannot be guaranteed.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Roads and Traffic Agency of the Flemish Government
title: Creation and management of semantic OTL relationships
source_description: The Flemish Roads and Traffic Agency’s semantic OTL project supports its transition towards data-driven infrastructure management. The operational problem is that road infrastructure assets, including roads, cycle paths, tunnels, bridges and related equipment, generate information across design, construction, maintenance and replacement phases, but this information must be standardised to remain usable throughout the asset lifecycle. The project aims to develop a tool for creating and managing semantic relationships in the Object Type Library, allowing asset data to be collected once, structured consistently and exchanged across models, databases and software systems. Its implementation builds on BIM and semantic data-management methods, defining relationships between infrastructure object types so that asset information can be shared uniformly among project partners. The expected impact is improved data quality, more efficient collaboration, reduced duplication and stronger lifecycle management of public infrastructure. By embedding semantic standards into asset management, AWV can strengthen interoperability and make infrastructure information more reliable for planning, maintenance and operational decisions.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Flemish Agency for Persons with Disabilities
title: Remote interpreting services - Communicating in Flemish sign language
source_description: The remote interpreting services project aims to improve communication between deaf and hearing people in Flanders by making Flemish Sign Language interpretation available more flexibly and consistently. The service problem is that several comparable services currently operate side by side, creating fragmentation and confusion for users, while existing technical and organisational arrangements do not yet ensure access anytime and anywhere. The project seeks to harmonise and scale remote interpreting so that deaf users can contact everyone by telephone, including emergency services, and can also be contacted by others such as colleagues or doctors in their preferred communication mode. Implementation requires innovation in hardware, software, service organisation, privacy protection and interoperability between existing systems. Conceptually, the solution combines video-remote interpreting, user authentication, service-routing, privacy safeguards and platform harmonisation. The expected impact is improved accessibility, lower organisational costs through consolidation, greater use of remote interpreting and stronger inclusion of deaf users in public, professional and personal communication. Its public value lies in treating language accessibility as an essential service rather than a fragmented accommodation.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Flanders Research Institute for Agriculture, Fisheries and Food (ILVO)
title: AI platform for agri-food applications from field to fork
source_description: Across ILVO’s living labs, food pilot, greenhouses, laboratories and test environments, large volumes of data are generated every day from IoT sensors, machine-mounted cameras, drones, satellites and analytical equipment. The operational challenge is that these data streams are not processed quickly enough, meaning potentially valuable signals for research, testing and operational improvement can be missed. The use case therefore focuses on helping ILVO researchers make better use of the information already being produced, while reducing the barriers that prevent advanced data methods from being used routinely in day-to-day work. Internal stakeholders across research and innovation teams were involved in defining the needs, with the objective of creating a platform that broadens access to data-driven methods and improves the speed and consistency of analysis from field to fork. The solution is being developed as an integrated platform for agri-food data and analytics, designed through a preparatory phase involving user-centred workshops with ILVO stakeholders and supported by consultancy partner Addestino. At a conceptual level, the platform is intended to connect heterogeneous data flows, support data science and model deployment, and provide functionalities that simplify the practical use of advanced analytics in research workflows. The expected impact is faster extraction of useful information, reduced loss of actionable insight and stronger scalability in handling complex agri-food datasets. More broadly, the platform improves research efficiency, supports innovation and creates value by democratising advanced analytical capabilities across ILVO’s operations.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: DigiPolis, IT provider for the City of Antwerp
title: ALTRUIS - Alternative Use of Imaging Systems through Artificial Intelligence
source_description: ALTRUIS was launched to help Antwerp respond to severe mobility pressures by extracting useful traffic and mobility insights from existing camera footage. The operational context was particularly challenging because Antwerp already experienced heavy congestion, while major infrastructure works placed additional pressure on mobility and quality of life. Digipolis sought to turn street images, which have limited value in raw form, into mobility intelligence for the city, especially in the Smart Zone. The implementation explored alternative use of imaging systems through artificial intelligence, initially focusing on anonymisation of visual material and then on image recognition and algorithms for mobility insights. The procurement later combined these phases into a single assignment and shifted the technological scope towards edge AI, meaning that interpretation would occur closer to the camera instead of relying only on cloud or on-premise GPU processing. The expected impact was better understanding of movement patterns, more responsive mobility management and support for smart-city traffic solutions. The case also highlights the importance of anonymisation, privacy-by-design and careful governance when repurposing urban camera infrastructure.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Capsat - Information from satellite images for a better agricultural policy in Flanders and Europe
source_description: Capsat was developed to support the Department of Agriculture and Fisheries in Flanders in monitoring compliance with agricultural policy requirements linked to the European Common Agricultural Policy. Farmers receiving direct support must respect several climate and environmentally oriented obligations, including crop diversification, grassland maintenance and the creation of ecological focus areas. Traditionally, supervision of these measures has relied on field spot checks, which are resource-intensive, limited in coverage and often unable to provide rapid insight across large agricultural areas. The objective of the use case is therefore to improve follow-up, guidance and control by using remote information that can complement or partially replace manual inspection. The implementation uses high-resolution satellite imagery to map relevant agricultural conditions and detect whether policy measures have been applied correctly and on time. Image-analysis techniques can help identify crops, land use, grassland status or ecological features, while also supporting faster objectification of crop damage caused by drought or flooding. This creates a more systematic evidence base for both compliance monitoring and farmer support. The expected impact is greater efficiency in controls, broader territorial coverage, faster detection of anomalies or damage, and more objective decision-making. In policy terms, Capsat strengthens the administration’s capacity to implement agricultural rules while supporting sustainable, liveable and competitive farming in Flanders and potentially at wider European scale.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: CATE - Continuous Auditing based on Technological Evolution and Data Mining
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: CATE was developed to rethink how the Flemish Audit Authority audits projects subsidised through European Structural Funds and Flemish co-financing. The operational problem is that a significant share of audits must be outsourced, often at high cost and with uneven added value, while the Flemish Audit Authority still needs to spend substantial time on quality control when external auditors lack sufficient expertise in public procurement or state aid. The project aims to redesign the audit process methodologically and technologically so that audits can provide greater assurance, lower costs, shorter turnaround times, higher added value and reduced loss of European resources. The implementation is based on continuous auditing, data mining and technological evolution, with an innovation partnership structured in phases from proof of concept to increasingly mature functionality. Conceptually, the system uses data-driven risk analysis, audit-process automation, analytical models and continuous monitoring of subsidised projects to identify where audit attention is most needed. The expected impact is a more efficient and targeted audit function, stronger detection of irregularities, better use of audit capacity and improved protection of public funds.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Smart Personalisation of the cultural offer in Antwerp Testing (SOCRATES)
source_description: The City of Antwerp and Digipolis launched SOCRATES to address a growing challenge in cultural participation: citizens are exposed to a broad and fragmented cultural offer, yet it is often difficult to connect individuals with activities and content that genuinely match their interests. The project therefore focuses on whether a more tailored, user-driven cultural experience can increase engagement and improve how residents discover literature, events and other cultural opportunities. The stakeholders include the city, Digipolis, cultural users and the wider digital-services ecosystem around Antwerp’s public platforms, with the objective of testing the feasibility and usefulness of an individual cultural profile that can power more relevant recommendations. The solution is implemented through a Digital Experience Platform built around a personal culture profile and enriched by recommendation logic, described as a “wonder algorithm”, that can suggest suitable cultural content. At a conceptual level, the platform is designed modularly so that it can connect with existing and future architecture, especially Antwerp City Platform as a Service, which already offers reusable backend components. SOCRATES extends this model to application front ends and digital touchpoints, allowing the user’s “digital cultural DNA” to inform personalised suggestions. The expected impact is more relevant cultural discovery, better use of digital channels and stronger engagement with Antwerp’s cultural offer. More broadly, the project creates value by testing a scalable, interoperable model for citizen-centred cultural personalisation.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Smart regulation - Using Artificial Intelligence to train computers to interpret regulation
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Smart Regulation responds to the difficulty of navigating fragmented, divergent and incoherent regulatory information. Regulations are essential for citizens, administrations, businesses and software systems, yet relevant provisions are often spread across basic laws, amendments, additions and corrections, making it hard to retrieve the exact rule that applies to a given situation. The Flemish Domestic Governance Agency and Information Flanders aim to create an engine that can process unstructured legal and regulatory sources and provide users with targeted data and insights according to their needs. The implementation uses artificial intelligence to train computer systems to interpret regulation, extract relevant information and make it available for specific target groups, including people, applications and machines. Conceptually, the solution combines natural language processing, legal text mining, semantic structuring, regulatory knowledge extraction and subscription-based access to structured outputs. The expected impact is faster access to applicable rules, reduced information silos, better reuse of regulatory data and stronger support for digital public services that depend on machine-readable legislation. By turning complex legal texts into more structured and queryable information, the project can improve administrative efficiency and regulatory transparency.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Turing - Automatically control Flemish road lighting with local and current data
source_description: Turing addresses the challenge of managing motorway lighting in Flanders in a way that balances energy efficiency, climate objectives, road safety and operational workload. The Agency for Roads and Traffic had already adopted a lighting strategy in 2011 in response to the European Union’s objective of reducing energy consumption by 20% by 2020, and the number of illuminated road sections has since fallen by almost half. However, the existing control approach relies mainly on historical traffic intensities and weather forecasts at provincial level, which limits the precision of decisions on whether lighting is necessary for a specific road segment. The Turing use case aims to make lighting control more localised, timely and evidence-based. Its implementation combines rule-based algorithms with machine-learning techniques to integrate internal and external data sources into the current road-lighting control system. Local and real-time information on traffic intensity and weather conditions can be processed to determine more accurately when lighting should be switched on or off. This allows the system to move from broad assumptions towards segment-level operational decisions. The anticipated results include lower energy consumption, stronger contribution to climate targets, maintained or improved road safety, and a significant reduction in manual workload for operators. The use case also demonstrates how existing infrastructure-management systems can be upgraded through data-driven automation.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Elsa - AI-assisted spreading decisions
source_description: Elsa addresses the need for more consistent winter-service decisions across Flemish road districts. The Agency for Roads and Traffic is responsible for controlling slippery road conditions on the roads it manages, but spreading decisions depend on local interpretation of real-time measurements, weather forecasts and staff experience. Because expertise varies across districts and road networks do not stop at administrative boundaries, inconsistent spreading policies can affect safety, environmental impact and operational efficiency. Elsa is intended to support district employees in deciding whether, when and how to spread de-icing material. The implementation combines physical rules and machine-learning techniques with data from AWV’s smoothness measurement system, which already integrates real-time measurements from monitoring points and stations with forecasts from the Royal Meteorological Institute. Conceptually, the system assesses road and weather conditions, estimates the risk of slipperiness and recommends the type of spreading material, quantity and timing needed to keep roads ice-free. The expected impact is more uniform decision-making, better road safety, reduced unnecessary salt use, lower environmental burden and stronger support for staff during winter operations.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Felmish Energy Company (VEB), Agency for Facility Operations (HFB) and Flemish Energy Agency (VEA)
title: Innovative functionalities and AI for energy saving in the public sector
source_description: The Flemish public sector manages a large and diverse portfolio of buildings and infrastructure, yet turning building and energy data into practical action remains a complex task. Within the Terra patrimony and energy database, substantial information already exists on asset characteristics and energy performance, but the challenge lies in using that information actively and systematically to identify savings opportunities, support renewable energy projects and guide long-term property strategy. This use case brings together VEB, Facilities and Services, and VEA, with the objective of improving how public-sector energy data is used to detect inefficiencies faster, plan interventions more effectively and monitor energy-saving measures with greater precision. The solution explores smart data use through advanced analytics, asset analysis and measurement models, while also assessing where algorithmic methods and a Software-as-a-Service model could add value. At a conceptual level, the approach uses the Terra database as the central information layer for identifying energy-saving potential, informing real-estate strategies, supporting the initiation and monitoring of OEPC contracts, and creating synergies with other digital and sustainability initiatives. The expected impact is earlier identification of savings opportunities, better-managed energy programmes and stronger evidence for investment decisions. In business and operational terms, the initiative supports cost reduction, improves the scalability of energy management and increases the long-term value of public assets through more informed and professionally managed interventions.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Naamsestraat - Reduce night noise through technology and nudging
source_description: Naamsestraat in Leuven is a busy transit route for people returning home after a night out, and this regularly generates disturbance for residents through late-night noise. The City of Leuven is addressing this as part of a broader strategy on nightlife nuisance in which preventive and enforcement measures are intended to work together. The use case therefore focuses on making the street more liveable while preserving the vitality of the city centre, involving municipal authorities and a range of local partners with the objective of detecting disturbing noise more accurately, understanding when and where it occurs, and intervening at the right moment. The solution is being developed as a living lab combining real-time data capture, objectified recognition of disturbing night noise, nudging techniques and predictive intervention planning. At a conceptual level, the implementation uses automated sound recognition to define and map nuisance, links live detections to behavioural nudges in the street environment, and supports scheduling of interventions through predictive models that identify likely high-disturbance moments. This creates a dynamic feedback loop between monitoring and action rather than relying solely on retrospective complaint handling. The expected impact is reduced nuisance, more targeted deployment of municipal measures and an improved nighttime environment for residents. More broadly, the initiative enhances urban liveability, supports evidence-based public-space management and creates a scalable model for tackling nightlife-related disturbance.

organization: Department of Mobility and Public Works (MOW)
title: Clearance of dumped war ammunition in the North Sea
source_description: On the North Sea sandbank De Paardenmarkt near Knokke, around 35,000 tonnes of First World War ammunition, including both conventional and chemical munitions, remain buried beneath the seabed. Although the site is currently regarded as stable, long-term risks persist as corrosion progresses and external factors such as ship strikes could trigger severe pollution, threaten marine safety and constrain coastal and port development. The Flemish government’s Maritime Access department launched this use case to test practical methods for addressing the problem safely and cost-effectively, with the objective of evaluating whether a larger-scale clean-up could be undertaken without creating unacceptable risks for people or the marine environment. The solution is being trialled through a combination of precision detection, environmental monitoring, sediment removal, deepening operations and robotic recovery of buried ammunition. At a conceptual level, the approach integrates seabed sensing, risk monitoring, controlled excavation and remote-handling technologies to locate and retrieve hazardous objects while limiting direct human exposure and minimising ecological disturbance. The expected impact is better understanding of feasible remediation methods, reduced uncertainty around operational risk and stronger preparedness for a full-scale clean-up. In strategic terms, the project supports environmental protection, enhances coastal safety and may unlock future value by reducing obstacles to maritime infrastructure and port development.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Customer call analysis - Finding patterns in the reasons for customer inquiries
source_description: The Social Insurance Board needed a clearer understanding of why citizens were contacting its services and where recurring pain points in service delivery were causing confusion, delays or repeated enquiries. Traditional review methods made it difficult to obtain both a broad statistical overview and a detailed picture of issues emerging across multiple communication channels. This use case therefore focused on helping managers identify patterns in customer concerns more quickly so that services could be improved in a targeted and timely way. The pilot involved an information-line manager and two service managers, with the objective of generating insights that would support managerial decision-making and lead to faster, more convenient public services. The solution was implemented with Feelingstream, which analysed customer contacts across calls, emails and chatbot interactions. During the pilot, calls from May to August 2020 were transcribed in Estonian and Russian, enabling the system to detect themes and recurring reasons for contact across language groups. At a conceptual level, the approach combines transcription, multilingual text analysis and cross-channel pattern detection to turn customer-contact data into actionable service intelligence. The expected impact is faster identification of service problems, better prioritisation of improvements and more informed management decisions. In practice, this enhances efficiency, improves the citizen experience and creates value by linking everyday customer interactions directly to service redesign.

organization: Department of Public Relations of the Ministry of Justice
title: Automatic translation of Riigi Teataja Ametlikud Teadaanded
source_description: Estonia’s Official Gazette introduced automated translation to make website content available in English, responding to the need for greater accessibility for foreign businesses and other international stakeholders while preserving Estonian as the only legally binding language. The operational challenge was to broaden access to official information without creating unsustainable translation costs or slowing publication processes. The use case therefore involved the publisher of the official notices service, external technology partners and users who require reliable access to administrative information in a language other than Estonian. Its objective was to support an open business environment and improve usability for non-Estonian speakers, while maintaining clear legal certainty about which language version is authoritative. The solution is implemented through a neural machine translation system developed with Tilde Eesti OÜ and Inversion OÜ and funded 80% by the European Commission. At a conceptual level, the system generates English versions of website content, captures corrections and feeds those improvements back into the model so that translation quality can improve over time. Quality is also monitored and adjusted by the publisher to maintain accuracy and fitness for use. The expected impact is lower translation cost, broader access to official information and improved convenience for foreign stakeholders. More broadly, the initiative strengthens transparency, supports international engagement and delivers scalable multilingual access without changing the legal status of official publications.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Center of Registers and Information Systems
title: Automatic translation in the Land Register search portal and Commercial Register
source_description: Estonia’s Centre of Registers and Information Systems introduced automatic translation in the e-Land Register and related registry environments to address a practical accessibility problem: non-Estonian speakers often found it difficult to understand detailed registry information, even when they needed only to read and interpret on-screen data rather than obtain a legally binding translation. Registry entries can contain highly technical content, such as information on easements and mortgages, and this can create barriers for foreign users engaging with official systems. The use case therefore involves citizens, businesses and other users of the e-Land Register and Commercial Register, with the objective of improving comprehension of registry data and making these digital public services more accessible internationally. The solution is implemented through a real-time machine translation tool launched in the e-Land Register web environment on 29 October 2021. At a conceptual level, the system uses neural-network-based translation methods that draw links across a large language database and improve over time as vocabulary and patterns are refined. The tool was developed in cooperation between Estonia, Latvia and Belgium, with middleware provided by the Latvian partner TILDE SIA. The translated text is explicitly informative and has no legal force, as Estonian remains the official language of the register. The impact includes improved usability for non-Estonian speakers, greater accessibility of registry information and a more inclusive digital-service experience.

organization: Information System Authority of the Republic of Estonia
title: Bürokratt – a virtual assistant for the Public Administration
source_description: Estonia’s public sector has sought to simplify how people access government services by reducing the need to navigate multiple agencies, channels and digital systems separately. The underlying operational problem is that citizens and businesses often have to move between different websites, interfaces and institutions to complete related tasks, even when they experience them as part of one life event or administrative need. Bürokratt was conceived to address this fragmentation by creating a more unified service experience in which users can obtain information and complete actions through a single conversational entry point. The stakeholders include citizens, public authorities, national information-system operators and, in some cases, private-sector service providers, with the objective of making service access more seamless, reducing friction and improving the efficiency of digital public administration. The solution is implemented as an interoperable network of public-sector virtual assistants, or “kratts”, connected to national information systems and capable of acting together as one channel from the user’s perspective. At a conceptual level, the system combines conversational interfaces, service orchestration and interoperability across public and selected private systems so that multiple tasks can be handled within one communication session and across devices. The expected impact is a more coherent user experience, reduced channel fragmentation and stronger scalability in digital service delivery. More broadly, Bürokratt creates value by supporting a whole-of-government approach to virtual assistance and making public services more accessible, integrated and citizen-centred.

title: Forecasting models Road Administration (Roads conditions and return of investments)
source_description: The Estonian Road Administration is developing forecasting models to address a key infrastructure-management problem: how to decide where road investments will have the greatest effect in terms of network condition and value for money. Road budgets are finite, and without stronger predictive insight it can be difficult to prioritise maintenance and improvement projects in a way that maximises long-term benefit. The use case therefore involves transport authorities, infrastructure planners and investment decision-makers, with the objective of improving planning quality by anticipating road conditions and directing funding towards the interventions most likely to deliver the best return. The solution is implemented through forecasting models that estimate both the future condition of roads and the likely return on investment associated with different projects. At a conceptual level, the system combines historical road data, condition trends and investment-analysis methods to identify where deterioration is likely to occur and where spending can produce the highest practical benefit. These outputs can then support prioritisation, maintenance scheduling and broader infrastructure strategy. The expected impact is better-targeted investment, improved road-condition management and more efficient use of public resources. More broadly, the initiative creates value by enabling evidence-based infrastructure planning, reducing the risk of poorly targeted spending and strengthening the long-term reliability and sustainability of the road network.
