organization: Ministry of Education and Research, University of Tartu, Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications
title: Kama - Multilingual multidisciplinary neuroma machine translation
source_description: In multilingual public and professional environments, the need to translate accurately across a range of languages and subject areas is essential for communication, cooperation and access to information. The operational problem addressed by Kama is that multilingual translation often requires separate tools, uneven language coverage or manual effort that reduces efficiency and consistency. This use case therefore focuses on providing a broader, more flexible translation capability that can support different domains and users working across several languages. Its objective is to enable reliable translation between multiple language pairs in a single system, making multilingual communication more practical and accessible. The solution is implemented as a multilingual neural machine translation system supporting seven input and output languages: Estonian, Latvian, Lithuanian, English, Russian, German and Finnish. At a conceptual level, the platform uses neural translation models trained to operate across multiple language directions, allowing users to move between different linguistic contexts within one shared architecture rather than relying on isolated bilingual tools. This design supports more efficient maintenance and broader applicability across disciplines and use cases. The expected impact is improved translation availability, greater consistency across languages and reduced dependence on manual translation for routine needs. In operational and business terms, Kama offers scalability, supports multilingual service delivery and creates value by widening access to information and collaboration across language communities.

title: ESTNLTK - Open source tools for Estonian natural language processing
source_description: Estonia’s digital ecosystem depends on high-quality language tools to support public services, research and software development in Estonian, yet language-technology resources for smaller languages often remain fragmented or incomplete. ESTNLTK was created to address this challenge by making existing Estonian language-technology tools easier to access and by developing new ones where gaps remain. The stakeholders include researchers, developers, public institutions and organisations working with Estonian-language data, with the objective of strengthening the technical foundation for processing Estonian texts and enabling wider reuse of language resources across different domains. The solution is implemented as an open-source toolkit, written mainly in Python, for analysing and editing Estonian text. At a conceptual level, the collection acts both as an integration layer for existing language-technology components and as a development framework for new tools, allowing users to perform a range of text-processing tasks within one extensible environment. Because it is open source and funded through the Estonian National Language Technology Programme, it supports both practical deployment and broader ecosystem building. The expected impact is improved availability of language-processing tools, lower barriers for developers and researchers, and better support for Estonian-language applications. More broadly, ESTNLTK creates value by reinforcing digital capability in a smaller language market, enabling innovation and reuse, and providing shared infrastructure that can support public-sector, academic and commercial work on Estonian text.

title: PPA Information Phone call transcription for customers analysis different languages
source_description: The Police and Border Guard Board needed a better understanding of why customers were contacting its information lines and how service bottlenecks were affecting the uptake of digital channels. Calls concerning the issuance of documents had already been identified as the largest category of enquiries, yet the organisation needed richer insight into customer difficulties, especially across different languages and over long service cycles in which people may only renew documents every five to ten years. The use case therefore focused on improving service design, encouraging greater use of e-channels and refining the content and presentation of customer information. The stakeholders include the Police and Border Guard Board, customer-service teams and citizens interacting with document-issuance services, with the objective of reducing avoidable calls and making digital services easier to use. The solution is implemented through an analytical application that processes customer contacts in several languages, including Estonian and Russian, and examines call content to identify recurring patterns and friction points. At a conceptual level, the system combines multilingual transcription and contact analysis to extract service insights from phone interactions and translate them into design improvements. The pilot showed that customers often forgot the correct steps because document requests are infrequent, and it identified specific bottlenecks hindering smoother digital use. The impact includes better-targeted service improvement, stronger support for e-channel adoption and more effective customer communication, creating value through more informed service design and reduced pressure on traditional contact channels.

title: Identification of forest tree species, forest clearing and forest height
source_description: Estonia’s remote forest monitoring information system was created to improve how forest resources are recorded, monitored and shared in georeferenced form. The forestry-management problem is that national forest assessment requires up-to-date spatial information on tree species, forest clearings, forest height and other structural characteristics, but traditional methods can be slow, fragmented or dependent on manual inspection. The Environmental Agency and KEMIT developed a system that supports the collection and sharing of operational forest information, using remote sensing as the main data source. The implementation is semi-automatic, combining machine-learning algorithms, visual inspection of remote-sensing data and third-party software tools. Inputs include satellite or other remote-sensing data, forest notifications, soil maps and teaching and validation datasets. The outputs include nationwide map layers for key assessment features, such as raster maps identifying dominant tree species. Conceptually, the system integrates geospatial data processing, classification models, human validation and forest-resource mapping. The expected impact is more consistent national forest monitoring, better evidence for forest management, improved detection of changes such as clearing, and more efficient sharing of forest data among competent bodies.

title: Transcription Kratt 1247 - Transcribing calls to to crisis number 1247
source_description: Estonia’s crisis-information services introduced this use case to make better use of the substantial volume of calls handled through the national 1247 crisis number. Spoken interactions often contain valuable information on citizens’ concerns, recurring service needs and operational bottlenecks, yet audio recordings are difficult to analyse at scale and manual review is time-consuming. The service therefore needed a way to convert calls into a format that could support structured analysis, service improvement and the development of additional digital-support tools. The stakeholders include the emergency and crisis-information service, public-sector innovation teams and future service designers working on Estonia’s “kratt” ecosystem. The technological implementation is based on automated speech transcription, which converts spoken conversations from the 1247 line into machine-readable text. Once transcribed, the material can be searched, analysed and reused to identify frequent topics, recurring questions, information gaps and patterns in public demand during crisis situations. The resulting text can also provide a practical evidence base for training or designing future conversational assistants. The main impact is improved reuse of call-centre knowledge, reduced effort in extracting insight from audio material and stronger support for evidence-based service design. More broadly, the solution transforms routine crisis-service interactions into a scalable knowledge resource for public administration.

title: Alarm Center Assistant for Risk Assessment
source_description: Estonia’s emergency notification process is highly time-critical and operationally complex: rescue operators must assess threats within roughly a minute while taking into account the information needs and resource rules of at least three different agencies. Under such pressure, mistakes in risk assessment or delays in gathering the right details can directly affect response quality. This use case was developed to support operators in one of the most demanding parts of emergency-call handling, with the objective of reducing error, speeding up assessment and improving the consistency of resource deployment. The stakeholders include the emergency centre, rescue operators and the agencies that depend on accurate threat classification, with the wider goal of making emergency call processing more reliable under severe time constraints. The solution is implemented through software that transcribes the incoming call and analyses it in light of previous actions in order to suggest the most likely event type and a typical case profile for the operator. At a conceptual level, the system combines real-time transcription, contextual analysis and historical pattern support to assist rather than replace the human operator during risk assessment. This allows critical information to be surfaced more quickly while keeping the operator in control of the final judgement. The expected impact is faster and more consistent threat assessment, reduced cognitive burden and better coordination of emergency resources, creating value through higher reliability in high-pressure public-safety operations.

title: Transcription Kratt 112 - Transcribing emergency calls dialed to the emergency number 112
source_description: Emergency-call centres handle high volumes of urgent voice data, yet spoken calls are difficult to search, analyse or reuse unless they are converted into text. Estonia introduced this use case to support the handling of 112 emergency calls by beginning the systematic transcription of those conversations. The operational challenge is that emergency communication must be processed instantly for response purposes, but afterwards authorities also need a usable record for review, quality improvement and possible integration into future support systems. The stakeholders include the emergency centre, call operators and related public-safety services, with the objective of making emergency-call content more accessible for analysis and process improvement while supporting a more modern digital workflow around voice data. The solution is implemented through automated transcription of calls to 112. At a conceptual level, the system applies speech-recognition technology to transform emergency conversations into text, allowing spoken interactions to become searchable, analysable and suitable for downstream use in training, quality monitoring or future decision-support development. Even where the immediate use is modest, the transcription layer creates a reusable digital asset from otherwise transient audio. The expected impact is improved access to operational information, better conditions for service analysis and stronger foundations for future emergency-support tools. More broadly, the project creates value by enabling voice-based public-safety interactions to be incorporated into broader data-driven improvement and digital-service development.

title: Appearance - Identification of objects at the Estonian National Archives
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: The Estonian National Archives wanted to make its vast photographic holdings more accessible by allowing users to search not only through metadata, but also through visual similarity in faces. Historical image collections are rich in public value yet often difficult to navigate when names are unknown, records are incomplete or users are trying to identify ancestors or historical figures from a single photograph. This use case therefore involved the National Archives, researchers, family historians and the wider public, with the objective of improving discoverability and opening new ways of engaging with archival photo collections. The solution is implemented through Ilme, a facial-recognition-based search service linked to Fotis, the National Archives’ photo database. At a conceptual level, users upload a photo, faces are detected and compared against more than half a million archive photographs spanning back to the 1840s, representing around three million faces in total, and the most similar matches are returned by email within 24 hours as a PDF. This creates a visual retrieval workflow that complements conventional catalogue search. The expected impact is easier access to archival imagery, improved usability of large photo collections and new opportunities for users to identify individuals across historical materials. More broadly, the system creates value by making cultural heritage more searchable, more personal and more meaningful for both specialist and public audiences.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Calculation of forest resources by remote sensing methods
source_description: Estonia’s forest monitoring system relies on annual field measurements from 5,600 plots, which provide the basis for national reporting and forest policy, but translating those point measurements into broader, map-based resource estimates remains a difficult and labour-intensive task. The operational challenge is to extend detailed statistical inventory information across large forest areas in a way that improves spatial coverage and supports both monitoring and stand-level economic decisions. This use case therefore involves forest-monitoring authorities, policy planners and users of national forest-resource data, with the objective of developing a methodology that can turn inventory data into maps of species composition, stand height and trunk volume. The solution is implemented by combining multispectral satellite imagery, airborne laser-scanning data and accurate tree measurements from sample plots. At a conceptual level, the system uses the plot-based measurements as model inputs and links them with remote-sensing variables in order to estimate forest characteristics spatially and produce map-based resource assessments. This moves the inventory system from pure sampling towards a hybrid model that supports both national reporting and more operationally detailed forest analysis. The expected impact is better spatial representation of forest resources, improved support for monitoring and stronger evidence for policy and economic planning. More broadly, the project creates value by increasing the usefulness of Estonia’s forest inventory, supporting smarter forest management and enabling more scalable environmental analysis through remote sensing.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Water level monitoring in coastal seas and lakes using satellite altimetry
source_description: Hydrological monitoring traditionally depends on in situ measurements of water levels and flows at national stations, but these observations do not always provide the spatial coverage needed for large lakes and coastal seas. This creates a challenge for flood monitoring and marine forecasting, where broader and more continuous visibility of water conditions can improve both warning and planning. The use case was developed to enhance water-level observation by combining conventional monitoring with remote methods, with the objective of improving hydrological information available to authorities and the public. The stakeholders include hydrological-monitoring services, marine forecasters and users of water-level information, with the broader aim of strengthening operational flood monitoring and sea-level prediction. The solution is implemented through prototypes that combine radar remote-sensing data, satellite altimetry, forecasting models and analytical methods. At a conceptual level, the platform integrates remote water-level observations with existing hydrometric data and modelling workflows so that water conditions can be observed over a wider area than is possible through ground stations alone. This is particularly relevant for improving observation coverage over the Great Lakes and for feeding better data into forecasting systems. The expected impact is improved spatial coverage, more accurate sea-level forecasts and stronger flood-monitoring capability. More broadly, the project creates value by making hydrological services more comprehensive and by supporting a more resilient, data-rich approach to water-level monitoring in coastal and inland waters.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Marakratt - Personal learning path infrastructure
source_description: Education systems increasingly need to support learners whose interests, prior knowledge and abilities differ widely, yet standardised content delivery can make it difficult to provide genuinely individual learning pathways. Marakratt was developed to explore how students could be supported more effectively through educational content and activities that are better matched to their personal learning needs. The use case therefore involved students, educators and digital-learning stakeholders, with the objective of testing whether recommendation models and automation could help build more individualised study paths and improve the relevance of educational material. Rather than redesigning the entire education process, the project focused on creating a proof-of-concept infrastructure able to personalise parts of the learner experience. The solution was implemented through machine-learning experimentation aimed at recommending educational materials and automating the personalisation of learning activities. At a conceptual level, the prototype used learner-related information such as interests, knowledge and abilities to generate recommendations and adapt content pathways, creating models that could serve as the basis for more personalised digital learning environments. This allowed the project to test how recommendation systems might support both educational planning and learner engagement. The impact is primarily exploratory, but it includes a clearer technical basis for individual study-path support, improved understanding of how recommendation models can function in education and a prototype framework for future scaling. More broadly, Marakratt creates value by laying the groundwork for more adaptive and learner-centred digital education services.

organization: Courts of Estonia and Registers and Information Systems Center
title: Salme - Speech recognition in courts
source_description: Estonia’s courts needed a faster and more efficient way to produce hearing transcripts, since manual transcription of court sessions is slow, labour-intensive and places a heavy burden on clerks. According to the Estonian courts, a single criminal case containing about 14 hours of hearings could require an average of 112 working hours to transcribe manually. The use case therefore involved the courts, the Centre of Registers and Information Systems and judicial staff, with the objective of reducing transcription effort, speeding up protocolling and improving the handling of spoken courtroom data in both physical and remote hearings. The solution is implemented through Salme, a speech-recognition tool developed with CGI Estonia and Tilde and integrated into the Court Information System via X-Road. At a conceptual level, Salme supports both real-time and offline transcription, assigns microphones to speakers, returns transcript text with only a short delay and links recordings, transcripts and notes back into court workflows. The system was trained using more than 800 hours of transcribed audio for acoustic models and over 800 million words of textual data for the custom language model, producing reported word-error rates between 8% and 15% and overall precision of about 92%. The impact includes major time savings, faster transcript production and better integration of courtroom recordings into digital judicial processes, creating value through efficiency, accuracy and secure operation on authorised court infrastructure.

title: Statistical characterization of the sea ice extent in the Gulf of Riga (Baltic Sea) using optical remote-sensing imagery
source_description: Monitoring sea-ice conditions in the Gulf of Riga is important for understanding winter dynamics, environmental conditions and maritime risks, yet consistent large-scale observation is difficult to achieve through field methods alone. This use case addressed the need for a more systematic way to characterise ice extent, ice occurrence probability and ice-season length across different winter scenarios in the Baltic Sea. The stakeholders include researchers, environmental analysts and organisations concerned with marine observation, with the objective of generating a reliable statistical picture of sea-ice behaviour over time and across locations. The solution was implemented using optical remote-sensing data from the MODIS instrument at 250 m resolution, covering the period from 2002 to 2011. At a conceptual level, the method relied on bimodal histogram analysis of remote-sensing reflectance data to distinguish ice from water, then used the resulting classifications to calculate sea-ice extent, occurrence probability and season length. The outputs were compared with official ice charts and multi-sensor products, showing strong agreement with reference data, with R² values above 0.83. The study found large year-to-year variation: the ice season ranged from 68 to 146 days and maximum ice extent from 329 to 15,350 km², with higher ice occurrence in waters shallower than 15 m. More broadly, the work creates value by providing a robust analytical basis for regional ice monitoring and winter-scenario classification.

title: Analysis of customer calls at the Estonian Social Insurance Board
source_description: The Estonian Social Insurance Board needed a better understanding of why customers were contacting its service channels and what recurring issues were driving calls and online chats. Routine contact analysis can be difficult to perform manually at scale, especially when interactions take place across multiple channels and in more than one language. This pilot was therefore designed to help the organisation detect patterns in customer appeals and use those insights to improve service design and communication. The stakeholders include the Social Insurance Board, service managers, call-centre staff and citizens using social-insurance services, with the objective of identifying the most common concerns more precisely and supporting more informed managerial decisions. The solution was implemented in cooperation with Feelingstream, whose application transcribed customer calls and chats over a three-month period from May to August 2020 in both Estonian and Russian. At a conceptual level, the system converted spoken and written interactions into analysable text and then examined these data to identify themes, recurring problems and patterns in customer needs. This provided a more detailed basis for service insight than high-level contact statistics alone. The impact includes better understanding of why citizens contact the organisation, improved potential to redesign problematic service areas and stronger evidence for decision-making. More broadly, the pilot creates value by turning everyday customer interactions into a usable source of operational intelligence and by supporting more responsive and efficient social-insurance services.

title: Identification of flammable dwellings
source_description: Estonia’s flammable-dwellings project aims to support fire prevention by identifying residential buildings that may present elevated fire risk. The public-safety problem is that fire services need to prioritise prevention activities, inspections and awareness measures, but risk factors may be distributed across building characteristics, location, past incidents, socio-demographic indicators and other administrative records. The Estonian Fire Department is developing an AI-based solution to detect dwellings that are more likely to be flammable or vulnerable to fire-related incidents. The implementation is described as an AI project under development, likely combining risk indicators, building or housing data, historical fire information and classification models to support prioritisation. Conceptually, the system would produce risk signals for fire-safety professionals, helping them decide where preventive outreach or inspection should be directed. The expected impact is better targeting of prevention resources, earlier identification of risky dwellings, fewer fire incidents and improved protection of residents. Because the system may concern private homes and potentially sensitive household data, its value depends on transparent criteria, appropriate legal basis, careful validation and use as a support tool rather than a fully automated enforcement mechanism.

title: Crop detection from Sentinel-1 and -2 time series using deep learning methods
source_description: Estonia needed a more objective and scalable way to identify agricultural crops for official monitoring and statistics, as traditional methods can be labour-intensive and difficult to apply uniformly across the country. The operational challenge was to create a methodology suited specifically to Estonian conditions and capable of supporting both agricultural administration and the production of consistent national statistics. The stakeholders include Estonian universities, agricultural authorities such as PRIA and the wider state administration, with the objective of improving crop identification, strengthening the quality of agricultural statistics and providing a more standardised evidence base for public-sector use. The solution was implemented through a methodology that combines Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 time-series data with contextual variables including soil type, average daily air temperature and precipitation. At a conceptual level, deep-learning techniques were used to model crop classes from these multi-source inputs and distinguish between different agricultural patterns over time. The results showed that several crop categories could be identified with over 90% accuracy, including potatoes, field peas and beans, summer and winter rapeseed, maize, rye, winter wheat and barley, while berry and fruit plantations, as well as carrot and beetroot plantations, could not yet be classified with sufficient reliability. The impact is a more uniform and objective basis for agricultural statistics, better support for monitoring and a scalable method that can be integrated into PRIA and wider state use.

title: Mapping of flooded areas from satellite images
source_description: Authorities responsible for flood response and environmental monitoring need a dependable way to identify inundated areas quickly, yet flood mapping can be difficult because water detection varies depending on weather, vegetation cover and sensor type. This use case focused on finding the most suitable operational methodology for mapping flooded areas under different conditions, with the objective of improving the reliability and timeliness of flood detection from satellite data. The stakeholders include environmental analysts, emergency-management actors and organisations working with Earth-observation data, all of whom benefit from more consistent flood mapping. The solution was implemented through an evaluation of Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery and the development of a prototype processing workflow. At a conceptual level, the work compared the suitability of radar and optical satellite data, identified the necessary preprocessing steps and selected the most appropriate vegetation index for characterising open water. These elements were then combined into an operational prototype capable of processing Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 data for flood-area mapping. By structuring the method in this way, the project moved beyond ad hoc interpretation towards a repeatable analytical workflow. The impact includes a clearer methodological basis for flood detection, improved operational readiness for mapping inundation and better use of satellite resources under varying environmental conditions. More broadly, the prototype creates value by supporting faster, more systematic flood monitoring and by enabling scalable geospatial analysis for hazard assessment and response planning.

title: Kratt for Estonian Internal Security Service - Combining video and GIS to identify people
source_description: Internal security agencies need tools that help them interpret large volumes of surveillance information quickly and accurately, particularly in situations where location, movement and visual identification must be assessed together. The operational challenge is that video streams and spatial data are often handled separately, which can limit the speed and effectiveness of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance work. This use case was developed to strengthen situational awareness by combining these sources into a more usable operational picture. The stakeholders include Estonian internal security agencies and the analysts or officers responsible for surveillance and reconnaissance, with the objective of improving identification capability, increasing efficiency in analysis and supporting more informed operational decisions. The solution is implemented as an ISR tool that integrates video streams with GIS data. At a conceptual level, the system links visual input from live or recorded footage with geographic information so that people and movements can be analysed in relation to location, routes and surrounding spatial context. This creates a more structured and operationally useful interface than reviewing video and maps separately. Although the public description is brief, the expected impact lies in faster identification, better situational interpretation and improved coordination of surveillance analysis. More broadly, the project creates value by enhancing the operational effectiveness of security services through integrated spatial and visual intelligence support.

title: Automatic border control - Facial Recognition at border controls
source_description: Estonia introduced automated border-control gates to improve the efficiency and security of border crossing at busy entry points such as Tallinn Airport and the Narva road border crossing. Border authorities face the dual challenge of processing travellers quickly while also verifying identity and right of entry with a high level of reliability. Manual control remains essential, but alone it can slow throughput and leave less room for automated support in detecting document misuse. The stakeholders include border guards, travellers and the authorities responsible for border management, with the objective of speeding up crossings, reducing the risk of identity fraud and strengthening the overall reliability of entry checks. The solution is implemented through biometric ABC gates that use facial-recognition-based identification algorithms alongside document verification. source_description: Kratt Sälli was developed by Estonia’s National Heritage Board to support museums in managing preservation and inventory activities more efficiently. title: Safe Spotter - AI platform to detect and transmit data of an accident
source_description: Safe Spotter was developed for the Municipality of Monserrato as part of a broader effort to create an innovative and sustainable smart-city model focused on citizen protection and territorial management. The use case responds to a critical road-safety challenge: when traffic accidents occur, emergency response depends on the rapid availability of reliable information on what happened, where it happened and which vehicles may be involved. Delays or incomplete information can affect the ability of public authorities and emergency services to intervene effectively. The objective is therefore to strengthen the municipality’s capacity to govern road safety by detecting accidents automatically and transmitting essential data quickly. The AI platform uses an advanced network of cameras and sound sensors installed on intelligent street lights. The sound sensors are designed to recognise noises associated with traffic accidents and activate a directional camera when a relevant event is detected. The system then collects Minimum Safe Data, including images or videos, time, location, vehicle direction and registration number. This information can be transmitted to support situational awareness and response coordination. The expected impact is faster accident detection, improved evidence for emergency intervention, stronger monitoring of road-safety events and better protection of citizens. The use case also demonstrates how urban lighting infrastructure can be repurposed as a platform for smart public-safety services.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Central Agency of Social Security Bodies (ACOSS):
title: Voice-bot ACOSS - answering questions from users
source_description: The Central Agency of Social Security Bodies developed the ACOSS voice-bot to answer questions from users of the Chèque Emploi Associatif, addressing a common service-delivery challenge in social-administration contexts: large volumes of routine enquiries can slow response times and place heavy demand on human support channels. The objective of the initiative was to provide faster, more accessible answers for users while easing pressure on administrative teams responsible for handling repeated questions. The stakeholders included ACOSS, users of the Chèque Emploi Associatif service and customer-support staff, with the intention of improving responsiveness and simplifying access to information by telephone. The solution was implemented as a conversational voice agent capable of interacting with callers and supplying responses automatically. At a conceptual level, the system used voice-based dialogue handling to recognise incoming questions, match them to relevant service information and deliver spoken answers within the call flow, creating an automated first-line support channel for the service. This allowed routine issues to be handled without immediate staff intervention and offered a more scalable way to provide information to users. While detailed performance figures are not provided in the source material, the expected benefits included faster access to answers, reduced administrative workload and more efficient handling of common queries. The voice-bot is no longer in use, but it remains a relevant example of how social-security institutions experimented with conversational voice technology to modernise user support.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Better guide environmental police checks
source_description: Environmental police services must decide where to direct limited inspection resources across large territories and a wide variety of ecological risks, from habitat degradation to unlawful activities affecting protected areas. Without strong targeting, inspections may be dispersed too broadly, reducing their deterrent effect and limiting the capacity of authorities to intervene where environmental harm is most likely or most severe. This use case addresses that challenge by helping the French Biodiversity Agency improve how controls are planned and prioritised. The stakeholders include environmental inspectors, biodiversity-protection teams and public authorities responsible for safeguarding natural ecosystems, with the objective of making inspections more efficient and strengthening the effectiveness of environmental enforcement. The solution is implemented through analytical methods that help identify patterns of risk and guide control activity towards higher-priority locations or situations. At a conceptual level, the system combines available environmental, territorial and operational information to support risk-based targeting of checks, enabling inspectors to focus attention where potential infringements or ecological pressures are more likely to occur. These outputs complement, rather than replace, field expertise and enforcement judgement. The expected impact is better allocation of inspection effort, more targeted interventions and stronger protection for vulnerable ecosystems. In operational terms, the approach improves efficiency, supports scalability in environmental policing and creates value by increasing the effectiveness of public controls without requiring a proportional increase in field resources.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: ASN: better use of the data contained in follow-up letter of inspections
source_description: The French Nuclear Safety Authority, ASN, developed this use case to improve how inspection knowledge is exploited in the regulation of nuclear installations. Following the Fukushima accident of 11 March 2011, ASN requested operators on 5 May 2011 to undertake complementary safety assessments of their installations, reinforcing the importance of systematic oversight and evidence-based inspection practices. A major operational challenge was the large volume of information contained in around 20,000 inspection follow-up letters. These documents include observations, recommendations and signals that may be relevant for identifying recurring issues or emerging trends, but manual analysis at this scale is demanding and limits the ability of inspectors to detect patterns across time, sites and themes. The objective was to transform unstructured inspection correspondence into structured information that could support inspectors in their work. The AI solution applies text-analysis techniques to inspection follow-up letters in order to detect weak signals, extract relevant information and identify statistical trends. At a conceptual level, the tool processes regulatory documents, organises their content and makes recurring themes more visible to inspection teams. Its value lies in providing a ready-to-use decision-support capability, improving the exploitation of accumulated inspection evidence, reducing time spent on manual document review and strengthening ASN’s ability to identify cross-cutting safety issues across the nuclear sector.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Departmental Directorate of Territories and the Sea (DDTM) of L'Hérault
title: Automatically detecting irregularities in occupancy soils
source_description: Monitoring land use across a territory is a complex responsibility, particularly when authorities need to identify irregular developments such as illegal construction, unauthorised land occupation or waste dumping over large areas. Manual inspection alone is costly, slow and often unable to provide timely visibility of emerging problems. This use case, developed by the Departmental Directorate of Territories and the Sea of Hérault, addresses that operational challenge by improving the detection of irregularities in land occupation and use. The stakeholders include territorial authorities, environmental and planning officers and inspection teams, with the objective of strengthening oversight, accelerating detection and improving the protection of land and natural environments. The solution is implemented through the analysis of aerial and satellite imagery to identify patterns that may indicate unlawful or abnormal land-use activity. At a conceptual level, image-analysis and classification techniques are applied to large-scale geospatial data in order to detect changes or anomalies associated with illegal constructions, dumping or other irregular uses of land. These findings can then be routed into administrative and inspection workflows for verification and follow-up. The expected impact is quicker identification of suspect sites, reduced reliance on labour-intensive visual review and better prioritisation of field controls. More broadly, the approach improves scalability in territorial monitoring, enhances the reliability of detection and creates public value by supporting more effective environmental and land-use enforcement.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: General Directorate of Food (DGAL) of the Ministry of Agriculture and Food:
title: Targeting establishment inspection - refine targeting of establishments for inspections
source_description: The General Directorate of Food of the French Ministry of Agriculture and Food developed this use case to improve the targeting of inspections in establishments that sell or deliver food directly to consumers, including restaurants, catering businesses and distributors. Food-safety inspection authorities must allocate limited inspection resources across a large and diverse population of establishments, where risks may vary depending on hygiene practices, customer experience, operational conditions and previous signals. Traditional targeting methods may not fully capture emerging problems or recent consumer concerns, particularly where relevant information appears first in public feedback channels. The objective of the use case is to refine the prioritisation of establishments to be inspected by using additional evidence from online consumer reviews. The AI component analyses reviews published on online platforms to identify signals that may suggest possible food-safety or hygiene concerns. Natural language processing can be used to detect relevant terms, patterns of complaints or sentiment linked to establishments, which can then inform inspection planning alongside existing administrative data and regulatory criteria. The system is intended to support, not replace, professional judgement by inspectors. Its expected impact is a more risk-informed allocation of inspection capacity, earlier identification of establishments requiring attention, better use of publicly available feedback and improved protection of consumers through more targeted food-safety controls.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Intelligence Emploi
source_description: Intelligence Emploi was introduced within Pôle emploi as a transformation initiative aimed at accelerating the return to sustainable employment. The use case addresses a central labour-market challenge: employment services must support large numbers of jobseekers with different profiles, skills, barriers and career objectives, while also responding to employer demand and changing labour-market conditions. Public employment counsellors need tools that help them identify relevant opportunities, personalise support and prioritise interventions without reducing the quality of human guidance. The objective is therefore to strengthen Pôle emploi’s capacity to help people move into stable work more quickly and effectively. The AI implementation acts as a lever within employment-service processes, using available labour-market, jobseeker and vacancy-related data to support matching, guidance and decision-making. At a conceptual level, models may analyse profiles, skills, employment histories, job offers and contextual indicators to identify suitable pathways or opportunities for users. These outputs can help advisers provide more tailored support and improve the relevance of recommendations made to jobseekers. The expected impact is faster return to sustainable employment, better targeting of support measures, improved efficiency for counsellors and greater personalisation of public employment services. For the administration, the use case supports a more data-driven service model while preserving the role of employment professionals in guiding complex individual transitions.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Ministry of Action and Public Accounts - DGFIP
title: AI for targeting fraud and valuing requests (CFVR) to improve the efficiency of tax audits
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Tax administrations must process very large volumes of information from multiple public sources in order to identify cases where individuals or companies may not be complying with their fiscal obligations. The difficulty lies in distinguishing the truly high-risk situations from the mass of ordinary declarations, especially where discrepancies may result from error, omission or deliberate fraud. This use case addresses that challenge by helping the Directorate General of Public Finances target tax audits more effectively and allocate investigative resources where they are most justified. The stakeholders include tax auditors, compliance teams and public-finance authorities, with the objective of improving the efficiency, fairness and consistency of fiscal controls. The solution is implemented within the CFVR system through large-scale processing and cross-checking of data collected by different administrations. At a conceptual level, the system analyses patterns such as abrupt changes in income, inconsistencies between declared situations and other indicators of risk in order to generate prioritised signals for tax-control teams. These signals support audit selection and case valuation while leaving the final judgement to tax professionals. The expected impact is more accurate targeting of audits, reduced time spent on low-yield controls and better recovery of irregular situations. In operational and public-value terms, the approach increases scalability, strengthens the credibility of tax enforcement and creates value through more efficient use of control resources and fairer treatment of compliant taxpayers.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Datascience
source_description: The Ministry of the Interior carries out a wide range of missions, from security and territorial administration to crisis management and public-policy coordination, all of which generate substantial volumes of data. The operational challenge is to turn that information into structured insight that can support strategic analysis consistently across the ministry rather than in isolated, ad hoc exercises. This use case focuses on expanding the activity of the scientific laboratory, or datalab, created in 2016 so that data-driven methods can be embedded more systematically across the organisation. The stakeholders include ministry analysts, operational departments and senior decision-makers, with the objective of strengthening strategic analysis, improving cross-cutting understanding of complex issues and enabling broader adoption of advanced analytical methods in support of ministerial missions. The solution is implemented by enlarging the datalab’s role, capabilities and analytical reach, creating a shared environment for data exploitation and the emergence of more advanced modelling approaches. At a conceptual level, this involves structuring data-science practices, developing reusable analytical workflows and promoting the use of predictive and exploratory techniques across multiple business areas of the ministry. The expected impact is better-informed decision-making, stronger analytical consistency and greater capacity to address diverse operational questions at scale. More broadly, the initiative improves institutional agility, supports innovation in public administration and creates value by making strategic analysis more systematic, reusable and relevant to the full range of the Ministry of the Interior’s responsibilities.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Ministry of Solidarity and Health - DREES
title: Health data hub - Creation of a big data infrastructure in health
source_description: Health systems produce vast quantities of information, yet the value of these data is often constrained by fragmentation, inconsistent access and a shortage of shared tools and expertise to make them usable for research and operational decision-making. This use case addresses that structural problem by creating a health data infrastructure capable of supporting analysis at scale and improving how data are mobilised across the healthcare ecosystem. Led by the Department of Research, Studies, Evaluation and Statistics of the Ministry of Solidarity and Health, the initiative involves researchers, policymakers, planners and healthcare stakeholders, with the objective of strengthening clinical research, improving support for resource-allocation decisions and enabling more predictive and effective forms of medicine. The solution is implemented through a big-data infrastructure in health that brings together datasets, analytical tools and specialist capabilities within a common framework. At a conceptual level, the platform is designed to facilitate secure data use, support large-scale analysis and provide the technical and organisational foundation needed for data-driven research and decision support. This creates an environment in which health information can be used more systematically to generate evidence and operational insight. The expected impact is improved efficiency in the health system, stronger support for clinical and policy analysis and better conditions for innovation in care and research. More broadly, the initiative enhances scalability, strengthens the value extracted from health data and creates public benefit through a more informed, coordinated and forward-looking healthcare system.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Ministry of Ecological and Inclusive Transition - Météo France
title: Expert systems in meteorology and climate to better forecasting
source_description: Weather and climate services must produce forecasts that are not only scientifically robust but also understandable, timely and useful for a wide range of users affected by meteorological risks. For Météo-France, this means continually improving predictive capability while also adapting communication tools and workforce practices to new operational realities. This use case addresses that dual challenge by modernising forecasting methods and supporting the organisation’s staff as their professional roles evolve alongside new technologies. The stakeholders include meteorologists, climate specialists, operational forecasters and end users of weather information, with the objective of improving the prediction of meteorological phenomena and their impacts while making forecast outputs more actionable and easier to communicate. The solution is implemented through expert systems and machine-learning-based approaches that enhance the modelling and interpretation of weather and climate data. At a conceptual level, these methods are used to refine forecasting processes, support impact-oriented analysis and integrate more effective communication tools into operational workflows. At the same time, the project supports staff in adapting to new modes of work and decision support. The expected impact is better forecasting performance, clearer communication of risks and stronger operational efficiency within the forecasting chain. More broadly, the initiative increases institutional resilience, improves the usefulness of meteorological services and creates value by combining technical innovation with organisational transformation.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Indexing of Government photos for better identification on photos using facial recognition
source_description: The Government’s Information and Press Service of Luxembourg implemented this use case to improve the management of a large media library of political photographs belonging to the Luxembourg State. The operational problem was the manual indexing of extensive photographic collections, a process described as laborious and time-consuming. Without efficient metadata, the value of the media library is reduced, as photographs are harder to retrieve, identify and reuse by public institutions. The objective was to accelerate the identification of politicians appearing in government photographs and to improve the quality and completeness of metadata associated with the collection. The AI project uses facial-recognition technology to identify political figures in images and generate enhanced metadata for the media library. At a conceptual level, the system analyses visual features in photographs, compares them with authorised reference material and supports the tagging of individuals appearing in the images. The resulting metadata makes the collection easier to search and manage, while reducing the manual effort required from staff. The impact has been to facilitate and accelerate metadata production, improve the usability of the State’s photographic resources and enable better exploitation of the media library’s content across government. The use case delivers administrative efficiency, strengthens information management and supports more consistent reuse of public visual records.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Extraction of topographical objects - AI to extract topographical objects from aerial images
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Updating national topographic and land-registry databases is labour-intensive, particularly when officials must identify newly built structures, new roads and emerging construction areas from large volumes of aerial imagery. This creates delays in keeping official spatial records current and can limit the quality and timeliness of services that depend on accurate geographic information. The use case therefore addresses the need to modernise how the Land Registry and Topography Administration detects changes in the built environment and maintains its databases. The stakeholders include mapping specialists, cadastral officials and public bodies that rely on up-to-date territorial information, with the objective of reducing manual workload, accelerating updates and improving the overall quality of topographical data. The solution is implemented through automated extraction of topographical objects from aerial images using computer-vision and object-detection techniques. At a conceptual level, the system analyses imagery to identify features such as buildings and roads, distinguishes new elements from the existing mapped environment and feeds these outputs into the database-update process. This creates a more efficient workflow for detecting construction areas and for enriching official geospatial records. The expected impact is faster database maintenance, improved data quality and lower administrative effort for State officials. More broadly, the initiative enhances scalability, supports the creation of new data and services, and strengthens the public value of official geospatial infrastructure through more timely and reliable mapping.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: CLAVIS project - Automatic recognition of old handwritten documents
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Historical archives contain vast quantities of handwritten material that remain difficult to exploit because older manuscripts are often challenging to read, search and interpret at scale. For the Luxembourg National Archives, this limits the accessibility of important seventeenth- and eighteenth-century sources and constrains the extent to which researchers can use them effectively. The CLAVIS project addresses this documentary bottleneck by improving the legibility and usability of digitised manuscript collections. The stakeholders include archivists, historians, researchers and cultural-heritage institutions, with the objective of making historic documents more accessible, searchable and useful for future generations while also improving archival description processes. The solution is implemented by submitting digitised manuscript images to Transkribus, a platform for automated handwriting recognition, transcription and search in historic documents. At a conceptual level, the system processes scanned archival pages, converts handwritten text into machine-readable transcriptions and enables downstream uses such as content search, structured retrieval and the automated generation of inventories or indexes of people and places. This transforms previously difficult-to-use archival sources into a more navigable digital resource. The expected impact is greatly improved accessibility to historical records, reduced manual transcription effort and stronger support for archival research and discovery. More broadly, the project improves the scalability of document processing, enriches cultural-heritage services and creates value by opening complex manuscript collections to much wider scholarly and public use.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: 3D scan underground infrastructure - Prevention damage of critical infrastructure
source_description: Arnhem’s 3D scan project focuses on preventing accidental damage to critical underground infrastructure during construction work. The operational issue is that sewer infrastructure is often located below ground in ways that may be difficult for construction teams to visualise accurately from the surface, creating a risk of costly damage, service disruption and safety hazards. The municipality’s approach combines a precise 3D scan of the main sewer with an application that visualises the sewer’s location above ground. The implementation therefore links geospatial surveying, three-dimensional infrastructure modelling and field-based visualisation, allowing users to understand the position of underground assets before or during works. Conceptually, the system turns hidden sewer infrastructure into a digital and spatially interpretable layer that can be consulted by staff or contractors. The expected impact is fewer accidental strikes, better planning of construction activities, reduced repair costs and improved protection of essential municipal infrastructure. By making underground assets more visible and usable in operational settings, the project supports safer, more data-driven public works management.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: 8Ting, business office Work & Income of the municipality of Enschede
title: 8TING - Analysis of drivers to keep people in class
source_description: 8TING was used in Enschede to apply psychology and web technology to support people participating in municipal work-and-income or training pathways. The operational problem is that people may drop out of programmes when support is not aligned with their personal motivation, behaviour, context or barriers. The system seeks to make clear who needs what type of attention by monitoring and adjusting more than 80 factors related to internal drivers. Its implementation uses profiles, behavioural data and contextual indicators to plan automatic or semi-automatic interventions, such as measurements, encouragement and targeted support activities intended to keep people engaged in class or training. Conceptually, the tool combines behavioural profiling, motivation analysis, web-based interaction, programme planning and adaptive support. The expected impact is better retention in training, more personalised support, earlier identification of disengagement risks and improved effectiveness of municipal activation services. At the same time, because the tool analyses behavioural and psychological drivers, careful safeguards are needed around transparency, consent, proportionality and the avoidance of overly deterministic profiling of participants.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Dutch Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA)
title: Aerial Inspection Drones
source_description: Aurea Imaging wants to develop image analysis technology for drones/Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) to use them in the agricultural sector in detecting anomalies. These abnormalities may indicate harmful organisms. In a testing ground of the Dutch Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA), we investigate the feasibility of this technology.

title: Agent system
source_description: ProRail’s agent system is designed to support train traffic controllers when disruptions or delays occur on the Dutch rail network. The operational challenge is that small delays can propagate quickly through interconnected railway services, requiring rapid decisions on routing, prioritisation and recovery measures. Train traffic controllers must assess complex operational conditions under time pressure, balancing passenger disruption, infrastructure capacity and the need to prevent knock-on effects. The agent functions as an autonomous computer programme that operates with defined goals and associated actions, providing advice to controllers on how to respond to delays and reduce further disruption. At a conceptual level, the system can be understood as a decision-support agent that analyses traffic conditions, expected train movements, available infrastructure and possible operational choices, then proposes interventions for human operators to consider. The expected impact is improved punctuality, better use of available rail capacity and more consistent support during disruption management. By assisting controllers rather than replacing them, the system can help preserve human responsibility while improving the speed and quality of operational advice in complex traffic situations.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI for public space notifications - Image recognition to analyse reports
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Municipalities receive many citizen reports about defects and inconveniences in public space, ranging from loose paving stones and broken streetlights to potentially dangerous situations requiring urgent intervention. Although these reports are valuable, they can vary greatly in clarity and completeness, which means staff must spend time interpreting the issue before deciding how to respond. This use case, explored by the municipality of Dordrecht, addresses that operational friction by seeking to make reporting easier for residents and the follow-up process more efficient for municipal teams. The stakeholders include citizens, municipal service staff and teams responsible for public-space maintenance, with the objective of improving intake quality, speeding up case assessment and supporting quicker resolution of local problems. The solution is implemented through image-recognition techniques applied to photographs submitted with defect reports. At a conceptual level, the system analyses the uploaded image to identify the type of issue reported, extract relevant visual cues and support routing or prioritisation within the municipal workflow. This gives staff a clearer starting point for action and may reduce the need for repeated clarification. The expected impact is faster processing of public-space notifications, reduced administrative effort and a smoother user experience for residents. More broadly, the approach improves service responsiveness, enhances consistency in case handling and creates value by linking citizen reporting more directly to operational action.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI Chatbot Robin - Answer questions about business transfers
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Agricultural entrepreneurs need accessible and consistent guidance when preparing or managing business transfers, as these processes involve administrative, financial and sector-specific questions that can be difficult to navigate through static information pages alone. AI Chatbot Robin addresses this need by providing a virtual agent for the Netherlands Enterprise Agency that answers questions on agricultural business transfers. The service builds on the earlier Pilot Watson and went live in April 2019, moving from an experimental conversational service towards a more operational support channel for users seeking information from the agency. Its purpose is to offer a first point of contact for recurring questions, helping business owners or prospective successors understand relevant procedures and obtain guidance without immediately relying on telephone or email support. The implementation uses chatbot technology to interpret user questions and match them with prepared knowledge on agricultural business-transfer topics. At a conceptual level, the system relies on natural language understanding, a structured knowledge base and conversational flows that guide users towards relevant answers. The main value is improved availability of information, more efficient handling of repetitive enquiries and a more user-friendly digital service for agricultural stakeholders. For the administration, Robin also supports channel shifting and allows staff to focus on more complex or case-specific requests.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AICrimePrediction (AICP) - Prediction of the risk of crime and terrorism
source_description: Police control rooms handle continuous streams of incident data and real-time reports, yet anticipating where risks may emerge remains a difficult task in fast-changing urban environments. The AICrimePrediction feasibility study, carried out by Amsterdam police and Ciphix, addresses the challenge of improving situational awareness and supporting earlier, better-informed deployment decisions in relation to crime and terrorism risks. The stakeholders include control-room staff, police planners and operational decision-makers, with the objective of understanding whether available data can be used to generate sufficiently accurate risk predictions to strengthen prevention and response. Rather than focusing only on historical review, the use case seeks to inform live operational choices by connecting past patterns with current signals. The solution is implemented by combining historical control-room data, including type of incident, time and location, with real-time reporting inputs. At a conceptual level, the system applies predictive modelling to spatio-temporal and incident-pattern data in order to estimate the likelihood of criminal or terrorism-related risk in particular contexts or locations. These predictions are intended to support operational awareness and resource allocation rather than replace police judgement. The expected impact is more targeted monitoring, improved readiness and better use of police capacity in high-risk situations. More broadly, the feasibility study explores whether data-driven forecasting can strengthen public-safety operations through greater precision, timeliness and coordination in risk assessment.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI machine learning supervised - Delivering learning reports
source_description: Educational and public-service organisations often hold large amounts of administrative and performance data, yet turning those data into useful learning insights for internal improvement can be slow and resource-intensive. This use case, piloted internally by DUO, addresses the need to produce learning reports more efficiently and in a more structured way. The stakeholders include internal analysts, programme managers and decision-makers within DUO, with the objective of improving how organisational learning is captured, reported and used to inform future action. In this context, the challenge is not simply to collect information, but to derive coherent reporting outputs that support reflection, oversight and service improvement from existing internal data. The solution is implemented through a supervised machine-learning pilot designed to support the production of a learning report. At a conceptual level, the system uses labelled data and supervised modelling techniques to identify relevant patterns, classify information or structure insights that can feed into report generation and internal evaluation processes. Rather than replacing expert interpretation, the tool is intended to support analysts in assembling evidence more systematically and efficiently. The expected impact is quicker preparation of learning reports, reduced manual processing and stronger consistency in how findings are compiled. More broadly, the pilot offers a foundation for scalable internal reporting, improved organisational learning and better use of data in steering, evaluation and continuous improvement activities within DUO.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI for detection of diseases in plants and trees
source_description: Plant and tree health monitoring is essential for protecting agriculture, biodiversity and wider environmental quality, yet disease detection across large areas can be difficult, time-consuming and dependent on scarce specialist expertise. The NVWA pilot addresses this challenge by exploring a more efficient way to identify signs of disease in plants and trees before problems spread or become more costly to manage. The stakeholders include inspectors, plant-health specialists and authorities responsible for biosecurity and environmental protection, with the objective of improving early detection, strengthening surveillance capacity and supporting more timely interventions. The use case responds to the practical need for broader, more scalable monitoring in contexts where manual inspection alone may not provide sufficient coverage or speed. The solution is implemented through a pilot that applies image-based analysis to detect disease-related patterns in vegetation. At a conceptual level, the system uses machine-learning techniques trained on visual indicators of plant or tree illness in order to distinguish healthy from potentially affected specimens and to support inspection prioritisation. These outputs can then be incorporated into plant-health workflows to guide follow-up checks and decisions. The expected impact is faster identification of potential disease outbreaks, better targeting of inspection resources and reduced reliance on purely manual screening. More broadly, the approach improves scalability, enhances the reliability of plant-health monitoring and creates value through stronger preventive action in environmental and agricultural protection.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI for detecting Asian Hornbill
source_description: Detecting the presence of the Asian hornet is a growing operational priority because this invasive species can threaten biodiversity, disrupt ecosystems and create risks for beekeeping and public safety. The challenge for inspectors is that suspected nests are not always easy to confirm quickly in the field, particularly across wide outdoor areas, and accurate species identification is essential to avoid unnecessary intervention. This use case, led by the NVWA, addresses that problem by improving how potential sightings and nest reports are verified. The stakeholders include inspectors, environmental authorities and members of the public reporting possible nests, with the objective of accelerating detection, improving species recognition and supporting more targeted intervention against the invasive hornet. The solution is implemented through two complementary tools: drone surveys equipped with thermal-imaging cameras for suspected nest areas, and an image-recognition application that helps distinguish between the Asian hornet and the European hornet. At a conceptual level, the system combines aerial thermal sensing with visual classification models to support both field detection and species verification. These capabilities can then be integrated into the NVWA’s inspection workflow to prioritise action and reduce uncertainty. The expected impact is faster confirmation of nest locations, more reliable differentiation between species and better use of inspection resources. More broadly, the approach enhances scalability, supports environmental protection and creates public value through a more responsive and accurate invasive-species control process.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI for fisheries inspections - Detecting illegal barrels
source_description: Inspection authorities face a recurring challenge when monitoring production and storage environments: potentially harmful anomalies may be difficult to identify quickly across large areas, yet delayed detection can weaken controls, increase operational costs and heighten risks to food safety. This use case, explored in a testing environment with the Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority, focuses on improving inspection efficiency by identifying suspicious deviations that may indicate harmful organisms or other non-compliant conditions. The stakeholders include inspectors, laboratory teams and operational managers, with the objective of directing scarce inspection resources more effectively, strengthening control methods and improving the quality of oversight in high-risk contexts. The solution is implemented through image-analysis technology mounted on drones or other unmanned aerial vehicles, designed to detect anomalies from visual data gathered during inspections. At a conceptual level, the system combines aerial imaging, machine-learning-based pattern detection and inspection workflows so that unusual features can be highlighted and assessed for follow-up. These outputs can then support decisions on where to deploy staff, laboratory analysis or specialist equipment. The expected impact is more efficient use of inspection capacity, improved targeting of controls and stronger food-safety protection through earlier and more reliable anomaly detection. More broadly, the approach enhances scalability, reduces wasted effort and creates value by modernising field inspection methods in a resource-constrained regulatory environment.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AIDA (Artificial Intelligence Disaster Advisor), and Horizon 2020 project
source_description: During major incidents, control rooms are confronted with a flood of potentially relevant information arriving from social media, public channels and other data sources, yet it is rarely possible for emergency staff to collect, validate and assess all of it in real time. This creates an information paradox: there is abundant data, but not enough operational clarity, which can hinder decision-making, slow coordination and ultimately endanger lives. AIDA was developed to address this challenge by helping emergency services identify and use the most relevant information during a crisis. The stakeholders include control-room operators, emergency responders and coordinating authorities, with the objective of improving situational awareness and enabling faster, more informed action in high-pressure scenarios. The solution is implemented by combining big-data processing, data-science methods and streaming architectures to ingest and filter information from multiple public and non-public sources. At a conceptual level, the system analyses incoming data flows, evaluates relevance and rapidly distributes prioritised information to emergency services so that operational teams can focus on the most important signals. This supports live crisis management rather than retrospective analysis. The expected impact is better-informed emergency handling, faster access to critical intelligence and improved coordination across services. In practical terms, AIDA strengthens responsiveness, increases the usability of complex data in crisis settings and creates public value by supporting actions that can better save and protect human lives.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: University of Rotterdam and other 14 dutch universities
title: Anti-cheat software for exams
source_description: Higher education institutions conducting remote examinations need to preserve the integrity of assessments while managing the practical limitations of supervising students outside traditional examination rooms. Anti-cheat software for exams refers to the use of Proctorexam by several Dutch higher education institutions, including the University of Rotterdam and other universities, to monitor students during online tests. The operational challenge is to detect possible cheating in a digital setting where invigilators cannot physically observe candidates, but where fairness, equal treatment and the reliability of qualifications remain essential. The software enables remote surveillance through a student’s webcam, microphone and web browser, allowing examination behaviour and the digital environment to be monitored during the assessment. Its technical implementation combines online proctoring functions with automated or semi-automated detection of behaviours that may be classified as suspicious, such as unusual movements, browser activity or environmental signals. The system can flag students for further review, rather than necessarily determining misconduct on its own. The expected benefit for institutions is greater capacity to run remote examinations while maintaining oversight and reducing manual invigilation constraints. However, the use of such systems also raises important concerns around privacy, proportionality, transparency and student trust, meaning that its operational value depends strongly on governance safeguards, review procedures and clear communication with candidates.

title: Artificial inspector - Self-learning system for the inspection of national roads and waterways
source_description: Rijkswaterstaat needed a more efficient and affordable way to inspect national roads and waterways, since traditional inspection approaches often depend on expensive professional camera equipment and limited collection capacity. Routine infrastructure inspection is essential for maintaining safety and service quality, but manual processes and specialist hardware can restrict coverage and raise costs. The use case therefore focused on expanding inspection capability while lowering the barriers to large-scale visual data collection. The stakeholders include Rijkswaterstaat, inspection teams and infrastructure managers, with the objective of automating a larger share of road and waterway inspection and improving the timeliness and consistency of asset monitoring. The solution is implemented through standard Android smartphones mounted on cars and ships, each running an application that captures an image every second. At a conceptual level, these images are combined with geographic data and used to train a cloud-based neural network that can recognise relevant infrastructure conditions and support automated inspection tasks. By using inexpensive, widely available devices instead of specialist cameras, the system creates a more scalable and flexible inspection model. The expected impact is lower equipment cost, broader inspection coverage and faster collection of infrastructure data. More broadly, the project creates value by modernising public-asset monitoring, improving operational efficiency and demonstrating how low-cost sensing combined with cloud-based analysis can reshape large-scale infrastructure inspection.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Province of North Holland, Municipality of Amersfoort, Bam infra, Province of Gelderland and other provinces
title: Asphalt scan - Detection of damage to roads
