source_description: Road authorities need reliable and up-to-date information on pavement damage and declining visibility of signage in order to plan maintenance before defects become more severe, more expensive and more disruptive for road users. Traditional inspection methods can be time-consuming and difficult to scale across large networks, particularly when both road-surface condition and associated roadside assets must be monitored regularly. This use case addresses that operational need by improving how defects in infrastructure are identified and prioritised. The stakeholders include road-maintenance teams, infrastructure managers and public authorities responsible for transport safety and asset performance, with the objective of detecting deterioration earlier and supporting more efficient maintenance planning. The solution is implemented through the Asphalt Scan, which gathers data from satellites and scanning vehicles and then applies analytical models to identify road damage and reductions in signage brightness. At a conceptual level, the system combines remote and mobile sensing with automated classification and anomaly-detection techniques to convert raw imagery and scan data into actionable maintenance signals. These outputs can then feed into infrastructure-management workflows and inspection planning. The expected impact is earlier detection of deterioration, reduced reliance on manual inspection and better-targeted maintenance interventions. More broadly, the approach improves scalability, enhances asset reliability and creates value through more efficient road-network management and safer travel conditions.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Combating Online Child Abuse
source_description: Authorities and online-safety stakeholders face the urgent challenge of identifying illegal child sexual abuse imagery on the internet quickly enough to support removal and limit further harm. The scale of online content makes manual review alone difficult, slow and distressing for staff, while delayed detection can allow illegal material to remain accessible for longer. This use case addresses that problem by exploring whether a technical model can be created and deployed to recognise illegal images and support rapid action. The stakeholders include enforcement and online-safety actors, specialist investigators and platform or service partners involved in the detection and removal process, with the objective of strengthening identification capability and improving the speed and consistency of intervention. The solution is being developed through an SBIR project in collaboration with PwC to assess the feasibility of creating and implementing a model that recognises illegal image content. At a conceptual level, the system uses image-classification techniques to analyse visual material, distinguish unlawful content from non-relevant imagery and generate outputs that can support review and takedown processes. These capabilities are intended to complement, not replace, human oversight in highly sensitive decision-making. The expected impact is faster detection of illegal material, reduced manual burden on specialist teams and more effective support for online removal. More broadly, the approach improves scalability, strengthens digital safeguarding and creates public value through better protection of children online.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Prediction of young people engagement in undesirable behaviour (Pilot Apeldoorn Youth)
source_description: The municipality of Apeldoorn explored this pilot to address concerns about youth-related nuisance and other forms of undesirable behaviour in public space, with the aim of identifying where preventive action might be most needed. Municipal authorities often face difficulty in deciding where to direct youth work, supervision and social intervention, especially when risks appear unevenly distributed across locations and groups. The use case therefore involved local authorities and youth-related service actors, with the objective of detecting patterns earlier and supporting more targeted preventive measures rather than relying only on reactive responses once incidents had already occurred. The solution was implemented by linking multiple data sources in order to estimate which groups of young people were more likely to engage in undesirable behaviour and in which locations this was more likely to happen. At a conceptual level, the system used cross-dataset analysis and predictive modelling to generate risk patterns that could inform municipal decision-making about attention, intervention and local policy. This created a data-driven view of behavioural risk across groups and places rather than depending solely on manual observation or isolated reports. The expected impact was earlier visibility of emerging risks, more focused use of local preventive resources and stronger operational support for youth policy. More broadly, the pilot created value by exploring how linked data could help municipalities move towards more anticipatory public-order and youth-support strategies, though such approaches also raise important governance and proportionality questions.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Blue Operational Prevention Service
source_description: Flood prevention requires timely decisions based on changing risk conditions, available response resources and the practical question of what action is most useful in a given moment. In many cases, however, decision-makers must interpret large volumes of information under pressure, making it difficult to determine the optimal deployment strategy quickly and consistently. This use case addresses that challenge by helping users prevent flooding through more precise and operationally relevant guidance. The stakeholders include flood-risk managers, emergency planners and operational users responsible for preventive action, with the objective of minimising risk through better real-time deployment choices and more tailored decision support. The solution is implemented through smart algorithms that combine live risk information with knowledge of the resources available. At a conceptual level, the system analyses evolving conditions, evaluates feasible response options and translates them into a user-specific action perspective, rather than producing a generic warning alone. This means the output is not simply descriptive, but directly linked to the operational choices that can still be made in time. The expected impact is more effective preventive deployment, quicker and better-targeted decisions and improved use of limited resources in flood-risk situations. More broadly, the approach enhances reliability, supports scalability in operational prevention and creates value by turning real-time information into practical, context-sensitive action for those managing water-related threats.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Province of Gelderland, NEO, Wageningen Environmental Research
title: Tree Monitor - Detecting illegal logging
source_description: Regional authorities responsible for environmental protection need reliable methods to identify tree loss and possible illegal logging across large territories where field inspections alone may be slow, selective or reactive. Tree Monitor gives the Province of Gelderland an additional monitoring tool for detecting potential illegal felling by comparing satellite images from different years. Operational since December 2017, the system helps authorities locate areas where trees appear to have disappeared and visualises these changes on a map. The objective is to improve the detection of irregular tree removal and support more targeted follow-up by enforcement or environmental-management teams. The implementation uses Earth observation data, with satellite imagery analysed across time to identify changes in vegetation cover. At a conceptual level, image-comparison techniques detect differences between historical and more recent satellite data, highlighting locations where tree cover has declined. These outputs can then be reviewed by officials and used to prioritise inspections or further investigation. The initiative involves the Province of Gelderland, NEO and Wageningen Environmental Research, combining public environmental responsibilities with specialist geospatial expertise. The main impact is broader territorial coverage, faster identification of potential illegal logging, better targeting of field checks and stronger evidence for environmental enforcement. It also demonstrates how satellite-based monitoring can support nature protection and land-use oversight at regional level.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Municipality of Enschede, Saxion, Winkelhart Enschede, University of Twente, Both Social, eLabbs, Marotura, Present Media, Squal Media, Think Public, University of Twente and Winkelhart Enschede
title: Brid.ge - Smart City Enschede
source_description: Urban mobility in Enschede is affected by congestion, inefficient parking usage and limited coordination between private vehicles and public transport, creating delays, emissions and poor user experience for residents and visitors. Local authorities, transport operators and travellers require accurate, timely information to support better travel choices and reduce pressure on the city centre. The objective of this pilot is to improve accessibility and sustainability by guiding users to appropriate parking facilities or encouraging a shift towards public transport based on real-time conditions. The implementation integrates traffic sensors, parking occupancy data and public transport information into a single digital platform. Data analytics and predictive models evaluate congestion patterns and parking availability, while user-facing services deliver recommendations through navigation tools and digital signage. The platform connects with existing smart city and mobility systems to ensure interoperability. The pilot resulted in reduced time spent searching for parking, smoother traffic flows and increased uptake of alternative transport modes. Qualitative benefits include lower emissions, improved travel experience and enhanced decision support for urban planners, demonstrating a scalable model for smart mobility management.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Business Intelligence and Analytics (BI&A) - Indication of tax fraud risks based on previous declarations
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Tax administrations must identify fraud and recovery risks across very large volumes of declarations and receivables, while using enforcement capacity in a targeted and proportionate manner. Business Intelligence and Analytics (BI&A) supports the Dutch Tax Authority by using self-learning models to indicate where risks may exist, based on previously inspected declarations and feedback from inspection outcomes. The broader operational objective is to move from uniform or purely rule-based selection towards more refined risk identification, allowing the administration to focus attention where available data suggest a higher probability of non-compliance or recovery opportunities. One example is Dynamic Monitoring, which links outstanding receivables to possible sources of redress, such as wages, cars, real estate or other assets, and generates lists of claims where new recovery options may be available. The implementation combines machine-learning methods with administrative tax data, inspection histories and feedback loops from previous control results. Models are progressively refined as additional outcomes become available, improving their capacity to identify relevant risk patterns. The potential impact is more efficient allocation of inspection and recovery resources, faster identification of actionable cases and improved use of existing administrative data. At the same time, such systems require careful governance to ensure transparency, legality, non-discrimination and appropriate human oversight in tax decision-making.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Case Law Engine
source_description: Prosecutors and legal researchers face significant information-management challenges when preparing criminal cases, as relevant case law, procedural material and hidden connections may be dispersed across large and complex legal datasets. Case Law Engine was developed by LexIQ for the Dutch Public Prosecution Service to reduce research time and improve the quality of case preparation. The Public Prosecution Service had explored how advanced digital tools could support daily working procedures, particularly where professionals need to search, analyse and draw insights from criminal-case information. The tool, also described as a “Jurisprudentierobot”, supports prosecutors and researchers in identifying relevant case law, understanding patterns and making better use of information during preparation. Its implementation combines machine-learning algorithms with intuitive search functions, data visualisations and analytical features that help users navigate large volumes of legal and case-related data. Rather than replacing legal judgement, the system provides indications, connections and possible outcome-related insights that professionals can assess within their own legal reasoning. The impact is reduced time spent on manual research, better handling of information overload and improved ability to detect relevant or previously hidden information. For the Public Prosecution Service, the tool offers business value by strengthening preparation quality, supporting consistency and enabling staff to approach criminal-case analysis in a more structured and evidence-informed way.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Municipality of Amsterdam and AMS Institute
title: CityFlows-Amsterdam
source_description: Busy pedestrian areas in Amsterdam require reliable crowd-management capabilities to safeguard public safety, maintain comfort and support evidence-based operational decisions in high-density urban spaces. The CityFlows initiative, developed as an EIT Urban Mobility flagship project, brought together the Municipality of Amsterdam, AMS Institute and a wider consortium of partners to address the need for better monitoring and management of pedestrian flows, particularly in locations affected by congestion, events, tourism and changing mobility patterns. The objective was to provide public authorities with a decision-support capability that helps them understand crowd dynamics and take timely measures to improve the use of public space. The emerging technology implementation centres on the Crowd Management Decision-Support System, a software-based platform licensed through City Analytics to government authorities. At conceptual level, the system combines pedestrian-flow data, urban analytics and operational decision-support functions to help authorities assess crowding conditions, anticipate risks and select appropriate interventions. Its deployment supports integration between urban data sources, monitoring tools and municipal crowd-management processes. The main impact is improved situational awareness for public authorities, enabling safer, more comfortable and more responsive management of busy pedestrian spaces. The creation of City Analytics as a dedicated start-up also strengthens scalability and reuse, allowing the solution to be offered beyond the original project context and supporting cities seeking reliable tools for managing public space during normal operations and crisis situations.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: CrossWalk in Smart City Rijswijk
source_description: The municipality of Rijswijk tested CrossWalk to address a concrete accessibility and road-safety challenge: standard pedestrian crossing times are often insufficient for older people, people with disabilities or citizens with reduced mobility. This can create unsafe situations at intersections and reduce the autonomy of residents who require more time to cross the road. The pilot involved the Municipality of Rijswijk and Dynniq, with the objective of making pedestrian infrastructure more responsive to the needs of vulnerable road users while avoiding permanent changes to signal timing for all pedestrians. The emerging technology implementation is based on a mobile application connected to traffic signal systems. When a registered user with mobility difficulties approaches or waits at a crossing, the app uses location data to communicate with the traffic control software and signal the user’s presence. The traffic light system can then automatically extend the green phase, allowing additional time for a safe crossing. At conceptual level, the solution integrates mobile positioning, traffic-light control logic and intersection management systems. Its impact lies in improving pedestrian safety, accessibility and user experience for residents who walk more slowly. It also demonstrates how smart-city infrastructure can provide targeted support without redesigning the entire traffic system, making the approach potentially scalable to other intersections and municipalities with similar accessibility objectives.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Municipality of The Hague and Phinion Data Engineering.
title: Improve data quality with AI - Machine learning to improve the data quality of registrations
source_description: Municipal services depend on accurate and consistent data registrations, because errors, inconsistencies or missing information can directly affect service quality, administrative reliability and decisions made for residents. Improve data quality with AI was piloted by the Municipality of The Hague with Phinion Data Engineering to analyse, monitor and continuously improve the quality of municipal registrations. The problem addressed is not a single faulty dataset, but the broader need to maintain trustworthy records across the systems that underpin local public services. Poor data quality can lead to delays, incorrect processing, duplicated work or reduced confidence in digital administration. The implementation uses Phinion’s Qbot product, which applies machine-learning techniques to discover patterns and deviations within and between registrations. At a conceptual level, the system examines relationships in administrative data, identifies anomalies and highlights inconsistencies that may require correction or further investigation. This enables the municipality to move from ad hoc data-quality checks towards more continuous monitoring. The expected impact is higher-quality registrations, earlier detection of data problems, improved operational reliability and better support for service delivery. By helping staff identify structural issues in the data, the pilot also contributes to more efficient back-office processes and strengthens the foundation for future digital services that depend on accurate municipal information.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: The Refinery: AI in investigation support
source_description: Police investigators need to process and interpret increasing volumes of information from multiple sources, including case files, operational records and digital evidence, without losing sight of relevant patterns or connections. The Refinery: AI in investigation support is a data-analysis facility developed by the Dutch National Police to enhance investigative capabilities and help officers work with complex information environments. The operational challenge is that valuable links between cases, suspects, events or pieces of evidence may remain hidden when data are fragmented across systems or too extensive to review manually. The platform enables investigators to access, interpret and visualise large volumes of police data drawn from diverse sources. Its implementation combines data integration, analytical tooling and AI-driven methods that support the detection of patterns, relationships and connections within investigative material. At a conceptual level, the system can help structure heterogeneous datasets, identify associations and present results through visual interfaces that make complex information easier to understand. The tool is intended to assist investigative judgement rather than automate final decisions. Its impact lies in faster analysis, improved situational awareness, better detection of links across cases and more effective use of available police data. For the Dutch National Police, The Refinery strengthens investigative capacity, supports evidence-led policing and provides a scalable analytical environment for complex criminal investigations.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Algorithm Impact monitor bridge openings
source_description: The Province of South Holland must manage the movement of both road traffic and shipping across a region where bridge openings can create delays, congestion and competing demands between transport modes. The smart bridge addresses this challenge by using digital monitoring and predictive analytics to support more informed bridge-operation decisions across an infrastructure portfolio that includes more than 100 bridges. The initiative forms part of South Holland’s wider work on smart shipping and focuses on linking up-to-date road-traffic information with live shipping information, so that the impact of bridge openings can be better understood and anticipated. In the project “impact monitor bridge openings”, the province has taken an important step towards predicting traffic intensities around several key bridges. The technological implementation combines sensor-based data collection, traffic information and algorithmic analysis, including Long Short-Term Memory neural networks designed to forecast traffic conditions up to 21 minutes ahead. These models are suited to time-series prediction because they can learn from sequential patterns in traffic behaviour and bridge-operation data. The reported correlation-efficient accuracy of 60–80% indicates that the approach can provide useful short-term forecasts for operational planning. The main value is improved anticipation of congestion, better coordination between road and waterway mobility, more evidence-based bridge management and a stronger basis for reducing disruption while keeping both transport networks accessible and safe.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Detection of aggression, panic and abnormal behaviour with smart cameras
source_description: This pilot investigates whether smart-camera analytics can support earlier recognition of aggression, panic and abnormal behaviour in crowded public environments. The operational problem is that incidents in stations, airports, city centres or entertainment districts can escalate quickly if security teams identify them too late. Traditional monitoring relies heavily on human operators observing multiple camera feeds, which can be demanding, inconsistent and slow. ViNotion develops technology that analyses the behaviour of individuals and detects signs of panic, aggression or deviant conduct at an early stage. The implementation uses video analytics and behaviour-recognition models to process visual information from cameras, identify movement or interaction patterns associated with abnormal events, and generate alerts for security or assistance personnel. Conceptually, the system combines computer vision, behavioural classification, anomaly detection and real-time alerting. The expected impact is faster deployment of staff, reduced harm to the public, more efficient incident response and better management of safety risks in large public areas. Its value depends on accuracy, proportionality and careful governance, because behavioural interpretation in public spaces can raise concerns around false positives, surveillance intensity and the treatment of individuals whose conduct is incorrectly flagged.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Firework nuisance detection system - AI to determine if bangs are firework
source_description: Dutch municipalities face recurring public order and safety issues linked to illegal fireworks, particularly during evenings and festive periods, placing strain on enforcement capacity and generating resident complaints. The firework nuisance detection system was introduced to help municipalities such as Amersfoort identify when and where fireworks are being set off, enabling more targeted enforcement. Stakeholders include municipal authorities, enforcement officers, residents and public safety services. The objective is to distinguish fireworks from other loud noises, identify nuisance hotspots and optimise patrol routes and response times without relying solely on citizen reports. The system combines a distributed network of acoustic sensors placed in public space, which capture sound events and triangulate their location when multiple sensors detect the same bang. Signal-processing and classification techniques analyse acoustic signatures to distinguish fireworks from other impulsive sounds such as slamming doors or vehicle backfires. When a sound is classified as fireworks, alerts are automatically sent to municipal enforcers via mobile devices, alongside spatial and temporal data. The pilot has improved situational awareness and allowed more selective deployment of enforcement resources. Qualitatively, municipalities report faster response times, better evidence-based planning and improved transparency around nuisance patterns, while residents benefit from more visible and timely enforcement.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Diagnosis Plan and Control Tool - Assessing the risk of home fraud
source_description: Municipal social services must prevent benefit fraud while ensuring proportional enforcement and safeguarding citizens’ rights. In complex housing situations, case officers faced difficulties in deciding when a home visit was justified, leading to inconsistent practices and inefficient use of limited inspection capacity. The objective of this use case was to support more consistent, evidence-based prioritisation of cases where discrepancies between declared circumstances and observed living conditions suggested elevated risk, while preserving human decision-making authority. The tool aggregated administrative data, including household composition, housing arrangements, declared living costs and registered debts, and applied statistical risk-scoring techniques to generate structured risk profiles. These profiles were integrated into existing municipal case-management systems and presented as decision support indicators rather than automated outcomes. Municipalities reported more focused inspections and fewer unnecessary home visits, improving resource allocation and operational efficiency. However, concerns regarding transparency, proportionality and potential bias prompted increased regulatory scrutiny, and similar profiling tools have since been restricted or discontinued in several municipalities
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Ministry of Social Affairs and Employment
title: Digital assistant for answering Parliamentary questions
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Policy officials must often answer Parliamentary questions under time pressure, while ensuring that responses are accurate, well-evidenced and consistent with publicly available information. Digital assistant for answering Parliamentary questions supports the Ministry of Social Affairs and Employment by helping policy staff search public sources more efficiently during the preparation of answers. The operational problem is that relevant information may be dispersed across documents, websites, policy files and other open sources, making manual retrieval slow and increasing the risk that important material is missed. The assistant is intended to strengthen the preparatory phase of drafting by accelerating information discovery and supporting staff in identifying relevant public evidence. From a technological perspective, the system functions as a search and retrieval tool that can scan public sources, interpret user queries and return potentially relevant material for policy officers to review. Depending on its configuration, such a tool may use natural language processing to understand questions, rank information by relevance and help structure the evidence base for a draft response. It does not replace the judgement of officials or the political and legal checks required before an answer is submitted. Its impact lies in reducing research time, improving consistency in source use, supporting more complete answers and allowing staff to focus more of their effort on analysis, drafting quality and institutional coordination.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Ministry of Justice and Security, Ministry of the Interior and Kingdom Relations
title: Digital identification and verification
source_description: Public authorities in the Netherlands have explored digital identification methods to improve security, efficiency and user experience in public services. This research initiative examined the potential use of biometric identifiers, such as facial recognition, within government contexts. Stakeholders include government agencies, technology researchers, citizens and data protection authorities. The objective was to assess feasibility, risks and governance requirements rather than to deploy an operational system. The research analysed biometric recognition techniques, enrolment and verification processes, and possible integration with existing identity infrastructures. Particular attention was paid to data quality, accuracy, false positives, and compliance with privacy and data protection frameworks. Technical studies focused on how biometric templates could be securely stored, matched and audited, and under what conditions such systems might be appropriate. No operational rollout followed the research, but the findings informed policy discussions on digital identity, highlighting significant legal, ethical and societal constraints. The impact lies primarily in improved understanding of technological limitations and governance requirements, contributing to more cautious and rights-aware approaches to digital identity innovation in the public sector.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: E-Discovery - automatic classifcation of incoming and outgoing emails
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: The National Archives of the Netherlands and ICTU explored E-Discovery to address a growing information-management challenge within public administration: the increasing volume of incoming and outgoing emails that must be classified, retained, searched and managed in accordance with archival and administrative requirements. Manual classification is time-consuming, inconsistent and difficult to scale, particularly for organisations that handle large volumes of official correspondence. In 2016, the Nationaal Archief launched a study into the potential of E-Discovery methods in information management, with the objective of testing whether automated support could improve the organisation, retrieval and governance of email records. The emerging technology implementation consisted of a prototype capable of classifying emails automatically. At conceptual level, the system used machine-learning techniques to analyse email content and metadata, identify relevant categories, and assign classifications that could support archival processes. The prototype was developed in cooperation with ICTU, linking information-management expertise with technical implementation capacity. The expected impact is a more efficient, consistent and scalable approach to managing public-sector email records. By reducing the burden of manual classification, the solution can support better compliance, faster retrieval of information and more reliable records management. Although described as a study and prototype, the case demonstrates the value of automated classification for public administrations facing rapidly growing volumes of digital correspondence.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Excess Material Exchange (EME)
task: Tracking of goods and assets along the supply chain
source_description: Organisations that generate residual materials often lack efficient mechanisms to identify potential reusers, assess the value of surplus flows and close material loops across sectors. Excess Material Exchange (EME) addresses this problem by creating a digital trading platform where supply and demand for excess materials can be matched at scale. The initiative involves organisations such as ProRail, Schiphol and other public and private actors seeking to reduce waste and improve circular-economy performance. The operational objective is to move residual materials away from disposal or low-value treatment and towards productive reuse by making information about available materials more visible, comparable and actionable. The technology implementation relies on artificial intelligence to read, interpret and structure data on material streams, including information on composition, availability, quality, location and potential applications. Matching algorithms then identify possible links between suppliers and buyers, including combinations that may not be obvious through manual brokerage. The platform’s intelligence lies not only in listing materials, but also in actively bringing together parties whose residual flows and needs may align. The expected impact is faster matching, greater scalability in circular-material exchange, reduced transaction costs and improved resource efficiency. For participating organisations, EME can support waste reduction, lower procurement or disposal costs, and contribute to broader sustainability and circular-economy objectives.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: FlowCube - a picture of the traffic of cyclists, vehicles and pedestrians
source_description: Street managers need reliable information on how different road users move through public space, especially where cyclists, pedestrians and vehicles interact in ways that are not fully captured by traditional traffic counts. FlowCube responds to this need by using compact camera-based modules to generate traffic intelligence for local mobility management. The system is intended to give authorities and transport planners a clearer picture of flows, routes and travel times without relying on manual observation or intrusive data collection. Its implementation combines compact video sensors with image-recognition algorithms that distinguish cyclists, pedestrians and, where configured, other types of traffic. At a conceptual level, the modules detect objects, classify road-user categories, track local movement and aggregate observations into usable mobility data. Multiple FlowCubes can also combine data to infer commonly used cycling routes and corresponding travel times. The expected impact is more accurate insight into active mobility, better evidence for infrastructure planning, improved monitoring of cycling and walking policies, and safer management of mixed-use streets. Technolution presents FlowCube as an operational product and emphasises privacy compliance, because the system generates mobility indicators rather than functioning as an identity-based surveillance tool. This makes it relevant for municipalities seeking granular traffic intelligence while remaining within data-protection constraints.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Forensic Image Recognition (FIRE) - Recognition of containers that have illegal cargo
source_description: FIRE is an experimental forensic image-recognition system developed to reduce the manual burden on detection staff when analysing large volumes of visual material. The operational problem is that forensic and investigative services may need to inspect extensive image datasets, including data carriers and other visual sources, to identify objects that could be relevant to criminal investigations. In this framed pilot area, the Netherlands Forensic Institute examines whether the system can learn to recognise sea containers that may contain illegal cargo. The implementation uses automatic image recognition, drawing on large datasets to train or test models capable of identifying relevant visual patterns. Conceptually, FIRE combines computer vision, dataset preparation, model training, image classification and explainability requirements, particularly because forensic applications must be legally robust and understandable. The expected impact is a substantial reduction in the time required for image-based screening, allowing staff to focus on higher-value forensic analysis. If the approach succeeds, work that might otherwise require extensive manual review could be narrowed to a more manageable set of flagged images. However, before broader use, the project must address dataset compilation, storage, lawful use and inter-agency sharing.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Geniq - reports wait times
source_description: Mental-health providers need accurate and current information on waiting times because delays affect access to care, referral choices, planning, accountability and communication with patients and commissioners. Geniq was developed for Dutch mental-health institutions as a reporting and analytics capability that calculates, analyses and reports waiting times so that managers and operational teams can maintain an up-to-date view of service accessibility. The practical problem is that waiting-time data can sit across electronic client records, intake processes, treatment-planning systems and reporting obligations, making it difficult to produce consistent insight without manual extraction and reconciliation. The implementation uses data-processing and reporting functionality connected to the care-administration environment, allowing institutions to calculate waiting-time indicators, analyse patterns and generate reports for internal management or external accountability. At a conceptual level, the system transforms operational registration data into structured management information, helping organisations distinguish where delays arise, which pathways are under pressure and where additional capacity or process changes may be needed. The expected impact is better planning of clinical capacity, faster identification of bottlenecks, stronger compliance with waiting-time transparency requirements and more informed dialogue with referrers, insurers and patients. In the wider Dutch mental-health context, reliable waiting-time insight remains important because national regulators continue to emphasise the need for dependable data on the scale and development of GGZ waiting times.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: GEO reference of documents - Gaining more insight into data on nitrogen emissions and soil pollution
source_description: The GEO reference of documents project supports the Province of Gelderland in analysing large volumes of unstructured information related to nitrogen emissions and soil pollution. The policy and administrative challenge is that environmental files, permits, reports and technical documents may contain relevant evidence, but their unstructured format makes it difficult for officials to extract patterns, locations and relationships efficiently. Bolesian developed an application to help the province gain more insight from this dispersed information base. The implementation uses natural language processing, document analytics and geographic referencing to process unstructured text and connect relevant information to territorial or environmental contexts. Conceptually, the system can identify key entities, themes, locations and relationships within documents, then structure them so that policymakers and specialists can examine nitrogen and soil-pollution issues more systematically. The expected impact is improved environmental intelligence, faster review of complex documentation and stronger evidence for policy, permitting and enforcement decisions. By converting unstructured material into more usable data, the application can support more transparent and data-informed environmental governance in a policy field where decisions are often technically complex and politically sensitive.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA)
title: Graasdierpremie - Use of drones in counting animals
source_description: The Graasdierpremie pilot examines whether drones and automated image analysis can improve the counting and monitoring of grazing animals. The operational problem is that animal-distribution and abundance monitoring is traditionally carried out manually on foot or through aerial recording from manned aircraft, both of which can be costly, slow and labour-intensive. For public authorities such as the NVWA, more efficient monitoring can support nature conservation, agricultural control and subsidy-related verification. The implementation uses drone imagery to collect visual data on animals in the field, combined with computer-vision methods that detect, classify and count animals automatically. Conceptually, the system replaces broad manual observation with aerial data capture, image-processing pipelines and automated counting models, while still requiring quality checks and validation by competent staff. The expected impact is faster monitoring of animal populations, reduced inspection costs, improved geographical coverage and more consistent evidence for administrative or conservation decisions. If validated, the approach could make field verification more scalable and less dependent on resource-intensive manual methods. It may also support more timely insights into animal distribution, enabling better planning and more targeted follow-up inspections.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Hansken - Recognizing images of narcotics in digital seizure
source_description: Criminal investigations increasingly involve very large volumes of seized digital material, making it difficult for forensic experts and investigators to manually review every phone, computer, hard drive or storage device in time-sensitive cases. Hansken - Recognizing images of narcotics in digital seizure responds to this challenge by helping the Netherlands Forensic Institute and investigative authorities identify relevant visual or textual evidence more quickly within large datasets. The operational aim is to accelerate the discovery of incriminating or case-relevant material while reducing the burden of exhaustive manual review. The technological implementation uses a self-learning algorithm integrated into the Hansken digital-forensics environment. The system can be trained to recognise specific categories of images, such as weapons or drugs, and to detect text elements appearing in images, including licence plates or account numbers on stolen bank cards. At a conceptual level, image-recognition and pattern-detection techniques classify visual content and highlight items that may deserve closer examination by experts. The tool supports forensic prioritisation rather than replacing evidentiary assessment, which remains subject to professional and legal review. Its impact is faster search across seized data, better use of investigative capacity, improved ability to find hidden or dispersed evidence and stronger support for serious-crime investigations where digital material is extensive and operational timelines are demanding.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: HKV Eye - Line in Water
source_description: HKVEYE supports the inspection and monitoring of dikes, water defences and water systems by adding data-driven visual analysis to water-management practice. The operational challenge is that water authorities and infrastructure managers face expanding management areas while staffing capacity for inspection can be limited. Manual inspection of dikes, structures and water systems can be time-consuming, and early recognition of deterioration is essential for flood safety and maintenance planning. HKV Lijn in Water developed HKVEYE to provide additional “eyes” on water infrastructure, using visual data to examine the condition of dikes and related assets in more detail. The implementation applies data-science techniques to interpret images and other visual data, supporting questions such as monitoring vegetation quality, assessing revetment condition, detecting sand-carrying boils and conducting difference analyses over time. Conceptually, the system combines visual monitoring, data interpretation, anomaly detection and inspection-support workflows. The expected impact is more precise, efficient and evidence-based inspection, helping managers focus attention on areas that require intervention. By extracting useful information from increasingly available visual data, HKVEYE can improve maintenance prioritisation, support flood-risk management and strengthen the reliability of water-safety monitoring.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Identifying people at risk of falling into large debts
source_description: Municipal debt-prevention services increasingly try to intervene before financial problems become unmanageable, because late intervention can lead to enforcement costs, housing insecurity, health impacts and long-term dependence on social support. The Amsterdam use case concerns the use of predictive or data-driven methods to identify residents who may be at risk of accumulating large debts, so that support can be offered earlier. The operational problem is that signs of debt distress may be distributed across different municipal or service-provider datasets, while front-line staff may only become aware of the situation once arrears have already escalated. At a conceptual level, the system would combine available administrative signals, risk indicators and historical patterns to prioritise cases for preventive outreach. The intended value is not to automate sanctions, but to surface possible vulnerability so that human professionals can offer assistance, advice or referral to debt-support services. The expected impact is earlier identification of residents in financial difficulty, better targeting of municipal support, reduced long-term debt escalation and more efficient use of social-service capacity. However, such systems require careful safeguards because financial-risk profiling can reproduce biases in historical data, affect vulnerable households and create opacity around why a person is flagged.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Public Prosecutor's Office, the National Police, the Tax Authorities, Customs, the FIOD and the Financial Intelligence Unit, the Social Affairs and Employment Inspectorate (Investigation Directorate), the Intelligence and Investigation Service of the Environment and Transport Inspectorate (ILT-IOD), the Intelligence and Investigation Service of the Dutch Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA-IOD), the Media Commissioner
title: Infobox criminal and unexplained assets (iCOV)
source_description: Financial crime investigations often require analysts to understand relationships between people, companies, assets, income, transactions and public records that are dispersed across different authorities. The Infobox Crimineel en Onverklaarbaar Vermogen, known as iCOV, provides Dutch public partners with data-driven reports that support the detection and disruption of money laundering, tax evasion, fraud and unexplained wealth. The operational problem is that individual agencies may each hold partial information, while criminal financial structures often exploit fragmentation between enforcement, tax, customs, labour and supervisory bodies. The implementation is a formal cooperation between public organisations, including the Public Prosecutor’s Office, National Police, Tax Authorities, Customs, FIOD, Financial Intelligence Unit and several inspection and investigative services. At a conceptual level, iCOV combines authorised data access, risk indicators, analytical models and reporting formats to generate insight into assets, income relationships, companies and suspicious patterns. The system is not a fully autonomous enforcement mechanism; its outputs support investigation, prosecution and asset recovery by giving professionals a richer picture of potential criminal or unexplained wealth. The expected impact is faster financial investigation, improved targeting of asset-confiscation work, stronger inter-agency cooperation and more effective action against organised financial crime. Current public information describes iCOV as an active cooperation that helps partners through data-driven reports, including practical examples of use by investigation and prosecution services.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Ministry of Instrastructures and market parties
title: Inspection bridges with drones
source_description: The bridge-inspection drone pilot explores how unmanned aerial vehicles can reduce reliance on manual inspection capacity for bridges and viaducts. The operational problem is that infrastructure inspections are often labour-intensive, require specialist access arrangements, and may expose inspectors to safety risks when structures are difficult to reach. Public infrastructure managers need reliable ways to detect deterioration, document structural conditions and prioritise maintenance without closing assets unnecessarily or deploying extensive human resources for every inspection. The implementation uses drones to capture visual data from bridges and viaducts, allowing inspection teams to review high-resolution imagery of structural elements that would otherwise require physical access. At a conceptual level, the approach can combine UAV-based image capture, georeferenced inspection records, visual analytics and, where developed further, computer-vision models for recognising cracks, corrosion, deformation or other signs of damage. The expected impact is faster inspection, lower operational burden, improved safety for inspection staff and more consistent documentation of asset condition. If validated, the pilot could support more risk-based infrastructure maintenance by helping authorities identify which structures require closer expert review and which can be monitored remotely.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Intelligent traffic control systems (I-VRI's) - Better traffic flow
source_description: Urban traffic intersections must balance the needs of private vehicles, buses, emergency services, cyclists and pedestrians while reducing congestion and improving journey reliability. In Gelderland, existing traffic lights at eight intersections in Arnhem and Velp were replaced with intelligent traffic-control systems, or iVRIs, to support better traffic flow. The objective was to move beyond fixed or locally reactive signalling by using digital information from road users and connected systems. The implementation uses mobile data and vehicle-to-infrastructure communication so that road users and traffic-control installations can exchange information. Buses and emergency services can receive priority when approaching an intersection, while other road users may receive up-to-date information about routes and speed advice. At a conceptual level, iVRIs combine connected traffic-light controllers, data exchange standards, road-user messages, priority rules and adaptive signal control. This allows the intersection to respond more dynamically to current traffic conditions and to support policy priorities such as public transport reliability or emergency response. The expected impact is smoother traffic flow, reduced waiting times, better journey predictability and more efficient use of existing road infrastructure. Dutch public portals continue to provide national visibility on iVRI deployments, while Gelderland’s own public material refers to implementation and execution documents for the Arnhem and Velp iVRIs.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Use of scan cars for underground containers - Determining type of waste
source_description: Municipal waste management services struggle with contamination of waste streams when incorrect materials are deposited in underground containers, leading to higher processing costs and reduced recycling rates. In The Hague and other cities, scan cars were introduced to monitor underground containers and improve waste separation. Stakeholders include municipal waste services, residents and environmental authorities. The objective is to detect incorrect waste disposal early and support targeted interventions. Vehicles equipped with cameras periodically capture images of open or overfilled containers. Image analysis techniques are applied to identify visible waste types, such as bulky items or mixed waste placed in recycling containers. The system integrates with municipal waste management platforms, allowing services to prioritise clean-up operations and identify recurring problem locations. The pilots have improved operational efficiency by reducing manual inspections and enabling faster responses to misuse. Municipalities report cleaner collection points, better data on citizen behaviour and more effective communication campaigns. While still limited in scope, the approach demonstrates scalable potential for data-driven waste management and supports broader circular economy objectives.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: iRN_iColumbo
source_description: Police investigations increasingly involve large volumes of online information, making manual monitoring of digital sources time-consuming and inconsistent. iColumbo was developed within the Dutch police’s Internet Research & Investigation Network (iRN) to support systematic online searches for suspicious material. Stakeholders included law enforcement investigators, digital forensics units and judicial authorities. The objective was to enhance investigative capacity by automating parts of open-source intelligence collection while preserving legal oversight. The service crawled publicly accessible online sources and forums using predefined search strategies, keywords and behavioural patterns. Collected material was indexed and presented to investigators for assessment, rather than triggering automatic enforcement actions. The project improved consistency and speed in early-stage investigations and reduced reliance on ad hoc manual searches. Although the specific iColumbo project has since been concluded, its concepts informed later police tooling for digital investigations. The main impact lies in professionalisation of online investigative practices and improved methodological consistency in handling internet-based evidence.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Artificial Intelligence Knowledge System for the judiciary searches for similar lawsuits
source_description: The Artificial Intelligence Knowledge System for the judiciary was developed to support legal professionals in identifying comparable lawsuits more efficiently. The operational challenge is that courts and judicial staff work with large volumes of case material, and finding relevant precedents or similar disputes can be time-consuming when searches rely only on keywords or manual legal knowledge. The District Court of East Brabant tested a system that allows users to enter text and receive the ten most similar lawsuits. The implementation is based on textual similarity search, likely combining natural language processing, document representation and ranking techniques to compare an input text with a database of past cases. Conceptually, the tool transforms legal documents into searchable representations, calculates similarity between the user’s text and available case records, and returns a ranked list of relevant results. The expected impact is faster legal research, more consistent retrieval of comparable cases and better support for judicial preparation. By assisting users in navigating case material, the system can improve internal efficiency without replacing judicial reasoning. Its value depends on the quality of the underlying case database, the transparency of similarity criteria and careful use by trained legal professionals.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: LAA - Address quality in Personal Records Database (BRP)
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Public authorities depend on accurate address records to deliver services, administer rights and obligations, and prevent misuse of public systems, but incorrect registrations in the Personal Records Database can undermine these functions. LAA - Address quality in Personal Records Database (BRP) supports the Dutch Ministry of Interior in improving address quality by using data analysis to recognise patterns that may indicate incorrect addressing. The underlying problem is that inaccurate address data can affect administrative decisions, public-service delivery and fraud prevention, particularly where residence information is used to determine eligibility, correspondence, enforcement or access to benefits. The initiative aims to help bring the BRP into better order by identifying records that may require verification or correction. The technological implementation applies analytical methods to administrative data in order to detect combinations, deviations or patterns associated with possible address-registration problems. These outputs can then guide further checks by competent authorities, who assess whether a registration is indeed incorrect and what follow-up is required. The system therefore functions as a risk-identification and prioritisation tool within a broader governance process. The expected impact is improved data quality, more targeted verification work, stronger reliability of the population register and better support for fraud prevention. Given the sensitivity of population data, the value of the system depends on clear legal safeguards, proportionality, transparency and appropriate human oversight.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Using smart algorithms to map whether building or demolishing certain homes improves liveability
source_description: Housing policy can affect liveability through tenure mix, housing type, density, neighbourhood composition, public-space quality and access to services, but the relationship between physical interventions and social outcomes is difficult to assess with simple indicators. Breda’s use case concerns the application of machine-learning methods to investigate whether building or demolishing certain types of homes could improve neighbourhood liveability. The operational problem is that urban-planning decisions often involve long-term effects and many interacting variables, making it hard for decision-makers to isolate which housing interventions are likely to improve local conditions. The implementation concept uses historical and spatial data to detect patterns between housing stock, neighbourhood characteristics and liveability outcomes. At a conceptual level, the model would compare combinations of housing and contextual indicators, identify correlations with liveability measures and support planners in evaluating possible redevelopment scenarios. The expected impact is more evidence-based housing policy, better targeting of regeneration measures and stronger analytical support for decisions on demolition, new construction or housing mix. The system should be understood as a planning-support tool rather than a substitute for political, social and participatory decision-making. Its value depends on combining model outputs with local knowledge, resident engagement and policy judgement.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Tackling undermining using AI
source_description: Municipalities and safety-domain partners can lose valuable intelligence on subversive crime when suspicions are reported through fragmented channels or fail to reach the right professionals quickly. Tackling undermining using AI builds on Milvum’s “Report a Suspicion” platform, which is already used by more than 300 professionals to share signals of undermining, such as illegal prostitution or drug production, directly with the relevant municipal actors. The operational challenge is to improve communication between municipalities and chain partners so that local safety information is not lost, delayed or handled inconsistently. The existing platform combines a mobile app and web portal, enabling professionals to submit and route suspicions in a structured way. The planned or added AI functionality strengthens this model by applying big-data analysis to identify, categorise and prioritise signals of subversive crime more effectively. At a conceptual level, the system can analyse reports and related data to detect patterns, cluster similar cases, highlight urgent risks and support prioritisation for follow-up. The impact is improved information flow, faster routing of relevant signals, better coordination between municipal and safety partners, and more systematic handling of local crime intelligence. For public authorities, the platform offers operational value by turning dispersed observations into structured knowledge that can support earlier intervention and more targeted action against undermining.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Detecting 'unknown' companies with environmental risk
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Environmental supervision depends on knowing which businesses operate in a municipality, what activities they carry out and whether those activities may create inspection or permitting risks. Eindhoven’s use case focused on mapping “unknown” companies that could pose a potential environmental risk by using data more intelligently. The operational problem is that companies may be invisible to inspectors because records are incomplete, activities change, addresses are inconsistent or information is distributed across multiple administrative sources. This creates the risk that environmentally relevant businesses are not prioritised for supervision or included in the appropriate regulatory process. The implementation uses data matching and analytical screening to identify companies that may fall outside established inspection lists but show characteristics associated with environmental risk. At a conceptual level, the system combines business-register information, location data, sector classifications, permit or enforcement records and risk indicators to generate candidate companies for further human review. The expected impact is better coverage of environmental supervision, earlier detection of potentially risky activities, more efficient targeting of inspections and improved data quality in municipal environmental registers. The system should be understood as a prioritisation and discovery tool: it does not determine guilt or non-compliance, but helps inspectors find entities that may require attention. Public case material records the project as an Eindhoven initiative to make otherwise hard-to-find companies visible through smarter data use.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Totta Datalab, municipality of Nissewaard, municipality of Brielle
title: Detecting welfare fraud - Prediction of the likelihood of unlawful behavior on the House Market
source_description: Municipalities administering welfare benefits face pressure to prevent fraud while ensuring fair and lawful treatment of beneficiaries. The Municipality of Nissewaard introduced a predictive model to identify cases with a higher likelihood of unlawful behaviour in the housing market, such as undeclared cohabitation or subletting. Stakeholders included social services, case officers and welfare recipients. The objective was to prioritise investigations and reduce random or unnecessary checks. The model analysed historical administrative data, identifying patterns associated with confirmed fraud cases and assigning risk scores to current clients. These scores informed decisions on whether further investigation was warranted, always requiring human review. While the system aimed to improve efficiency, concerns emerged around transparency, bias and legal safeguards. Following national scrutiny of similar systems and evolving legal standards, Nissewaard discontinued the model in 2021. The case significantly influenced Dutch policy discussions on automated risk profiling, reinforcing the need for strict governance, explainability and proportionality in data-driven public services.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Municipality of Deventer, Municipality of Goirle
title: Detecting welfare fraud in the municipality of Deventer and Goirle (SyRI system)
source_description: The Deventer and Goirle welfare-fraud detection pilot used risk profiling to identify welfare recipients whose files might require additional investigation. The administrative problem was the need to target limited enforcement capacity towards cases considered more likely to involve irregularities, while managing public funds and ensuring compliance with welfare rules. The stakeholders included the municipalities of Deventer and Goirle, welfare recipients, municipal social-service staff, enforcement teams and citizens affected by decisions based on risk scores. The implementation generated risk profiles for welfare recipients, with the resulting score used to decide whether a dossier should be examined more closely. At a conceptual level, such a system links administrative datasets, applies risk indicators or algorithmic scoring rules, and routes selected cases to additional human investigation. The intended impact was more efficient fraud detection, better prioritisation of municipal control resources and earlier identification of possible unlawful behaviour. However, because SyRI-style systems involve sensitive personal data and profiling of welfare recipients, they raise significant concerns around transparency, discrimination, proportionality and legal accountability. These concerns are particularly relevant given the broader Dutch SyRI judgment, where the system’s legal basis was found incompatible with privacy protections.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Detection of crime and subversion in the Municipality of Leudal (SyRI system)
source_description: Local authorities may seek to detect organised or “subversive” crime where administrative records suggest unusual patterns around buildings, businesses or permits. The Leudal use case concerns the reported use of algorithmic profiling to identify locations where paperwork or administrative signals may indicate possible criminal or irregular activity. The operational problem is that suspicious activity may not be visible through a single inspection file, but may emerge from combinations of property records, business information, permits, registrations, enforcement history or other municipal data. At a conceptual level, the system would combine multiple administrative indicators and generate risk signals for further investigation by officials. The intended impact is to help local government and enforcement partners prioritise inspections, detect hidden misuse of premises and support more coordinated action against organised crime. However, this type of system is high-risk because it can involve profiling of people, addresses or businesses without clear visibility for those affected. It therefore requires strict legal basis, transparency, proportionality, data-quality controls and human review. The use case should be treated cautiously because “subversion” is a broad policy category and algorithmic indicators may produce false positives or reinforce biased inspection patterns.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Detection of crime and subversion in the municipality of Dronten (SyRI system)
source_description: Dronten’s pilot examined whether algorithms could help identify patterns associated with subversive crime at municipal level. The operational challenge was that forms of organised or undermining crime can be difficult for local authorities to detect because relevant signals may be dispersed across administrative records, enforcement data and local intelligence. The municipality therefore explored how algorithmic analysis could support earlier detection and prioritisation of cases requiring further attention. The implementation is described as an experiment using algorithms to detect subversive crime. Conceptually, the system may combine municipal data sources, risk indicators, pattern detection and case-selection workflows to flag locations, activities or dossiers that appear to warrant additional scrutiny. The expected impact would be improved situational awareness for local enforcement actors, more targeted investigation and better use of limited municipal capacity. At the same time, the use of predictive or profiling tools in public-order contexts requires strong safeguards. Risks include opaque criteria, inaccurate suspicion, disproportionate targeting of specific groups or areas, and weak routes for contesting decisions. The pilot therefore needs careful legal, ethical and operational governance if algorithmic signals are used to trigger further enforcement action.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Detection of crime and subversion in the municipality of Maastricht (SyRI system)
source_description: Municipal enforcement teams may use data analysis to identify properties or situations where administrative inconsistencies suggest possible criminal use of buildings, fraudulent activity or other forms of subversion. Maastricht was reported as one of the Dutch municipalities using algorithmic systems in this field. The operational problem is that subversive crime may be hidden behind apparently ordinary businesses, rental arrangements or property uses, and manual inspection may not be able to cover all possible risk locations. At a conceptual level, the system would process administrative records and other available indicators to flag addresses or cases where the combination of data points appears unusual or suspicious. The expected impact is more targeted inspection, earlier detection of hidden criminal structures and better coordination between municipal services and enforcement partners. The system’s role should be framed as risk signalling for human review, not as automatic proof of wrongdoing. This distinction is important because the consequences of being flagged can be significant, including inspections, enforcement attention or reputational harm. The use case therefore raises strong requirements around explainability, proportionality, auditability and safeguards against discriminatory targeting of neighbourhoods, businesses or residents.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Detection of crime and subversion in the municipality of Nederweert (SyRI system)
source_description: Smaller municipalities can face complex enforcement challenges when criminal or improper activity is hidden behind legal-looking administrative structures, property records or business registrations. Nederweert was reported as using algorithmic methods to support detection of subversive crime. The operational problem is that municipal datasets may contain weak signals of irregularity, but individual records may not be meaningful unless combined with other information. A risk-based system can help identify buildings or cases where paperwork “smacks of suspicious cases”, allowing limited inspection capacity to be focused where further review appears justified. At a conceptual level, such a system would aggregate administrative indicators, score or classify cases and provide signals to officials for follow-up. The expected impact is more efficient local enforcement, earlier identification of hidden misuse of property and better support for multi-agency responses to organised crime. However, the system can also create legal and ethical risks if residents, owners or businesses are profiled through opaque combinations of data. The case therefore needs to be presented as an enforcement-support system requiring human verification, rather than an automated determination of criminal conduct. Transparency and safeguards are particularly important because flagged persons may not know that algorithmic profiling influenced official attention.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Municipality of Amsterdam (Parking, Team Analysis & Advice), the Hague, Rotterdam and Utrecht
title: Parking control in various Dutch municipalities - Parking control by means of scan cars
source_description: Large municipalities need to enforce parking rules across dense urban areas efficiently, while limiting manual checks and maintaining consistent treatment of vehicles using paid or restricted parking spaces. Parking control in various Dutch municipalities - Parking control by means of scan cars supports parking enforcement in Amsterdam, The Hague, Rotterdam and Utrecht through vehicles equipped with cameras that inspect parked cars while driving through city streets. The operational problem is that conventional on-foot inspection can be labour-intensive and difficult to scale across large numbers of parking spaces, particularly in cities with high vehicle turnover and complex parking regimes. The scan cars capture licence plates and use an image-recognition algorithm to identify registration numbers. These readings can then be checked against parking-payment or permit databases to determine whether a vehicle appears to be compliant. Cases that require further verification can be reviewed before enforcement action is taken, depending on local procedures. The technology therefore combines mobile sensing, automated number-plate recognition and integration with municipal parking-administration systems. Its impact is greater inspection coverage, faster detection of possible parking violations, more efficient deployment of enforcement staff and improved consistency in parking control. For municipalities, the approach can also generate better operational data on parking behaviour and support more responsive management of urban parking policy.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Passer-by count
source_description: City centres increasingly require reliable insights into pedestrian flows to support economic development, urban planning and public safety. The municipality of Nijmegen introduced passer-by counting to better understand how people move through the city centre, how busy specific areas are at different times, and how these patterns relate to retail performance and public space use. Stakeholders include municipal planners, economic development teams, local businesses and event organisers. The objective is to generate continuous, objective data on footfall without relying on manual counts or surveys, enabling evidence-based decisions on zoning, infrastructure investments and city marketing. The system uses fixed sensors placed in public space to detect and count passers-by while avoiding direct identification of individuals. The sensors process visual or signal data locally to extract movement counts and directional flows, which are then aggregated and transmitted to municipal dashboards. Data is anonymised at source and integrated with other urban indicators, such as time of day, weather and events. The solution has improved the municipality’s ability to monitor urban vitality in near real time and to evaluate the impact of interventions such as street redesigns or events.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Analysing data to help people on welfare get back to work for Social Assistance in The Hague
source_description: The Hague’s social-assistance pilot used data analysis to identify welfare recipients who could be supported towards employment at an earlier stage. The operational problem was not only benefit administration, but also timely activation: municipalities need to recognise which people may benefit from rapid support before unemployment becomes prolonged or more difficult to address. The stakeholders included the Municipality of The Hague, social-assistance recipients, reintegration advisers, municipal employment services and residents whose welfare trajectory could be affected by early intervention. The implementation analyses administrative data to find people at an early stage so that they can be guided towards work more quickly. Conceptually, the system may combine historical welfare data, employment indicators, case characteristics and predictive or segmentation methods to identify groups requiring specific support. The expected impact is improved targeting of reintegration services, faster outreach to residents, more efficient allocation of municipal staff and potentially shorter welfare dependency where appropriate support is available. The value of the tool depends on using the analysis to offer assistance rather than punitive control, and on ensuring that data-driven categorisation remains transparent, fair and subject to professional judgement.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AviaTor - Pilot detection child abuse
source_description: AviaTor was developed to support law-enforcement authorities in processing referrals related to child sexual abuse material, a sensitive and resource-intensive operational area where delays can affect the identification of perpetrators and the protection of victims. Police services receive large volumes of reports, including referrals from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, and need to assess them quickly, prioritise the most urgent cases and enrich available information for investigative follow-up. The project involved Dutch and Belgian police expertise, ZiuZ as solution developer, and funding from the European Union’s Internal Security Fund – Police. Its objective was to reduce the time and effort required to process reports while improving completeness and prioritisation. The emerging technology implementation combines augmented visual intelligence with targeted online research capabilities. Developed from research into a working prototype within 12 months, the tool uses expert insight from police interviews to structure workflows, prioritise reports and support the analysis of visual and contextual information. It also helps combine report data with relevant online sources at an investigative-support level. The impact is faster, more efficient and more complete processing of referrals, allowing law-enforcement officers to focus their attention on high-priority cases, victim identification and perpetrator detection. The case provides clear operational value by improving triage, reducing repetitive workload and supporting more targeted investigative action.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Municipality of Rotterdam, TNO and BZK
title: Pilot Youth Policy Rotterdam - Influencing factors socio-emotional development of young people
source_description: Rotterdam’s youth-policy pilot explored which factors influence the socio-emotional development of young people by combining linked datasets with statistical and machine-learning methods. The policy challenge is that youth outcomes are shaped by multiple interacting variables across education, family context, neighbourhood conditions, health, welfare and social participation. Local authorities need stronger evidence on these relationships to design interventions that are preventive, targeted and proportionate. The stakeholders included the Municipality of Rotterdam, TNO, the Dutch Ministry of the Interior and Kingdom Relations, young people, families, youth-service professionals and policymakers.
