The implementation links datasets and applies a combination of statistical analysis and machine learning to examine which factors are associated with socio-emotional development. Conceptually, the pilot functions as a data-driven policy lab: it integrates relevant administrative or research data, tests associations, identifies patterns and supports policy learning rather than producing a direct automated decision on individual young people. The expected impact is improved understanding of risk and protective factors, better targeting of youth policies and stronger evidence for preventive interventions. Its usefulness depends on data quality, careful interpretation, privacy protection and avoiding deterministic conclusions about individual young people based on statistical correlations.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Project Jurisprudence Robot - AI tool to support prosecutors and investigators
source_description: Public prosecutors and investigators face growing volumes of legal material and case law, making it increasingly difficult to identify relevant jurisprudence efficiently and consistently. To address this challenge, the Dutch Public Prosecution Service collaborated with the legal technology company LexIQ to develop the Jurisprudence Robot, a tool designed to support daily prosecutorial work by improving access to relevant judicial decisions. The main stakeholders include prosecutors, investigators, and judicial support staff, with the objective of reducing time spent on legal research while improving consistency in legal reasoning. The solution processes large collections of court rulings and legal texts and matches them to case-specific queries using automated text analysis techniques. The system structures legal documents, extracts relevant concepts, and presents ranked jurisprudence results to users through an interface integrated into existing prosecutorial workflows. Human decision-making remains central, with the tool acting strictly as an advisory aid rather than an automated decision-maker. According to publicly available judicial documentation, the Jurisprudence Robot has been tested in controlled environments and limited operational settings, with no evidence of nationwide deployment or discontinuation. Reported benefits include faster legal research, improved consistency in case preparation, and reduced administrative burden, while maintaining judicial accountability and professional autonomy.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: VIALIS Real-time incident detection
source_description: VIALIS Real-time Incident Detection focuses on preventing traffic problems by analysing urban traffic data in real time. The operational challenge is that incidents, congestion and disruptions can develop quickly in urban road networks, and traffic managers need early signals to intervene before delays escalate. The stakeholders include Vialis B.V., municipal or transport authorities using the system, road users, traffic-management centres and public bodies concerned with road safety and mobility performance. The implementation uses artificial intelligence to process urban traffic data and detect patterns that may indicate emerging incidents or traffic disruptions. Conceptually, the system can combine sensor data, traffic-flow information, anomaly detection, predictive analytics and alerting functions to support operational decisions. The expected impact is earlier detection of incidents, faster traffic-management responses, reduced congestion and improved reliability for road users. By shifting from reactive monitoring to proactive analysis, the tool can help cities deploy interventions more efficiently, such as adjusting traffic signals, informing road users or dispatching response teams. Its added value depends on integration with existing traffic-control systems, the quality of real-time data streams and the accuracy of alerts produced by the model.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Rain radar Rijnmond - Prediction of rain to prevent flooding and damage
source_description: Rijnmond’s rain radar was developed to provide highly localised measurement and prediction of precipitation in the Rotterdam region, where intense rainfall can quickly create flooding risks and damage to public space, buildings and infrastructure. The operational challenge is that conventional weather information may be too coarse to support timely urban water-management decisions at neighbourhood or street level. Municipal services, emergency planners, water managers, residents, businesses and researchers therefore require more granular rainfall intelligence to anticipate localised disruption. The implementation combines radar-based precipitation measurement with predictive analytics to estimate rainfall patterns at a fine spatial scale. Conceptually, the system collects local meteorological data, processes it into short-term precipitation forecasts and supports decisions on drainage management, preparedness and response. Its value lies in moving from general weather awareness to actionable local prediction. The expected impact is improved prevention of flooding, faster operational response, reduced damage from heavy rainfall and stronger climate-resilience planning. By helping authorities understand where and when rain is likely to become problematic, the tool supports more targeted deployment of resources and better protection of vulnerable urban areas.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Remote sensing for monitoring nature reserves on the Frisian Wadden Islands
source_description: The Frisian Wadden Islands remote-sensing pilot tested whether vegetation in protected nature reserves could be monitored more frequently and efficiently using satellite data. The environmental-management problem is that field-based monitoring of vegetation can be slow, costly and labour-intensive, while ecological conditions may change more rapidly than traditional inspection cycles can capture. The Province of Friesland and Ilionix explored whether annual vegetation monitoring could be supported through data-driven models, giving nature managers a more regular view of habitat conditions. The implementation uses satellite imagery combined with machine-learning techniques to classify and monitor vegetation patterns. Conceptually, the models process remote-sensing data, identify vegetation characteristics and optimise classifications so that ecological changes can be assessed over time. This allows authorities to compare areas, detect developments in habitat composition and prioritise follow-up inspection or management action. The expected impact is more continuous insight into nature reserves, reduced dependence on manual fieldwork and improved evidence for conservation planning. By enabling annual monitoring, the pilot can support more responsive ecological management and help public authorities safeguard sensitive island habitats with more timely and consistent data.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management
title: Rijkswaterstaat vital assets - Predictive maintenance on bridges
source_description: The Dutch Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management needs to maintain bridges and hydraulic civil-engineering works in a way that prevents failures, reduces unnecessary interventions and uses maintenance budgets more efficiently. Rijkswaterstaat vital assets - Predictive maintenance on bridges supports this objective by using data to estimate when maintenance should be carried out on critical infrastructure assets. The operational challenge is that bridges and related water-management structures are subject to wear, environmental pressure and intensive use, while traditional maintenance planning can be either reactive or based on fixed schedules that do not always reflect the actual condition of the asset. The initiative, funded by the Dutch Ministry of Infrastructure and developed with Vitale Assets and the Water cluster of the CAMINO Smart Industry Field Lab, explores how predictive maintenance can be applied to hydraulic civil-engineering works. The technological implementation combines sensors, Internet of Things infrastructure, Big Data techniques and predictive modelling to collect and analyse information on asset condition, use patterns and potential deterioration. These data are used to estimate maintenance needs more accurately and to support planning before faults become critical. The expected impact is more efficient maintenance scheduling, fewer unnecessary inspections or interventions, improved reliability of vital infrastructure and reduced risk of disruption for road and waterway users. The approach also strengthens long-term asset management by helping authorities move from routine maintenance cycles towards condition-based decision-making.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Scan car for checking group formation and complying with corona measures
source_description: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the municipality of Rotterdam needed ways to monitor compliance with public-health measures in urban space, particularly rules concerning group formation and distancing. Manual enforcement alone could be difficult to scale across a large city, especially when conditions changed quickly and authorities needed timely information about where crowding or non-compliance might be occurring. The use case therefore focused on supporting oversight of coronavirus measures in public areas, with the objective of improving situational awareness and helping the municipality respond more effectively to risky gatherings. The stakeholders include the municipality, enforcement and public-safety teams and people using public space, with the wider aim of reducing infection risk during the emergency period. The solution was implemented through a scan car used to observe public-space conditions and check for group formation linked to corona rules. At a conceptual level, the system combined mobile sensing and automated analysis to identify patterns of crowding or gathering while moving through the city, creating a more mobile form of monitoring than fixed observation points alone. This allowed the municipality to gather information on compliance across different locations and support operational responses where required. The expected impact was improved visibility of non-compliant situations, more efficient deployment of enforcement attention and stronger support for pandemic management. More broadly, the use case created value as an example of crisis-time urban monitoring, showing how mobile automated observation could support local public-health enforcement in exceptional circumstances.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Sia - Online notification system of the municipality of Amsterdam
source_description: The Municipality of Amsterdam must respond to a high volume of reports about public-space issues, ranging from street cleaning and repairs to unsafe traffic situations, nuisance and problems in parks or around restaurants. Sia provides a digital channel through which residents and other users can submit notifications when something in the public space needs attention. The core operational problem is that urban maintenance and enforcement services depend on timely, structured and actionable information from the public, while fragmented reporting channels can make it harder to prioritise, route and resolve issues efficiently. SIA enables reports to be made for several types of situations, including objects or areas that need to be repaired or cleaned, dangerous traffic conditions and nuisance caused by people or establishments. The technology implementation consists of an online reporting platform that captures user-submitted information and supports its classification and routing within municipal workflows. Where algorithmic support is used, incoming reports can be categorised, prioritised or assigned to the appropriate service teams based on the content and type of notification. The main impact is a more accessible reporting route for citizens, better structuring of municipal case handling, faster allocation of tasks to relevant departments and improved oversight of recurring public-space problems. For the municipality, SIA contributes to more responsive local service delivery and a stronger evidence base for managing urban maintenance and liveability.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Smart Cameras - Analyzing road situations
source_description: Rijkswaterstaat needs to manage traffic flow on busy roads safely and efficiently, particularly when decisions such as opening or closing rush-hour lanes must be taken quickly and with reliable situational awareness. Smart Cameras support road operators by enabling cameras to interpret traffic conditions and assist with operational decisions on the road network. The problem is that conventional camera monitoring depends heavily on human observation, which can be demanding when many road sections must be supervised simultaneously and when traffic conditions change rapidly. The initiative, involving Rijkswaterstaat, the Innovation Centre and ViNotion, focuses on smart cameras that can “read” the road situation and thereby make the management of rush-hour lanes faster, easier and safer. The implementation uses camera images and computer-vision techniques to detect relevant traffic conditions, such as the presence of vehicles, congestion, incidents or lane availability. These outputs can be integrated into traffic-management processes to support decisions on whether a rush-hour lane can be opened or should be closed. The technology therefore adds an analytical layer to existing camera infrastructure, helping operators interpret visual information more consistently. The expected impact includes faster operational responses, improved safety when changing lane status, reduced workload for traffic-control staff and smoother traffic flow. By enhancing the use of visual data, the solution strengthens real-time road management and supports a more efficient transport network.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Smart enforcement cameras - Enforcement of drivers driving through red road crosses
source_description: Road authorities and enforcement bodies need to prevent drivers from ignoring red crosses above closed lanes, because such violations create serious safety risks for road workers, emergency responders and other road users. Smart enforcement cameras were tested by the Public Prosecutor’s Office and Rijkswaterstaat along the A28 motorway near Amersfoort to detect and reduce these violations. The operational problem is that a red cross indicates that a lane must not be used, often because of incidents, roadworks or traffic-management measures, yet manual enforcement is difficult and dangerous on high-speed roads. The pilot uses smart cameras positioned along the motorway to identify vehicles that continue driving through lanes marked with a red cross. Technically, the system combines camera-based monitoring with automated image analysis to capture relevant evidence, including vehicle passage in relation to the active lane-control signal. The data can then support enforcement processes, subject to verification and applicable legal safeguards. The purpose is not only to sanction non-compliance, but also to increase deterrence and promote safer behaviour around closed lanes. The expected impact is fewer red-cross violations, improved protection for road personnel and road users, better enforcement coverage on motorways and stronger compliance with traffic-control measures. The pilot also demonstrates how digital enforcement tools can complement existing road-safety policies where direct human monitoring is impractical.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Smart decision aid - Determining if a case is a scam or not
source_description: The National Internet Reporting Centre receives around 42,000 reports of buying and selling fraud every year, yet in approximately 10,000 cases a police officer later determines that the reported situation does not constitute a criminal offence. Smart decision aid helps address this mismatch by supporting the initial assessment of online fraud reports and providing direct feedback to the person submitting the report. The operational challenge is that police capacity can be absorbed by reports that require review but do not meet the legal threshold for criminal investigation, while citizens still need clarity on what has happened and what they can do next. Developed within the National Police Lab Artificial Intelligence, the decision aid assists in determining whether a reported buying or selling incident is likely to be a scam. The system uses information entered by the declarant and applies decision-support logic, potentially combining rule-based criteria and data-driven indicators derived from previous reports, to assess whether the case fits known fraud patterns. When the situation does not appear to be a criminal offence, the tool can provide an alternative action perspective to the user. The impact is faster clarification for citizens, reduced unnecessary workload for police officers, better triage of internet-fraud reports and more consistent initial handling of cases. It also supports more efficient use of investigative capacity for reports that are more likely to require police action.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Smart lampposts for combating burglaries - Detection of suspicious movements and audio
source_description: Rotterdam’s smart lampposts pilot in the Lombardijen district was introduced to test whether street infrastructure could support earlier detection of burglary-related signals. The public-safety problem is that burglary attempts may occur before residents, police or municipal services become aware of suspicious activity, limiting the opportunity for rapid intervention. The Municipality of Rotterdam installed lampposts equipped with sensors able to record suspicious movements and microphones able to detect sounds such as tapping on a window. The implementation combines urban sensor infrastructure, motion detection, audio analysis and alerting logic to identify patterns that may suggest attempted burglary or abnormal activity. Conceptually, the lampposts function as distributed detection points in the neighbourhood, using environmental signals to support situational awareness. The expected impact is faster recognition of possible incidents, improved capacity to deploy security or police resources and stronger deterrence in areas affected by burglary risk. The pilot also illustrates the governance challenges of sensor-based urban safety systems, as microphones and movement detection in public or semi-public spaces require careful safeguards, transparency, proportionality and clear limits on data use.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Smart sensor waste containers
source_description: The Municipality of Rotterdam needs to keep neighbourhood waste collection reliable and clean while avoiding both overflowing containers and unnecessary collection trips to bins that are not yet full. This use case addresses this operational problem by installing sensors in waste containers to measure filling levels and support more efficient collection planning. In dense urban areas, conventional waste collection based on fixed routes or schedules can result in two opposite inefficiencies: waste accumulating beside overcrowded containers when emptying is too late, and staff time and vehicle kilometres being wasted when containers are emptied too early. The system uses “filling degree meters” that transmit the status of containers every hour, providing regular information on how full each bin is. This data is made available to collection teams, and drivers can use a tablet to see which route should be taken next. The technological implementation combines sensor-based monitoring, data transmission and route-support tools that translate container-level information into operational guidance for waste-collection services. The expected impact is cleaner public space, fewer complaints about overflowing containers, more efficient use of collection vehicles and reduced unnecessary driving. For waste-management staff, the system improves day-to-day planning by showing where intervention is actually needed. For the municipality, it supports a more responsive and resource-efficient approach to urban waste services.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Aincient B.V., Picturae, Sioux Technologies, Islands of Meaning, Amsterdam City Archive.
title: Amsterdam City Archive - Handwritten Text Recognition for eabling searches on old handwritten texts
source_description: The Amsterdam City Archive holds millions of scans of historical handwritten documents that are valuable for research and public This initaitves aim to make these archival materials more discoverable by automatically converting handwritten scans into text transcriptions. The operational challenge is that manual transcription of such large volumes would be extremely time-consuming, while image-only records limit the ability of researchers, citizens and archivists to search across complete texts. The initiative involves Aincient B.V., Picturae, Sioux Technologies, Islands of Meaning and the Amsterdam City Archive, combining archival expertise with specialist technology providers. The implementation uses Handwritten Text Recognition to analyse scanned handwritten pages and generate machine-readable transcriptions. Natural language processing is then used to support further interpretation, structuring and searchability of the resulting text. At a conceptual level, the system identifies handwriting patterns, converts them into textual output and enables full-text search across materials that were previously far less accessible. The impact is a major improvement in archival discovery, faster access to historical information, reduced dependence on manual indexing and greater reuse of cultural-heritage collections. By making complete handwritten texts searchable, the project strengthens public access to Amsterdam’s documentary heritage and supports more scalable digital-archive services.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Smart Street Scan really sets up municipal services differently
source_description: Municipalities need to keep public spaces clean, yet litter and other waste in streets and public areas are often detected only after complaints or routine inspections, which can delay action and make municipal services less efficient. Smart Street Scan was developed to address this challenge by enabling faster identification and registration of litter so that waste-collection and street-cleaning operations can be organised more effectively. The stakeholders include municipal service providers, waste-collection teams and residents using public space, with the objective of improving cleanliness, reducing response time and optimising service deployment through better information. The solution is implemented by combining sensor and camera technology with image-recognition methods to scan public space automatically. At a conceptual level, the system detects, classifies and registers litter in the street environment, creating a digital feed of observed waste conditions that can be linked to operational planning. This allows downstream services, such as sweeping and waste collection, to adapt routes and interventions on the basis of current conditions rather than relying solely on fixed schedules or resident reports. The expected impact is quicker detection of litter, more efficient route planning and improved street-cleaning performance. More broadly, the project creates value by changing how municipal services are organised around public-space maintenance, reducing unnecessary effort and supporting a more data-driven, responsive and scalable approach to keeping urban environments clean.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: UWV, SVB, the Tax And Customs Administration, DUO, Justid, CJIB and RDW
title: Enforcement of social policy laws with AI
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: This national Dutch pilot concerns the use of data analysis to support enforcement of social-security legislation, particularly in relation to fraud detection and compliance with the duty to inform. The administrative problem is that several public bodies are responsible for schemes, payments, registrations and enforcement processes that may involve overlapping information on citizens, benefits, education, taxation, vehicles and justice-related records. Coordinated analysis can help authorities understand enforcement risks, identify inconsistencies and evaluate how social-security rules are implemented. The implementation involves organisations including UWV, SVB, the Tax and Customs Administration, DUO, Justid, CJIB and RDW. Conceptually, the system can combine cross-agency data analysis, risk indicators, policy evaluation and compliance monitoring to support enforcement of social-policy laws. The expected impact is more structured insight into enforcement practice, better targeting of checks and improved understanding of where errors, omissions or potential fraud may occur. However, because the use case involves sensitive personal and administrative data across multiple bodies, it requires strong safeguards on legality, purpose limitation, transparency, proportionality and independent oversight. The business value for public administration depends on using analytics to improve fairness and efficiency without creating opaque or discriminatory risk profiling.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Dutch Police, with Speech lab B.V.
title: Speaker Tracking in Time and Space
source_description: Speaker Tracking in Time and Space supports police analysis of audio recordings by separating and labelling speech from different speakers. The operational issue is that investigations can involve lengthy recordings with multiple voices, requiring officers or analysts to listen manually to identify who is speaking and when. This is time-consuming and can also expose investigators to conversations unrelated to the subject of interest, creating unnecessary privacy intrusion. Spraaklab develops technology that can largely disassemble, distinguish and label speech from different speakers, allowing police teams to work more efficiently and with higher analytical quality. The implementation uses speech-processing techniques, likely including speaker diarisation, voice-separation, audio segmentation and speaker-labelling models. Conceptually, the tool structures raw audio into speaker-specific segments, helping analysts locate relevant parts of recordings without reviewing unrelated material repeatedly. The expected impact is faster audio review, improved investigative productivity, better-quality evidence handling and stronger privacy protection for people whose conversations are not relevant to the investigation. Its value depends on accuracy in difficult acoustic conditions, careful validation and appropriate human review, since mistaken speaker attribution could affect investigative interpretation.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Road safety model The Hague - Providing a risk score for all road sections and intersections
source_description: Urban road authorities require proactive tools to reduce traffic accidents and prioritise safety interventions across complex road networks. The Municipality of The Hague developed a road safety model to assess and compare risk levels for all road sections and intersections within the city. Stakeholders include municipal traffic engineers, urban planners, and road safety policymakers. The objective is to move from reactive accident analysis to preventive, data-driven traffic safety management. The model combines historical accident records with a comprehensive dataset describing traffic conditions, infrastructure characteristics, environmental factors, and usage patterns. Each road segment and intersection is described using approximately 250 variables, enabling systematic comparison across the network. These datasets are processed to generate a relative risk score that highlights locations with a higher likelihood of future accidents. The results are visualised through analytical dashboards used by traffic experts to prioritise inspections, redesigns, and enforcement measures. According to official government documentation, the model is actively used as a decision-support instrument rather than an automated enforcement mechanism. The approach has improved the municipality’s ability to identify high-risk locations before accidents occur, allocate resources more effectively, and justify infrastructure investments transparently, contributing to a more systematic and preventive road safety strategy.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Road safety model Rotterdam - Predictive model for road accidents
source_description: The Municipality of Rotterdam faces similar challenges to other large cities in managing road safety across a dense and diverse transport network. To support preventive traffic policy, Rotterdam implemented a road safety model that predicts accident risks by analysing the relationship between historical accidents and contextual road data. Key stakeholders include municipal traffic authorities, safety analysts, and infrastructure planners. The objective is to identify hazardous road locations proactively and guide targeted interventions. The model links accident records with data describing road geometry, traffic intensity, surrounding land use, weather conditions, and environmental characteristics within the influence area of each accident location. These combined datasets are analysed to identify patterns associated with elevated accident risks, allowing the municipality to generate predictive insights rather than relying solely on past accident counts. The results are used internally by experts to prioritise safety audits, redesigns, and policy measures. According to sector knowledge platform documentation, the model is operational as a decision-support tool and does not replace expert judgement. Its use has strengthened Rotterdam’s capacity to focus safety investments where they are most needed, improved transparency in traffic safety planning, and supported a shift towards data-informed preventive road management.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Movable Traffic Predictor
source_description: The Movable Traffic Predictor pilot was designed to support traffic-management decisions by forecasting traffic conditions before congestion becomes visible in real time. The operational problem is that traffic-control centres often react to current data, while non-recurrent congestion caused by incidents, sudden bottlenecks or unusual flows may require earlier warnings to deploy effective measures. File radar B.V. developed a new type of AI-based traffic forecaster capable of predicting traffic up to about one hour ahead, with testing carried out in collaboration with traffic-control centres, particularly the national VCNL centre near Utrecht. The implementation applies predictive analytics to traffic data to generate short-term forecasts in the range of approximately 20 to 60 minutes. Conceptually, the system analyses current and historical traffic conditions, identifies emerging disruptions and provides predictive information for operational decisions such as congestion detection, deployment of mobile assets or traffic-management measures. The expected impact is earlier intervention, improved traffic flow, reduced delay and better use of transport-management resources. By shifting traffic control from purely real-time monitoring to anticipatory decision support, the pilot can improve resilience to irregular and incident-driven congestion.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Reference Index Recherche Onderzoeken en Subjecten - Detection of unusual transactions
source_description: Law enforcement agencies must efficiently identify suspicious financial transactions that may be linked to ongoing criminal investigations while operating within strict legal frameworks. In the Netherlands, unusual transactions are partly assessed through comparison with the Reference Index Recherche Onderzoeken en Subjecten (VROS), a database managed by the National Police. Stakeholders include financial institutions, law enforcement bodies, and investigative authorities. The objective is to support criminal investigations by identifying whether reported unusual transactions are linked to existing police investigations. Transaction data flagged by reporting entities is compared through a partly automated process with entries in the VROS. A positive match indicates a potential connection between the transaction and an active investigation, triggering further human-led assessment. The system does not autonomously label transactions as criminal but acts as an investigative signal within a broader legal process. VROS is formally embedded in Dutch legislation and remains operational as part of the national framework for combating financial crime. Its use has improved investigative efficiency by enabling faster cross-referencing of financial intelligence, reducing manual searches, and supporting coordinated law enforcement action, while maintaining procedural safeguards and human oversight.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Viralcom Egg - accidents in the water
source_description: Viralcom Egg is a prototype designed to detect accidents in water and communicate relevant alerts to rescue services. The safety problem is that drownings or underwater incidents can be difficult to identify quickly, especially where visual monitoring from the shore is limited or delayed. The Municipality of Dordrecht is linked to the pilot context, with Viralcom seeking to test the Egg remotely from the quay in Zwijndrecht to the opposite quay in Dordrecht. The implementation uses artificial intelligence and neural networks for pattern recognition and drowning detection. Conceptually, the system monitors activity in or around the water, analyses visual or sensor patterns that may indicate an accident, and sends information to emergency or rescue services when a potential incident is identified. The expected impact is faster detection of water accidents, shorter response times and improved public safety in areas where people may fall into or become distressed in water. The prototype’s value depends on reliable detection under varying environmental conditions, low false-alarm rates and effective integration with rescue-service workflows. If validated, it could strengthen prevention and emergency response in urban waterfront areas.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Predict which residents have a higher risk of care or debt problems in Twenterand (SyRI)
source_description: Residents experiencing debt, care needs or social vulnerability often interact with multiple services, but early warning signs may remain fragmented until problems become acute. Twenterand’s reported use case concerns profiling residents to map debt and care-related problems, with the aim of identifying people who may need help earlier. The operational problem is that social problems often develop gradually and may only become visible once enforcement, crisis care or intensive support is required. A predictive system can bring together administrative indicators and historical patterns to identify households or individuals whose situation resembles earlier cases of debt escalation or care need. At a conceptual level, the system would classify or prioritise residents according to risk signals, enabling municipal professionals to consider preventive outreach or support. The expected impact is earlier intervention, better coordination between social services, reduced crisis escalation and more efficient targeting of limited municipal capacity. The use case must be handled carefully because it involves potentially sensitive social and financial data, and because predictive profiling can unintentionally stigmatise residents or neighbourhoods. Its legitimacy depends on clear purpose limitation, strong human oversight, transparency to affected people and safeguards ensuring that the system is used to offer support rather than punishment.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Early school leavers in the municipality of Amersfoort - Estimation of students at risk
source_description: Preventing early school leaving requires timely identification of pupils whose educational trajectory suggests a higher risk of dropping out before completing their programme. The Amersfoort and Dordrecht use case concerns the use of an algorithm to estimate which students may be at risk of becoming early school leavers. The operational problem is that schools and municipalities may hold relevant signals, such as school changes, grade repetition or attendance-related patterns, but these signals may not be systematically combined for early intervention. At a conceptual level, the algorithm compares current pupils with patterns observed among previous early school leavers and assigns an indication of risk. Professionals can then decide whether additional guidance, counselling or follow-up is appropriate. The intended value is preventive: the model is meant to help education and youth-support services act before disengagement becomes irreversible. The expected impact is better targeting of support, lower dropout rates, more efficient use of guidance capacity and improved educational outcomes. However, the case also raises important governance issues because educational-risk profiling can affect young people’s opportunities and may be difficult to understand or contest. It should therefore be presented as decision support for human professionals, with transparent explanation of the indicators used and safeguards against discriminatory effects.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Wabo assistant - Automated environmental permits
source_description: The municipality of The Hague needed a more efficient way to manage the intake of environmental-permit applications governed by the Environmental Law General Provisions Act, known as Wabo. Permit procedures in this area can involve large volumes of documents and varied applicant questions, creating an administrative burden at the earliest stages of the process and slowing the movement of cases into proper review channels. The use case therefore focused on improving intake efficiency and reducing repetitive administrative work, while helping the municipality process environmental permits more consistently. The stakeholders include municipal permit teams, applicants and environmental-administration staff, with the objective of automating part of the intake process and improving the speed and quality of early-stage handling. The solution is implemented through a Wabo assistant that uses natural language processing to support permit-related tasks. At a conceptual level, the system analyses incoming textual information, identifies relevant content and helps structure or route permit applications so that initial handling requires less manual intervention. This creates a more standardised intake workflow and allows staff to spend less time on repetitive front-end processing. The expected impact is faster handling of permit submissions, reduced clerical burden and improved efficiency in the administration of environmental permits. More broadly, the Wabo assistant creates value by modernising a document-heavy municipal process, supporting better service for applicants and enabling a more scalable model for managing regulatory intake under environmental law.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Water fields - purification system for rainwater
source_description: Cities increasingly face pressure to manage water sustainably while reducing reliance on potable water for non-drinking purposes. The City of Breda implemented “water fields”, a nature-based purification system that collects, buffers, and treats rainwater at district level. Stakeholders include municipal water managers, urban planners, and local residents. The objective is to optimise water use, reduce pressure on drinking water supplies, and improve climate resilience. Rainwater from the surrounding area is collected and filtered through a series of natural purification layers before being stored for reuse. Sensors continuously monitor system performance, rainfall volumes, and storage levels. Operational data is analysed to optimise purification processes and forecast water availability, supporting adaptive system management. According to reporting on the project, the water fields are fully implemented and integrated into Breda’s water infrastructure. The initiative has improved water efficiency, reduced operational costs, and enhanced resilience to drought and heavy rainfall. It also demonstrates how data-driven monitoring can support sustainable urban water systems while maintaining transparency and reliability.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Hoogheemraadschap de Stichtse Rijnlanden en Tauw en HAL24k
title: Water management SR - Predicting of water levels
source_description: Water authorities need to manage treatment plants and water levels proactively, because delayed detection of operational issues can affect service reliability, maintenance planning and the ability to respond to changing environmental conditions. The Water management system supports Hoogheemraadschap De Stichtse Rijnlanden, Tauw and HAL24K in applying data science to complex water-management challenges. The case focuses on improving how real-time operational data can be used to understand conditions at water treatment plants and anticipate changes in water levels, rather than relying only on periodic checks or reactive maintenance. The technological implementation is based on HAL24K’s Dimension data-intelligence platform, demonstrated through the use of live sensor data. At a conceptual level, the platform collects and processes streams from sensors installed in water-management infrastructure, enabling the analysis of current conditions, anomalies and trends relevant to maintenance or level management. Predictive models can use these data to support earlier identification of risks and more timely operational decisions. The expected impact is more efficient maintenance, faster detection of emerging problems, better use of real-time information and improved capacity to manage water systems proactively. For the responsible organisations, the value lies in strengthening operational resilience, reducing avoidable interventions and creating a more data-driven basis for water-level control and treatment-plant management.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Municipality of Houten, Ijsselstein, Lopik, Nieuwegein and Vijfheerenland
title: WIL Leak Current - Discover abuse and improper use of benefits
source_description: Welfare administrations need to ensure that people who are entitled to benefits receive support while also detecting improper use or abuse of public funds. WIL Lekstroom, a cooperation of municipalities in the Utrecht region, was reported as using algorithms to support detection of abuse and improper use of social-assistance benefits. The operational problem is that benefit-control processes are labour-intensive, and staff may need to identify which cases deserve additional review without checking every file manually. At a conceptual level, the system would use historical benefit, case-management or administrative data to detect patterns associated with previous improper use, then generate signals or risk scores for officials. The expected impact is more targeted investigation, reduced unnecessary checks, improved administrative efficiency and better protection of public resources. However, welfare-fraud prediction is a high-risk area because historical data may reflect biased enforcement patterns and flagged residents may not know that an algorithm influenced additional scrutiny. The system should therefore be understood as decision support only, not as automatic sanctioning or benefit withdrawal. Any responsible use would require clear documentation, explainability, human review, appeal routes and monitoring for discriminatory impact, especially because the affected population may already be socio-economically vulnerable.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Brightlands Techruption, OU (CAROU), UM (BISS), Police NL (iLAB)
title: Nexus - speech-operated expert system
source_description: Nexus is designed to support community police officers who require timely, structured and locally relevant information before engaging with neighbourhoods. Officers often need to review recent incidents, local risks and operational context, but conventional briefing processes can be fragmented, time-consuming or dependent on manual searches across different systems. The case involves Brightlands Techruption, the Open University’s CAROU, Maastricht University’s BISS and the Dutch Police iLAB, with the objective of providing officers with an accessible expert system that delivers detailed neighbourhood briefings through speech interaction. The emerging technology implementation consists of a speech-operated expert system that allows officers to request and receive information verbally. At conceptual level, the system combines speech recognition, knowledge retrieval and expert-system logic to transform operational data on recent incidents into a concise briefing tailored to a specific neighbourhood. The interface reduces the need for manual interaction and supports use in operational contexts where officers may benefit from hands-free access to information. The impact is improved situational awareness, more efficient preparation and a better user experience for community police officers. By making local incident information easier to access and interpret, Nexus can support more informed decision-making, strengthen neighbourhood policing and reduce the time spent searching for relevant background information before field activities.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Municipality of Heerlen, CBS, VNG, CoTown, Heerlen Mijn Stad, Brightlands
title: W(e). Service.Heerlen (WESH)
source_description: W(e). Service.Heerlen, or WESH, addresses the challenge of maintaining the public environment while promoting citizen participation and supporting local economic activity. Municipalities often face pressure to keep public spaces clean, safe and well maintained, while citizens may have limited structured opportunities to contribute to neighbourhood improvements. In Heerlen, the municipality and partners including CBS, VNG, CoTown, Heerlen Mijn Stad and Brightlands developed an application that enables citizens to take on maintenance tasks in the public environment. The objective is to create a participatory model in which residents can contribute directly to local upkeep and receive a financial reward that can be spent with local small and medium-sized enterprises. The emerging technology implementation is based on a digital platform that connects available municipal maintenance jobs with citizens willing to complete them. At conceptual level, the app supports task publication, citizen participation, completion confirmation and reward allocation, linking civic engagement with local economic circulation. The solution may also generate useful operational data on maintenance needs, participation patterns and service delivery. Its impact is both operational and social: the municipality can mobilise additional capacity for small-scale public-space maintenance, citizens gain a practical role in improving their environment, and local SMEs benefit from reward spending. The case demonstrates how digital public-service platforms can combine urban maintenance, participation and local value creation.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Brightlands Techruption, CBS, municipality of Heerlen, CZ, Maastricht University, TNO
title: Poverty prevention - Identification of poverty and debt early
source_description: Early signs of financial vulnerability are often missed because relevant data is distributed across multiple public agencies that cannot easily share information without infringing privacy regulations. Municipalities, social services and welfare organisations require new approaches to identify citizens at risk before situations escalate into severe poverty or debt. The objective of this pilot is to enable preventive social interventions while fully safeguarding personal data. The implementation applies privacy-preserving computation techniques that allow organisations to analyse combined indicators without revealing individual-level data. Secure algorithms process variables such as income changes, benefit dependency and arrears to identify risk patterns, and results are integrated into existing social support workflows. When risk thresholds are reached, case workers are alerted to initiate early assistance. The pilot improved the timeliness and targeting of interventions, reducing long-term social and financial costs. Qualitative impacts include stronger inter-agency collaboration, increased trust from citizens and full compliance with data protection requirements. The project demonstrates that data-driven prevention policies can be effectively implemented without compromising confidentiality or individual rights.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: INZNAK Project - Intelligent road signs for adaptive vehicle traffic control
source_description: The INZNAK project responds to the need to improve road safety and traffic management by providing drivers with timely, location-specific warnings about hazards, disruptions and recommended speeds. Many highway collisions are linked to speed that is not adapted to current weather, road-surface or traffic conditions, particularly during sudden braking, congestion, fog, storms, blizzards or black ice. In Gdańsk, the project aims to develop a network of autonomous intelligent road signs capable of warning drivers earlier and supporting adaptive traffic control. The emerging technology implementation includes three types of signs: standing, hanging and mobile. Each sign has a display showing text and image messages, including suggested speeds and information on current disruptions. The signs communicate with each other through LoRaWAN and with the traffic control centre through LTE, creating a two-level communication architecture that improves resilience if telecommunications infrastructure fails. Each sign is equipped with sensors such as Doppler radar, lidar, acoustic probes, RGB cameras, Bluetooth receivers and a local weather station. This multimodal approach allows the system to combine different detection methods, for example using lidar when standard cameras are less effective at night. The expected impact is earlier hazard detection, more reliable traffic information and better adaptation of driver behaviour to real-time road conditions, with potential benefits for safety, traffic flow and operational resilience.
