title: Lombardia Chatbot Coronavirus
source_description: The Lombardia Coronavirus Chatbot was developed during the COVID-19 emergency to respond to the urgent need for clear, accessible, and structured public information on symptoms and appropriate behavioural measures. The operational problem was the rapid increase in citizen enquiries during a public health crisis, which placed pressure on regional information channels, healthcare services, and emergency communication systems. The stakeholders included residents of Lombardy, the regional administration, ARIA SpA as the Regional Company for Innovation and Purchasing, healthcare authorities, and public health bodies responsible for issuing guidance. The objective was to provide a guided self-orientation tool that helped users understand which actions to take based on their selected symptoms and official recommendations. The implementation consisted of an automated information chatbot that led users through predefined interaction paths, using symptom selection, rule-based decision flows, natural language interaction elements, and curated guidance from the Ministry of Health and relevant international organisations. The service was made available through a digital channel and integrated conceptually with regional communication infrastructure and authoritative public health content. The impact was immediate and visible, as the tool generated very high access numbers shortly after launch. Its main value was the ability to scale public communication rapidly, reduce repetitive enquiries to human operators, improve consistency of advice, and support citizens in navigating uncertainty during the emergency. The chatbot also strengthened the user experience by offering a simple, guided route to trusted information.

title: Sentilo BCN - Plataforma de Sensors i Actuadors de Barcelona
source_description: Smart-city services depend on the ability to collect, share and reuse information from many heterogeneous sensors and urban systems without creating isolated vertical platforms. Barcelona City Council developed Sentilo as an open-source sensor and actuator platform to support its smart-city strategy and provide a reusable infrastructure layer for real-time urban data. The practical challenge was to connect diverse devices, applications and legacy systems in a way that was open, interoperable and scalable across city domains. The implementation provides a cross-platform architecture through which sensors and actuators can publish and consume data, allowing different applications to reuse information from the same urban infrastructure. At a conceptual level, Sentilo acts as a middleware layer between physical devices and smart-city applications: sensors send data to the platform, applications subscribe to relevant streams, and the city can manage urban information through open standards and shared interfaces. This avoids fragmented one-purpose solutions and supports integration across environmental monitoring, mobility, public space, energy and other municipal services. The expected impact is improved interoperability, lower integration cost, stronger reuse of urban data and a larger ecosystem of cities and companies using free software. Current sources describe Sentilo BCN as providing real-time information on Barcelona and confirm that Sentilo remains available as open-source software with public documentation and code repositories.

title: SKRINJA 2.0 - Business Intelligence in the civil service (BI)
source_description: SKRINJA 2.0 provides Slovenia’s public administration with a horizontal data warehouse and business-intelligence service hosted on the Government Computer Cloud. The administrative problem is that ministries and public bodies often need better access to structured data, analytical tools and shared reporting capabilities to support evidence-based decisions, but such functions can be fragmented across institutions. The main stakeholders include the Ministry of Public Administration, its ICT department, government bodies, civil servants, procurement officials and policy managers using data for planning or oversight. The system was implemented as a cross-government service to promote data-driven decision-making in the civil service. Its implementation combines data warehousing, business-intelligence tools, cloud infrastructure and horizontal service configuration, enabling different parts of the administration to store, process, analyse and visualise data. Since the Ministry of Public Administration also handles national procurement activities, the system may also be used to support procurement procedures in the future. Conceptually, SKRINJA 2.0 provides common analytical infrastructure rather than a single sector-specific application, allowing public institutions to reuse data capabilities across policy areas. The expected impact is improved analytical capacity, more consistent reporting, reduced duplication of BI infrastructure and stronger support for strategic management in government. By centralising business-intelligence functions in the public cloud, the solution can enhance efficiency and create a foundation for broader data-driven governance.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: ProZorro, Bid prediction
source_description: Public procurement platforms need to understand tender behaviour in order to improve competition, reduce failed procedures and support better design of purchasing processes. ProZorro’s bid-prediction work applies artificial intelligence and machine-learning techniques to procurement data with the aim of estimating whether a tender is likely to take place successfully and whether a participant may leave the platform before completing the process. The operational problem is that public buyers, suppliers and platform administrators all face uncertainty: tenders may attract insufficient competition, bidders may drop out, and procurement processes may fail or require repetition. The implementation uses data from past tenders, participant behaviour, procurement categories and platform interactions to train predictive models. At a conceptual level, the system identifies patterns associated with successful or unsuccessful tenders and generates risk or probability signals that can help platform teams and procurement authorities focus attention on procedures that may require improvement. The expected impact is better procurement planning, fewer failed tenders, improved supplier experience and stronger evidence for platform design. Because ProZorro is a central national e-procurement system, even modest improvements in prediction and user support can have systemic value. Current public ProZorro services remain active, and recent Ukrainian procurement-analytics discussions continue to describe AI and analytics as relevant to the ProZorro ecosystem, but the exact operational status of this specific bid-prediction model is not clearly documented in current official sources.

title: ProZorro, CPV Prediction
source_description: Correct procurement classification is essential because CPV codes affect searchability, competition, market analysis and reporting in public procurement systems. ProZorro developed an AI tool to predict the correct CPV codes and units of measurement for procurement items, with the objective of reducing misclassification and making user-facing procurement platforms easier to use. The operational problem is that buyers may choose incorrect codes or inconsistent measurement units, which can make tenders harder for suppliers to find, distort procurement statistics and reduce the usefulness of open procurement data. The implementation uses machine-learning methods trained on historical procurement descriptions, item names, categories and code assignments. At a conceptual level, a user enters or uploads procurement information, and the model proposes likely CPV codes and measurement units based on similarity to previous tenders and learned classification patterns. The expected impact is fewer classification errors, faster tender creation, improved supplier discovery, more accurate analytics and better-quality procurement data for monitoring and policy. Because ProZorro depends on open data and marketplace interoperability, standardised classification has value beyond individual tenders. However, the source information indicates that this tool had not yet been implemented at the time of documentation. Current ProZorro remains operational, but I found no current official source confirming that this specific CPV-prediction tool has since been deployed in production.

title: DoZorro AI tool
source_description: Public procurement oversight requires identifying high-risk tenders among very large numbers of procedures, a task that is difficult for experts and civil-society monitors to perform manually. DoZorro, linked to Ukraine’s ProZorro procurement ecosystem and Transparency International Ukraine, applies AI-supported risk analysis to help detect tenders that may involve corruption, collusion, unjustified disqualification or unfair selection of winners. The platform already enables suppliers, buyers, control authorities and citizens to provide feedback on procurement processes. The AI tool strengthens that function by prioritising tenders with suspicious patterns, allowing experts to focus on cases with the highest probability of irregularity. At a conceptual level, the system combines open procurement data, complaint data, risk indicators, machine-learning models and expert review. It does not replace legal investigation or procurement-control decisions; rather, it narrows the search space and supports human monitors by highlighting tenders that deserve closer analysis. Reported beta-test results included 26% more cases of unfounded winner selection, 37% more cases of groundless disqualification and 298% more cases of participant conspiracy being identified. The expected impact is better targeting of oversight resources, stronger anti-corruption monitoring, improved transparency and more efficient use of civil-society expertise. Recent open-contracting material describes DoZorro analytics platforms as continuing to interact with ProZorro’s central database.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Kommers (KAI) semantics check tool
source_description: Public procurement processes in both public and private sector organisations require clear, unambiguous tender documentation to ensure fair competition and avoid misinterpretation by potential bidders. However, procurement texts often contain complex legal and technical language, which can lead to misunderstandings, increased bidder risk, additional clarification rounds and, ultimately, delays in contract award and project execution. Stakeholders in this context include procurement officers, legal advisors, potential suppliers and contracting authorities, all of whom benefit from improved clarity and reduced ambiguity in procurement materials. The objective of this initiative is to enhance the quality and precision of procurement documentation by identifying semantic inconsistencies, ambiguous phrases and unclear requirements before tender publication. The solution integrates an AI assistant into Primona’s Kommers e-procurement platform, extending its existing modules with natural language processing (NLP) capabilities. The AI component performs semantic analysis on requirement statements, specifications and other textual elements within procurement documents to detect unclear wording, potential contradictions and language that might be misinterpreted by bidders. The tool leverages trained language models and domain-specific lexicons, combined with syntactic and semantic rule sets, to highlight problematic segments to the procurement author. It is embedded within the Kommers workflow, allowing users to run checks directly within their document preparation interface and receive actionable feedback in real time. By automating semantic validation, the tool reduces the risk of ambiguous or poorly phrased procurement documents reaching the market, improving clarity and fairness in competitive tendering. This leads to fewer clarification requests, faster procurement cycles, reduced administrative burden for contracting authorities and a lower risk of bid disputes. Enhanced document quality contributes to better supplier engagement, more accurate tender responses and ultimately more efficient public and private sector procurement outcomes.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: State Treasury e-invoicing plans
source_description: The Finnish State Treasury is responsible for overseeing and supporting financial management processes across central government entities, including the handling of a high volume of electronic invoices. Despite Finland’s advanced adoption of e-invoicing, invoice processing still requires manual verification of key data such as agreement numbers, amounts, supplier information and accounting references, creating inefficiencies and limiting full automation. A significant challenge identified by the State Treasury is the inconsistent structuring and placement of invoice data by suppliers and IT service providers, which hinders seamless machine processing. The objective of the initiative is to increase the level of end-to-end automation in public sector invoice handling, reduce manual workload and improve accuracy and processing speed across government financial operations. The planned solution combines artificial intelligence techniques and robotic process automation to analyse structured and semi-structured invoice data. Machine learning models are designed to automatically extract and validate relevant invoice fields, such as contract identifiers and payment amounts, while rule-based automation tools integrate with existing financial management systems to route, verify and post invoices. The system relies on standardised e-invoice formats and interoperability frameworks, and is embedded within the State Treasury’s digital financial infrastructure to enable scalable, centralised processing. The initiative aims to enable near real-time invoice validation, significantly reduce manual intervention, minimise processing errors and accelerate payment cycles. By improving data quality requirements and promoting standardisation among suppliers, the State Treasury strengthens the reliability and efficiency of public financial management, reduces administrative costs and enhances transparency and scalability in government accounting processes.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: YPO, Procurement Information Provider
source_description: Public-sector buyers often need help navigating procurement frameworks, services and specialist teams, especially when they must purchase quickly while complying with public procurement rules. YPO introduced the Procurement Information Provider, known as PIP, as a chatbot to help users find relevant frameworks, understand YPO services and reach the right procurement teams. The operational problem is that procurement information can be spread across web pages, framework documentation and service categories, which makes self-service navigation difficult for schools, local authorities and other public organisations. The implementation uses a conversational interface on YPO’s website, allowing users to ask questions or follow prompts rather than manually search through procurement content. At a conceptual level, the chatbot retrieves relevant information from the site, directs users to appropriate frameworks and provides hand-off to human procurement specialists where needed. The expected impact is faster access to procurement guidance, reduced friction for public buyers, fewer routine enquiries and better use of YPO’s framework catalogue. The chatbot’s role is advisory and navigational rather than transactional: it helps users identify procurement routes, but does not replace procurement judgement or formal tendering processes. UKAuthority reported the launch in 2018 as a chatbot built to help public-sector buyers, while YPO itself remains an active public-sector procurement organisation.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Dashboard to Explore state spending in Finland
source_description: Open procurement data can strengthen public accountability only if citizens, companies and analysts can understand what the government is buying and from whom. Finland’s Explore State Spending service, Tutkihankintoja.fi, provides a public dashboard for examining government purchase-invoice data, including spending by procuring organisation, supplier and category of goods or services. The operational problem was that e-invoicing data from the state system was not originally categorised according to a standard procurement taxonomy, making it difficult to search, compare or analyse. Hansel piloted a machine-learning solution to automatically categorise state e-invoicing data according to the United Nations Standard Products and Services Code taxonomy. At a conceptual level, the system takes invoice-level procurement data, classifies spending into meaningful procurement categories and makes it searchable through a public web interface. This enables users to explore areas such as ICT procurement, administrative services, equipment or transport-related purchases. The expected impact is greater transparency, easier spending analysis, better procurement oversight and improved data quality for public buyers. Other AI-enabled analysis is also used internally for procurement authorities. Current sources confirm that the portal remains online and that Hansel continued expanding the service by adding new organisations in 2023.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: eNest solution
source_description: Finland’s eNest solution was designed to simplify supplier verification during public procurement by reducing the need for bidders to submit official records manually. In tendering processes, contracting authorities must check that suppliers meet legal and administrative requirements, while companies often need to gather and attach documents that already exist in official databases. This creates duplication, administrative burden and avoidable friction for both public buyers and service providers. eNest aims to make the tendering process more efficient by automatically verifying information submitted by suppliers against official records. The implementation relies on the European Single Procurement Document as a standardised structure for supplier declarations, allowing the system to connect tender information with authoritative public registers. At a conceptual level, the solution combines procurement workflow integration, automated data checks, standardised supplier self-declarations and register-based verification. By replacing repeated document submission with automated confirmation, the system can improve reliability, reduce processing time and make participation easier for companies. The expected impact is lower administrative cost, fewer errors in tender documentation, faster assessment of suppliers and a better user experience for both contracting authorities and bidders. It also supports interoperability in public procurement by aligning national processes with European procurement standards.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Finnish Government Shared Services Centre for Finance and HR
title: Palkeet - RPA Project
source_description: Shared service centres handle large volumes of repetitive finance and HR tasks where accuracy, consistency and processing speed are essential. Palkeet, the Finnish Government Shared Services Centre for Finance and HR, introduced robotic process automation to automate routine business processes across public administration support services. The operational problem was that tasks such as purchase-invoice validation, supplier-register maintenance and other administrative checks required structured but repetitive work by staff. The implementation used UiPath software robots, alongside other tools where appropriate, to model and execute automated workflows. At a conceptual level, RPA bots log into existing systems, follow predefined process rules, validate data, move information between applications and flag exceptions for human review. This approach allowed Palkeet to automate without immediately replacing all underlying legacy systems. The expected impact is higher productivity, improved processing quality, fewer manual errors, faster throughput and better use of staff time for expert work. The project is recognised as one of the first major RPA implementations in the Finnish public sector and formed part of a wider government digitalisation agenda. UiPath’s case material states that Palkeet began considering RPA in spring 2015 and became one of the first Finnish organisations to foresee its benefits, while Palkeet remains an active shared-services provider in Finnish government.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: mTender in France
source_description: Public procurement reform requires digital systems that increase transparency, reduce administrative friction and create structured data across the full procurement cycle. Moldova’s Ministry of Finance developed mTender with support from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development as an open-source electronic procurement system. The platform supports electronic open tenders, reverse auctions, aggregated procurement planning and online framework agreements, while using the Open Contracting Data Standard to make procurement information more accessible and reusable. The operational problem was to move from fragmented or paper-heavy procurement processes towards a transparent digital system connecting public buyers, private platforms and a central data layer. The implementation consists of a public portal, an open-data central database and accredited private-sector platforms that support electronic procurement by public and private users. At a conceptual level, mTender digitises procurement planning, tender publication, bidding, data disclosure and contract-related monitoring. The reported use of robotic process automation for tracking contract execution reflects the wider goal of automating repetitive controls and improving visibility across the procurement lifecycle. The expected impact is more transparent public spending, greater competition, easier supplier participation, stronger data-driven monitoring and alignment with international open-contracting practice. The current MTender portal remains accessible and describes the system as supporting procurement from planning through payment, while recent Moldovan reporting indicates that a new e-Achiziții system has been approved as the next stage of modernisation.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: SUVE - Chatbot for questions about the emergency situation and the coronavirus
source_description: During the COVID-19 emergency, citizens needed quick, consistent and accessible answers to frequently asked questions about restrictions, services and official guidance. Estonia’s SUVE chatbot was introduced across the websites of several government agencies to provide automated responses in Estonian and English, reducing pressure on public-service channels and helping users find reliable information from official sources. The operational problem was typical of the pandemic period: public rules changed rapidly, citizens repeatedly asked similar questions, and government agencies needed to maintain a single, trustworthy information layer while avoiding overload on call centres and staff. The implementation used an automated conversational interface able to answer frequently asked questions about general services and the emergency situation. At a conceptual level, the chatbot connected user queries to curated government information, allowing citizens to receive immediate guidance through agency websites without navigating multiple pages or waiting for human assistance. Its expected impact was faster access to public information, reduced administrative burden, greater consistency of answers and improved communication during a fast-moving crisis. Because SUVE relied on official sources and supported both Estonian and English, it also helped reach residents and foreign users who needed emergency information. The case illustrates how conversational automation can be rapidly deployed for crisis communication when public demand is high and information needs are repetitive.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: KRATID - Detecting traffic anomalies and incidents of the Estonian data exchange layer (X-Road)
source_description: Digital government depends on reliable data exchange between public institutions, and Estonia’s X-Road is a critical infrastructure layer for secure communication between public and private-sector systems. KRATID uses machine learning to monitor traffic patterns in the Estonian data exchange layer and detect anomalies or possible incidents. The operational problem is that very large numbers of exchanges take place through X-Road, making it difficult for human administrators to identify unusual behaviour, technical faults or unexpected changes in service use manually. The implementation compares current data-exchange behaviour with previous periods and searches for differences that may indicate an error, abnormal usage or another event requiring attention. At a conceptual level, the system combines traffic monitoring, anomaly detection, historical pattern comparison and human review. If the system cannot determine whether an observed situation is erroneous or permitted, a user still decides how to interpret the signal. The expected impact is stronger operational awareness for the Information System Authority, faster detection of incidents, better guidance for X-Road users and more resilient digital public infrastructure. The use case should be separated from other Estonian AI examples sometimes listed in the same source, such as job matching, land-mowing detection or police traffic deployment; the core KRATID case concerns X-Road anomaly and incident detection.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: COVID19 AragonBot
source_description: Regional emergency communication during the pandemic required fast responses to recurring citizen questions, particularly when telephone support lines were saturated. COVID19AragonBot was launched by the Government of Aragon with the support of ITAINNOVA to provide an automated response service through Telegram. The initiative emerged from a practical service-delivery problem: citizens repeatedly asked similar questions about COVID-19 rules, symptoms, services and procedures, while more complex or specific issues still required specialised human attention. The chatbot therefore acted as a first-level digital assistant, guiding users through common questions and helping redirect more complicated cases. The implementation used artificial intelligence and conversational automation within the Telegram messaging environment, making the service accessible through a familiar mobile channel. At a conceptual level, the bot classified user requests, matched them to prepared official information and provided immediate answers or orientation. Its expected impact was to reduce pressure on public helplines, accelerate responses, improve consistency of public information and allow human operators to focus on cases requiring judgement or escalation. The use case is strongly linked to the exceptional conditions of the pandemic, when speed of deployment, channel accessibility and operational relief were more important than building a long-term administrative assistant. It demonstrates how regional governments used lightweight conversational tools to manage sudden surges in public-service demand.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Covid-bot - France
source_description: Public-health authorities needed scalable tools to help people assess possible COVID-19 risk and obtain guidance without immediately contacting medical services. In France, the Pasteur Institute, Greater Paris University Hospitals and the chatbot start-up Clevy released an open-source COVID-19 auto-diagnosis chatbot in March 2020. The objective was to provide a structured questionnaire through which users could report symptoms and receive an indication of their possible risk of contamination or need for further action. The implementation relied on a conversational questionnaire rather than a free-form diagnostic system: users answered predefined questions, and the bot mapped responses to risk-assessment guidance based on the available public-health knowledge at the time. At a conceptual level, the service translated triage logic into an accessible digital interface, supporting early self-assessment, orientation and public communication. Its expected impact was to reduce unnecessary pressure on health services, help citizens understand their situation, and provide a rapid channel for standardised information during the first wave of the pandemic. The open-source character also allowed the tool to be reused or examined by other actors. The service should not be understood as a substitute for medical diagnosis; its role was to provide preliminary orientation during an emergency, when demand for health information was exceptionally high and official communication needed to scale quickly.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Automated parking control
source_description: Managing scarce parking space in a dense city requires regular enforcement, reliable permit checks and a process that can cover large numbers of parked vehicles without excessive manual patrol effort. Amsterdam uses automated parking control to determine whether parked vehicles have the right to occupy paid parking spaces, either because a fee has been paid through a parking meter or app, or because the vehicle has a valid parking permit. The implementation uses scan cars equipped with cameras and automatic number-plate recognition to identify licence plates and check them against relevant payment and permit systems. At a conceptual level, the scan car captures the plate, converts it into machine-readable data, checks the data against back-office records and flags cases where no valid parking right appears to exist. Human procedures can then verify and handle enforcement actions where needed. The expected impact is more efficient street-parking enforcement, better compliance with parking rules, reduced fraud and improved turnover of parking spaces. The system operates at large scale: Egis reports that Amsterdam’s on-street parking service uses ANPR to monitor more than six million vehicles per month.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Reporting issues in public space
source_description: Cities receive large volumes of reports about waste, broken infrastructure, unsafe traffic situations, nuisance and maintenance issues, and the value of such reporting depends on routing each case to the correct municipal team. Amsterdam’s public-space reporting system allows residents to submit issues online, by phone or through external applications. The earlier approach depended heavily on users choosing the right category from many drop-down options, which could lead to errors and delays because the municipality has many service departments and categories. The implementation uses an algorithm within the Signals reporting system to recognise relevant words and phrases in the user’s description, infer the likely category and support routing to the responsible department. At a conceptual level, the system applies natural-language processing or keyword-based text classification to citizen-submitted reports, then links the classification to municipal workflow allocation. This reduces the administrative burden on the person making the report and improves the chance that the case reaches the correct team quickly. The expected impact is faster processing, fewer misrouted reports, less manual reclassification and better responsiveness in public-space management.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Parking chatbot
source_description: Parking rules can be difficult for residents and visitors to navigate because they differ by location, permit type, vehicle, time period and payment situation. Helsinki’s parking chatbot provides an automated customer-service channel for parking-related questions through the city’s parking website. The operational problem is that many parking enquiries are repetitive and informational, but still require users to interpret municipal rules or find the correct page. The implementation uses a chatbot interface to answer common questions about parking services and guide users towards relevant information. At a conceptual level, the system recognises user intent, retrieves or matches the appropriate parking guidance, and presents an answer in conversational form. It does not replace formal permit decisions or enforcement processes; its role is to improve access to parking information and reduce routine enquiries. The expected impact is better customer experience, quicker answers outside conventional service channels, reduced pressure on human customer-service staff and more consistent communication of parking rules. The chatbot is part of Helsinki’s public AI register, which documents AI and algorithmic systems used by the city to improve transparency, accountability and civic participation.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Health center chatbot
source_description: Health-service users often need basic guidance before deciding whether to use a digital service, contact a health station, seek dental or mental-health support, or use social-service counselling. Helsinki’s health center chatbot provides anonymous, secure and round-the-clock advice for common health and illness-related questions. The operational objective is to improve access to information while directing users to the right digital health or social-service channel, such as Omaolo, Omakanta, social counselling chat or other city services. The implementation uses natural-language processing to analyse users’ searches, identify their intended service need and match that need with reliable instructions. At a conceptual level, the chatbot combines intent recognition, service navigation, evidence-based guidance and integration with digital health-service pathways. Clinical guidance is based on national practices, including evidence-based treatment, Current Care guidelines and emergency-care evaluation criteria. The expected impact is wider access to health-centre services, reduced queuing for routine guidance, improved consistency of advice, better user experience and a more efficient front door to digital health services. The service also supports staff by automating responses to frequently asked questions and collecting background information where appropriate.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Oodi's book recommendation service Obotti
source_description: Large public libraries hold collections that many visitors only partly discover, particularly when users do not know which titles, themes or authors match their interests. Obotti was developed for Helsinki Central Library Oodi as a recommendation chatbot that helps customers find books from Oodi’s collection. The objective is to make library material easier and more engaging to explore, especially by recommending works that users might not otherwise encounter through ordinary catalogue searches. The implementation is a mobile application for Android and iOS, divided into six thematic chatbot characters that recommend content according to different interests. Users can interact through predefined answer options or free search terms in text or speech. At a conceptual level, the service uses contextual natural-language analysis to infer the user’s interests and connect them with available materials in Oodi’s collection at the time of recommendation. The expected impact is improved discovery of library resources, a more playful and personalised customer experience, greater use of the collection and broader experimentation with AI in cultural services.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: ChatBot Botty Bonn
source_description: Municipal service information can be difficult for residents to locate when it is distributed across websites, offices and specialised service pages. Bonn’s chatbot Botty was developed to provide a conversational access point to municipal information and services, making the city’s website more intuitive for users seeking administrative guidance. The objective was to create an open community-oriented platform that could include municipal service information and earlier expert bots, while giving developers a live and development environment for further improvement. The implementation involved a technical foundation and server hosting financed and operated by the City of Bonn and GovBot, with municipal service information made available through the chatbot. At a conceptual level, the system recognises user questions, searches or maps them to municipal service descriptions, and responds in a chat-style interface. Its expected impact is easier access to public information, fewer routine enquiries, better digital availability outside office hours and a more collaborative ecosystem for chatbot development. Recent reporting indicates that Bonn now uses a data-protection-compliant AI chatbot on the city website, developed by the GovTech start-up neuraflow, to expand online information on municipal services.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Noa - chatbot
source_description: Entrepreneurs and start-ups often face fragmented administrative procedures, especially when they need to understand which obligations, forms or public services apply to their situation. Noa was designed as an online public-service chatbot to guide start-ups through administrative processes in the Île-de-France context. The operational objective was to simplify access to administrative guidance by offering a conversational entry point rather than requiring users to search across multiple institutional pages. The implementation used a chatbot interface to answer common questions, orient users through procedures and provide practical information on relevant public services. At a conceptual level, the system acted as a digital navigation layer over administrative content: users described their need, and the bot directed them towards the appropriate process or information. Its expected impact was reduced friction for start-ups, faster access to administrative guidance, lower demand for repetitive human support and a clearer user journey through public administration. The case reflects a broader shift towards user-centred government services, where chatbots are used not because the underlying procedures are simple, but because users need help navigating them. In this sense, Noa’s value lay in reducing uncertainty at the first point of contact and making public administration more approachable for new businesses.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Bobbi - Berlin administration
source_description: Citizens often need information from local administration outside normal service hours, and many requests concern recurring topics that can be answered through standardised guidance. Berlin’s chatbot Bobbi was introduced as an additional channel alongside the ServicePortal and the 115 citizen hotline, helping residents obtain quick answers to administrative questions at any time. The objective was not to replace existing service channels, but to provide a convenient first point of contact for common concerns, especially when users wanted immediate orientation rather than a telephone conversation. The implementation used a conversational interface connected to administrative information from Berlin’s public-service ecosystem. At a conceptual level, the chatbot interpreted user questions, matched them with relevant service descriptions or procedural information, and directed citizens towards the correct administrative pathway. Its expected impact was faster access to information, reduced pressure on human service channels, improved availability outside hotline hours and a more user-friendly digital front door for the city administration. The use case also illustrates the role of municipal chatbots in large metropolitan administrations, where the volume and variety of citizen requests make navigation support valuable. Bobbi was best understood as a supplementary digital assistant: useful for standard questions, but dependent on escalation or redirection where individual circumstances required human assessment.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: HoPE - Holistic Personal public Eco-mobility
source_description: HoPE was conceived as a user-centred mobility platform intended to encourage more conscious, convenient and sustainable use of public transport and eco-mobility services. Urban and regional travellers often face fragmented information across transport modes, ticketing systems, payment channels and journey-planning tools, which can make sustainable transport less attractive than private car use. The project therefore aimed to bring together mobility information and service functions in a single platform that could support greener travel choices while improving the user experience. The implementation combined info-mobility, trip planning, ticket reservation, fare calculation and mobile payment functions within a digital platform oriented around individual users. Conceptually, it integrated transport data, journey-planning algorithms, payment services, user-interface design and personalised mobility information to help people compare and access transport options more easily. The expected impact was greater awareness of public transport and eco-mobility, smoother journey planning, better access to multimodal services and increased attractiveness of low-emission travel. By combining information, reservation and payment capabilities, HoPE sought to reduce friction in everyday mobility decisions and create value for both users and transport providers. Its broader contribution lies in demonstrating how digital platforms can support behavioural change towards more sustainable transport systems.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: FLOBOT - Floor Washing Robot for Professional Users
source_description: FLOBOT addressed the difficulty of cleaning very large indoor surfaces in professional environments such as supermarkets, airports, trade fairs, hospitals and industrial or commercial premises. These facilities often require floor washing every day, and sometimes several times during the day, creating repetitive, physically demanding and time-consuming work for cleaning staff. Existing robotic solutions did not meet the standards expected by professional cleaning-service providers, particularly in relation to performance, safety, reliability and usability in busy environments. The project therefore developed and validated a professional robotic scrubber-dryer capable of washing and drying large floor areas. Its implementation combined robotics, autonomous navigation, floor-cleaning hardware, perception systems, safety controls and user interfaces suitable for professional operators. At a conceptual level, the robot needed to map and move through large premises, avoid obstacles, apply brushes and suction effectively, and operate in spaces shared with people and equipment. The expected impact was reduced manual effort, improved cleaning productivity, more consistent service quality and better scalability for cleaning operations across large buildings. By automating repetitive floor-maintenance tasks, FLOBOT could allow cleaning staff to focus on supervision, detailed tasks and service quality. The project also offered business value to cleaning providers by addressing labour intensity and operational efficiency.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: FIRST - A Flexible Interactive Reading Support Tool
source_description: FIRST was developed to improve reading accessibility for people with Autism Spectrum Disorders, who may experience difficulty understanding complex instructions, figurative language, uncommon words, ambiguous phrasing or imprecise documents. The practical problem is that many everyday texts are written in ways that assume strong inferential and contextual reading skills, which can create barriers in education, employment, public services and independent living. The project aimed to give users a tool that could convert standard documents into personalised versions that are easier to understand. Its implementation used language technology to simplify text according to the needs of people with ASD. Conceptually, the system analysed source documents, identified linguistic features that may create comprehension barriers, and generated clearer alternatives through simplification, explanation, rephrasing or adaptation of wording. The expected impact was improved comprehension, greater autonomy, reduced reliance on intermediaries and better access to written information. For educators, carers, service providers and public bodies, such a tool could make communication more inclusive and reduce misunderstandings. By focusing on personalisation rather than one-size-fits-all simplification, FIRST recognised that accessibility depends on individual reading profiles and contexts. Its business and public value lie in making complex documents more usable for a group often underserved by mainstream text technologies.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: DE-ENIGMA (Multi-Modal Human-Robot Interaction for Teaching Social Imagination in Autistic Children)
source_description: DE-ENIGMA focused on the use of robot-based interaction to support social imagination and social communication skills among autistic children. Many children with autism spectrum conditions may find social cues, imaginative interaction and reciprocal communication challenging, while therapists, educators and families need tools that can provide structured, engaging and repeatable support. The project aimed to create and evaluate technology that could help children practise social interaction in a controlled and motivating environment. The implementation used multi-modal human-robot interaction, combining robotic behaviour, sensors, affective computing, speech or gesture processing and adaptive interaction design. At a conceptual level, the robot acted as an interactive teaching partner, recognising child responses and supporting exercises designed to expand social understanding and imaginative engagement. The expected impact was more personalised therapeutic support, increased child engagement, improved consistency of social-skills training and new evidence on the role of robots in autism interventions. By combining robotics with behavioural and educational expertise, DE-ENIGMA sought to support professionals rather than replace them, offering an additional tool for structured learning. Its value lies in creating repeatable, measurable and potentially scalable interaction scenarios for children who may respond positively to predictable robotic partners.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Smart sENsor Devices fOr rehabilitation and Connected health - SENDoc
source_description: SENDoc introduced wearable sensor systems to support rehabilitation, independent living and connected health in ageing communities across remote areas of Northern Ireland and northern Scotland. The operational challenge is that older people in rural and remote settings may have limited access to continuous rehabilitation support, mobility assessment and preventive monitoring, while health and care providers need better information on functional decline, wellbeing and safety. The project therefore aimed to test how wearable technologies could measure mobility, strength, balance, exercise, wellbeing and safety in everyday contexts. Its implementation used smart sensor devices worn by users, collecting physiological or movement-related data that could inform rehabilitation and care decisions. Conceptually, the system combined wearable sensing, connected-health data flows, remote monitoring, user feedback and clinical or community-care interpretation. The expected impact was improved support for independent living, earlier identification of deterioration, more personalised rehabilitation and better continuity of care for older people living far from specialist services. By allowing data to be gathered outside traditional clinical settings, SENDoc could reduce travel burdens, support preventive care and improve service reach. Its broader value lies in demonstrating how connected health tools can strengthen ageing-in-place strategies and make rehabilitation more responsive in underserved rural communities.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Institute for Computer Science and Control
title: ADVANCE - Advanced predictive-analysis-based decision-support engine for logistics
source_description: ADVANCE was designed to help logistics operators make better decisions in transport planning, dispatching and strategic network management. Logistics environments generate large volumes of data on routes, orders, partners, traffic conditions, capacity constraints and delivery performance, yet operational decisions are often made under uncertainty and with incomplete visibility. The project therefore sought to provide a decision-support platform capable of combining the most recent operational information with higher-level intelligence derived from longer-term data analysis. Its implementation used predictive analytics, data mining, machine learning and optimisation techniques, including heuristics, ant colony optimisation and evolutionary algorithms. The platform was intended to analyse massive datasets, including 50 million or more data elements, and to process new information rapidly for real-time or near-real-time decisions. Conceptually, it linked structured logistics data, forecasting models and optimisation routines to support tasks such as local dispatching, deadheading reduction, early detection of missed due dates and partnership planning. The expected impact was improved transport efficiency, more competitive logistics strategies, lower operational waste and better responsiveness to changing conditions. By making the software framework available as open source, the project also aimed to reduce initial investment barriers and encourage smaller logistics actors to exploit predictive decision-support tools.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: PROTEUS (Scalable online machine learning for predictive analytics and real-time visualisation)
source_description: PROTEUS addressed the challenge of analysing very large datasets and continuous data streams in situations where decisions must be made quickly and supported by interpretable visual information. Organisations in sectors such as industry, energy, environment and knowledge-intensive services increasingly need predictive analytics that can operate at scale, but conventional batch-processing methods are not always suitable for fast-changing data. The project therefore aimed to develop ready-to-use scalable online machine-learning algorithms and interactive visualisation techniques for real-time predictive analytics. Its implementation focused on online learning methods, stream-processing architectures and visual analytics tools capable of handling extremely large datasets as they are generated. The developed algorithms and techniques were intended to form a library integrated into an enhanced version of Apache Flink, strengthening the capacity to process, model and visualise high-volume data streams. Conceptually, PROTEUS combined machine learning, distributed computing, real-time analytics and interactive user interfaces so that users could both forecast developments and understand emerging patterns. The expected impact was faster insight generation, more scalable predictive modelling, improved usability of complex analytics and stronger decision support in data-intensive environments. By integrating algorithms with visualisation, the project sought to make real-time predictive analytics more operationally usable rather than only technically feasible.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: CITADEL - Empowering Citizens to TrAnsform European PubLic Administrations
source_description: CITADEL focused on helping public administrations understand why citizens do not always use digital public services and how those services can be redesigned to become more inclusive, efficient and citizen-centred. Good public services are central to quality of life, regional competitiveness and entrepreneurship, but digital uptake may be limited by lack of skills, fear of errors, low trust, service complexity or poor alignment with user needs. The project therefore aimed to provide public authorities with tools, recommendations and methods to identify barriers to use and bring citizens back into digital service channels. Its implementation combined ICT-enabled service analysis, citizen engagement, public-sector transformation methods and evidence-based recommendations. CITADEL created an ecosystem of best practices and tools that allowed administrations to use existing knowledge and new data to shape services around what matters to users. Conceptually, it linked service-design insight, administrative data, stakeholder feedback and co-creation approaches to support better digital public services. The expected impact was improved digital-service adoption, more inclusive access, greater administrative responsiveness and better alignment between public services and citizen expectations. By examining not only technology but also trust, skills and usability, CITADEL treated digital transformation as an organisational and social challenge as much as a technical one.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: ENLARGE - ENergies for Local Administrations: Renovate Governance in Europe
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: ENLARGE examined how public authorities, experts and civil society can work together to design and deliver more effective public policies and services, with a particular focus on sustainable energy. Local administrations often face complex energy-transition challenges that require public acceptance, technical expertise and coordinated action across stakeholders. Traditional top-down policy design may not capture local knowledge or ensure long-term legitimacy, especially when energy measures affect daily life, costs and public-service delivery. The project therefore used intense policy dialogue to analyse existing models of co-design and co-production, drawing lessons on how collaborative governance can improve both sustainable-energy policies and broader public-administration performance. Its implementation relied on comparative analysis, case-study work, deliberative processes and structured engagement between policymakers, experts and civil-society actors. Conceptually, ENLARGE was less about a single digital tool and more about a governance methodology for identifying conditions under which co-production can increase policy quality, efficiency and public value. The expected impact was improved capacity of local administrations to involve stakeholders, stronger evidence on participatory energy governance and better guidance for designing public services that are both effective and legitimate. By focusing on co-design, the project supported administrative innovation in the energy-transition field.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Mobile-Age
source_description: Mobile-Age explored how open government data and mobile technologies could support public services for older people in European cities. Ageing populations create new demands for accessible, relevant and locally grounded services, particularly in relation to social isolation, safe mobility, inclusion and personal health information. Many older residents may also face digital barriers, meaning that services must be designed with them rather than simply delivered to them. The project therefore used a co-creation approach in which older people, public administrations, researchers and community actors worked together on services related to the production and use of open urban data. Its implementation combined mobile applications, open data, participatory design, local service scenarios and user-centred development. The project addressed themes including loneliness, social inclusion, safer and more accessible cities, data curation and personal health information. Conceptually, Mobile-Age linked civic data infrastructures with mobile interfaces and co-designed service models, ensuring that data-driven services responded to real needs in everyday urban life. The expected impact was improved accessibility of public services, stronger inclusion of older citizens in digital innovation, better reuse of open government data and more responsive local service delivery. By involving older people directly, the project strengthened both usability and democratic legitimacy.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: OpenGovIntelligence (Fostering Innovation and Creativity in EU through Pub Administration Modernization)
source_description: OpenGovIntelligence sought to modernise public administrations by using Linked Open Statistical Data to co-produce innovative public services with citizens, businesses and public-sector actors. Public administrations hold substantial statistical information, but its value is often limited by fragmented formats, weak interoperability and insufficient mechanisms for external reuse. The project therefore focused on new processes, policies and tools that would enable society and businesses to participate actively in data sharing and service co-production. Its implementation used Linked Open Statistical Data technologies and ran pilot studies in six countries, testing how structured, interoperable data could support new public-service models. Conceptually, the project combined linked data, semantic technologies, statistical datasets, co-creation methods and public-administration process redesign. It followed an iterative approach, using development and evaluation cycles to refine the OpenGovIntelligence framework and associated tools. The expected impact was greater transparency, more innovative public services, improved reuse of official statistics and stronger collaboration between administrations and external stakeholders. By treating data as a shared resource for service design, the project aimed to stimulate innovation and creativity while strengthening evidence-based administration.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: RECAP - Reliable Capacity Provisioning and Enhanced Remediation for Distributed Cloud Applications
source_description: RECAP supported the implementation of the Common Agricultural Policy by developing personalised public services for farmers, agricultural consultants and administrations responsible for monitoring compliance. CAP rules create complex obligations, particularly around cross-compliance, and public authorities need efficient ways to monitor whether requirements are being met across diverse agricultural contexts. Farmers and consultants also benefit from clearer, more transparent information on obligations and potential breaches. The project implemented a cloud-based Software-as-a-Service platform using open Earth Observation data, user-generated information and geospatial data to support compliance monitoring. Conceptually, the system extracted relevant features from satellite and other open data, correlated them with information available to public organisations and modelled potential breaches of CAP requirements. This enabled authorities and inspectors to focus attention on likely non-compliance while giving users more personalised support. The expected impact was more efficient administrative control, lower monitoring burden, greater transparency for farmers and better targeting of inspections. By combining Earth Observation with cloud services and user-generated data, RECAP demonstrated how agricultural public services can shift from document-heavy compliance checks towards more continuous, data-supported monitoring.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: SIMPATICO - Platform for PS - Italian Usecase
source_description: SIMPATICO was developed to improve the way citizens and companies interact with online public services, addressing a common weakness in digital administration: many services are standardised replicas of offline procedures, designed mainly around internal organisational logic rather than the needs, language and behaviour of users. In the Italian use case, the Municipality of Trento provided a public-service context in which administrative procedures could be simplified and adapted through continuous feedback. The objective was to make digital services easier to understand, reduce the distance between users and administrations, and identify why online procedures remain difficult or underused. The implementation combined language-processing technologies, machine-learning techniques and community contributions. Public administrations supplied formal knowledge about procedures, while citizens, companies, civil servants and professionals contributed questions, doubts, explanations and improvement suggestions. At a conceptual level, the platform linked service interfaces, text simplification, workflow guidance, user feedback and collaborative knowledge creation, allowing interactions to be progressively refined. The expected impact was improved usability of online services, fewer errors during administrative procedures, better citizen satisfaction and stronger capacity for administrations to learn from recurring difficulties. By combining institutional knowledge with bottom-up input, SIMPATICO treated service improvement as a continuous, participatory process rather than a one-off redesign of digital forms.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Empirica Gesellschaft für Kommunikations- & Technologieforschung mbH.
title: WeGovNow: Collective and participative approaches for addressing local policy challenges
source_description: WeGovNow explored how local public services and policy challenges could be addressed through collaborative digital participation, treating citizens as partners in public-service delivery rather than passive users or customers. Local authorities often need to respond to issues such as neighbourhood improvement, service quality, environmental concerns or community planning, but conventional consultation channels can be fragmented, episodic and disconnected from day-to-day civic action. The project therefore aimed to provide public administrations, citizens, civil-society organisations and local businesses with digital tools for co-production, collective proposition development and shared problem-solving. Its implementation integrated emerging civic technologies into a pilot platform tested under day-to-day conditions in the London Borough of Southwark, the City of Turin and San Donà di Piave. Conceptually, the platform combined participatory mapping, issue reporting, discussion, collective proposal development and community coordination functions. The project also examined legal, ethical and organisational conditions to ensure democratic legitimacy and practical exploitability. The expected impact was stronger citizen engagement, more responsive local services and improved evidence on how digital co-production works in real administrative contexts. During the final project year, 9,976 pilot user accounts were registered across the three pilot municipalities, showing meaningful uptake in real-life settings.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: REBUILD - ICT toolbox providing support to both migrants and refugees
source_description: REBUILD aimed to improve how migrants and refugees access services in Europe while helping local service providers manage integration support more effectively. The operational challenge was two-sided: newcomers often face fragmented information, language barriers, unfamiliar administrative systems and difficulties identifying relevant opportunities, while public authorities and support organisations need better tools to understand needs, coordinate services and evaluate impact. The project adopted a user-centred and participatory design approach, involving migrants, refugees and service providers from the early stages so that ethical, cultural and practical requirements could shape the solution. Its implementation developed an ICT toolbox using user profiling, skills-and-needs matching, chatbot functions and accessible service interfaces. Conceptually, the ecosystem connected information about individuals’ needs, skills and preferences with local service offers, guidance pathways and administrative workflows. It also included mechanisms to monitor and validate socio-economic impact. The expected value was more personalised support, easier access to services, improved communication between users and administrations, and better evidence for integration policies. By combining digital tools with co-design, REBUILD sought to avoid imposing a generic integration platform and instead build services around the lived experience of migrants and refugees and the operational realities of local providers.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: NADINE - platform to promote migrant inclusion
source_description: NADINE was designed to support migrant inclusion by improving the way public authorities and guidance professionals understand skills, needs and available services. Migration brings significant human capital to Europe, yet integration systems may struggle to match people’s abilities, career ambitions, educational requirements and social or cultural needs with real opportunities in host societies. The project therefore aimed to build a platform that could support employability, career guidance and service matching on the basis of richer evidence about both migrants and local environments. Its implementation used open data, large-scale data repositories and analytical tools to create two main information banks: one concerning host societies and services, and another concerning migrants’ profiles, needs and skills. As users interacted with the platform, further data could be collected to refine the system and improve recommendations. Conceptually, NADINE combined skills assessment, labour-market intelligence, local-service mapping, guidance tools and personalised support interfaces. The expected impact was more tailored assistance for migrants, better use of skills, improved decision support for professionals and stronger alignment between integration services and actual needs. By linking social, educational, cultural and employment dimensions, NADINE approached inclusion as a multidimensional process rather than only a labour-market matching exercise.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: WELCOME(Multiple Intelligent Conversation Agent Services for Reception, Management and Integration)
source_description: WELCOME focused on supporting the reception and integration of third-country nationals, migrants and refugees through personalised digital assistance for both newcomers and public administrations. Reception and integration processes often involve complex registration steps, orientation needs, language barriers, civic education, access to local services and social inclusion challenges, while administrations must provide guidance across diverse profiles and contexts. The project aimed to create a psychologically and socially competent support environment that could help users navigate these processes in a more accessible and personalised way. Its implementation developed intelligent multilingual conversational agents, including embodied assistants, designed for contexts such as registration, orientation, language learning, civic education and community integration. The system used personalisation techniques so that agent behaviour could adapt to the user’s profile and situation, and it also explored immersive virtual and augmented reality technologies to make interaction more realistic and engaging. Conceptually, WELCOME combined conversational interfaces, multilingual processing, user profiling, interaction adaptation and immersive service design. The expected impact was better access to integration guidance, reduced pressure on frontline administrations, more consistent information provision and improved user experience for migrants and refugees. The services were validated through pilot use cases in Catalonia, Spain, Germany and Greece.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Department of Public Expenditure and Reform
title: DPER Robotic Process Automation (RPA) Pilot
source_description: The DPER Robotic Process Automation pilot examined whether routine, stable and fully computer-based administrative processes in Irish central government could be automated to improve efficiency and service delivery. Public bodies often manage high-volume tasks that require staff to copy, check or transfer information between digital systems, even when the rules are clear and human judgement is limited. In 2017, the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform coordinated a pilot in which four government departments selected suitable processes to test the potential of robotic process automation. The implementation used software robots to operate existing applications at user-interface level, automating labour-intensive, rules-based tasks without requiring wholesale replacement of legacy systems. Conceptually, RPA was applied as a non-invasive automation layer that could log into systems, follow predefined steps, transfer data, validate entries and generate outputs consistently. The expected impact was improved accuracy, fewer manual errors, faster processing and the release of staff time for higher-value work. The pilot also helped the Irish public service understand which process characteristics make automation feasible and what governance, procurement and implementation arrangements would be needed for wider adoption. A later government RPA framework indicates that the pilot contributed to a broader national approach to automation services.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Housing Assistance Payment Shared Service Centre
title: Housing Assistance Payment Robotics Pilot
source_description: The Housing Assistance Payment Robotics Pilot addressed the operational pressure faced by the HAP Shared Service Centre, operated by Limerick City and County Council on behalf of the local government sector. The centre manages very large payment and tenancy volumes, including more than 47,000 tenancies, 27,000 landlords, over €400 million in payments and more than €100 million in rent collection, with projected growth to 80,000 tenancies, 55,000 landlords and €600 million in payments by 2021. These volumes create substantial administrative workload and a strong incentive to identify processes that can be automated safely. In 2018, Agilisys carried out a proof-of-concept pilot examining three micro-processes within the centre. The implementation used robotic process automation to test whether repeatable, rule-based activities could be executed by software robots across existing business systems. Conceptually, the pilot assessed process suitability, automation feasibility, savings potential and opportunities for wider business-system integration. The results demonstrated that efficiencies and savings could be achieved, and the subsequent business case suggested that replacing 10 complex processes with RPA could generate considerable savings while improving services for tenants, landlords and administrative stakeholders. The use case therefore provided a practical basis for identifying further immediate automation opportunities within the HAP SSC.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Artificial intelligence finds disease-related genes
source_description: This use case addresses a central challenge in biomedical research: disease mechanisms are often distributed across large numbers of interacting genes, making it difficult for researchers to identify meaningful patterns in high-dimensional gene-expression data. Scientists at Linköping University led a study exploring how these complex datasets could be used to discover groups of genes associated with disease and, in the longer term, support more precise diagnosis and treatment. The objective was not to replace biological interpretation, but to give researchers a stronger exploratory method for finding structures that may otherwise remain hidden in very large molecular datasets. The implementation used an artificial neural network trained on extensive gene-expression information, allowing the system to learn patterns without relying only on predefined disease categories or manually selected markers. At a conceptual level, the model processed expression profiles, detected relationships between genes and organised them into groups that could reveal disease-relevant biological signals. The expected impact is improved discovery of candidate genes, better understanding of disease pathways and stronger foundations for precision medicine and individualised treatment. Although the work remains research-oriented, its value lies in showing how neural-network methods can support biomedical knowledge discovery by extracting interpretable signals from datasets that exceed the capacity of conventional manual analysis.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Estonia to give citizens Alexa-like access to public services
source_description: Digital public services can still be difficult to use when citizens must navigate multiple portals, forms and institutional websites to complete a life event or obtain an answer. Estonia’s Bürokratt initiative aims to create a network of public-sector virtual assistants that allow people to interact with the state in natural language. The operational problem is that even highly digital government systems can remain fragmented from the user’s perspective, especially when a request requires cooperation between different agencies. The implementation concept connects chatbots across public-sector institutions into a shared assistant network. At a conceptual level, a citizen can ask a question or request a service through a conversational interface, while the system identifies the relevant institution, retrieves information and, where possible, supports service routing or administrative action. The longer-term vision is for personalised AI agents to cooperate across domains and help citizens solve problems without navigating complex portals or repeating information. The expected impact is simpler access to public services, better customer support, reduced administrative friction and more human-centred digital government. The initiative is significant because it moves beyond isolated chatbots towards an interoperable assistant layer for the public sector, building on Estonia’s wider digital-state infrastructure.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Artificial intelligence "Wuhan model"" at the biomedical campus in Rome"
source_description: During the early COVID-19 emergency, hospitals needed rapid tools to support diagnosis and monitoring of pneumonia from lung imaging, especially when clinical pressure was high and radiology teams faced urgent triage demands. Campus Bio-Medico University Hospital in Rome acquired an imaging system originally used in Wuhan to assist with early diagnosis and monitoring of COVID-19 pneumonia. The objective was to help radiologists interpret lung CT scans more quickly and consistently, while supporting clinical assessment rather than replacing specialist judgement. The implementation used an artificial-intelligence system trained to analyse chest CT images and identify patterns associated with COVID-19 pneumonia. Public reporting described a response reliability of 98.5% in around 20 seconds, and the system was tested successfully on anonymised patients by radiologists at the Rome hospital. At a conceptual level, the software processes CT image data, identifies relevant lung abnormalities and provides a rapid diagnostic support output for clinicians. The expected impact was faster radiological triage, improved monitoring of disease progression and better allocation of clinical resources during pandemic peaks. Its longer-term significance lies in demonstrating how emergency deployment of image-analysis systems can support hospital workflows, although public sources describe this primarily as a COVID-era installation and test rather than an enduring, general diagnostic platform.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Against the infection comes Minerva, a "robot"" invented by an engineer from Noci (IT)"
source_description: The early pandemic period generated intense demand for reliable information, while misinformation and rapidly changing rules made it difficult for citizens to know which guidance to follow. Minerva was created as a chatbot intended to share information about coronavirus using data drawn from the Italian Ministry of Health website. The objective was to provide a simple digital assistant that could answer recurring questions and direct users towards official public-health information. Although described publicly as a “robot”, the use case was essentially a conversational information service rather than a physical robot or clinical diagnostic tool. The implementation relied on an automated interface that processed user queries and returned relevant content based on official sources. At a conceptual level, the system acted as a bridge between citizens and institutional information, reducing the need to search manually through government webpages and helping standardise the messages received by users. Its expected impact was faster access to trusted information, improved public awareness and reduced confusion during a period of high uncertainty. The case was connected to a specific emergency context and should be interpreted as a lightweight crisis-communication tool rather than a long-term health-service platform. Its value lay in rapid deployment, official-source orientation and accessibility for users seeking immediate guidance.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Italian National Institute for Insurance against Accidents at Work (INAIL)
title: E-health 4.0, chatbots at the service of diagnostic units
source_description: Healthcare facilities faced extraordinary pressure during the COVID-19 emergency, especially where citizens needed preliminary symptom guidance and hospitals had to manage information demand at scale. Through collaboration between Microsoft and INAIL, Italian healthcare organisations were able to use the Healthcare Bot solution free of charge to create digital assistants for self-assessment of coronavirus symptoms. The initiative supported facilities such as Spallanzani, San Giovanni Addolorata Hospital and ASL Napoli 3 Sud, giving them a rapid way to deploy online symptom-checking and orientation tools. The implementation used a healthcare chatbot configured for COVID-19 self-assessment, allowing users to answer questions about symptoms and receive guidance through the healthcare provider’s portal. At a conceptual level, the service translated triage and public-health information into a conversational workflow, supporting preliminary risk orientation and directing users towards appropriate next steps. Its expected impact was reduced pressure on phone lines and diagnostic units, faster information access for citizens, and more consistent communication from healthcare organisations. The service did not replace medical evaluation; it provided a first layer of digital interaction at a time when health systems needed to reserve human capacity for urgent or complex cases.
