title: AI for anonymisation of court decisions in Croatia
source_description: Publishing court decisions is essential for transparency, legal certainty and consistency of case law, but it requires strong safeguards for personal data and confidential information. Croatia’s AI anonymisation initiative addresses this problem by preparing judicial decisions for online publication while protecting the identities of parties and other individuals mentioned in the text. The operational challenge is that courts produce large volumes of decisions, and manual anonymisation can be slow, inconsistent and resource-intensive. The project therefore uses AI-powered tools to support automatic pre-anonymisation, helping identify personal names, addresses and other sensitive elements before decisions are reviewed and published. At a conceptual level, the system combines document analysis, named-entity recognition, anonymisation rules, search functionality and publication workflows. Its purpose is not only to remove personal data, but also to preserve the legal meaning of the decision so that judges, lawyers, researchers, businesses and citizens can search and understand case law. The expected impact is greater transparency, faster publication of judgments, improved consistency in anonymisation and stronger public access to judicial information. The initiative also sits within a wider digital-justice agenda, including e-communication between courts, prosecutors, litigants and other justice stakeholders.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Judicial Anonymisation Tool
source_description: Courts must publish judicial decisions to ensure transparency and legal certainty, while strictly complying with personal data protection requirements. Manual anonymisation of court rulings is time-consuming, resource-intensive and prone to inconsistencies, particularly given the volume and complexity of decisions issued by public courts. Stakeholders include judicial authorities, court clerks, data protection officers, legal professionals and citizens accessing published rulings. The objective of this use case is to streamline and standardise the anonymisation process prior to publication, ensuring legal compliance while preserving the substantive content and readability of decisions. The solution combines rule-based expert systems with natural language processing techniques to automatically detect and classify personal data elements such as names, addresses and identifiers within judicial texts. Predefined legal rules guide masking, redaction or pseudonymisation, and the tool integrates with court document management and publication platforms to support human validation workflows. Expected impacts include significant reductions in manual workload, faster publication cycles, improved consistency in anonymisation practices and strengthened compliance with data protection legislation, thereby enhancing trust in digital justice services.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI to anonymise judicial courts in Denmark
source_description: Judicial transparency depends on publishing court judgments in a form that is accessible to the public, while privacy law requires that parties and other individuals are protected from unnecessary identification. Denmark’s court judgment anonymisation project supports publication of decisions in Domsdatabasen, the Danish courts’ judgment database, by using machine learning to pseudonymise judgments before they are made public. The operational problem is that judgments contain names, pronouns, descriptions, contextual details and other linguistic elements that can reveal identity directly or indirectly. The implementation uses a machine-learning system to pre-screen documents and suggest text passages that may need anonymisation or pseudonymisation. At a conceptual level, the solution combines named-entity recognition, privacy-risk detection, text marking and human quality control. Each judgment is reviewed by human participants after the software has identified potentially sensitive content, creating a hybrid workflow in which AI accelerates the process but does not make publication decisions alone. The expected impact is faster preparation of judgments, more consistent protection of personal data, broader access to case law and better public understanding of judicial practice. The system is particularly important because anonymisation quality affects both privacy and the usefulness of judgments for legal analysis.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI to plan meeting dates, times and locations for prosecutors
source_description: Court and prosecution services depend on effective scheduling, because hearings, meetings and procedural events must bring together busy professionals, appropriate locations and case-specific priorities. Denmark’s meeting-planning AI use case focused on allocating meeting dates, times and locations for prosecutors according to profile and logistical constraints. The administrative problem is that meeting organisation can consume staff time, generate inefficient schedules and make it difficult to distinguish between urgent or high-priority meetings and less critical coordination tasks. The implementation concept uses profile-based allocation, prioritisation and scheduling logic to reduce manual planning effort. At a conceptual level, the system would combine information about prosecutors’ roles, calendars, availability, meeting importance, location constraints and procedural requirements. It could then propose suitable meeting slots and venues, helping administrative staff organise work more efficiently. The expected impact is reduced clerical burden, fewer scheduling conflicts, better use of court and prosecution resources, and more consistent prioritisation of important meetings. The use case is administrative rather than adjudicative: it does not assess legal merits or influence prosecutorial decisions, but supports the logistics around justice work. This distinction is important because automation in scheduling can improve efficiency while leaving professional judgement and procedural responsibility with human officials.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Automatic anonymisation and content description of documents containing personal data
source_description: Judicial and administrative documents contain information that is valuable for transparency, research and decision-making, but wider electronic availability is constrained by the need to protect personal data. In Finland, the Ministry of Justice led the Anoppi project to address this challenge for court decisions and other official decisions issued by public authorities. Manual anonymisation can be slow, costly and inconsistent, particularly when large collections of documents must be prepared for publication, research use or legal-information services. The objective was therefore to provide tools that help authorities make documents more accessible while preserving privacy and legal safeguards. The implementation uses language-technology and semantic-computing methods to support two functions: automatic or semi-automatic anonymisation and pseudonymisation of personal data, and content description or annotation of legal documents. At a conceptual level, the system applies natural language processing, named-entity recognition, semantic annotation and document-structuring techniques to identify sensitive elements and generate metadata that improves searchability and reuse. The expected impact is faster document processing, broader access to legal information, improved support for research and more efficient publication workflows. By reducing the burden on courts and authorities, Anoppi strengthens digital justice services while maintaining data-protection requirements. It also supports the wider development of open, anonymised legal data for intelligent legal applications and the Semantic Finlex environment.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Robot process automation (RPA) in Finnish judicial system
source_description: Judicial administrations handle many repetitive financial and register-based tasks that require accuracy but do not necessarily require complex human judgement. Finland’s Ministry of Justice applied robotic process automation in the enforcement-of-fines area to improve administrative efficiency and reduce manual handling. The operational problem concerns recurring enquiries, overpayment checks and payment allocation tasks linked to fines and other financial sanctions. The implementation uses software robots to carry out structured actions such as sending enquiries by email to banks and the Finnish Population Centre, reviewing data to identify erroneous overpayments and supporting the return or allocation of payments to citizens. At a conceptual level, RPA interacts with existing administrative systems by following predefined rules, retrieving information, comparing records, triggering messages and flagging cases that require human attention. The expected impact is faster processing, fewer manual errors, better handling of overpayments, more consistent financial administration and reduced staff time spent on routine clerical activity. The use case shows how justice-system digitalisation is not limited to courtrooms or judicial decisions: substantial value can come from automating back-office processes that support the enforcement and correction of financial sanctions.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: DataJust
source_description: Compensation for bodily injury is a legally sensitive field because victims, parties, lawyers and judges need reliable information on comparable cases while preserving the independence and discretion of judicial decision-making. In France, the Ministry of Justice launched DataJust to explore whether past civil and administrative liability decisions could support a more consistent understanding of compensation levels. The project aimed to carry out retrospective and prospective evaluations of public policies, develop an indicative framework for bodily-injury compensation, inform parties during amicable settlement discussions and provide documentation for judges ruling on damages claims. The implementation was authorised by Decree No. 2020-356 of 27 March 2020, following CNIL review, and involved automated processing of personal data from relevant judicial decisions. At a conceptual level, the system was intended to extract compensation-related information, structure legal and factual variables, conduct statistical analysis and generate decision-support or information outputs. The expected value was greater transparency for parties, better-informed settlement negotiations and more documented policy evaluation in civil liability. However, the initiative raised concerns because it involved sensitive personal and judicial data and could influence perceptions of standardisation in damages assessment. The project ultimately did not reach operational deployment, showing the difficulty of applying algorithmic tools in domains where individual harm, legal nuance and institutional legitimacy are closely intertwined.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Commission for information technology in the judiciary
title: Land register analysis component in the project Development of a federal database land register
source_description: Digitising land-register information requires converting legally important legacy documents into structured, accurate and reusable data without weakening the certainty attached to property records. In Germany, this project component focused on automating the analysis of existing PDF files containing land-register information so that their contents could be fragmented, interpreted and assigned to appropriate database fields. The operational problem is that land-register material may exist in document formats that are difficult to search, integrate or process electronically, creating manual workload for justice administrations and limiting interoperability between systems. The objective was to support the development of a federal land-register database by transforming unstructured or semi-structured documents into structured records. The implementation is based on expert systems and rule-based techniques, reflecting the formalised structure of land-register documents and the need for deterministic interpretation rather than open-ended prediction. At a conceptual level, the tool analyses document content and layout, separates relevant sections, recognises values according to predefined rules and maps them into corresponding database fields. The expected impact is reduced manual transcription, improved consistency of digitised records, faster migration of legacy information and stronger support for electronic workflows involving courts, land-registry authorities, notaries and other authorised users. The case demonstrates that rule-based automation remains valuable where legal formats are stable and accuracy requirements are high.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Application of AI for early recognition of criminal offences that relate to hate crime
source_description: Online hate crime creates a difficult enforcement problem because potentially criminal content circulates at high volume, changes quickly and may be embedded in ambiguous linguistic, social or political contexts. In Germany, the Federal Criminal Police Office participated in a research project examining how police organisations could use automated support to detect, prevent and prosecute hate crime while respecting legal, ethical and organisational constraints. The objective was not only to classify online statements, but to define the conditions under which such tools could be responsibly adopted by law-enforcement bodies. The implementation investigated technical approaches for classifying hate speech according to criminal-law categories, hate-speech phenomena and thematic content. At a conceptual level, the project combined natural language processing, supervised classification, domain-specific annotation, organisational analysis and legal-ethical assessment. This holistic design was intended to ensure that any prototype would be evaluated not only for technical accuracy, but also for its suitability within police workflows and fundamental-rights safeguards. The expected impact was faster identification of potentially criminal hate messages, better prioritisation of police review, and stronger evidence on how automated tools can support, rather than replace, human legal judgement. FRA records the output as reports and a technical prototype to be evaluated by police, while later project reporting indicates that a tool recognising criminal hate messages from social media posts was developed through KISTRA.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Future criminal court rooms
source_description: Criminal proceedings increasingly rely on digital evidence, remote participation, audio-visual material and complex case records, while many courtrooms remain organised around paper-based or manually documented hearings. In North Rhine-Westphalia, the Central Cybercrime Department developed a pilot project aimed at modernising criminal courtrooms through technologies that could reduce the time and effort required to record, review and present proceedings. The objective was to create a courtroom environment in which hearings could be videotaped, speech could be converted into written transcripts, and participants could access both the transcription and embedded audio material. The implementation concept combined audio recording, video recording, speech-to-text recognition and digital document production inside the courtroom workflow. A further element under consideration was the 3D projection of crime scenes, which could support the presentation of spatially complex evidence in cybercrime or other criminal cases. At a conceptual level, the system would connect hearing capture, automated transcription, evidentiary presentation and case-file integration, allowing judges, prosecutors, lawyers and other authorised participants to work with richer digital records. The expected impact was reduced administrative effort, faster review of hearings, more accurate documentation and broader modernisation of criminal justice infrastructure. The available European Commission study records the project as a pilot within the wider mapping of innovative technologies in justice, but does not confirm full operational roll-out.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Speech recognition and transcription
source_description: Court proceedings generate spoken information that must be transformed into written minutes, decisions and procedural records, but manual transcription can be time-consuming and places a heavy burden on clerical staff. Hungary’s National Office for the Judiciary examined the use of speech-recognition and transcription software in courts to accelerate the production of written judicial documents. The operational challenge is that hearings and procedural events contain substantial spoken content, and delays in putting decisions or minutes into writing can affect court efficiency. The implementation applies automatic speech recognition to convert audio from proceedings into text, creating a draft transcript or written basis for further review. At a conceptual level, the system combines audio capture, speech-to-text processing, language modelling, transcription correction and integration into court workflows. It is intended to assist court staff rather than replace the official validation of minutes or decisions. The expected impact is reduced transcription time, better compliance with procedural deadlines, more efficient use of clerical capacity and faster availability of written records. For courts, the quality of such tools depends heavily on legal vocabulary, acoustic conditions, speaker variation and the ability to correct outputs reliably. The use case therefore illustrates both the potential and the implementation challenges of applying speech technology to judicial administration.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR)
source_description: Road-policing and law-enforcement operations often require rapid identification of vehicles without manual reading or recording of registration plates. Ireland’s Automatic Number Plate Recognition use case concerns deployment of ANPR technology by justice and policing authorities to support traffic and law-enforcement operations. The operational problem is that officers may need to identify vehicles of interest, verify registration information or process large numbers of passing vehicles quickly and accurately. The implementation uses optical character recognition, later capable of being augmented by artificial-intelligence techniques, to read and record vehicle registration plates automatically from camera feeds. At a conceptual level, the system captures an image of a vehicle plate, converts it into text, compares it with relevant records or alert lists, and produces information for policing or administrative follow-up. The expected impact is faster identification of vehicles, more efficient enforcement, reduced manual input, and stronger operational capacity in roads policing. The technology also raises privacy and governance questions because vehicle movements can reveal sensitive information about individuals’ behaviour. For that reason, legal authorisation, retention rules, access controls and oversight are important elements of responsible deployment. The tool should be understood as an investigative and traffic-management support capability rather than an autonomous sanctioning system.

title: Evaluate the potential of facial matching technologies as an aid to the intelligence gathering process
source_description: Law-enforcement and justice authorities face recurring challenges in identifying persons of interest, comparing image material and supporting intelligence processes, but facial-matching technologies raise significant questions about accuracy, proportionality, bias and fundamental rights. In Ireland, the Department of Justice and Equality developed a 2019 project to evaluate whether facial matching could assist intelligence gathering as part of a broader European mapping of innovative technologies in justice. The objective was exploratory: to assess potential use rather than to present a fully deployed policing system. The implementation concerned facial-matching technologies, which compare facial images to identify possible similarities or candidate matches. At a conceptual level, such a tool would require image inputs, biometric feature extraction, similarity scoring, human review and governance controls to ensure that any result remains investigative support rather than automatic identification or evidentiary determination. The expected value would be faster screening of image material, better support for intelligence workflows and improved prioritisation where large visual datasets are involved. However, the use case also sits in a high-risk area, because biometric matching in justice and policing contexts requires a clear legal basis, strict necessity and proportionality assessment, data-protection safeguards and transparency. The European Commission study records the Irish project as an evaluation initiative, and I found no evidence that it progressed to full operational deployment.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Predictive justice - a database to provide predictable guidelines and timing in particular areas
source_description: Judicial users, lawyers and citizens often need to understand how similar cases have been decided and how long proceedings may take, especially in areas where case-law orientation can affect litigation strategy and settlement decisions. In Brescia, the Court of Appeal developed a predictive justice initiative to organise selected decisions from the Brescia Court of Appeal and Ordinary Court into a navigable database. The objective was to provide predictable guidelines, relevant precedents and procedural orientation in particular legal areas, while supporting legal professionals rather than automating judicial decisions. The implementation uses a structured jurisprudence database supported by natural language processing and rule-based or expert-system logic. At a conceptual level, users choose a legal area and follow a guided path that progressively identifies the judicial situation most similar to their own issue, using essential linguistic and graphical presentation to make the case-law material easier to consult. The platform focuses on legal similarity, orientation and knowledge access rather than on generating binding outcomes. The expected impact is improved transparency of local case-law, faster retrieval of relevant decisions, better preparation by lawyers and parties, and greater consistency in understanding judicial tendencies. Current online material shows that the Brescia predictive justice platform remains publicly accessible and presents selected decisions grouped by thematic areas, notably labour and business law.

title: ITA.CA (Italian Case-Law On Private Antitrust Enforcement )
source_description: Private antitrust enforcement depends on access to specialised case law, but judgments in this field can be difficult to locate, compare and analyse across courts. ITA.CA was developed to collect and systematise Italian case law on private enforcement of competition law, initially around the Milan courts and later with broader contributions. The operational problem is that practitioners, judges, scholars and public stakeholders need a coherent view of decisions relating to damages actions, competition infringements and related civil litigation. The implementation uses a structured online database hosted by the Eurojus scientific journal, collecting judgments and organising them so that users can search and analyse relevant material. At a conceptual level, the system combines legal information retrieval, classification, expert curation and rule-based structuring of case-law content. It is not an autonomous legal decision-maker; rather, it supports legal knowledge management by making decisions easier to find and compare. The expected impact is improved legal transparency, better access to antitrust jurisprudence, stronger doctrinal analysis and more consistent understanding of private enforcement across Italy. The case is relevant to digital justice because curated and searchable databases are a foundation for more advanced legal analytics, even when the underlying technology is primarily rule-based or expert-system oriented.

title: Voice recognition in court administration
source_description: Court and prosecution services generate large volumes of spoken material, including hearings, interviews, procedural acts and internal administrative communication. Latvia’s voice-recognition use case for the Prosecutor’s Office applied AI-based speech technology to support court-administration or prosecution-office workflows. The operational problem is that transcription and document preparation can be labour-intensive, especially where staff must convert spoken material into structured written records. The implementation uses voice-recognition technology to transform speech into text, reducing the need for purely manual typing and helping legal-administrative staff prepare records more efficiently. At a conceptual level, the tool combines audio capture, automatic speech recognition, language processing and human correction or validation. Its expected impact is faster production of written records, reduced clerical burden, more efficient use of prosecution staff and better standardisation of documentation. In justice settings, such systems must handle legal vocabulary, speaker variation, Latvian-language recognition requirements and confidentiality constraints. Human review remains essential, because transcript errors can have procedural consequences. The use case should therefore be understood as an administrative support tool: it can improve efficiency in preparing and managing documents, but it does not replace prosecutorial judgement or court decision-making.

title: Just - virtual assistant of the State Unitary Computerized Land Book
source_description: Land-register services can be difficult for citizens and professionals to navigate because users must understand property identifiers, cadastral information, service categories and procedural steps. Latvia’s Court Administration introduced the virtual assistant Justs into the Land Register portal to help users find their way around the services of the State Unified Computerised Land Book. The objective was to provide a conversational guidance layer for people seeking land-register information or digital services. The implementation uses a virtual assistant on the land-register portal, allowing users to ask questions or obtain orientation without relying only on static navigation menus. At a conceptual level, the assistant maps user questions to service information, helps identify relevant procedures and supports navigation through the portal. Its expected impact is easier access to property-information services, fewer routine support enquiries, better digital self-service and improved user experience for citizens, businesses and legal professionals. Because land-register data are legally significant, the assistant’s role is informational: it supports navigation and service access, while formal registry records, rights and procedural acts remain governed by official systems and staff. The case is a useful example of conversational support in a specialised justice-administration domain where users may not know the correct terminology or route to obtain information.

title: Automatic Ship Classification from Optical Aerial Images with Convolutional Neural Networks
source_description: Maritime surveillance, coastal monitoring and aerial reconnaissance generate large volumes of visible-spectrum imagery in which ships or small unidentified floating objects may be difficult to identify quickly and consistently. Traditional approaches to ship detection have often relied on manually designed image-processing features, followed by conventional supervised classifiers, which can be sensitive to changing image conditions and may not capture complex visual patterns. Researchers at the University of Alicante addressed this challenge by developing a method to determine whether an optical aerial image contains a ship. The implementation used a convolutional neural network architecture adapted to visible-spectrum aerial imagery. At a conceptual level, the model extracted neural visual codes from images and combined them with a k-nearest neighbour method to improve classification performance. This approach moved feature extraction away from manually engineered descriptors and towards representations learned from image data. The expected impact is faster and more accurate screening of aerial image collections, reduced manual inspection effort and stronger support for maritime monitoring applications such as traffic surveillance, search and rescue, environmental control or security tasks. The work is research-oriented, but it demonstrates how deep-learning methods can improve remote-sensing image interpretation when the operational question is binary and clearly framed: whether a ship is present or absent in the observed scene.

organization: EWZ - Service Division of the Department of Public Utilities and Transport of the City of Zurich
title: LoRaWAN - The IoT network for Zurich
source_description: Chronic-disease care requires continuity across hospitals, community services, clinicians, patients and caregivers, especially where repeated outpatient visits or avoidable hospitalisations can reduce quality of life and increase pressure on health systems. COReHealth was developed in Puglia as a regional telemedicine operations centre for chronic diseases and clinical networks, with a particular role in turning the Apulian Oncological Network into a digitally enabled care ecosystem. The operational problem is that patients with chronic conditions often need monitoring, therapeutic adherence support, clinical follow-up and timely intervention without necessarily being physically present in hospital. The implementation provides a telemedicine platform through which patients can be cared for from home, send measurements, monitor their therapeutic plan, receive support for self-management and access remote-care services. At a conceptual level, the system connects patients, clinical networks and regional operational coordination through digital tools, enabling data collection, monitoring, communication and escalation where intervention is needed. The expected impact is reduced hospitalisation, fewer outpatient visits, better continuity of care, improved patient comfort and more proactive disease management. COReHealth is also significant because it positions telemedicine as a regional operating model rather than a single disease-specific application, creating infrastructure that can support chronic-care pathways and clinical networks across multiple territories.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Sen4Weeds: automatic detection in-field weeds
source_description: Farmers need timely and reliable information on weed pressure, because uncontrolled weeds reduce yields, increase inspection workload and often lead to broad herbicide use even when infestation is spatially uneven. Sen4Weeds was developed within AI4Copernicus to create an automated system for detecting and mapping weed patches at large scale, using Earth-observation data rather than relying only on field scouting. The objective is to support earlier, more targeted interventions that improve productivity while reducing environmental impact and input costs. The implementation combines high-resolution and super-resolved Sentinel-2 imagery, automated field delineation, weed classification and AI-based spectral unmixing of multi-spectral satellite data. At a conceptual level, the system identifies field boundaries, enhances satellite-image detail, detects spectral patterns associated with weeds and produces maps showing where weed pressure is likely to be concentrated. These outputs can then help farmers, advisers or agri-tech platforms decide where treatment is needed. The expected impact is more efficient crop monitoring, reduced manual inspection, lower herbicide use and improved scalability across different crops, weed species and regions. By linking Copernicus data with machine-learning models, Sen4Weeds demonstrates how satellite-based precision agriculture can move from general vegetation monitoring towards actionable, within-field weed-management intelligence.

title: Scaviho: scalable vegetation index and harvesting forecaster
source_description: Precision agriculture already uses NDVI widely to monitor crop condition, but intermediate NDVI values during the growth stage can be difficult for farmers to interpret despite containing important information on crop development. In Spain, Scaviho was developed to make vegetation-index information more actionable for vineyards and other agricultural contexts, helping users assess growth evolution, anticipate hidden problems and forecast harvesting dates. The operational problem is not the absence of satellite data, but the difficulty of translating seasonal vegetation signals into practical decisions for field management and harvest planning. The implementation uses historical Sentinel-2 NDVI data, crop phenological information and artificial-intelligence methods to broaden the interpretation of intermediate vegetation-index values. At a conceptual level, the solution builds a scale that links NDVI patterns to crop-growth stages and uses past satellite observations to identify deviations or signals relevant to expected harvest timing. The project involves ENCORE LAB and Castillo de Maetierra, combining digital-agriculture capabilities with vineyard operational experience. The expected impact is better crop monitoring, earlier detection of hidden stress, improved harvest planning and more precise use of remote-sensing information in everyday farm decisions. AI4Copernicus and the AI-on-demand platform describe Scaviho as an Open Call success story whose results have been developed in a consortium already using satellite images in daily agricultural operations.

title: Planning for flexible manufacturing with robots
source_description: Heavy-vehicle axle production involves many machining stages, machine constraints, stock dependencies and planning decisions that are difficult to automate when they rely heavily on human expertise. In this Swedish use case, the challenge is to support flexible manufacturing of front axles by transforming expert production knowledge into a form that automated planning and scheduling systems can use. Human planners understand which operations are possible, which machines can perform them, how available stock affects production routes and how orders should be sequenced, but this knowledge is often implicit and hard to scale. The implementation combines planning and scheduling techniques to generate machining plans from three main inputs: expert knowledge extracted from human planners, incoming order requirements and available stock. At a conceptual level, the system formalises production rules, links them to machine capabilities and uses scheduling-based reasoning to identify feasible and efficient machining sequences. This allows planning decisions to be produced more systematically while remaining grounded in operational know-how. The expected impact is faster production planning, better use of machinery, reduced dependence on individual planners and improved ability to respond to changing orders or stock availability. By combining knowledge representation with automated scheduling, the use case demonstrates how industrial planning systems can support flexible, small-batch or variable manufacturing without requiring a complete redesign of production infrastructure. organization: German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence
title: Planning and execution for a mobile indoor robot
source_description: Indoor mobile manipulation requires a robot to act in environments where object positions, task conditions and execution outcomes may not be fully known in advance. This German use case explores how task planning and execution can control a mobile robot performing manipulation tasks in such settings. The practical challenge is that a robot may need to find boxes or other objects placed on tables, move through the environment, decide which actions to perform and adapt when observations differ from the initial model. The implementation combines task-planning methods with execution control on a mobile robotic platform. In the demonstration scenario, the robot starts without knowing where objects are located and must plan, perceive, move, manipulate and update its knowledge as the task progresses. At a conceptual level, symbolic planning represents goals, actions and preconditions, while execution modules dispatch actions to the robot, monitor results and trigger replanning if expected conditions fail. This creates a loop between high-level reasoning and low-level robotic control. The expected impact is more robust service robotics, improved ability to operate in uncertain indoor environments and a clearer path from planning research to physical deployment. The use case is valuable because it demonstrates not only plan generation, but also the operational challenge of making plans executable on real robots. (research.aiodp.eu

title: AI planning for integrated urban traffic control
source_description: Connected and autonomous vehicles create new possibilities for traffic management because they can exchange information with infrastructure rather than only reacting independently to road conditions. In Kirklees and related research settings, this use case examines how urban traffic control could combine conventional signal management with route guidance for connected vehicles. The operational problem is that urban networks experience congestion, emissions, delays and safety risks, while traffic-control systems often act through limited instruments such as traffic-light timing. Vehicle-to-infrastructure communication adds a further control channel: vehicles can provide information about traffic conditions and receive guidance about preferable routes. The implementation uses planning techniques to coordinate traffic-light decisions and connected-vehicle routing so that the two mechanisms work together rather than separately. At a conceptual level, the system represents the traffic network, vehicle movements, signal states and possible interventions, then generates control strategies able to respond to expected or unusual conditions. The expected impact is reduced congestion, lower emissions, time savings, improved accident prevention and more integrated management of urban mobility. Research linked to this area shows that model-based planning can address both normal patterns and unexpected traffic conditions in real time, making it relevant for future traffic-control systems as connected vehicles become more common. title: AI for predicting the climate change impact in RES and energy demand at regiona and local level
source_description: Regional energy planners need more precise information on how climate change will affect renewable-resource availability and local energy demand, because high-level climate projections are often too coarse for operational decisions. In Asturias, FAEN led a pilot focused on downscaling climate information to support regional and local energy planning. The problem is that changing weather patterns can alter heating and cooling demand, solar and wind generation potential, and the reliability of renewable-energy planning assumptions. Existing climate models may describe long-term trends, but their spatial resolution is often insufficient for local infrastructure, investment or policy decisions. The implementation uses artificial intelligence to connect broad climate projections with in situ data, producing finer-scale estimates of local climate impacts and their consequences for renewable energy and demand. At a conceptual level, the system combines climate-model outputs, local measurements, energy-demand data and renewable-generation indicators to generate geographically relevant forecasts. The expected impact is better regional energy planning, improved assessment of renewable potential, stronger adaptation strategies and more resilient investment decisions. By translating climate projections into actionable local energy intelligence, the use case supports public authorities and energy agencies in aligning climate adaptation, renewable deployment and demand management. organization: Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communication
title: Business Viability Index: AI support for business planning and avoiding failures
source_description: Small and medium-sized enterprises and regional development actors often lack timely, data-driven insights to assess business resilience, market positioning and risk exposure. Fragmented data sources and delayed financial indicators can hinder proactive decision-making, increasing the likelihood of business failure. Stakeholders include entrepreneurs, investors, financial institutions and regional authorities. The objective is to provide an integrated, real-time assessment framework that supports strategic planning and early risk detection. The solution aggregates heterogeneous data sources, including market trends, financial performance indicators and operational metrics, and applies supervised and unsupervised machine learning models alongside deep neural networks to detect behavioural patterns and correlations. Feature engineering and predictive analytics generate a composite viability index, delivered through dashboards and decision-support interfaces integrated with enterprise management systems. Anticipated impacts include improved strategic foresight, earlier identification of financial distress signals, more informed investment decisions and strengthened regional economic resilience, with scalability across sectors due to modular data integration and cloud-based deployment.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: COReHealth – operating centre of telemedicine for chronic conditions and clinical networks
source_description: COReHealth (Regional telemedicine operations centre for chronic diseases and clinical networks) addresses the challenges posed by the COVID-19 emergency and aims to transform the Apulian Oncological Network into a digitally-enabled ecosystem. Thanks to COReHealth, people with chronic diseases can be treated at home, i.e. in a comfortable environment, thus reducing hospitalisations and visits to outpatient clinics. It enables self-management of one's illness and the possibility of being constantly followed, monitored and treated even at a distance or with timely interventions.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: VR4SAW | RESCUESAW VR - Virtual exercise for disaster response
source_description: Forestry workers, firefighters and rescue-service personnel face serious risks when using chainsaws or rescue saws, particularly because recoil, cutting errors and unstable working conditions can cause severe injuries. VR4SAW, also presented as CHAIN SAW VR or RESCUESAW VR, addresses the need for frequent, safe and cost-effective training without fuel consumption, equipment wear or exposure to dangerous practice conditions. The implementation uses virtual reality to simulate chainsaw handling, cutting techniques and work steps in a controlled environment. Trainees wear a VR headset and interact with a secured saw-like device, allowing them to practise procedures and understand hazards before operating in real emergencies. At a conceptual level, the simulator combines immersive visual scenarios, tool handling, procedural instruction and risk-feedback mechanisms. The expected impact is safer chainsaw use, more repeatable training, reduced material cost and better preparation for rescue or forestry operations. It is particularly useful where personnel need to rehearse high-risk movements regularly but cannot reproduce dangerous field conditions safely. Public product material and reporting present the solution as a VR training product for foresters and emergency services, rather than only a research prototype.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Digital assistant for forest management
source_description: Forest managers must plan harvesting under conditions that are becoming more uncertain because of climate change, biodiversity requirements, market pressures and the loss of experienced local knowledge. In Germany, the EDE 4.0 project focuses on logging planning as a central task of forest management, covering the type, quantity and quality of wood to be harvested. District foresters and forest enterprises need recommendations that reflect inventory data, stand conditions, regional climate forecasts and operational constraints, but established decision-making routines may be too static for rapidly changing forests. The implementation develops a digital assistant that uses district and inventory-related data together with medium-term and regional climate forecasts to support harvesting decisions in real time and in the field. At a conceptual level, the system combines forest data, growth modelling, predictive analytics and mobile decision support, extending established processes with data-based recommendations rather than replacing professional judgement. The expected impact is more resilient harvesting planning, better adaptation to climate risks, improved use of local forest information and stronger support for less experienced decision-makers. Project reporting indicates that EDE 4.0 integrates multiple data sources and forest-growth modelling to create predictive recommendations for dynamic logging planning. (www.fnr.de
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: PhenoRob proejct - Fertilise crops more specifically
source_description: Crop production must become more resource-efficient while maintaining yields under climate, biodiversity and environmental pressures. PhenoRob, the Cluster of Excellence led by the University of Bonn with Forschungszentrum Jülich, addresses this challenge by combining robotics, phenotyping, digitalisation and machine learning for sustainable crop production. The objective is to understand plant growth, nutrient use and water efficiency more precisely so that fertiliser and crop-protection measures can be applied only where and when needed. The implementation uses ground robots, drones, sensor-based phenotyping, field monitoring and large-scale data analysis. At a conceptual level, robotic platforms collect high-resolution data on crop growth, soil, canopy structure and field conditions, while machine-learning models transform these observations into knowledge about plant performance and resource needs. This supports more targeted agronomic interventions and helps researchers explore crop adaptability to climate conditions and biodiversity-preserving practices. The expected impact is lower input use, reduced environmental burden, better yield stability and more robust evidence for sustainable farming systems. PhenoRob is not a single deployed product but a major interdisciplinary research cluster whose work feeds methods, prototypes and scientific knowledge into future agricultural practice. In 2025, the cluster received further funding for a second phase extending to 2032, confirming continued institutional support.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI)
title: FlatFish - Autonomous inspections in the deep sea
source_description: Inspection of offshore oil and gas infrastructure is expensive, technically complex and risky when it depends on remotely operated vehicles, support vessels and specialist divers. FlatFish was developed to simplify repeated subsea inspection by using an autonomous underwater vehicle capable of operating for extended periods around underwater structures. The objective is to reduce inspection cost and risk while improving the frequency and quality of monitoring for industrial assets. The implementation combines autonomous navigation, acoustic and optical sensors, subsea docking concepts and robotic inspection capabilities. At a conceptual level, the vehicle maps and localises itself underwater, follows inspection missions, collects visual and sensor data, and performs tasks such as structure and pipeline inspection without continuous tethered control. Original research involved DFKI, the Brazilian Institute of Robotics and Shell, while later industrial development connected FlatFish to Saipem’s Hydrone underwater robotics programme. The expected impact is lower reliance on maintenance ships, reduced exposure of personnel to hazardous offshore work, better repeatability of inspections and more efficient asset monitoring. Recent public information indicates that FlatFish has advanced beyond laboratory research: Saipem reported successful functional testing with Petrobras in 2026, including autonomous inspection missions, cathodic-protection measurements and wall-thickness assessments.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Flora Incognita app – recognise wild plants using an app
source_description: Biodiversity awareness depends on people being able to recognise the plants around them, but botanical identification can be difficult without specialist knowledge. Flora Incognita addresses this gap through a free mobile application that uses artificial intelligence to identify wild plants from images taken with a smartphone or tablet. The objective is both educational and scientific: users receive immediate help identifying species, while the observations generated through the app can contribute to research on plant distribution, biodiversity change and environmental monitoring. The implementation applies deep-learning models to photographs of plant parts such as flowers, leaves, bark or fruit. At a conceptual level, the app analyses the visual characteristics of the plant, compares them with learned species patterns and returns a likely identification together with supporting information on characteristics, distribution and protection status. Its expected impact is wider public engagement with nature, easier access to botanical knowledge, increased participation in citizen science and better data for conservation research. The app is especially useful for schools, universities, nature-protection initiatives and individual users who want to learn more about local flora. By combining image recognition with educational content and observation recording, Flora Incognita turns everyday encounters with plants into structured biodiversity data and public learning opportunities.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: HoloMed – precise puncturing during brain operations
source_description: Neurosurgical ventricular punctures require extremely precise placement of a needle or catheter into deep brain structures that are not directly visible during the operation. Freehand procedures can be challenging because the target lies inside the brain, the permitted angle may have only a few degrees of tolerance and every minute can matter in acute cases such as brain haemorrhage or stroke. HoloMed was developed to support surgeons by making patient-specific anatomical information visible in their field of view. The implementation creates a three-dimensional model of the patient’s brain from CT or MRI images and displays relevant guidance through augmented-reality glasses. At a conceptual level, the system combines medical imaging, model generation, spatial registration, augmented-reality visualisation and surgical navigation. Graphic elements help the medical team identify the puncture point and insertion angle, allowing hidden structures to be mapped onto the patient during the procedure. KIT notes that only about 60% of freehand punctures reach an optimal position, which explains the clinical rationale for navigation support. The expected impact is higher first-attempt accuracy, improved safety, reduced cognitive load and more efficient surgical workflows. Prototype testing at Günzburg hospital was reported positively, although the available sources present HoloMed as a research and prototype system rather than routine clinical deployment. (kit.edu
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Wearable exoskeleton for stroke patients
source_description: Stroke and other neurological conditions can leave patients with severe movement limitations, creating a need for intensive, repetitive and adaptive rehabilitation that is difficult to provide continuously through therapist-led sessions alone. In Bremen, DFKI’s Robotics Innovation Center developed Recupera REHA as a mobile whole-body exoskeleton and modular assistance system for robot-supported rehabilitation. The aim was to expand therapy options by helping patients practise gripping, arm movement, standing or walking with robotic support adapted to their impairment. The implementation uses a metal exoskeleton structure with modular actuators, sensor systems and control software. Individual actuator modules can support the body directly or be reconfigured as gripper arms attached to a wheelchair, enabling assistance for different mobility needs. At a conceptual level, the system combines rehabilitation robotics, biosignal analysis, sensor fusion and adaptive “assist-as-needed” control so that support can match the patient’s capability and therapy goals. The expected impact is more intensive rehabilitation, greater patient autonomy, reduced dependence on constant therapist assistance and new possibilities for home or near-home training. The project ran from 2014 to 2017, and later research continued to advance the Recupera-Reha exoskeleton’s modelling and control for actions such as sitting, standing and static walking. (dfki.de
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Georg-August University of Göttingen (UGOE) and Julius Kühn Institute (JKI
title: NOcsPS (Agriculture 4.0 without chemical-synthetic crop protection)
source_description: Pressure to reduce chemical-synthetic plant protection products is reshaping agricultural research, because farmers still need systems that protect yields, manage weeds and diseases, and remain economically viable. NOcsPS develops a cultivation model that sits between conventional and organic farming: it avoids chemical-synthetic crop protection while retaining mineral fertilisation and using new cultivation measures, data-driven monitoring and agronomic optimisation. The initiative brings together the University of Hohenheim, the University of Göttingen and the Julius Kühn Institute to test whether more sustainable cropping systems can be designed without seriously impairing yield performance. The implementation combines field trials, crop-rotation design, soil and fertilisation strategies, digital monitoring and Agriculture 4.0 methods. At a conceptual level, data from experimental plots, crop growth, management practices and environmental conditions are used to compare production systems and support decisions on how to control pests, weeds and diseases without conventional pesticides. Initial research indicates that systems without chemical-synthetic plant protection generally achieve lower yields than conventional systems, but considerably higher yields than organic systems, suggesting a potential middle path for sustainable intensification. The expected impact is reduced pesticide dependency, improved evidence for future farming systems, and better support for farmers facing regulatory and environmental pressure. NOcsPS has moved into a second phase, with 18 scientific consortium partners working across cropping systems, sustainability and transformation.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: ARMAR-6 – Cooperative robot in industrial environments
source_description: Industrial maintenance often requires workers to perform varied physical tasks in environments where tool use, unexpected situations and human cooperation are central. ARMAR-6 was developed by Karlsruhe Institute of Technology as a humanoid assistance robot able to support people in industrial contexts, especially where tasks cannot be fully anticipated at programming time. The objective is to create a robot that can recognise when a human partner needs help, use human-designed tools and perform or assist with maintenance activities. The implementation combines a human-like upper body, bimanual manipulation, mobile movement, perception, action planning and interaction capabilities. At a conceptual level, the robot observes the work situation, interprets human activity, identifies opportunities to assist and executes tasks such as handing tools, holding components or operating equipment. Its human-like morphology allows it to interact with objects and tools designed for people, such as drills or hammers. The expected impact is safer and more flexible industrial support, reduced physical burden on workers and better handling of tasks that are difficult to automate with fixed machinery. ARMAR-6 remains primarily a research platform for collaborative humanoid robotics, but it is important because it demonstrates how industrial assistance can move from pre-programmed automation towards proactive, context-aware cooperation with human workers.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Dublin's Balbriggan district 3D Model to visualise in VR
source_description: Public consultation on urban regeneration can be difficult when residents are asked to interpret technical plans, drawings or planning documents that do not clearly show how a place will feel once works are completed. Fingal County Council developed the Balbriggan 3D Model to help citizens visualise the planned transformations in the Our Balbriggan 2019–2025 Town Rejuvenation Plan, particularly around Quay Street and the Harbour. The objective is to make proposed public-realm changes more understandable, tangible and accessible, enabling local people to engage with the future of the town through an intuitive visual environment. The implementation uses aerial survey photography and ground-level photo surveys to create a digital 3D map, or digital twin, of Balbriggan. This model can be explored through a web viewer and virtual-reality experience, allowing users to see planned changes to streets, the harbour and public spaces in a spatially realistic way. At a conceptual level, the system connects geospatial capture, three-dimensional modelling, visualisation and citizen-engagement workflows. The expected impact is better-informed public consultation, higher-quality feedback, improved trust in regeneration planning and stronger community participation in place-making. Fingal County Council now presents Balbriggan as part of a wider digital-twin portfolio covering public-realm projects, while the Quay Street and Harbour works have progressed as a €15 million transformation scheme.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Bristol city council virtual reality program to train caregivers
source_description: Care staff supporting people with dementia need to understand how sensory, visual and motor challenges shape everyday tasks, but classroom training may not fully convey what dementia can feel like from the resident’s perspective. Bristol City Council funded a virtual-reality dementia training programme at Redfield Lodge, its council-owned care home specialising in dementia care. The objective was to improve person-centred care by helping staff experience simulated challenges that residents may encounter when completing basic activities. The implementation uses VR headsets to immerse trainees in scenarios that replicate aspects of dementia-related perception and movement difficulty. At a conceptual level, the training converts experiential simulation into practical reflection: staff observe how tasks become confusing or physically difficult, then use this insight to design better care plans and support environments that set residents up for success. The expected impact is greater empathy, improved staff awareness, more appropriate care planning and better daily support for residents. The programme began with around 30 caregivers and was expanded to managers and supervisors, indicating organisational uptake beyond a single training session. Public reporting describes the initiative as complete, with the council funding VR training to improve dementia-care practice.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Use of IoT technologies to gather data from the City of Ferrara
source_description: Cities that manage tourism, air quality, shared mobility and public-space use need timely information from many urban systems, but these data are often fragmented across departments, platforms and service providers. Ravenna’s smart-city work has explored the use of IoT technologies to monitor sensitive urban indicators, including air quality, tourist flows and mobility-sharing patterns. The operational objective is to help the municipality understand how people move through the city, how tourism affects local areas and where environmental or mobility pressures require intervention. The implementation is based on connected sensors, data collection from urban infrastructure and analytical platforms that support monitoring and planning. At a conceptual level, IoT devices and digital services collect local observations, which can then be integrated into dashboards or planning tools to inform mobility, tourism and environmental policies. This approach is consistent with Ravenna’s wider digital transition trajectory, including the DARE programme and the more recent FOOTPRINTS initiative, which focuses on sustainable tourism, accessibility, mobility, digital facilities and flow management. The expected impact is improved situational awareness, better management of tourist pressure, more evidence-based mobility planning and stronger capacity to reduce the ecological footprint of visitors. Current public information suggests that Ravenna continues to develop smart mobility and sustainable destination tools, although the precise status of the individual IoT pilots described in the original source is not fully specified.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Veovo BlipTrack Guest Predictability solution in Amsterdam Airport Schiphol
source_description: Large airports need to manage passenger flows through security, border control, gates and terminal areas while avoiding congestion and maintaining predictable journey times. Amsterdam Airport Schiphol adopted Veovo’s BlipTrack / Passenger Predictability technology to measure queues and passenger movement automatically, beginning with security-process wait-time measurement. The operational problem was that airport staff needed real-time information on where congestion was forming and how long passengers were waiting, especially during irregular operations or periods of high demand. The implementation uses sensors and analytics to detect passenger movement and estimate queue length, dwell time and flow across terminal processes. At a conceptual level, the system collects movement signals, converts them into operational indicators and provides airport teams with dashboards or alerts that support proactive capacity management. The expected impact is faster response to bottlenecks, improved staffing and resource allocation, more reliable passenger information and better long-term planning of terminal infrastructure. The technology also supports a shift from reactive airport management to predictive flow management, where data from multiple stages of the passenger journey helps identify pressure points before they become severe. Its value lies in combining real-time operational awareness with evidence for future process and facility improvements.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Smart monitoring system of tourism footprint
source_description: Tourism destinations seeking carbon neutrality need reliable information about the environmental impact of visitor activity, but tourism emissions are distributed across accommodation, mobility, restaurants, attractions, events and other services. Visit Valencia adopted GO2, a blockchain-based tool, to calculate and manage the carbon footprint of tourism activity. The objective is to support data-driven decision-making and make sustainability performance more visible for destination managers and tourism actors. The implementation uses smart labels or smart tags assigned to different tourism activities, breaking each activity into a calculation scheme that estimates its carbon footprint. At a conceptual level, data from tourism organisations and activities are processed through a digital platform, with blockchain technology used to provide traceability, verification and integrity for the information. This makes it possible to monitor emissions more systematically and to connect individual activities with the destination’s broader sustainability strategy. The expected impact is better measurement of tourism-related emissions, stronger accountability for climate commitments, more informed mitigation measures and improved communication with visitors and businesses. The use case is relevant because it applies blockchain to environmental verification rather than financial speculation, focusing on trust, auditability and shared sustainability data across a destination ecosystem.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Germany analyses big data with AI to manage tourist trends
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: National tourism organisations need to understand how marketing campaigns, origin markets, travel behaviour and external events influence visitor demand. The German National Tourist Board developed a data-driven analytics solution to monitor visitor trends and assess tourism-market dynamics using large datasets and machine-learning techniques. The operational problem was that tourism demand is influenced by many variables, including flight reservations, campaign exposure, traveller preferences, seasonality and source-market conditions. The implementation combined data from Global Distribution Systems and other travel-data sources with business-intelligence tools and trend-prediction algorithms. A specialised data-analytics provider supported the analysis by supplying near-real-time market data, reports and visualisation capabilities. At a conceptual level, the solution integrates large-scale booking and campaign datasets, identifies patterns before and after marketing actions, and generates insights on visitor origin, travel routes, popular cities and segment-specific preferences. The expected impact is better allocation of marketing investment, more targeted destination promotion, improved forecasting of demand and more tailored tourism offers for visitors. The use case also shows how AI can support destination management indirectly: tourists may not interact with the system, but its insights help shape campaigns, services and strategic decisions that affect the visitor experience.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Goochem - a pioneering interactive chatbot created as a marketing tool to bring culture closer to young people
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Cultural institutions and destination-marketing organisations often struggle to reach younger audiences with relevant information, especially when cultural offers are spread across many venues, events and platforms. Goochem was created by Amsterdam Marketing and the City of Amsterdam as an interactive chatbot to bring culture closer to young people through personalised recommendations. The chatbot was available through Facebook Messenger and used conversational interaction to learn about a user’s interests, build a simple profile and suggest relevant cultural activities. The implementation was developed by digital technology companies Raft and Axendo after an open call for innovative pitches. At a conceptual level, Goochem combines dialogue-based profiling, recommendation logic and cultural-event information to guide users towards activities that match their preferences. Rather than presenting a static calendar, the chatbot asks questions and uses the user’s responses to filter and prioritise cultural suggestions. The expected impact is easier access to cultural information, stronger engagement with younger audiences, better promotion of Amsterdam’s cultural offer and more personalised destination marketing. The case is significant because it treats a chatbot not only as a customer-service tool, but as an active marketing and cultural-discovery interface that can make a city’s cultural ecosystem feel more accessible and relevant.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI application developed for Dubrovnik visitors predicting the number of visitors in the Old Town
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Historic city centres can become difficult to manage when visitor flows peak unpredictably, especially where tourism pressure affects residents, local businesses, transport and heritage conservation. Dubrovnik developed an application to predict the number of visitors in the Old Town and surrounding contact zones as part of the wider “Respect the City” measures. The objective is to help tourists, citizens and businesses plan their activities using clearer information about expected crowd levels. The implementation uses machine learning to estimate the number of people in the historic core on a selected day, drawing on parameters associated with tourism flows and urban demand. At a conceptual level, the application translates historical and contextual data into visitor-number predictions, making crowd pressure more visible before people decide when to visit. The expected impact is better distribution of visitors across time, reduced pressure on the UNESCO-listed Old Town, improved planning for local businesses and more informed daily choices by residents. The system is also relevant for urban mobility and destination management, because crowd forecasts can support operational decisions beyond individual visitor planning. Its value lies in shifting from reactive crowd management to anticipatory visitor-flow intelligence in a city where tourism intensity is a central policy issue.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Smart parking in Dubrovnik with IoT
source_description: Parking pressure in tourist cities can generate congestion, emissions and frustration, particularly when visitors circulate near historic centres searching for available spaces. Dubrovnik’s Smart Parking initiative uses Internet of Things technology to provide real-time information on parking availability across the city. The operational problem is acute because the city receives large visitor numbers and has constrained access around the old town. The implementation connects sensors and digital systems to parking spaces and car parks, providing information on the number of free spaces, prices, opening hours and distance from the user’s location. Integration with Google Maps helps route drivers to available parking, while payment functionality supports quicker transactions and reduces queues at machines. At a conceptual level, NB-IoT sensors detect occupancy, transmit parking-space status to a central platform and make the information available through a mobile or map-based interface. The expected impact is reduced search traffic, improved use of parking capacity, lower congestion, easier payment and better data for city mobility management. The project also contributes to broader smart-city strategy by showing how connected infrastructure can address a very practical urban-management problem in a high-pressure destination.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Augmented Reality Technologies Enter Slovenian Schools and Companies - THINK XR Project
source_description: Education systems and companies increasingly need staff who can understand, design and apply extended-reality technologies, but many schools lack curricula, equipment and trained mentors for augmented and virtual reality. THINK XR was created in Slovenia to introduce new teaching modules and practical training in this field, linking formal education, vocational training and industrial use cases. The initiative involves Konjice Secondary School and Slovenian education and research partners, with the objective of making immersive technologies more accessible for students, teachers and companies. The implementation includes the establishment of an XR Academy, training for future XR trainers, development of 3D content and use of tools such as Blender and Unity. At a conceptual level, the project combines curriculum design, teacher training, immersive content development, specialised equipment and cooperation between education and industry. Its purpose is not only to demonstrate augmented reality, but to embed it into learning pathways and practical skills development. The expected impact is improved student engagement, better understanding of complex subjects, stronger digital competences among teachers and more direct links between schools and companies using XR. The first Slovenian XR trainer course took place in spring 2023, while the national and final conference in Ljubljana in April 2024 reported strong participation and results that exceeded expectations.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: "Chatta col David"" - Chatbot on the Galleria dell'Accademia di Firenze website"
source_description: Museums increasingly need digital tools that make collections more accessible, engaging and conversational, especially for audiences who may approach cultural heritage through informal online channels. “Chatta col David” was created by the Galleria dell’Accademia di Firenze as an AI chatbot that allows users to interact with a digital alter ego of Michelangelo’s David. The objective is to communicate historical, artistic, religious and anecdotal information about the statue in a more immediate and engaging form than a conventional web page. The implementation uses automated chatbot technology and deep-learning-based interaction developed with Querlo, allowing users to ask questions and receive responses about the artwork, its context and its symbolism. At a conceptual level, the system transforms museum interpretation into a dialogue: rather than reading a fixed description, users can explore their curiosity through questions and answers. The expected impact is broader public engagement, a more accessible entry point to Renaissance art, improved digital museum experience and increased interaction with the museum’s online presence. The use case is notable because it turns a single iconic object into a conversational interface, using AI not to replace curatorial interpretation but to make it more discoverable, playful and personalised for digital visitors.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Venice smart monitoring systems for tourists
source_description: Overtourism threatens the liveability and heritage of Venice, requiring precise understanding of visitor flows to support management decisions. This use case involves the city administration, residents, and visitors, with the objective of monitoring and managing tourist density. The solution combines data from pedestrian sensors, cameras, and anonymised mobile phone information to analyse real-time and historical flows. Integrated monitoring enables modelling of crowd dynamics and supports timely interventions. The system improves situational awareness, supports sustainable tourism policies, and enhances safety. It delivers data-driven management of a fragile urban environment while balancing tourism and resident needs.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: DATAESTUR to understand tourism in Spain via big data
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Tourism policy requires timely, comprehensive data, particularly during crises such as the Covid-19 pandemic. Spain lacked a unified, open platform to consolidate tourism intelligence. DATAESTUR addresses this gap by involving public agencies and private data providers, with the objective of improving decision-making and transparency. The platform aggregates national tourism data from multiple authoritative sources and publishes them openly across structured categories. It improves accessibility to insights on demand, economics, transport, and accommodation. DATAESTUR supports evidence-based policy, industry analysis, and research, delivering long-term value through openness, coordination, and data-driven governance.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: MyHelsinki Open API
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Tourism, event promotion and city discovery services depend on high-quality local data that can be reused by developers, businesses and public-sector actors. The MyHelsinki Open API was created to provide structured access to information about places, events and activities in Helsinki and the surrounding region. The objective was to make city-curated content available as open data, encouraging reuse in digital services while maintaining quality standards and multilingual accessibility. The implementation exposed three databases through an application programming interface, allowing users to query and filter content by location, category, time and other criteria. At a conceptual level, the API turned Helsinki Marketing’s curated destination information into machine-readable resources that third-party applications could integrate into websites, mobile apps or digital services. Content was maintained by experts, updated regularly and made available in Finnish, Swedish, English and Chinese, improving both local and international reuse. The expected impact was stronger tourism innovation, easier development of city-service applications, improved visibility of Helsinki’s events and attractions, and reduced duplication of content maintenance across public and private platforms. The case illustrates how open APIs can serve as public digital infrastructure, enabling an ecosystem of services around trusted municipal data. Although not an AI use case in itself, it was an important example of data-driven public-service enablement and reuse.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Helinki Tourist info chatbot
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Visitors to a city often need immediate practical information about attractions, transport, events, services and local recommendations, but traditional tourist-information channels may not be available at all hours or in the user’s preferred format. Helsinki’s virtual tourist-information assistant, Lokki, provides a chatbot interface on the MyHelsinki website to help travellers and other users find relevant city information. The operational problem is that tourism information is broad and situational: users may ask about what to see, how to move around, where to get help, what events are taking place or how to plan a visit. The implementation uses a chatbot that answers questions through a conversational interface and guides users towards relevant information from Helsinki’s tourism ecosystem.
