The operational problem is that environmental monitoring datasets can contain gaps, missing measurements or discontinuities, making it harder for public authorities to understand hydrological conditions and anticipate changes in water availability. The implementation used dense neural-network techniques to estimate and reconstruct missing flow-rate data by learning relationships between available observations and expected water-flow patterns. At a conceptual level, the model supports prediction-measurement comparison: where sensor or historical data are incomplete, the neural network can infer plausible values and help reconstruct the hydrological series needed for environmental assessment. This creates a decision-support layer for monitoring glacier-fed systems, reservoir inflows and broader environmental status. The expected impact is improved continuity of hydrological monitoring, better evidence for water-resource planning and stronger public-sector capacity to use existing environmental datasets. The case is also relevant because it shows how an open-innovation challenge can introduce AI methods into provincial administration without requiring a full internal AI development team. Trentino Innovation describes the Public AI Challenge as a mechanism through which students develop predictive models and intelligent systems for public-administration needs.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI for Water in Garda Lake area
source_description: Wastewater-treatment and water-infrastructure operators need to manage variable inflows while controlling energy consumption, maintenance risks and service continuity. The Trentino / Garda-area AI for Water use case involved NIRIS and AI Challenge participants working on data from public water-treatment infrastructure to forecast incoming water variations using historical plant data and meteorological information. The operational problem is that treatment plants consume significant energy, and rainfall-driven changes in inflow can create operational peaks that are expensive or inefficient if not anticipated. The implementation used historical purifier data, weather data from the Stenico area and machine-learning methods to identify correlations between meteorological conditions, anthropic impact and plant behaviour. At a conceptual level, the system learns from past inflow, weather and operational patterns to forecast future water loads, enabling plant managers to prepare equipment and optimise energy use. The expected impact is lower energy consumption, better remote management, improved predictive maintenance and more resilient operation of depuration infrastructure. The use case is notable because it applies AI to a highly practical utility-management problem, where small percentage savings can matter because water-treatment systems operate continuously and at high energy intensity across many plants.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Fondo Caproni Project (AI for Culture)
source_description: Large cultural collections can become difficult to preserve and make accessible when the volume of material exceeds the capacity of manual cataloguing teams. The Caproni Collection contains approximately 200,000 historic photographs and aviation-related assets, including valuable images, memorabilia and documentation linked to Italian aeronautical history. The administrative challenge is to count, catalogue, classify, preserve, assess image quality and prepare selected materials for public exposure without imposing unsustainable labour requirements on cultural staff. The implementation explored the use of artificial intelligence to automate parts of the catalogue-building process, with particular emphasis on image-quality assessment and primary thematic classification. At a conceptual level, computer-vision models can identify damaged, blurred or low-quality photographs, group images into broad themes, support metadata generation and prioritise items requiring human review or conservation attention. This does not remove curatorial responsibility, but it can shift expert effort towards validation, interpretation and public presentation. The expected impact is faster digitisation, improved quality control, better searchability and broader public access to the Caproni heritage. Provincial material also confirms that the wider Caproni archive is being digitalised using PNRR funding, making the AI challenge part of a larger cultural-heritage digitisation trajectory. The case demonstrates how AI can support public cultural institutions when archive scale makes purely manual processes impractical.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: ‘Outpost’ autonomous towers to monitor Greek islands for threats
source_description: Remote island monitoring requires persistent situational awareness across land, sea and air, but continuous human surveillance can be costly, difficult and operationally limited. “Outpost” is an autonomous surveillance tower concept developed by Lambda Automata for monitoring Greek islands and other remote or sensitive areas. The operational problem is to detect and track diverse possible threats, including people, drones, vessels, aircraft, vehicles and smoke columns, across locations where infrastructure and personnel may be limited. The implementation uses autonomous towers equipped with sensors and artificial-intelligence software for geolocation, classification and tracking. At a conceptual level, the system observes the surrounding environment, processes sensor inputs, classifies detected objects or events and supports operators with alerts or situational information. The expected impact is stronger border and island surveillance, earlier detection of threats, reduced reliance on continuous manual observation and improved response coordination. The use case is security-focused and therefore distinct from civilian smart-city monitoring, but it illustrates a broader pattern in public-sector AI: distributed sensor infrastructure combined with automated classification to provide decision support in environments where rapid detection matters. It also raises typical governance issues around surveillance, oversight, proportionality and the human role in interpreting alerts.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: I-CAN Police Crime Predictive System against Ndrangheta Network Crime
source_description: Investigating organised and transnational criminal networks such as the ’Ndrangheta requires law enforcement agencies to analyse vast volumes of heterogeneous data, including communications, financial records, multimedia material and relational information. Traditional investigative tools struggle to cope with this complexity, leading to lengthy investigations and fragmented insights. INTERPOL launched the I-CAN initiative to strengthen the analytical capacity of police forces involved in combating Italian mafia-type organisations, supporting national and cross-border investigations. Stakeholders include INTERPOL, national police forces, judicial authorities and specialised organised crime units. The objective is to accelerate investigations, improve detection of hidden criminal relationships and enhance international cooperation. The system builds on technologies developed in EU-funded research projects such as ROXANNE, integrating network analysis, multilingual text and speech processing, and video analysis into a single interoperable platform. Data from multiple investigative sources are correlated to generate visual network graphs, behavioural patterns and relationship mappings, while remaining compatible with existing law enforcement databases and legal safeguards. I-CAN is operational as an INTERPOL cooperation framework, with tools progressively deployed to support investigations. Reported impacts include faster case analysis, improved situational awareness, reduced investigative workload per case and stronger cross-border intelligence sharing, contributing to more effective disruption of organised crime networks.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Venice Smart Control Room
source_description: Managing Venice requires coordination across pedestrian flows, water traffic, road access, tourism pressure, public transport, weather, tides, security and parking. The Venice Smart Control Room was developed as an integrated urban “control tower” to aggregate information from sensors, video feeds, municipal systems and service operators. The operational problem is that Venice’s urban mobility is unusually complex: boats, pedestrians, road transport and tourist flows interact with weather and tidal risks in a fragile historic environment. The implementation, developed by the Municipality of Venice with TIM and local public-safety stakeholders, brings together data on people present in the city, types of boats in canals, water and road transport movement, tourist flows, forecasts and parking. At a conceptual level, the platform combines sensor networks, camera feeds, telecommunications data, urban analytics and predictive modelling to support monitoring and decision-making. It can help detect mobility issues, identify congestion, support public safety and provide evidence for planning. The expected impact is improved city management, faster operational coordination, better regulation of water and land mobility, and more informed decisions during high-pressure events. The case is significant because it combines heritage-city governance with smart-city operations in a territory where urban management has both everyday and exceptional-risk dimensions.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: ChatGPT as a tool for Education
source_description: Schools and higher-education institutions face a pedagogical challenge when generative AI can produce coherent written answers, summaries and draft texts in response to ordinary prompts. This use case concerns the educational use of ChatGPT not as an autonomous teaching system, but as a tool for critical collaboration between students, teachers and AI-generated text. The operational issue is that students may use the system to produce assignments mechanically, while educators can instead redesign activities so that learners interrogate, verify, contextualise and improve AI outputs. The implementation is therefore mainly pedagogical: ChatGPT can be used to generate examples, draft outlines, propose questions, create exercises, provide writing models, support translation, or produce material that students then analyse against sources and disciplinary knowledge. At a conceptual level, the tool offers syntactically coherent and semantically connected responses, but it does not independently establish a situated, critical or interpretative perspective. The expected impact is a shift from banning AI to teaching students how to question it, evaluate its limitations and use it to accelerate constructive thinking. The case is particularly relevant in arts and humanities education, where human contextualisation, semiotic reading and critical interpretation remain central to the learning process.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Evaluate science and business cooperation in terms of knowledge usage efficiency
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Public innovation agencies need to understand whether scientific knowledge generated by universities and research institutions is effectively used by businesses and economic sectors. In Lithuania, GovTech Lab supported a challenge to create an AI-enabled tool for evaluating science-business cooperation and knowledge-use efficiency. The operational problem is that data on publications, graduates, joint projects and institutional knowledge-transfer activities can be dispersed, delayed or difficult to compare across sectors. This limits the ability of public authorities to assess which forms of cooperation produce value and where additional policy support is needed. The implementation develops an innovative, user-friendly tool to collect, process, classify and systematise relevant data from institutions of science and studies. At a conceptual level, the solution combines data integration, automated classification, interactive visualisation and analytical summaries, allowing users either to compare information quickly through diagrams or conduct deeper cross-sectional analysis. The expected impact is more transparent monitoring of knowledge-transfer effectiveness, better evidence for science and innovation policy, and improved capacity to identify sectors where scientific knowledge is being underused.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Intelligent traffic control in the port of Hamburg - various applications
source_description: Ports are complex logistics ecosystems in which road, rail, vessel, terminal and warehouse operations must be synchronised to avoid congestion, emissions and wasted capacity. Hamburg Port Authority’s smartPORT approach applies digital intelligence to improve the efficiency and sustainability of port operations. The operational problem is that freight movement and traffic flows depend on many actors and real-time conditions, including vessel arrivals, truck movements, parking availability, road capacity, environmental constraints and terminal operations. The implementation uses sensor technology, analysis, forecasting and information systems to support intelligent traffic and goods management. At a conceptual level, data from infrastructure, vehicles, logistics systems and operational platforms are integrated to produce traffic information, forecasts and decision support for port users and managers. This can improve routing, parking, congestion management and the utilisation of existing infrastructure. The expected impact is reduced delays, lower greenhouse-gas and air-pollutant emissions, fewer unnecessary vehicle kilometres, better reliability for logistics operators and stronger environmental performance. The case is important because it treats port digitalisation as a system-level optimisation problem: AI and analytics do not only improve one process, but help coordinate the port as an urban-industrial infrastructure.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: 5G test field planned in the Port of Duisburg
source_description: Inland ports need low-latency, high-capacity connectivity to support automation, traffic control and real-time logistics coordination. The Port of Duisburg 5G test field was designed to explore how private or local 5G infrastructure can improve port operations, especially the partially automated control of container cranes and future smart logistics applications. The operational problem is that conventional connectivity may not provide the responsiveness, reliability or flexibility needed for semi-automated equipment, sensor networks, drones and real-time traffic-management systems. The implementation established a 5G test environment in Europe’s largest inland port, with support from North Rhine-Westphalia’s 5G.NRW funding framework and technology partners including Deutsche Telekom. At a conceptual level, cameras, sensors, industrial equipment and control systems communicate over the 5G network, enabling data to be collected and interpreted rapidly for operational decisions. The expected impact is higher container-handling capacity, more flexible port operations, better congestion prevention and a foundation for future AI- and IoT-enabled logistics use cases. The project illustrates how next-generation connectivity can be a prerequisite for more advanced automation: AI-driven prediction or control depends on timely data transmission from distributed port assets.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Procurement data quality and CPV improvement for TED data
source_description: European public procurement transparency depends on high-quality, standardised data, but procurement notices can contain missing, inconsistent or incorrectly classified information. The TED data-quality and CPV improvement use case focuses on using AI and natural language processing to improve the quality of Tenders Electronic Daily data and generate more reliable procurement statistics. The operational problem is that Common Procurement Vocabulary codes and notice metadata are essential for search, monitoring, analytics and expenditure analysis, but they may be incomplete or inaccurate when submitted. The implementation concept includes extracting or validating CPV codes from procurement documents, detecting inconsistencies, deriving missing fields, harmonising data and producing improved statistics on expenditure, contractors and contracting authorities. At a conceptual level, NLP models read tender text and metadata, infer likely classifications or corrections, and support data-quality auditing. More advanced analytical objectives include identifying patterns in awards and forecasting likely bidders or awardees under certain tender characteristics. The expected impact is better procurement transparency, more accurate public spending analysis, improved searchability of tenders and stronger evidence for policy, audit and market-intelligence work. The use case is important because high-quality procurement data is a foundation for accountability, competition analysis and anti-corruption monitoring across the EU.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Finland Tax Agency AI support
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Tax administrations process large volumes of returns, declarations, payments, risk signals and taxpayer interactions, making them natural candidates for automation and data-driven decision support. The Finnish Tax Administration use case concerns the controlled use of artificial intelligence in taxation, within the legal framework governing tax assessment and administrative procedure. The operational problem is that taxation requires both efficiency and legal certainty: AI can support risk selection, classification, service delivery or internal analysis, but the consequences for taxpayers mean that each use must be assessed separately. The implementation approach is therefore governance-led rather than based on one single model. Different AI solutions may be used for different functions, and the degree of automation depends on the purpose, legal basis and procedural safeguards of each system. At a conceptual level, AI can either generate recommendations for tax officials or, where legally permitted, support more automated processing. The expected impact is more efficient tax administration, improved targeting of checks, better consistency in routine processing and faster taxpayer service. The case is significant because it emphasises that AI in taxation is not merely a technical matter: it must be aligned with administrative-law principles, taxpayer rights, transparency, accountability and the distinction between decision support and independent automated decision-making.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Speeding up judicial proceedings with Transkit, an AI-based tool that transcribes trials
source_description: Court proceedings generate large volumes of spoken material that may later need to be searched, quoted, reviewed or used in higher-instance appeals. In the Basque Country, Transkit was developed to reduce the burden of manually reviewing court-session videos and preparing transcripts. The operational problem is that legal staff may need to locate exactly where a phrase was said, who said it, or which named entities were mentioned, but manual video review is slow and does not create searchable text. The implementation uses neural-network-based speech-to-text technology capable of transcribing Spanish, Basque and bilingual Spanish-Basque audio or video content. At a conceptual level, the system converts recorded proceedings into timestamped text, links speech with searchable terms and allows staff to focus on correction, validation and completion rather than full manual transcription. The expected impact is faster judicial administration, improved productivity for clerks and court staff, easier review of appeal material, better searchability of proceedings and more efficient preparation of judgments or records. The tool does not replace official legal validation of transcripts; it provides a draft and search layer that supports human professionals in managing recorded procedural content more efficiently.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: ISA2 Action 1.7 – AI Pilot for Document Classification
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: Public administrations frequently handle large volumes of unstructured documents and emails that must be reviewed within strict deadlines, particularly in investigative and compliance contexts. Manual classification is labour-intensive and may lead to inconsistencies. Stakeholders include administrative bodies, investigative units and IT departments. The objective is to assess the added value of machine learning for document review and classification within public administrations. The pilot evaluates multiple machine learning algorithms and modelling approaches, including supervised text classification models based on natural language processing techniques. The system is designed to integrate with existing document repositories and review platforms, addressing interoperability, organisational and legal considerations. Anticipated impacts include faster document triage, improved consistency in classification decisions, reduced administrative burden and clearer understanding of governance implications associated with automated document analysis.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Portugal Ministry of Justice – GPJ Digital Assistant
source_description: Citizens and businesses in Portugal often face difficulties understanding legal procedures due to complex language and fragmented information sources. The Ministry of Justice sought to improve access to justice by making procedural information clearer, more accessible, and easier to navigate. This use case involves the Ministry, citizens, companies, and legal professionals, with the objective of simplifying access to information about legal proceedings. The GPJ digital assistant is implemented as a conversational system trained on official justice content and written in plain language. It responds to user questions through natural dialogue, guiding them through procedures, requirements, and next steps. The system is integrated with Ministry information sources and designed to evolve as regulations change. The solution improves comprehension, reduces the need for in-person or phone enquiries, and supports more equal access to justice information. It enhances user experience by lowering language barriers, improves efficiency within the justice system, and delivers public value by making legal information more transparent and accessible.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Blockchain to certify energy services delivery
source_description: Small islands face distinctive energy challenges because they often rely on isolated grids, imported fuels and limited flexibility, while renewable generation requires coordination between producers, consumers and local distributors. BloRin was developed for Sicilian islands such as Favignana and Lampedusa to test whether blockchain-based systems could support decentralised renewable-energy communities and transparent energy-service delivery. The objective is to manage exchanges between prosumers, aggregate distributed resources, support balancing services and coordinate energy flows without relying on opaque or intermediary-heavy processes. The implementation uses a blockchain-like platform for secure data transfer between users, developed with the University of Palermo and industrial partners including Exalto Energy & Innovation and Regalgrid. Tests are linked to Mediterranean island settings and the University of Palermo campus. At a conceptual level, the system records energy production, consumption, exchange and service-delivery information in a tamper-resistant environment, helping coordinate microgrid operations and interactions with electricity distributors. It can also support electric-vehicle charging infrastructure in vehicle-to-grid mode. The expected impact is greater transparency in renewable-energy management, stronger participation by local prosumers, better integration of distributed generation and a replicable model for sustainable small-island energy communities. Public sources continue to describe BloRin as a project being developed and tested, rather than a mature commercial utility platform.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Artificial Intelligence and advanced Data Analytics for Law Enforcement Agencies
source_description: Law-enforcement agencies investigating cybercrime and terrorism must process large, heterogeneous and fast-moving datasets, including online content, digital traces, multilingual material, network information and intelligence records. AIDA was created to provide European law-enforcement bodies with a modular platform for descriptive and predictive analytics that could support investigation and proactive prevention while operating in a secure environment. The objective was to improve the full analytical workflow, from content acquisition and information extraction to fusion, knowledge management, enrichment, visual analytics and operational decision support. The implementation combines big-data processing, machine learning, deep learning, predictive analytics, multilingual scene-text recognition and task-specific analytical tools for cybercrime and terrorism investigations. At a conceptual level, AIDA integrates data ingestion, automated mining, entity and relationship extraction, knowledge representation and visual interfaces so that analysts can identify patterns, links and risks across large datasets. The tools were intended to be made available to law-enforcement agencies through a secure sandbox environment using real data, raising the technological readiness level towards TRL 7. The expected impact is faster intelligence analysis, more efficient investigations, improved situational awareness and stronger ability to detect complex criminal activities. The project also produced work on safeguards and citizen perspectives, reflecting the sensitivity of AI use in policing.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: The Hague uses AI to reduce laughing gas nuisance
source_description: Urban enforcement teams in busy nightlife and tourist areas must respond to nuisance quickly, but reports may arrive too late or lack precise location information. In Scheveningen, The Hague tested whether smart cameras could help detect nitrous oxide, or laughing gas, abuse around the boulevard, where nuisance was linked to parking problems, traffic violations, noise and other undesirable behaviour. The objective was to give municipal enforcement staff timely information while avoiding unnecessary collection of identifiable footage. The implementation used AI-enabled cameras from Avutec trained to recognise nitrous oxide balloons and related paraphernalia, with Monotch’s TLEX platform forwarding detection data to the enforcement organisation. At a conceptual level, the system combines video analytics, object recognition, privacy-preserving event reporting and real-time notification workflows. Smart Cities World reports that no footage was sent because of privacy considerations; only detection data were forwarded. The pilot assessed algorithm functionality, camera accuracy, notification speed and privacy protection during a test day on the Scheveningen boulevard. The expected impact is quicker enforcement response, better targeting of patrols and reduced nuisance linked to laughing gas use, without creating a general-purpose surveillance stream. The test confirmed the algorithm’s functionality and gave a “green light” for refinement, but public sources describe it as a trial rather than full deployment.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Digital identity verification for financial services in Gibraltar
task: Authentication of self-sovereign Digital ID services
source_description: Financial services require robust identity verification to prevent fraud, meet compliance obligations and support trust in digital transactions. Gibraltar’s blockchain-related digital-identity use case concerns the use of distributed-ledger and secure credential technologies to streamline identity verification and strengthen the integrity of financial-service interactions. The operational problem is that financial institutions and regulated digital-asset firms must verify customers reliably, but repeated checks across different services can be inefficient and burdensome. A blockchain-enabled approach can support certified credentials, tamper-evident records and shared assurance mechanisms while preserving appropriate access controls. At a conceptual level, government-issued or institutionally verified credentials can be stored or referenced in a secure digital environment, allowing authorised parties to validate identity attributes without relying entirely on repeated manual document checks. The expected impact is reduced fraud, faster onboarding, improved regulatory confidence and greater efficiency for Gibraltar’s fintech and digital-asset ecosystem. The use case aligns with Gibraltar’s wider strategy of positioning itself as a regulated fintech and distributed-ledger jurisdiction. Its success depends on governance, compliance, data protection and regulatory supervision, because digital identity in financial services involves sensitive personal and transactional information.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Blockchain-enabled land registry in Gibraltar
source_description: Property markets depend on reliable land records, because ownership, transfers and encumbrances must be trusted by buyers, sellers, lenders, lawyers and public authorities. Gibraltar’s blockchain-enabled land-registry use case concerns the integration of distributed-ledger technology into government systems to support trusted digital records and more efficient public-service delivery. The operational problem is that land-related transactions can involve multiple documents, institutions and verification steps, creating time, cost and administrative friction. A blockchain-based approach can create tamper-evident records or certificates that help verify the authenticity and integrity of government-held information. At a conceptual level, the system links official land or property records with cryptographic proofs, enabling authorised users to confirm that a document or register entry has not been altered after certification. The expected impact is faster property transactions, lower administrative cost, stronger trust in land-title records and greater attractiveness for investors operating in Gibraltar’s real-estate market. The use case is best understood within Gibraltar’s wider effort to apply blockchain to legacy government systems, rather than as a standalone cryptocurrency project. Its value lies in using distributed-ledger features such as immutability, auditability and shared verification to strengthen conventional public administration.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Republic of Georgia’s National Agency of Public Registry (NAPR)
title: Blockchain-enabled land registry in Georgia
source_description: Secure land registration is central to property rights, investor confidence and citizens’ trust in government, particularly where land-title disputes or weak records can undermine economic development. Georgia’s National Agency of Public Registry partnered with Bitfury to introduce blockchain technology into the land-title registry. The operational objective was to strengthen the security and integrity of property records by anchoring land-title information to a cryptographic proof. The implementation generates a hash of relevant land-registry data and records that proof on a blockchain, allowing future verification that the record has not been altered. At a conceptual level, the authoritative register remains a government land-registry system, while the blockchain layer provides an additional tamper-evident certification mechanism. Citizens can receive digital certificates linked to their property assets, and officials can use the system to reinforce confidence in registry data. The expected impact is stronger protection of ownership rights, better trust in public records, reduced risk of manipulation and a more modern land-administration service. The project is significant because it was widely presented as one of the first government blockchain land-registry systems, applying distributed-ledger technology to a concrete public-administration function rather than a speculative digital-asset use case.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: E-residency program in Gibraltar
source_description: Digital entrepreneurs and internationally mobile business owners increasingly seek remote access to legally recognised business environments, but establishing a trusted online presence across borders requires secure identity, credentials and public-service infrastructure. Gibraltar’s e-residency idea is linked to its broader blockchain-enabled government-services programme, which aims to modernise legacy public systems and improve interaction between government departments, individuals and organisations. The operational problem is that remote business users need verifiable credentials, trusted access to services and a clear legal environment without necessarily being physically present in the territory. The implementation concept builds on blockchain and distributed-ledger technology to support government-issued certified credentials and improve interconnection between public systems. At a conceptual level, an e-residency model would allow eligible users to establish a recognised digital relationship with Gibraltar, authenticate themselves securely and access administrative or business services online. The expected impact is greater attractiveness for digital entrepreneurs, easier company formation or service access, stronger digital trust and a more competitive fintech and digital-business ecosystem. The use case should be treated carefully because the source confirms a blockchain pilot for government-issued credentials, while the e-residency component appears more as a strategic direction than a fully documented operational programme.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: WHO Europe launched an innovative virtual reality training tool on ship sanitation inspection
source_description: International ports and ships play a frontline role in preventing, detecting and responding to public-health events linked to maritime travel and trade, but high-quality ship sanitation inspection training can be difficult to deliver consistently across countries. WHO/Europe introduced a virtual reality training tool to strengthen the capacity of port health officers and International Health Regulations focal points, especially after the COVID-19 pandemic showed how vulnerable maritime inspection systems can be when travel restrictions and port closures disrupt normal practice. The tool was first tested during a four-day training in Istanbul with 13 professionals from Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan. The implementation uses immersive virtual reality to familiarise trainees with realistic ship environments, technical areas and inspection procedures, allowing them to practise end-to-end sanitation inspection, risk assessment and interaction with captains and crews. At a conceptual level, the system converts inspection guidance into scenario-based simulation, combining visual immersion, procedural learning and public-health decision-making. The expected impact is more standardised training, improved inspection readiness and stronger public-health capacity across more than 230 ports in the WHO European Region and 41 IHR State Parties with authorised ports for issuing ship sanitation certificates. Once fully launched, the tool should help scale specialist training without requiring constant access to vessels or in-person inspection settings.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Assisted Living and Safe Aging Services in the Region of Central Macedonia (Greece)
source_description: Ageing populations create increasing demand for social-care models that help people remain independent at home while reducing isolation and improving safety. The Region of Central Macedonia introduced Assisted Living and Safe Aging Services as a telecare model for elderly people who live alone, have chronic conditions, face health risks or are socially isolated. The operational problem is that older people may need rapid help after a fall, health incident or emergency, but cannot always rely on family members or nearby carers. The implementation combines a 24-hour call centre with trained social workers and psychologists, home monitoring devices, fall-detection systems, panic buttons, outdoor tracking and locator devices. At a conceptual level, the service links personal devices, monitoring infrastructure and human support teams so that alerts can be assessed and responded to quickly. The expected impact is safer independent living, reduced loneliness, faster response to emergencies and greater confidence for elderly people and their families. The service is also important as a preventive social-care intervention: rather than waiting for institutionalisation or crisis, it provides continuous, personalised support that can help people remain in familiar home environments while still being connected to public care services.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Brønnøysund Register Centre under the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries
title: Automated disbursement of the Covid-19 Business Compensation in Norway
context: General economic, commercial and labour affair
source_description: The economic shock of the COVID-19 pandemic required governments to deliver financial support quickly while still preventing fraud, error and misuse of public funds. Norway’s digital compensation scheme was created to help businesses withstand pandemic-related revenue losses through a highly automated application, verification and payment process. The operational objective was to provide rapid liquidity to eligible firms without creating a slow, manually administered grant system. Applications were approved by an auditor and then automatically processed through checks against multiple official sources and registers. At a conceptual level, the system combined digital application intake, pre-disbursement validation, register-based verification, automated decision support, transparency mechanisms and rapid payment workflows. Information about grants was published every hour, applicants could receive a reply within minutes, and payments were made within 72 hours. This design reduced the need for extensive post-payment verification because key checks were performed before disbursement, lowering both administrative burden and misconduct risk. The expected impact was fast crisis support, protection of business continuity, transparent use of public money and reusable capacity for future emergency schemes. The Norwegian case is a strong example of digital-era public administration: automation was used not merely for efficiency, but to combine speed, control, auditability and public transparency during an exceptional economic crisis.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Forecasting Sweeish GDP with Explainable AI
source_description: Macroeconomic forecasting is essential for public financial management, but machine-learning models can be difficult for officials to trust if their predictions are not interpretable. The Swedish National Financial Management Authority developed an explainable-AI application to improve GDP forecasting and help analysts understand the behaviour of black-box models. The operational problem was not only to produce accurate forecasts, but also to make visible which variables influenced a prediction and how their importance changed over time. The implementation used machine-learning forecasting models alongside explainability tools developed in collaboration with a scholar from KTH Royal Institute of Technology. At a conceptual level, the web application analyses the contribution of individual variables to GDP predictions, showing both temporal variation and aggregated effects over longer periods. This allows economists to inspect model behaviour, compare it with domain knowledge and improve forecasting practice. The expected impact is more accountable use of AI in public financial management, better integration of machine learning into economic forecasting and stronger confidence among officials who must interpret forecasts for policy and budgetary purposes. The use case is significant because it focuses on explainability as a core requirement for government AI, rather than treating predictive accuracy alone as sufficient.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: NHS Flu and COVID-19 Vaccines Chatbot
source_description: Seasonal vaccination programmes require clear public information because citizens may have many questions about eligibility, timing, safety, booking and the relationship between different vaccines. The NHS Winter Vaccines Virtual Helper was developed to turn vaccine search into a conversational experience, giving users a single place to ask questions about flu and COVID-19 vaccination. The operational problem was that search results often returned only one answer even though users’ questions were complex or sequential, while misinformation and uncertainty could reduce vaccination uptake. The implementation created a “one stop vaccination shop” that answered common vaccine questions and directed users towards booking their jab. At a conceptual level, the chatbot interprets vaccination-related questions, retrieves trusted NHS information and supports the user journey from uncertainty to action. The expected impact is improved access to authoritative public-health information, reduced confusion, more efficient digital guidance and stronger encouragement for eligible people to book vaccination appointments. The use case is notable because it applies conversational AI to a public-health communication problem where trust, clarity and behavioural nudges are central. Rather than replacing clinical advice, it provides a scalable front-line information channel aligned with NHS messaging during seasonal vaccination campaigns.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Semantic Analyser – Smart Text Search Engine
source_description: Public administrations work with large collections of legal, policy and administrative texts, but conventional keyword search may miss related documents where different terminology is used. Slovenia’s Semantic Analyser was developed as an open-source smart text-search prototype for Slovenian-language documents. The operational problem is to help officials analyse collections of laws, proposals, vocabularies and other public-administration texts by identifying key concepts and relationships between them. The implementation uses natural-language processing to extract characteristic concepts from documents, identify concepts that co-occur, group texts with related content and visualise semantic relationships. At a conceptual level, the tool turns terms into links between documents, enabling users to find related materials, identify missing concepts in vocabularies and compare texts across collections. Users can also search by a set of terms and discover documents connected by synonyms, broader terms or related concepts. The expected impact is more efficient document analysis, better management of legal and administrative knowledge, improved development of public-sector vocabularies and stronger reuse of textual data. The use case is important because it shows how AI can support everyday knowledge work in government, especially in smaller-language contexts where off-the-shelf NLP tools may be less mature.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Goteverse - Expanding Gothenburg's digital twin within the metaverse
source_description: Urban development increasingly depends on the ability to communicate future plans visually, coordinate stakeholders and make city information accessible to wider audiences. Gothenburg’s digital twin, Virtual Gothenburg, provides a three-dimensional model of the city that can be used to visualise development projects, support analysis and improve shared understanding of urban change. Goteverse extends this digital twin into more immersive and public-facing virtual experiences, allowing audiences to visit representations of Gothenburg and explore how future cities can use virtual technologies for services, communication and participation. The implementation uses game-engine and metaverse techniques to transform geographic information and collected city imagery into interactive digital environments. The city’s own material describes Virtual Gothenburg as an 800 km² 3D model based on municipal geographic information, designed to support visualisation, simulation and more informed urban decisions. At a conceptual level, Goteverse connects urban digital-twin data, immersive storytelling, virtual access and digital placemaking. The expected impact is better communication of future projects, stronger public engagement, more accessible city experiences and new opportunities for tourism, planning and co-creation. Gothenburg & Co also describes Goteverse as a hub for shared exploration and notes related virtual initiatives such as Gothenburg Arena in Fortnite, showing that the digital-twin strategy has expanded beyond technical planning into public digital experience.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI-assisted diagnostic and rehabilitative tools for personalised support of children with cerebral palsy
source_description: Children with unilateral cerebral palsy require highly personalised assessment and rehabilitation because motor impairments, upper-limb function and treatment response vary substantially across individuals. The AInCP project, led by the University of Pisa, addresses this need by developing clinical decision-support tools that can help clinicians provide functional diagnosis, prognosis and tailored home-based intervention for children with unilateral cerebral palsy. The operational problem is that conventional care can rely on fragmented clinical observations, periodic assessments and limited real-time information on how children use their upper limb outside the clinic. The implementation uses a multimodal approach that combines clinical phenotyping, advanced brain imaging and real-time monitoring of upper-limb function. Artificial intelligence methods are used to integrate these sources into personalised assessment and rehabilitation tools, supporting both clinical interpretation and home-based treatment planning. At a conceptual level, the system links diagnostic data, imaging features, movement monitoring and intervention recommendations in an evidence-based decision-support framework. The expected impact is more precise functional profiling, better prediction of rehabilitation needs, improved personalisation of therapy and stronger continuity between clinical and home settings. The project also aims to validate the tools through observational and rehabilitation studies, making clinical reliability and trustworthiness central to its development. CORDIS lists AInCP as running from 1 June 2022 to 31 May 2027.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: VR in wound care in Denmark
source_description: Wound treatment can be painful and stressful for citizens, while nurses need practical ways to reduce discomfort without making procedures more complex or resource-intensive. Viborg Municipality tested the use of virtual reality glasses during wound care in its home-care and everyday-rehabilitation services, with the aim of distracting citizens from pain and improving the experience of treatment. The context is municipal healthcare, where wound care may take place repeatedly in health centres, nursing clinics or citizens’ homes, and where small improvements in comfort can affect cooperation, anxiety and staff workload. The implementation uses VR headsets as a sensory distraction technology during wound treatment. At a conceptual level, the citizen is immersed in a visual and auditory environment that draws attention away from the procedure, while nurses continue their ordinary clinical tasks. The project does not replace wound-care expertise; it adds a non-pharmacological support layer to reduce perceived pain and make treatment more tolerable. The expected impact is improved citizen experience, easier completion of wound procedures and better working conditions for staff managing painful treatments. Viborg Municipality reports that the project confirmed the pain-distraction effect indicated by research and produced good results for both citizens and employees. As a result, VR glasses are now being used further in home nursing and nursing clinics.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Aarhus University, Municipality of Aalborg and DigiRehab
title: AI-enabled Rehabilitation in danish municipalities
source_description: Municipal rehabilitation for older citizens requires caseworkers to assess training needs, assistive aids, fall-prevention measures and expected self-sufficiency, often under pressure from ageing populations and limited care resources. The AIR project was designed to support these professional assessments with data-driven decision support rather than replace municipal judgement. With Aalborg Municipality as project owner, Aarhus University, DigiRehab, Syddjurs Municipality and Viborg Municipality collaborated on one of Denmark’s municipal AI signature projects. The implementation uses models and statistical analysis based on municipal rehabilitation data, including information on granted assistive devices and completed training pathways, to support decisions about which rehabilitation measures may be most appropriate for older citizens. At a conceptual level, the system analyses patterns in previous rehabilitation cases and translates them into recommendations or decision support for case managers, with performance measured through improved self-sufficiency and reduced reliance on home help. The expected impact is more consistent rehabilitation planning, better use of assistive aids, earlier fall-prevention attention and improved targeting of training resources. A proof-of-concept was conducted in 2018–2019, while the AIR signature project ran from 2020 to 2022 and delivered a prototype by the end of the project period.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Me@Gis - AI-powered webcams in the Municipality of Messina to enhahnce public security
source_description: Urban areas face growing challenges in preventing crime and ensuring public safety, particularly where surveillance systems and data sources are fragmented. In Messina, local authorities needed a more coordinated approach to monitoring public spaces and supporting police operations. The ME@GIS project addresses this need by creating an integrated urban security infrastructure that enhances situational awareness and investigative capacity. Stakeholders include the municipal administration, local police forces, and citizens. The objective is to reduce crime risk, improve response times, and modernise public security governance through a scalable digital model. The solution integrates a network of webcams, sensors, and data sources into a unified platform that enables real-time monitoring and analysis of urban environments. Advanced analytics support the detection of suspicious patterns and events, while shared dashboards improve coordination between operational units. The pilot nature of the project allows solutions to be tested and refined before replication in other cities. The impact includes improved detection and prevention of criminal activity, more efficient investigations, and strengthened trust in public safety services. ME@GIS demonstrates how integrated digital infrastructures can enhance urban resilience and deliver measurable public security benefits.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Vaxjo Kommun chatbot
source_description: Municipal websites contain information for residents, businesses and visitors across many service areas, from permits and schools to care, traffic, culture and local democracy. Växjö Municipality’s chatbot use case concerns the use of conversational support to help users navigate municipal information and reach the right service more quickly. The operational problem is that users may not know which department, page or e-service corresponds to their question, particularly when municipal terminology differs from ordinary language. The implementation places a chatbot or AI-supported contact layer within the municipality’s digital service environment, allowing users to ask questions and receive guidance in a more accessible form than browsing menus alone. At a conceptual level, the assistant interprets a user’s request, searches or maps it against municipal content and returns relevant links, answers or next steps. The expected impact is improved accessibility of local-government information, reduced pressure on the contact centre for routine enquiries, better user experience and clearer pathways to e-services. Such systems are most useful where they remain tightly connected to official content and where complex or sensitive cases can still be escalated to human staff. The chatbot is therefore best understood as a navigation and first-line information tool, not as a replacement for municipal decision-making.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Syddjurs, DK and neighboring cities map employment service processes with AI-powered platform
source_description: Employment services often involve complex citizen journeys across unemployment benefits, municipal departments, job-search support and follow-up activities, making it difficult for caseworkers and managers to see which pathways are effective. Syddjurs Municipality and four partner municipalities used AI-based process mining to analyse how citizens move through employment-service systems and where delays, detours or inefficient steps occur. The objective was to create a more holistic and effective employment effort by turning administrative process data into maps of real user experiences and predictive insights. The implementation combines municipal data on unemployment benefits, service contacts and departmental interactions with process-mining and predictive-monitoring techniques. At a conceptual level, the platform reconstructs actual citizen pathways, identifies patterns in service sequences and recommends the most suitable route for each resident’s employment search. This allows municipalities to understand not only which services are provided, but how citizens experience the sequence of interventions. The expected impact is better prioritisation of employment support, improved coordination between municipal teams, faster identification of bottlenecks and more personalised guidance for jobseekers. The participating municipalities received DKK 4.1 million from a national innovation fund, and the dedicated project site remains active with resources on process mining, data strategy and evaluation.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Hertfordshire County Council implemented a AI-powered traffic monitoring platform
source_description: Traffic surveys are essential for highways planning, junction design and transport policy, but manual traffic counts can be slow, inconsistent and labour-intensive. Hertfordshire County Council developed an AI-powered traffic monitoring platform with AWS to automate and standardise the analysis of local traffic-camera footage. The operational problem was to reduce the staff time required to classify vehicles, directions and speeds while producing more consistent data for decision-making. The implementation sends video from local traffic cameras through an application built on AWS Amplify to Amazon Rekognition for automated analysis. At a conceptual level, the system processes video, identifies traffic types, direction and speed, records the relevant survey data and then deletes imagery to reduce data-retention risks. Twelve-hour video segments can be categorised much faster than manual review, and the interface is designed to be usable without specialist training. The expected impact is faster traffic surveys, lower administrative burden, better standardisation, improved evidence for transport planning and more scalable monitoring of road use across the county. The case demonstrates how cloud-based computer vision can automate a narrow but high-volume local-government task when privacy and deletion rules are built into the workflow.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Municipality of Aalborg and Municipality of Rødovre
title: AI-powered platform for hospital rehabilitation recommendations in two danish municipalities
source_description: Municipal rehabilitation planning after hospital admission requires clinicians to assess each patient’s needs, available services and likely recovery pathway, but this can consume substantial staff time and vary across cases. Aalborg and Rødovre developed an AI-powered platform to support recommendations for rehabilitation pathways. The operational problem was that municipal staff spent thousands of hours each year planning rehabilitation for patients discharged from hospitals, while historical patient data contained patterns that could help inform future treatment plans. The implementation uses data from around 18,000 previous patients to generate insights on how comparable future patients might be treated. At a conceptual level, the platform analyses patient characteristics, prior rehabilitation trajectories and outcomes to suggest possible treatment pathways. Licensed clinicians then review the recommendations and develop final plans in collaboration with the system, ensuring that professional judgement remains central. The expected impact is reduced administrative planning time, more consistent rehabilitation recommendations, better use of historical data and improved support for patients moving from hospital to municipal rehabilitation services. The case is important because it applies AI to a care-planning workflow where recommendations are decision-support outputs, not automated treatment decisions. Human clinicians remain responsible for adapting pathways to individual clinical and social circumstances.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Graz outfits intersection with smart sensors to improve cyclist commute
source_description: Cycling policy depends on accurate evidence about how different road users behave at intersections, especially where safety, illegal manoeuvres and modal shift are priorities. Graz trialled LMT’s smart traffic monitoring platform at a busy central intersection to collect real-time data and support improvements for cyclists. The operational problem was that conventional sensor systems can struggle to distinguish between cars, mopeds, bicycles, scooters and other users, limiting the usefulness of traffic data for active-travel policy. The implementation uses light-mounted smart sensors and a GDPR-compliant video analytics platform that applies AI algorithms at the edge to classify traffic and detect behaviours such as bus-lane use by passenger vehicles, illegal turns and red-light violations. At a conceptual level, the system analyses video streams, categorises road users, measures traffic patterns and produces data that can inform future junction design or enforcement priorities. The expected impact is better safety analysis, more evidence-based cycling infrastructure, improved understanding of violations and a lower-cost alternative to infrastructure-heavy monitoring systems. The case is relevant because it shows how AI-enabled sensing can be deployed quickly at existing street infrastructure to support urban mobility and climate-policy goals.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Staffordshire County Council implemented AI technology for road assessments
source_description: Road-condition assessment is a core highways function, but traditional surveys can be slow, resource-intensive and dependent on manual inspection or resident reports. Staffordshire County Council introduced Vaisala RoadAI to give its highways team a more consistent and scalable way to assess carriageway condition. The operational problem was that inspectors previously relied heavily on manual checks and ReportIt submissions, which could make it harder to build a complete and comparable picture of defects across a large road network. The implementation allows highway inspectors to capture road video using mobile devices while carrying out their normal work. The RoadAI system then processes the footage and converts it into mapped road-condition data, identifying defects such as potholes, surface deterioration, pavement settlement, standing water, road-marking issues and traffic-sign problems. At a conceptual level, the tool applies computer-vision analysis to ordinary inspection footage and turns it into geospatial intelligence for maintenance planning. The expected impact is faster defect detection, more accurate prioritisation of repairs, improved asset-management data and stronger long-term planning for highways investment. The use case is significant because it embeds AI into routine field inspection rather than requiring a separate specialist survey process, helping road teams update condition evidence more frequently and consistently.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Air quality sensors in Trim (Ireland)
source_description: Local air quality can vary sharply by street, traffic pattern, weather condition and time of day, but many towns have historically relied on sparse monitoring data that does not reflect neighbourhood-level exposure. Meath County Council’s Trim air-quality project installed sensors in the town to generate hyperlocal environmental information and make it visible through a public dashboard. The operational problem was to provide residents and decision-makers with more granular evidence on pollutants, traffic-related exposure and the health implications of air quality. The implementation combines air-quality sensors, the Meath Environment Platform and Trilateral Research’s STRIAD:AIR platform. At a conceptual level, sensors collect local readings, the platform stores and displays the data, and analytical tools help identify trends and potential health impacts. The expected impact is better public understanding of local air quality, stronger evidence for environmental policy, support for behaviour change and improved ability to assess whether local interventions are working. The use case is relevant because it makes environmental data directly available to residents rather than keeping it only inside council systems. It also supports a more participatory model of climate and air-quality governance, where local evidence can inform both public debate and operational decisions.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Sheffield City Council works with VivaCity on AI-powered monitoring of its Clean Air Zone
source_description: Clean Air Zones require careful evaluation because their effects depend on how traffic patterns, vehicle types and emissions change after implementation. Sheffield City Council worked with VivaCity to monitor the impact of its Clean Air Zone using AI-enabled traffic sensors. The operational problem was to understand how traffic on key routes changed during peak and off-peak periods, and how those changes related to air-quality outcomes. The implementation uses seventeen VivaCity sensors along the A61 and associated areas to collect traffic-flow data, classify road users and track changes in movement patterns. This data is then considered alongside readings from existing air-quality sensors. At a conceptual level, computer vision classifies vehicles and movement flows, while environmental monitoring provides evidence on pollutant levels. Combining these datasets allows the council to evaluate whether policy measures are changing traffic behaviour and contributing to community-health objectives. The expected impact is more evidence-based Clean Air Zone management, better understanding of displacement or peak-period effects, stronger air-quality evaluation and improved transparency around policy outcomes. The case demonstrates how AI-enabled sensing can support environmental regulation by connecting mobility behaviour with public-health evidence.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Greater Manchester adopts virtual reality for training on gender based violence
source_description: Professionals who support people affected by gender-based violence need to understand coercive control, trauma, survivor experience and the behaviour patterns that may not be immediately visible in standard casework. Greater Manchester funded the Unbroken virtual-reality training programme to improve awareness and response across relevant professional and support sectors. The operational problem is that traditional training can struggle to convey the lived experience and psychological dynamics of coercive control. The implementation uses VR headsets to immerse learners in scenarios based on survivor accounts, helping them experience situations from the perspective of people affected by abuse. The programme includes different learning tracks, including “Insight” for professional awareness and “Flourish” for support contexts. At a conceptual level, immersive simulation creates experiential learning: users do not simply read guidance, but encounter a structured scenario that prompts empathy, reflection and better recognition of abusive patterns. The expected impact is improved professional understanding, stronger support for survivors, better multi-agency awareness and more effective local responses to gender-based violence. The use case is significant because it applies VR to safeguarding and social policy, where emotional understanding and behavioural recognition are central to service quality.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Virtual reality (VR) application for people living with dementia in Suffolk
source_description: People living with dementia can benefit from familiar, calming and stimulating experiences, but access to meaningful places, memories or environments may become restricted by mobility, care setting or cognitive challenges. Suffolk County Council developed a specialist virtual-reality application to support wellbeing, cognition and communication among residents with dementia. The council’s Digital Care Team based the proposal on evidence that supported immersive experiences can improve quality of life when they are designed carefully and co-produced with users. After a competitive tender, Spark Emerging Technologies was awarded an £80,000 contract to build the platform with people living with dementia in Suffolk. The implementation resulted in Reverie, a VR solution that offers supported immersive experiences intended to help people reconnect with memories, engage cognitively and communicate in a safe environment. At a conceptual level, the system combines VR content, user-centred design, care support and reminiscence-style engagement. It is not a general entertainment device placed in care settings without mediation; the value lies in structured, supported use by carers or professionals who understand the person’s preferences and needs. The expected impact is improved wellbeing, enhanced communication, more personalised care activities and new tools for social care teams. Suffolk County Council announced the launch of Reverie in February 2025, confirming that the project progressed from procurement to an implemented VR product.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: South Dublin County Council's Think Big Space stimulates STEM learning among community members
source_description: Communities need accessible routes into science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics, particularly where young people and adult learners may not otherwise encounter advanced digital tools such as cloud computing, robotics or virtual reality. South Dublin County Council and Amazon Web Services created AWS Think Big Space in Tallaght as a dedicated educational lab for STEAM learning. The operational objective is to provide a place beyond the classroom where students, teachers and community members can explore technologies that are increasingly relevant to future work and public-service innovation. The implementation offers free workshops, monthly events, virtual-reality and robotics sessions, cloud-computing courses and AWS certification pathways for adult learners. At a conceptual level, the facility combines physical learning space, digital tools, structured workshops and community outreach. The expected impact is stronger digital literacy, increased interest in STEAM careers, improved access to high-quality technology resources and broader community participation in future-skills development. The use case is relevant because it treats emerging technology as a civic-learning asset, not only as an operational tool. By locating advanced learning resources in a public-library and community context, the initiative links digital inclusion, workforce development and local innovation capacity.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Cornwall Council brings Newquay Futures development project to life with a VR experience
source_description: Public consultation on town-centre regeneration can be limited when residents must judge proposed changes from drawings, written plans or static visualisations. Cornwall Council used virtual reality to make the Newquay Futures project more tangible, helping residents experience proposals for active travel infrastructure and new community spaces before they are built. The initiative supported public engagement around the future of the coastal town and its investment plan, working with Newquay Business Improvement District, Newquay Town Council, Newquay Town Team and Digital Urban. The implementation created a VR version of Newquay using immersive visualisation, 360-degree images, environmental sound and a cyclist’s perspective to show how proposed improvements might feel at street level. At a conceptual level, the system transforms planning proposals into experiential consultation, allowing citizens to see, hear and navigate potential changes rather than only read about them. After experiencing the VR environment at community events, residents could provide feedback that informed local decision-making. The expected impact is more inclusive consultation, better understanding of spatial change, richer feedback from residents and stronger legitimacy for regeneration choices. Cornwall Council described the approach as giving residents a real insight into the difference proposed changes could make, while Digital Urban framed the experience as a way to make future-place consultation more engaging and accessible.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Eskilstuna Kommun develoeped virtual reality training tool for its Jobbcirkus youth employment program
source_description: Young people making education and career choices often have limited direct experience of workplaces, particularly in sectors with labour shortages or unfamiliar technical roles. Eskilstuna’s Jobbcirkus programme developed a VR tool to make career guidance more experiential and less stressful for students in grade 9 and other residents facing career decisions. The objective is to help users explore industries, post-secondary options and work environments before making choices that can affect education, training and employment pathways. The implementation was developed with Combitech AB and Reality Labs as a 360-degree VR programme, allowing users to simulate career and education decisions and experience work settings virtually. At a conceptual level, the application combines immersive workplace visits, guided career reflection and information about sectors with talent shortages. It can be used by study and career advisers, schools and other organisations supporting young people or adults in transition. The expected impact is better-informed career choices, stronger motivation to explore shortage occupations, and more equal access to workplace insight for students who may not otherwise visit such environments. Jobbcirkus VR app is available for download on the Meta Quest Store, indicating that the project advanced towards implementation.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Virtual reality technology programme used to tackle youth violence in Greater Manchester
source_description: Youth violence prevention requires interventions that help children understand consequences, peer pressure and decision-making before harmful behaviour escalates. Greater Manchester’s Violence Reduction Unit worked with Greater Manchester Magistrates’ Association and Round Midnight to deliver Virtual_Decisions, a prevention programme using virtual reality as part of a wider educational curriculum. The project began with a pilot across 31 schools, involving 1,395 pupils, and focused on helping young people examine the roots of violent behaviour and make safer choices. The implementation places students inside an immersive simulated situation with multiple possible outcomes, then uses facilitated discussion and a 12-week curriculum to explore decision points, consequences, empathy and alternatives to violence. At a conceptual level, the technology creates an emotionally engaging scenario, while the educational programme converts that experience into reflection and behavioural learning. The expected impact is improved awareness of knife crime and serious violence, better decision-making among pupils and stronger prevention work in schools. Following the pilot, the programme was rolled out across Greater Manchester for pupils from Year 5 to Year 8. Later youth-justice resources continue to describe it as a 12-week virtual programme to help children avoid serious violence and knife crime.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Municipality of Härnösand is building a training center that utilizes realistic virtual reality environments
source_description: Practical training for social interaction, conflict management, workplace behaviour and difficult scenarios can be hard to deliver safely through conventional classroom methods. Härnösand’s VR studio was developed as a virtual-reality training environment where learners can practise in realistic simulated settings. The operational problem is that some skills require embodied experience, feedback and repetition, but real-world practice may be costly, risky or difficult to stage. The implementation is based in Technichus Science Center and is linked to Härnösand Municipality’s Learning Centre, creating a shared environment for training, education and development. The VR studio can be used to create scenarios for specific educational needs, allowing participants to interact with digital environments and practise situations such as social encounters, conflict handling or demanding work tasks. At a conceptual level, virtual reality provides a controlled simulation space where behaviour, movement and responses can be observed and reflected upon. The expected impact is more engaging learning, safer practice of challenging situations, better preparation for real-world interactions and a local platform for developing digital education. The use case demonstrates how a municipality can treat VR as part of adult learning and workforce capability-building, rather than as a standalone demonstration technology.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Municipality of Horn created the “360° Horn” website for visitors to experience the city in virtual reality
source_description: Smaller municipalities often need cost-effective ways to promote local heritage, cultural venues and tourism assets to people who may not yet be physically present. Horn’s 360° virtual experience was created to allow visitors to explore the city and associated cultural locations through panoramic digital media. The operational objective is to make the city more visible and attractive as a destination by offering a remote, immersive preview of places such as Kunsthaus Horn and the surrounding urban environment. The implementation uses high-quality 360-degree imagery that can be viewed on a computer, smartphone or VR headset. At a conceptual level, the website converts physical locations into navigable panoramic scenes, allowing users to look around as if standing in the space. This supports trip planning, cultural promotion and digital access for users who cannot visit immediately. The expected impact is stronger destination marketing, improved online visibility for local attractions, wider access to cultural spaces and a more engaging digital presence for the municipality. The use case is significant because it shows how virtual-reality-style content can support local economic development and cultural communication even without highly complex interactive modelling.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Turku Municipality produces Save Turku augmented reality game for resident engagement with local history
source_description: Local history can be difficult to communicate to younger audiences or visitors when it is presented only through plaques, static museum text or traditional guided tours. Save Turku was created as an augmented-reality mobile game that turns Turku’s historic centre into an interactive adventure. The operational objective was to celebrate the city’s long history and encourage residents and visitors to engage actively with historical sites around the Old Great Square and Cathedral Park area. The implementation was developed with CTRL Reality Oy and uses AR to place actors and narrative elements into the real environment when users reach specific locations. At a conceptual level, the game combines geolocation, augmented video content, historical storytelling and puzzle-based exploration. Users follow clues, observe monuments and urban spaces carefully, and try to recover the city’s founding document with help from local characters. The expected impact is stronger public engagement with cultural heritage, more attractive history education, increased footfall in historic areas and a playful way to connect residents with place identity. The case is relevant because it uses AR as a civic storytelling tool, making local heritage experiential and participatory rather than purely informational.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: London Borough of Redbridge addresses root causes of domestic violence with VR training
source_description: Addressing domestic violence requires behavioural change interventions that help perpetrators understand the impact of their actions, yet traditional programmes often struggle to foster empathy and reflection. In Redbridge, local authorities sought innovative approaches to strengthen existing intervention programmes. The objective of this pilot is to enhance offender awareness by enabling participants to experience domestic violence scenarios from a child’s perspective. The implementation introduces immersive virtual reality training capsules integrated into an eight-week behavioural programme. Participants are exposed to realistic scenarios designed to evoke emotional understanding and reflection, supported by structured facilitation. Academic researchers assess participant responses and attitudinal changes. Expected impacts include deeper emotional engagement, improved programme effectiveness and stronger evidence for behaviour change.
