title: Lab.ai: the heart of artificial intelligence in public administration
source_description: Public administrations and local businesses increasingly need structured support to explore advanced digital solutions responsibly, yet innovation efforts are often dispersed across separate projects without shared coordination, training or ethical oversight. Lab.ai was launched by Informatica Alto Adige under a broader strategy for introducing advanced digital capabilities into public administration in South Tyrol. Based at NOI Techpark in Bolzano, the initiative addresses the need for a central coordination point capable of linking research, development and skills-building across both public-sector use cases and local economic actors. The stakeholders include public administrations, local businesses, research partners and innovation leaders, with the objective of accelerating practical adoption, strengthening organisational capability and ensuring that innovation proceeds under clear strategic and ethical guidance. The solution is implemented as a coordinated innovation hub, supported by partnerships with Microsoft and Eurac Research and reinforced by a dedicated competence centre for strategic oversight, compliance and capacity-building. At a conceptual level, Lab.ai connects experimentation, training and application development in a shared framework that allows public-sector and local-business use cases to benefit from common expertise and infrastructure rather than operating in isolation. The expected impact is stronger innovation coordination, improved institutional readiness and better-quality deployment of advanced digital solutions. More broadly, Lab.ai creates value by building a sustainable ecosystem for public-sector modernisation, strengthening skills and governance, and making innovation more structured, scalable and aligned with public interest.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Digital Twin: a digital replica for efficient management
source_description: Public administrations often struggle to plan and deliver services efficiently when information about citizens, territories and service environments is fragmented across multiple systems and difficult to interpret as a whole. This limits transparency, slows decision-making and makes it harder to design services that are inclusive, responsive and grounded in real conditions. The Digital Twin initiative led by SIAG addresses this challenge by creating virtual models of real entities, such as users or geographic areas, to improve monitoring, planning and service management. The stakeholders include public administrators, service planners and decision-makers responsible for territorial and citizen-facing services, with the objective of enabling more data-driven, transparent and efficient public administration. The solution is implemented through digital-replica models that mirror relevant characteristics and behaviours of real systems. At a conceptual level, these twins integrate data from operational environments and translate them into virtual representations that can be used for simulation, monitoring and decision support. Depending on the use case, this may involve modelling individual service users, territorial systems or public-service environments so that administrators can analyse conditions, detect changes and assess options more effectively. The expected impact is improved service efficiency, better situational awareness and more informed public decision-making. More broadly, the initiative creates value by supporting inclusive and responsive governance, strengthening the practical use of data in administration and providing a scalable framework for smarter management of both people-centred and place-based public services.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Automated bus lane and bus stop enforcement pilot with Hayden AI
source_description: Bus reliability in dense urban corridors is frequently undermined by vehicles that stop or park illegally in reserved bus lanes or at bus stops, disrupting service regularity and slowing public transport operations. In Barcelona, this creates an operational challenge for Transports Metropolitans de Barcelona, which must keep buses moving efficiently while also understanding how frequently such obstructions occur and where they have the greatest impact. The six-month pilot was therefore launched to improve evidence on bus-lane and bus-stop misuse and to assess whether a larger-scale monitoring approach could support future operational improvements. The stakeholders include TMB, bus operators, city mobility authorities and public transport users, with the objective of enhancing bus circulation, reducing interference with service and gathering robust information for possible future enforcement action. The solution is implemented on four buses running on the H12 and D20 routes through cameras mounted inside the front of the vehicles and supplied by Hayden AI. At a conceptual level, the system uses computer-vision techniques to identify static violations, such as unauthorised stopping or parking in restricted areas, while avoiding the recording of licence plates or people during the trial phase. No fines are issued; instead, the system collects statistical and contextual data for evaluation. The expected impact is improved understanding of obstruction patterns, better-informed decisions on rollout and a scalable model for supporting faster, more reliable bus services across the network.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Decidim - digital and democratic platform for citizen participation
source_description: Barcelona City Council created Decidim.Barcelona to address a core governance challenge: how to involve citizens more meaningfully, transparently and inclusively in municipal decision-making. Traditional participation processes can exclude parts of the population, limit visibility of how contributions are used and make it difficult for residents to engage consistently across different policy issues. The platform was therefore designed to give citizens a more direct role in shaping the city’s development by enabling debate, proposal submission and voting on public initiatives. The stakeholders include residents, municipal departments, civic organisations and elected representatives, with the objective of strengthening democratic engagement, improving transparency and making participation more accessible through a combination of online and in-person channels. The solution is implemented through an open-source digital participation platform that supports structured consultations, deliberation spaces, proposal management and voting mechanisms. At a conceptual level, the system integrates digital workflows with physical participation methods, allowing contributions gathered through different channels to be managed within a common and transparent framework. Because the software is open source, it can be continuously improved, adapted and reused according to changing civic and institutional needs. The impact includes broader citizen participation, greater visibility of decision-making processes and improved trust in municipal governance. More broadly, Decidim creates public value by supporting scalable, transparent and inclusive democratic participation while giving the city a flexible platform for long-term civic engagement.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: PlatOne - PLATform for Operation of distribution Networks (Italian Pilot)
source_description: As renewable generation, storage technologies and electrified demand become more common, distribution networks need new ways to balance local supply and demand without compromising reliability. The Italian PlatOne pilot, led by Areti in the Rome metropolitan area, addressed this challenge by exploring how a local flexibility market could help manage electricity flows more intelligently. The stakeholders included the distribution-system operator, households, commercial users, technology providers and energy-service actors, with the objective of supporting reliable electricity supply while enabling greater use of distributed energy resources and more active citizen participation in energy management. The solution was implemented through a pilot that connected advanced grid automation and monitoring with flexible assets such as cogenerators, residential renewable systems with storage, smart office energy management and electric-vehicle charging infrastructure. At a conceptual level, the platform coordinated these distributed resources through market-oriented and technical mechanisms that allowed flexibility to be identified, exchanged and used in support of network operations. This created a practical environment in which local balancing services could be tested under real operating conditions. The expected impact was more efficient management of electricity demand and supply, improved integration of renewables and stronger operational visibility for the grid operator. More broadly, the pilot created value by demonstrating a pathway towards smarter, more flexible distribution networks that can accommodate electrification and decentralised generation while keeping citizens and local users actively involved.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: RWTH Achen University - Institute for Automation of Complex Power Systems
title: PlatOne - PLATform for Operation of distribution Networks (Germany Pilot)
source_description: Before local flexibility markets can be deployed widely, core technical components must be validated in a secure and controlled setting to ensure that distributed energy resources, measurement systems and market platforms can interact reliably. The German PlatOne reference implementation addressed this need by creating a laboratory-based environment in which the project’s open framework could be tested before real-world deployment. The stakeholders included RWTH Aachen University, Engineering Ingegneria Informatica, distribution-system operators and technology developers, with the objective of building a scalable and secure framework capable of supporting local flexibility markets and improving the integration of renewable energy into distribution grids. The solution was implemented by connecting key elements of the PlatOne architecture, including the Blockchain Access Layer and the DSO Technical Platform, with a real-time power-system simulator, a prototype Synchronized Measurement Unit and development work on a low-cost phasor measurement unit. At a conceptual level, this environment enabled secure data exchange, interoperability testing and validation of flexibility-service tools under realistic electrical conditions without the risks of direct field deployment. It also helped raise the maturity of enabling technologies before use in European pilots. The expected impact was stronger technical readiness, more reliable coordination of distributed energy resources and better assurance that the framework could function securely at scale. More broadly, the reference implementation created value by reducing deployment risk and strengthening the foundations for flexible, efficient and sustainable electricity distribution.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Pioneering Use of Microsoft Copilot - Barnsley Council
source_description: Barnsley Council introduced Microsoft Copilot to tackle a familiar public-sector challenge: high volumes of administrative work that consume staff time and reduce capacity for more meaningful, citizen-facing tasks. The council began with 300 licences in late 2023, quickly expanded to 2,000, and by January 2024 had rolled the tool out across the organisation. The initiative involved a wide range of internal stakeholders, including teams in finance, business support and social care, with the objective of improving staff efficiency, automating routine work and supporting wider digital transformation without compromising governance in sensitive public-service settings. The solution is implemented through Microsoft Copilot embedded into staff workflows, supported by training, stakeholder engagement and a governance model that includes an ethics board and specific protocols for higher-risk areas such as children’s social care. At a conceptual level, the system uses generative-assistance capabilities within office productivity environments to help staff draft, summarise and organise information more efficiently while maintaining organisational oversight of where and how the tool is used. Early adoption has already improved productivity in several service areas and reduced time spent on repetitive administration. The impact includes better use of staff capacity, stronger confidence in digital working practices and improved organisational readiness for responsible adoption of emerging tools. More broadly, the programme creates value through efficiency gains, more purposeful work and faster public-service modernisation.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Foundry - Birmingham City
source_description: Birmingham City Council launched the Foundry in 2023 to respond to a combination of budget pressure, rising service demand and the need to build stronger internal digital capability while reducing reliance on external consultants. Rather than pursuing isolated technology projects, the council created a collaborative model in which multidisciplinary teams work with frontline staff to identify practical interventions that improve efficiency, reduce cost and enhance the experience of work. The stakeholders include service teams, operational staff, digital specialists and council leadership, with the objective of embedding a culture of data-informed improvement under the principle of “think big, start small, learn and scale quickly”. The solution is implemented as an internal transformation engine that co-develops and deploys digital and automation tools across priority back-office functions. At a conceptual level, the Foundry combines workflow redesign, user-centred development and a portfolio of technologies, including Microsoft Copilot for administrative automation, UiPath for automated redaction, SharePoint-based translation for simple documents in 30 languages, and an AI-powered communications-mining solution that analyses emails and routes thousands of incoming messages to the right teams. These solutions are integrated into day-to-day operations rather than treated as stand-alone pilots. The impact includes faster compliance, reduced manual sorting, lower fine risk, improved staff efficiency and better citizen response times. More broadly, the Foundry creates business value by building internal capability, cutting avoidable cost and fostering a digitally confident workforce.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Buckinghamshire Council: Early adoption of Microsoft Copilot
source_description: Buckinghamshire Council became one of the first UK local authorities to adopt Microsoft Copilot in October 2023, granting early access to 300 staff across digital services, business support, customer service and other departments. The council’s operational challenge was to improve productivity and work quality while also reducing risk, identifying savings and supporting staff wellbeing in a context of growing service pressure. The rollout therefore aimed not only to test a new productivity tool, but also to uncover practical use cases that would align with strategic priorities across the organisation. The stakeholders included staff from multiple service areas, senior leaders and governance teams, with the objective of ensuring that adoption was purposeful, collaborative and well controlled. The solution is implemented through Copilot embedded in staff workflows, supported by a structured engagement model that included a “Dragon’s Den”-style event where teams pitched high-value use cases for the technology. At a conceptual level, this was combined with a governance board meeting fortnightly to oversee implementation, share lessons and address emerging issues. This governance-and-engagement structure allowed the council to pair experimentation with oversight and cross-departmental learning. The impact includes improved staff productivity, stronger collaboration between teams and earlier identification of valuable operational uses. More broadly, the initiative creates value by reducing implementation risk, supporting digital confidence and demonstrating how early adoption can be aligned with strategic public-sector outcomes.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Greater Cambridge Shared Planning: AI-Driven Summarisation for Local Plan Consultations
source_description: Greater Cambridge Shared Planning, a partnership between South Cambridgeshire District Council and Cambridge City Council, faced a substantial administrative burden in processing around 9,500 public comments for each Local Plan consultation. Summarising this feedback manually took approximately 18.5 hours of officer time, limiting the capacity available for deeper analysis, stakeholder engagement and planning judgement. The use case was therefore developed to reduce the time and effort required to process consultation responses while preserving the ability of officers to focus on higher-value planning work. The stakeholders include planning officers, partner councils and members of the public who contribute to consultations, with the objective of making the consultation process more efficient and improving the quality of how feedback is handled. The solution is implemented through a summarisation tool developed with support from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government’s PropTech Innovation Fund. At a conceptual level, the system processes large volumes of consultation text and produces structured summaries in under an hour, compared with the previous 18.5 hours of officer effort. This allows response data to be organised and reviewed much faster within the planning workflow. The impact includes a major reduction in administrative time, quicker turnaround in consultation processing and better use of professional planning capacity. More broadly, the tool creates value through efficiency gains, improved responsiveness and a more scalable consultation process for complex planning exercises.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: The Family Hub in Halton Borough Council: Digital front door in family hub services
source_description: Families seeking support often need timely, clear and accessible information, yet service pathways can be difficult to navigate, especially outside standard working hours. Halton Borough Council addressed this challenge by creating a “Digital Front Door” for Family Hub Services so that parents and carers could access guidance and practical support more easily and without unnecessary delay. The stakeholders include families, children’s services teams and service administrators, with the objective of improving accessibility, simplifying contact with family services and making routine transactions more efficient for both users and staff. The solution is implemented in partnership with Beebot AI as an interactive platform offering 24/7 access to family and children’s services. At a conceptual level, the system combines conversational interfaces with automated service functions, including personalised guidance through chat-based interactions and automated booking processes for appointments. This creates a single, always-available access point that can handle common enquiries and direct users towards appropriate support pathways. By integrating these digital interactions into Family Hub operations, the platform is intended to reduce friction in first contact and routine service access. The impact includes improved accessibility for families, faster handling of standard requests and more streamlined service delivery. More broadly, the initiative creates value by improving the user experience, supporting a more responsive family-services model and freeing staff capacity for more complex cases requiring direct human support.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Hertfordshire County Council: AI road maintenance robot
source_description: Hertfordshire County Council, working with Robotiz3d and the University of Liverpool, set out to address a costly and persistent infrastructure problem: small cracks in roads are often left untreated until they develop into potholes, by which point repairs are more expensive, more disruptive and more damaging to road quality. The objective of the project is to intervene earlier by identifying minor defects before they worsen and by carrying out preventative maintenance in a more efficient way. The stakeholders include highway maintenance teams, local government infrastructure managers and road users, all of whom benefit from more reliable roads and lower lifecycle maintenance costs. The solution is implemented through an autonomous road-maintenance robot capable of detecting and repairing defects such as cracks. At a conceptual level, the robot combines sensing, defect-identification models and automated repair functions so that it can inspect road surfaces, locate issues likely to become potholes and carry out preventative treatment without relying on entirely manual workflows. This shifts maintenance activity from reactive repair to earlier intervention. The impact includes improved maintenance efficiency, better targeting of preventative repairs and reduced likelihood of more severe road deterioration over time. More broadly, the project creates value by lowering long-term maintenance costs, improving asset reliability and demonstrating a scalable model for proactive highway management that can reduce disruption for both councils and road users.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Kent County Council: Using predictive analytics to prevent homelessness in Maidstone and Kent
source_description: Kent County Council leveraged predictive analytics to identify individuals and households at risk of homelessness in Maidstone and across Kent. By analysing data from multiple sources, the council can proactively intervene, provide targeted support, and allocate resources more effectively, aiming to reduce homelessness and improve community well-being.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Lancashire County Council – A strategic approach to deploying AI in transport
source_description: Lancashire County Council is taking a structured approach to a persistent transport-management challenge: how to improve traffic flow, reduce congestion and make better use of existing infrastructure in a context of rising demand, constrained budgets and growing expectations for smarter mobility. Rather than treating digital tools as isolated experiments, the council is positioning this work as part of a broader transport-planning and network-management strategy. The stakeholders include transport planners, highways managers, operational teams and road users, with the objective of improving journey reliability, supporting more efficient use of the road network and strengthening the council’s ability to respond to changing mobility patterns. The solution is being implemented through analytical and predictive technologies designed to support traffic optimisation and infrastructure management. At a conceptual level, these tools use transport and operational data to identify congestion patterns, model likely network behaviour and support decisions on planning, intervention and traffic management. By embedding these capabilities within existing transport processes rather than operating them separately, the council is creating a more strategic and scalable basis for deployment. The expected impact is improved traffic efficiency, better-informed planning decisions and more effective use of public infrastructure. More broadly, the initiative creates value by supporting smarter urban mobility, reducing avoidable delay and building a stronger foundation for data-driven transport management across the county.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Northumberland County Council- FloodAI, using AI to detect flash floods
source_description: Northumberland County Council launched FloodAI to address a serious public-safety and resilience issue: flash floods can develop rapidly, leaving little time for authorities and communities to respond. In a changing climate, local authorities need earlier and more reliable warning mechanisms to reduce disruption, protect people and support a more coordinated response to local flooding events. This pilot, funded by Defra through the £200 million Flood and Coastal Innovation Programmes managed by the Environment Agency, involves council teams, resilience planners and public-safety stakeholders, with the objective of detecting flood conditions in real time and enabling faster operational action. The solution is implemented as a live monitoring and early-warning system that analyses environmental data to identify signs of flash flooding as they emerge. At a conceptual level, the system draws on relevant local data streams, processes them through detection and forecasting models, and converts these outputs into warning signals that can support operational response and risk mitigation. By linking analysis to real-time monitoring, the pilot is intended to shorten the time between environmental change and public action. The expected impact is earlier flood detection, improved readiness and stronger public safety outcomes. More broadly, FloodAI creates value by enhancing local climate resilience, supporting more proactive flood management and providing a scalable model for data-driven adaptation in vulnerable areas.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: North Yorkshire Council: Using AI to reimagine Children’s Social Care
source_description: North Yorkshire Council is exploring how to improve children’s social care in a service environment where case complexity, workload pressures and the need for timely, well-informed decisions place heavy demands on professionals. The council’s proof-of-concept project was developed to address the challenge of modernising case management so that staff can make better decisions, allocate resources more effectively and tailor support more closely to the needs of children and families. Funded by the Department for Education’s Data and Digital Solutions Fund, the initiative involves social-care practitioners, service managers and digital teams, with the objective of improving outcomes while making the service more responsive and better equipped for complex casework. The solution is implemented through a case-management proof of concept built on Microsoft Azure and designed to support data-driven analysis within children’s social care workflows. At a conceptual level, the system uses analytical and decision-support capabilities to organise case information, surface relevant patterns and support more informed judgements about intervention, prioritisation and support planning. This is intended to complement professional expertise rather than replace it. The expected impact is better-quality decision-making, more effective deployment of resources and more personalised support for children and families. More broadly, the project creates value by strengthening service capability, improving workflow efficiency and laying the groundwork for a more modern and evidence-informed model of children’s social care.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Peterborough City Council: Hey Geraldine, a personalised AI assistant
source_description: Peterborough City Council introduced “Hey Geraldine” to improve how residents access information and guidance from the council, particularly in situations where generic web content or traditional contact routes may not provide a quick or sufficiently tailored response. Local authorities increasingly need to offer services that feel more responsive to individual needs, while also managing service demand efficiently. This use case therefore focuses on improving resident engagement and making council information easier to access in a more personalised way. The stakeholders include residents, customer-service teams and council departments, with the objective of providing more relevant support, improving satisfaction and making interactions with the council simpler and more effective. The solution is implemented through a personalised digital assistant that interprets user needs and preferences in order to provide tailored information and guidance. At a conceptual level, the system combines conversational interaction with user-context understanding, enabling it to respond in a way that is more specific and useful than a standard one-size-fits-all information service. This allows the council to offer a more adaptive digital front end while maintaining consistency in information delivery. The expected impact is stronger resident engagement, higher satisfaction and easier access to council support. More broadly, “Hey Geraldine” creates value by improving the user experience, supporting service modernisation and offering a scalable model for more personalised local-government interaction.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: South Cambridgeshire - Contact centre chatbot to improve resident satisfaction
source_description: South Cambridgeshire District Council deployed a contact-centre chatbot to address a common local-government challenge: high volumes of routine enquiries can slow response times, reduce service efficiency and leave staff with less capacity to deal with complex or sensitive cases. Residents increasingly expect immediate answers for straightforward questions, yet traditional contact-centre models often struggle to provide this without increasing cost or pressure on staff. The initiative was therefore designed to improve resident satisfaction while making the council’s service model more efficient. The stakeholders include residents, contact-centre teams and service managers, with the objective of providing faster responses to common queries, reducing unnecessary waiting and allowing staff to focus their effort where human judgement adds the greatest value. The solution is implemented through a chatbot integrated into the contact-centre environment and configured to respond instantly to routine enquiries. At a conceptual level, the system uses conversational question handling and service-routing logic to identify common issues, provide immediate answers and direct unresolved matters towards the appropriate teams. This creates a layered service model in which simple requests can be handled automatically while more complex cases continue to receive staff attention. The expected impact is quicker response times, improved service efficiency and better resident satisfaction. More broadly, the chatbot creates value by reducing friction in frontline service delivery and supporting a more scalable, responsive contact-centre operation.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: St Helens Borough Council – augmenting TEC with AI
source_description: St Helens Council launched its Technology Enabled Care Hub in 2024 as part of its 2024–2027 Adult Social Care strategy and wider “reablement – home first” approach, responding to the challenge of supporting people more proactively after hospital discharge and helping them regain confidence in everyday life. Adult social care services need to identify the right support quickly, plan effectively and avoid unnecessary dependency on reactive models of care. This initiative therefore focuses on improving how Technology Enabled Care is selected, planned and embedded within care pathways. The stakeholders include adult social care teams, people leaving hospital, care planners and digital service leads, with the objective of shifting from reactive support to more preventative and person-centred intervention. The solution is implemented through in-house tools developed with Microsoft Copilot Studio, including predictive analytics used to match individuals with the most suitable TEC solutions and to build cost models for care planning. At a conceptual level, the system combines person-level data, predictive matching and planning support within the council’s digital-care framework so that TEC can be used more strategically and consistently. The expected impact is better alignment between individual need and care technology, improved planning efficiency and stronger support for reablement outcomes. More broadly, the initiative creates value by optimising the impact of TEC, strengthening the council’s next-generation digital strategy and enabling more sustainable adult social care delivery.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Swindon Borough Council: Simply Readable, an AI easy-read solution
source_description: Swindon Borough Council developed Simply Readable to tackle a significant accessibility gap in public communication: producing Easy-Read documents for residents with learning disabilities can be slow, expensive and difficult to scale, even though accessible information is essential for fair access to public services. Traditional production methods often take weeks and cost hundreds of pounds, which limits how much information can realistically be adapted. The council therefore set out to create a faster and more inclusive way to generate accessible documents. The stakeholders include residents with learning disabilities, council communication teams and wider community users who benefit from clearer information, with the objective of improving understanding, reducing production barriers and extending access across more languages and formats. The solution is implemented as an Easy-Read generation tool developed in collaboration with residents and designed to produce simplified documents using clear language, larger fonts and helpful visuals. At a conceptual level, the system automates document adaptation and supports translation into 75 languages, allowing accessible content to be created rapidly while still reflecting the practical needs identified through co-design. The impact is substantial: production time has fallen from weeks to minutes and costs from hundreds of pounds to pennies per page. More broadly, Simply Readable creates value through major efficiency gains, stronger inclusivity and a scalable model for accessible public information.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Tunbridge Wells Borough Council: The Amelia Scott, Collecting Tomorrow
source_description: At The Amelia Scott cultural hub, Tunbridge Wells Borough Council sought to address two linked challenges: preserving historical artefacts more efficiently and creating richer ways for visitors and local communities to engage with collections. Traditional digitisation workflows can be time-consuming and resource-intensive, limiting how quickly objects can be documented, interpreted and reused in exhibitions or educational settings. The project therefore involved museum and cultural staff, local residents, learners and visitors, with the objective of improving preservation processes, widening access to heritage and building new skills and opportunities around digital culture. The solution is implemented by integrating generative tools into 3D-scanning workflows to accelerate and refine the creation of digital twins of historical objects. At a conceptual level, scanning, modelling and digital-content production are combined so that artefacts can be transformed into high-quality virtual representations for immersive exhibitions, tactile displays and virtual-reality experiences. The project also includes training activity that helps community participants develop practical digital skills linked to cultural preservation and interpretation. The impact includes faster and more accurate production of digital replicas, improved visitor engagement and broader accessibility to collections through interactive formats. More broadly, the initiative creates value by opening commercial opportunities, strengthening local capability and demonstrating how cultural institutions can combine preservation, education and innovation in a scalable and socially meaningful way.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Warwickshire County Council: “Access to Food” – exploring LLMs for citizen needs
source_description: Warwickshire County Council developed the “Access to Food” project to better understand how residents, particularly those living in deprived areas, access healthy and affordable food options. The operational challenge was that identifying and classifying local food-related businesses and services manually required significant staff effort and limited the speed with which the council could generate useful insights for policy and service design. The stakeholders included council analysts, service planners and communities facing barriers to food access, with the objective of improving the evidence base for local decision-making while exploring whether new tools could reduce manual workload and support future analysis. The solution was implemented through an in-house experiment using the open-source Llama 2 model to classify local businesses, allowing the council to retain full data sovereignty. At a conceptual level, the project tested large language model capabilities against more conventional data-science methods in a controlled environment, examining performance, infrastructure needs, governance implications and operational fit. Although traditional analytical methods proved more accurate in this case, the pilot showed that language-model tools may still have value for automating parts of labour-intensive classification tasks. The impact lies less in immediate performance gains and more in strategic learning: the project generated valuable insight on hardware, security and governance requirements, while highlighting where future time savings and productivity improvements might be realised through carefully controlled adoption in local government settings.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Wigan Council: QuickAction in adult social care
source_description: Wigan Council introduced QuickAction to address a pressing operational issue in adult social care: professionals were spending substantial time on repetitive administrative tasks, reducing the time available for direct support to residents. Activities such as writing needs assessments, recording meeting minutes, carrying out case audits and analysing survey responses are essential, but they can absorb large amounts of staff capacity in already pressured services. The initiative therefore involved adult social care practitioners, housing teams and transformation partners, with the objective of reducing administrative burden, improving workflow efficiency and allowing staff to focus more on frontline support. The solution was implemented in partnership with Agilisys Transform as a suite of tools designed around real service needs, with social workers involved directly in the design process. At a conceptual level, the system automates core administrative processes, supports case documentation and analysis, and includes an AI chatbot to assist service users and staff. The approach has also been extended beyond social care into housing services, creating wider organisational value. Robust governance arrangements were embedded to support secure and ethical use throughout deployment. The impact has already been measurable, with more than 100 staff days saved, alongside qualitative gains in productivity, consistency and user experience. More broadly, QuickAction demonstrates how carefully designed automation can improve service quality, reduce operational pressure and create a more sustainable and responsive model for care delivery.

organization: Scottish Government’s Directorate for Equality, Inclusion & Human Rights
title: SignPort: Transforming access to BSL interpreters through technology
source_description: Access to British Sign Language interpreters is essential for Deaf BSL users to participate fully in work, healthcare, public services and social life, yet existing booking systems are often fragmented, inefficient and unable to match users with available interpreters reliably. This creates a practical barrier even where interpreter capacity exists, because the process of finding the right person at the right time can be slow and opaque. SignPort was developed to address this access problem, with Deaf Action and Burrotech focusing on choice, control and equity for Deaf BSL users rather than simple administrative efficiency alone. The stakeholders include Deaf BSL users, interpreters, public-service organisations and booking agencies such as the NHS, with the objective of improving interpreter access and making the process more user-centred and scalable. The solution is implemented as a mobile app that matches users to interpreters according to need, availability and timing. At a conceptual level, the platform combines booking logic, user preferences and service coordination into a digital matching workflow that reduces fragmentation and improves responsiveness. The team is also extending the service through additional features, including a fully integrated web version, to make it more attractive for interpreters and easier for agencies to adopt. The expected impact is faster and more reliable access to interpreters, improved user autonomy and a more efficient matching process, with broader value in accessibility, inclusion and service scalability.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Scottish Government’s Directorate for Equality, Inclusion & Human Rights
title: DeepMiner: Transforming business support through data integration
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: The Scottish Government identified a significant structural problem in the design and delivery of business support: information about businesses was fragmented across multiple organisations, making it difficult to generate a coherent view of need, target support effectively or evaluate outcomes across the public sector. This lack of integration weakened both efficiency and policy responsiveness, particularly during periods of economic uncertainty when timely evidence is critical. DeepMiner addressed this challenge by creating a common data foundation that could improve how business support services are designed, delivered and assessed. The stakeholders include policymakers, business-support teams, public agencies and the wider Scottish economy, with the objective of making business data more accessible, connected and useful for decision-making. The solution is implemented through the Data Spine, a platform designed as a single point of truth for businesses in Scotland. At a conceptual level, it integrates and structures economic data from diverse sources, creating a unified and queryable environment that supports insight generation, early identification of economic shocks and more targeted policy responses. Originally founded through CivTech in 2017 and refocused in 2020 on advanced data technologies, DeepMiner has built a model that reduces data silos and increases analytical capability. The impact includes stronger policy intelligence, better targeting of support services and improved efficiency in the use of economic data. More broadly, the platform creates societal and economic value by enabling smarter, faster and more coordinated public decision-making.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Bath and North East Somerset Council
title: ConsultAI: Bath and North East Somerset Council parking charge proposals
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: When Bath and North East Somerset Council consulted on proposed parking-charge changes in 2024, it received more than 4,300 responses and over 18,000 free-text comments. Processing such a large volume of qualitative feedback manually would normally require weeks of officer time, slowing decision-making and making it harder to provide clear, consistent and accountable reporting on what residents had said. The council therefore needed a way to accelerate analysis without losing visibility of the issues raised. The stakeholders included council officers, decision-makers and residents participating in the consultation, with the objective of improving the speed, clarity and reliability of consultation analysis. The solution was implemented through ConsultAI, deployed in partnership with The Future Fox. At a conceptual level, the platform processes large volumes of consultation responses, identifies themes, analyses longer comments and produces editable reports in Excel and Word format, enabling officers to review and refine outputs within familiar working tools. The system completed the full analysis within three days, compared with an estimated six weeks of manual effort. The impact was therefore both substantial and measurable: major time savings, quicker decision support and more consistent reporting. More broadly, the use case creates value by improving transparency and accountability in public consultation, while giving councils a scalable way to handle large volumes of citizen feedback more efficiently.

title: PlaceBuilder - Unlocking community-driven development
source_description: Hanwood Park, one of the UK’s largest planned housing developments, required an approach to consultation that could keep local communities involved throughout a complex and long-term planning process. Large developments often struggle to sustain meaningful engagement, especially when conventional consultation formats are slow to launch, difficult to access or unable to provide timely insight into what communities actually think. The developers therefore sought a more agile and inclusive method of involving residents in discussion about key themes such as sustainability, wellbeing and the masterplan itself. The stakeholders included Hanwood Park LLP, local communities and planning teams, with the objective of capturing broad, representative feedback and remaining responsive to local needs during the planning process. The solution was implemented through The Future Fox’s PlaceBuilder platform, a mobile-first digital engagement tool that enabled a branded consultation to be designed and launched in under seven days. At a conceptual level, the platform combines accessible digital polling, targeted online promotion and built-in analytics so that engagement can be broadened while results are analysed in real time, rather than through lengthy manual review. The impact included strong participation, faster interpretation of feedback and improved visibility of community priorities. More broadly, PlaceBuilder creates value by reducing consultation friction, improving the quality and representativeness of engagement, and giving developers a scalable method for community-driven planning.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government (MHCLG)
title: Strategic spatial planning: inclusive engagement and AI in strategic spatial planning
source_description: In 2020 and 2021, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government commissioned a large-scale digital consultation across the Oxford-Cambridge Arc, a region spanning five counties and 3.3 million residents, to inform the development of a long-term Spatial Framework. The operational challenge was to gather meaningful input across a very large and diverse geography while ensuring that participation extended beyond the usual respondents and generated usable evidence for strategic planning. The initiative therefore aimed to improve both the inclusiveness and analytical strength of spatial consultation. The stakeholders included national and local policymakers, residents, underrepresented groups and planners shaping the region’s future growth and sustainability, with the objective of obtaining richer, broader and more actionable public insight. The solution was implemented through The Future Fox’s PlaceBuilder platform using a two-phase engagement model: visually led polls to attract younger audiences and a formal consultation site for wider participation. At a conceptual level, targeted social-media campaigns were combined with automated analysis of over 66,000 responses, producing spatial heatmaps that visualised public sentiment on themes such as environment, economy, connectivity and place-making. The project achieved a 28% conversion rate, significantly higher than traditional surveys, and successfully engaged groups often underrepresented in consultation, including people under 35 and ethnic minorities. The impact was a more inclusive, data-rich and strategically useful consultation process, demonstrating the value of digital engagement and analytical tools in large-scale spatial planning.

title: Simplyhealth supports their digital transformation with PolyAI
source_description: Simplyhealth, a leading UK health insurer, partnered with PolyAI to develop a customer-led voice assistant aimed at modernising their customer service operations. The voice assistant efficiently handles common FAQs and identifies vulnerable callers, directing them to appropriate departments for personalised support. This AI-driven solution has successfully resolved 25% of calls, enhancing customer experience and optimising resource allocation.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI traffic system in Pittsburgh
source_description: Pittsburgh needed a more effective way to manage congestion caused by a difficult urban road network shaped by hills, bridges and irregular street layouts. Traditional pre-programmed traffic signals were poorly suited to these changing conditions and contributed to delays, excess idling and inefficient traffic flow. The use case therefore focused on improving mobility through smarter signal control, with the objective of reducing travel time, cutting emissions and creating a more responsive traffic-management system. The stakeholders include city authorities, transport planners, drivers, pedestrians and researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, who developed the SURTRAC system to support a more adaptive model of urban traffic control. The solution is implemented through a decentralised signal-management platform that uses sensors and cameras to detect traffic in real time, predict short-term flows and adjust signal timings dynamically. At a conceptual level, intersections communicate with one another while still making local decisions, creating a coordinated network without relying on a single central controller. First deployed in 2012 across nine intersections in East Liberty, the system quickly demonstrated strong results: travel times fell by about 25%, idling by more than 40%, braking by 30% and emissions by roughly 21%. The project was later expanded to dozens of intersections and spun off into Rapid Flow Technologies for wider deployment. More broadly, the case shows how adaptive traffic control can improve mobility, reduce environmental impact and offer a scalable model for smarter urban infrastructure.

title: Chatbot for Mental Health and Wellbeing Support
source_description: North Lanarkshire introduced this use case in response to rising suicide rates and the need for more accessible, immediate and low-barrier routes into mental health support. Many people experiencing distress do not engage easily with traditional services, especially when support is difficult to access outside normal service hours or when stigma discourages direct contact. The initiative, delivered through Hello Lamp Post as part of the council’s “Let’s Talk” campaign, sought to provide constant and approachable guidance in both public spaces and online. The stakeholders include the council, local communities, adults, under-18s and mental-health support services, with the objective of improving access to timely advice, identifying people at risk earlier and directing them towards appropriate support. The solution is implemented through interactive signage in public locations and a linked digital chat platform that offers tailored guidance and resource signposting through conversational interaction. At a conceptual level, the system uses rule-based and adaptive dialogue flows to identify user needs and route them towards relevant support pathways, including urgent services where necessary. The early impact was notable: within 24 hours of launch in Airdrie, one person self-identified as being at risk; about a third of users were directed to critical mental-health support and 23% were guided to emergency services. More broadly, the initiative creates value by providing always-available support, strengthening early intervention and demonstrating a scalable model for community-based mental-health engagement.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Chatbot for Collecting Patient Feedback
source_description: The Royal United Hospital in Bath needed a more effective way to gather patient feedback without overloading staff or relying on low-response manual survey processes. In urgent care and orthopaedic outpatient settings, traditional feedback collection created administrative burden for nurses and produced very limited response volumes, making it difficult for the hospital to gain representative insight into patient experience. The use case therefore focused on improving both engagement and operational efficiency through a more accessible and automated feedback mechanism. The stakeholders include patients, nurses, departmental managers and hospital administrators, with the objective of raising response rates, reducing staff workload and generating more useful evidence for service improvement. The solution is implemented through Hello Lamp Post’s interactive chat platform, structured around the Friends and Family Test and deployed directly in the relevant hospital wards. At a conceptual level, the system automates survey delivery through conversational interaction, allowing patients to respond more easily while the hospital receives structured and analysable feedback without depending on manual administration. The results were substantial: completion rates rose from just 2% to 70%, and each department saved around 300 staff-hours annually, representing staffing-cost savings calculated at GBP 11 per hour. The hospital also obtained richer insight into care quality, with 58% of orthopaedic patients rating their care as good and 5% identifying areas for improvement. More broadly, the project creates value by transforming patient engagement, improving operational efficiency and strengthening service improvement through better-quality feedback.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: ExploreStation - Virtual Reality (VR) in Designing the Stations of the Future
source_description: Railway stations are public spaces used by passengers, communities, businesses and staff, so their future design requires engagement beyond technical rail specialists. ExploreStation used virtual reality to involve the public in shaping the design of small and medium-sized railway stations in the UK. The operational problem was that proposed station layouts, accessibility features and community functions can be hard for people to understand from drawings or consultation documents alone. The implementation created immersive VR experiences in which participants could walk through proposed station environments, experience platforms and waiting areas, and consider how design choices affected comfort, safety, accessibility and integration with local places. At a conceptual level, virtual architectural visualisation turns design consultation into embodied experience: users can form opinions based on spatial perception rather than abstract plans. The expected impact is more meaningful public feedback, better-informed station design, stronger inclusion of passenger and community needs, and improved collaboration between designers, planners and users. The use case is significant because it applies VR to democratic infrastructure design, using immersive technology to make complex built-environment decisions more accessible and participatory.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Virtual Reality (VR) in the Nottinghamshire Hospice
source_description: Palliative and end-of-life care settings need approaches that support comfort, emotional wellbeing and meaningful experience for patients who may have limited mobility or cannot easily access outdoor environments. Nottinghamshire Hospice worked with Digital Urban on a virtual-reality experience designed to bring natural landscapes into the care environment. The operational problem was to enhance patient experience and wellbeing without requiring physical travel or demanding activity. The implementation used a pop-up VR installation themed “Adding Life to Days”, allowing patients and residents to enter a virtual natural landscape with mountains, a pond, meadow, birds, butterflies, bees and other countryside elements. At a conceptual level, VR provides an immersive sensory environment that can support relaxation, reminiscence, emotional connection and temporary escape from clinical surroundings. The expected impact is improved wellbeing, reduced stress or anxiety, richer engagement for patients and families, and a more accessible way to experience nature within a hospice setting. The use case is relevant because it shows how immersive technology can be applied in compassionate care, not merely for training or entertainment. Its value depends on careful facilitation, sensitivity to patient comfort and integration with broader palliative-care support.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Virtual Reality (VR) in the Paxton’s Conservatory at Chatsworth House
source_description: Lost heritage structures can be difficult for visitors to understand when no physical building remains, even where archival drawings and historic descriptions survive. The Chatsworth project used virtual reality to reconstruct Joseph Paxton’s Great Conservatory, a major nineteenth-century glasshouse completed in 1840 and demolished in 1920. The operational objective was to make a vanished architectural and engineering landmark visible again for contemporary audiences, allowing visitors to experience its scale, iron-and-glass structure, planting and spatial drama. The implementation used detailed 3D modelling, historic drawings, archival research and immersive visualisation to create a virtual reconstruction of the conservatory. At a conceptual level, the project turns documentary evidence into a spatial experience: users can step inside a building that no longer exists and understand how its design, heating systems and botanical displays worked together. The expected impact is richer heritage interpretation, stronger public appreciation of Paxton’s engineering innovation, improved accessibility to lost architectural history and a more memorable visitor experience. The use case is important because it shows how VR can revive heritage spaces without physical reconstruction, supporting education and interpretation while preserving the integrity of the historic landscape.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Virtual Reality (VR) in Seacombe
source_description: Regeneration proposals can be hard for residents to assess when plans are presented as maps, drawings or abstract policy language. The Seacombe VR project used immersive 3D modelling to support community engagement around possible future changes to Seacombe and nearby waterfront areas. The operational objective was to help residents and stakeholders visualise regeneration ideas before decisions were finalised, especially in a context where public trust and early involvement were important. The implementation created a virtual experience that allowed participants to move through imagined urban, waterfront and public-realm spaces, including a playful classroom-based experience in which children could virtually pedal through future scenarios. At a conceptual level, VR converts masterplanning concepts into embodied experience: users can see scale, spatial relationships and design possibilities in a more intuitive way than through traditional consultation documents. The expected impact is broader participation, more informed feedback, better engagement with younger residents and stronger alignment between regeneration proposals and community expectations. The case is significant because it uses immersive technology as a consultation method, not merely as a visual presentation tool, helping local authorities gather reactions from people who might not otherwise engage with planning processes.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Virtual Reality (VR) in New Brighton
source_description: Seaside regeneration involves sensitive choices about density, waterfront design, tourism, community identity and public space, so residents need ways to understand proposals before they become fixed plans. The New Brighton VR project used immersive visualisation to support early engagement with the town’s regeneration process. The operational problem was that people may react differently to proposals once they can see how buildings, promenades and public spaces might feel in situ. The implementation created a 3D model and VR experience for New Brighton, including a virtual journey along the promenade on a simulated open-top bus. Ideas from local young people and wider engagement were incorporated into the experience, making it a participatory tool rather than a purely technical model. At a conceptual level, the system turns planning options into an interactive environment where residents can assess scale, movement, views and atmosphere. The expected impact is more informed consultation, better representation of youth perspectives, reduced misunderstanding about regeneration proposals and stronger community influence on masterplanning. The case is relevant because it shows how VR can help move consultation beyond static boards and surveys, making future urban change easier to debate collectively.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Virtual Reality (VR) in Visualising the Future of Farnham High Street
source_description: High-street regeneration programmes need public input, but consultation can struggle to reach younger or less-engaged residents when proposals are shown through conventional documents. The Farnham project used a digital twin and immersive VR experiences to help the public explore proposed changes to the town centre. The operational objective was to make future high-street designs easier to understand, more engaging and more inclusive as part of the Farnham Infrastructure Programme. The implementation created a 3D model of the town centre and deployed pop-up VR experiences directly on the high street, including playful modes where participants could “fly” through the future town using a jet-pack metaphor or explore the space through joystick-controlled alternatives. At a conceptual level, the project converts transport and public-realm proposals into a navigable digital environment, allowing people to experience scale, movement and design implications before providing feedback. The expected impact is broader consultation participation, more informed responses, stronger engagement with younger demographics and better evidence for planners and local decision-makers. The case demonstrates how immersive consultation can make urban-design choices more accessible, helping residents interact with planned changes in the place where those changes would occur.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI4Gov - Trusted AI for Transparent Public Governance fostering Democratic Values
source_description: Public administrations are increasingly interested in using advanced analytical systems to improve policy design and service delivery, yet this raises difficult questions around transparency, bias, discrimination, legality and public trust. AI4Gov addresses this governance challenge by helping policymakers and public institutions develop tools and frameworks that support automated, evidence-based decision-making while protecting democratic values and fundamental rights. The stakeholders include public authorities, policymakers, researchers and citizens, with the objective of making technological adoption in government more trustworthy, interpretable and aligned with frameworks such as GDPR and the EU AI Act. The solution is implemented through a European programme that develops governance models, practical tools and pilot use cases to improve transparency, explainability and ethical oversight in public-sector applications. At a conceptual level, the project combines technical methods for trustworthy systems with policy-oriented design and user-friendly interfaces, enabling public bodies to test how advanced automation can be introduced without sacrificing accountability or fairness. This also supports greater citizen understanding and confidence in the use of digital systems in governance. The expected impact is better-quality public decision support, reduced risk of harmful bias and improved institutional readiness for responsible adoption. More broadly, AI4Gov creates value by strengthening democratic legitimacy, supporting more transparent public innovation and helping governments modernise in a way that is both effective and rights-conscious.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Diputación Provincial de Badajoz (DPB) is a local government body coordinating municipalities to promote economic and social development across the province. As part of the AI4Gov project, the DPB pilot focuses on sustainable water cycle management, covering both drinking and wastewater. The council oversees 63 drinking water treatment plants serving 137,910 residents, along with wastewater treatment. The pilot aims to develop intelligent tools that leverage existing water management systems and data to identify inefficiencies—such as leaks, water losses, or off-hour energy use—enabling technicians to implement non-obvious, day-to-day solutions. The insights will also support policymakers in infrastructure planning, budget allocation, and optimising water services by training AI models to detect system malfunctions.
title: AI4Gov - Trusted AI for Transparent Public Governance fostering Democratic Values (Spain)
source_description: In the province of Badajoz, water-cycle management spans both drinking water and wastewater services, creating an operational challenge in identifying inefficiencies across a distributed infrastructure of treatment plants and networks. The provincial council oversees 63 drinking-water treatment plants serving 137,910 residents, alongside wastewater responsibilities, and needs better ways to detect leaks, losses, malfunctioning equipment and avoidable energy use. This pilot addresses that problem by helping technicians and policymakers use existing operational data more effectively in day-to-day management and long-term planning. The stakeholders include technical staff, infrastructure planners and provincial decision-makers, with the objective of improving service efficiency, targeting investment more intelligently and strengthening sustainable water management. The solution is implemented by building intelligent tools on top of existing water-management systems and datasets. At a conceptual level, the pilot uses analytical models to identify non-obvious inefficiencies, abnormal patterns and possible system malfunctions, translating these findings into operational insights for maintenance and service optimisation. The same evidence base can also inform budget allocation and infrastructure planning decisions. The expected impact is earlier detection of leaks and losses, more efficient energy use and better-informed technical interventions. More broadly, the pilot creates value by improving reliability in public water services, supporting sustainable infrastructure management and showing how existing municipal data can be turned into practical governance and operational benefits.

title: AI4Gov - Trusted AI for Transparent Public Governance fostering Democratic Values (Slovenia - Pilot1)
source_description: Many promising initiatives claim to contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals, but comparing them systematically and evaluating their ethical quality and practical impact at a global level is difficult. The Top100 Projects pilot, led by the Jožef Stefan Institute in partnership with UNESCO’s IRCAI, addresses this challenge by strengthening the application and evaluation process behind IRCAI’s annual showcase of one hundred initiatives linked to the 17 UN Sustainable Development Goals. The stakeholders include researchers, project applicants, evaluators and policymakers interested in socially beneficial innovation, with the objective of creating a more robust global platform that highlights projects not only for technical novelty but also for ethical practice and real-world value. The solution is implemented by enhancing the digital system through which initiatives are submitted, assessed and compared. At a conceptual level, the pilot applies structured analysis and evaluation support to make project selection more transparent, consistent and evidence-based, while giving greater visibility to considerations such as impact, fairness and responsible implementation. This transforms the showcase from a listing exercise into a stronger governance and learning instrument. The expected impact is improved quality and comparability of applications, better visibility for ethically grounded initiatives and more useful insights for organisations tracking innovation for the SDGs. More broadly, the pilot creates value by supporting a more credible and globally relevant framework for recognising technology-enabled projects with genuine societal benefit.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI4Gov - Trusted AI for Transparent Public Governance fostering Democratic Values (Slovenia - Pilot2)
source_description: Policymakers and researchers need accessible ways to monitor progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals, yet relevant indicators are often dispersed across different sources and not always presented in a form that supports rapid understanding or action. The JSI SDG Observatory pilot addresses this challenge by creating a clearer and more usable evidence base for tracking sustainability progress. The stakeholders include researchers, policymakers and institutions working on SDG implementation, with the objective of making indicators easier to gather, visualise and interpret so that they can inform strategy, monitoring and public decision-making more effectively. The solution is implemented as a web-based toolkit that aggregates and displays SDG-related indicators in a structured and accessible format. At a conceptual level, the observatory combines data collection, harmonisation and visual analytics so that users can explore trends, compare indicators and identify areas requiring policy attention. This turns fragmented sustainability information into a more coherent monitoring environment and supports more timely use of evidence in governance. The expected impact is better visibility of SDG progress, improved usability of indicator data and stronger support for evidence-based policy discussions. More broadly, the pilot creates value by enhancing transparency in sustainability monitoring, reducing friction in the use of complex datasets and giving policymakers and researchers a more practical tool for understanding where action is succeeding and where additional intervention may be needed.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI4Gov - Trusted AI for Transparent Public Governance fostering Democratic Values (Slovenia - Pilot3)
source_description: National strategies on advanced digital technologies are now widespread, but understanding how these policy documents address issues such as bias, fairness and responsible governance remains a complex analytical task. The OECD AI policy-analysis pilot addresses this challenge by helping institutions examine national strategies in a more systematic way, with particular attention to how bias is treated in policy frameworks. The stakeholders include policymakers, governance researchers and organisations interested in responsible digital regulation, with the objective of improving understanding of policy quality, highlighting best practices and supporting more informed development of future governance approaches. The solution is implemented through analytical and visual tools that examine national policy documents and generate comparative summaries of how bias-related questions are addressed. At a conceptual level, the pilot combines policy-text analysis, thematic categorisation and visual presentation methods to reconcile large numbers of documents and make differences in emphasis, completeness and good practice easier to identify. These outputs can then support reflection and policy learning rather than replacing expert interpretation. The expected impact is clearer visibility of policy strengths and gaps, better benchmarking across national strategies and stronger support for more ethical policy development. More broadly, the pilot creates value by improving the transparency and usability of policy analysis, helping decision-makers move from broad strategy statements towards more concrete, informed and responsible approaches to governance.

title: AI4Gov - Trusted AI for Transparent Public Governance in Transport (Greece - Pilot1)
source_description: Vari-Voula-Vouliagmeni (VVV) is a municipality in eastern Attica with 50,585 residents and a significant influx of seasonal and weekend visitors drawn to its coastline, cultural sites, and events. The municipality faces the challenge of optimising policies across transportation, waste management, sanitation, healthcare, security, and public works to adapt dynamically to varying citizen flows, including spatiotemporal patterns and ad-hoc situations like severe weather. Coordinating updates across domains—for example, aligning parking management with waste collection—is crucial. Within AI4Gov, VVV proposed a use case focuing on parking ticket monitoring. The aim is to predict citizen flows and design efficient, multi-domain policies to manage people and vehicle movement effectively.
