title: Brainscan Telemedicine - AI for brain diagnostics
source_description: Rapid diagnosis of brain injuries and neurological conditions is critical because delays can directly affect survival, treatment options and long-term patient outcomes. The BrainScan telemedicine pilot in Odesa addresses this problem by using artificial intelligence to analyse computed tomography images of the brain and provide doctors with a faster diagnostic “second opinion”. The operational challenge is that radiologists and emergency clinicians must detect pathological changes quickly, especially when patients may have trauma, stroke-related signs or other acute brain conditions. Manual analysis can take longer, and in wartime or strained healthcare settings specialist capacity may be limited. BrainScan uses a neural network to process CT images automatically and identify possible pathological changes. According to the source, results can be available around five minutes after image processing, allowing doctors to decide on further treatment more quickly than in ordinary workflows. At a conceptual level, the AI does not replace the clinician; it provides rapid image analysis and decision support, helping reduce the risk of missed findings and supporting faster triage. The project was implemented within Ukraine’s national telemedicine strategy, with support from USAID’s LHSS project, and the Odesa experience was subsequently extended to frontline Kramatorsk in Donetsk region. The expected impact is faster diagnosis, fewer medical errors, more timely treatment decisions and stronger access to specialist-style diagnostic support in locations under pressure. The case is significant because it links AI diagnostics with telemedicine and emergency care in a high-stakes wartime health context.

organization: Public Health Center of the Ministry of Health of Ukraine (PHC)
title: AI helps diagnose tuberculosis and other lung pathologies
source_description: Tuberculosis screening and diagnosis require rapid reading of chest X-rays, but radiology capacity can be limited, especially in regions where mobile outreach and specialised services are needed. Ukraine’s Public Health Center reports the use of AI-enabled systems to assist the diagnosis of tuberculosis and other lung pathologies by analysing chest X-ray images. The operational problem is that radiologists must review large volumes of images and detect subtle changes, while delays can slow the start of treatment and reduce the effectiveness of public-health interventions. The AI systems support automated analysis of chest images, highlighting potentially affected lung areas with heat maps and helping identify primary tuberculosis, residual changes after disease, pneumonia, tumours and other thoracic pathologies. At a conceptual level, the tool works as a diagnostic-support layer: it does not replace medical professionals, but accelerates image interpretation and helps clinicians focus attention on suspicious findings. The system is particularly relevant for mobile screening teams, where AI-supported portable X-ray equipment can be deployed in territorial communities and underserved areas. The expected impact is faster diagnosis, reduced radiologist workload, earlier detection of lung disease and improved access to screening outside large hospitals. The case is significant because it shows practical AI deployment in public health under difficult operating conditions, where speed, portability and scarce specialist capacity are central constraints.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: CheckEye: The first AI-based platform in Europe implementing a national chronic disease screening
source_description: Chronic diseases such as diabetes can lead to severe complications when early signs are not detected, and diabetic retinopathy is a major preventable cause of vision loss. CheckEye addresses this problem through an AI-based platform for large-scale screening of diabetic retinopathy and, more broadly, chronic-disease complications. The operational problem is that many patients do not receive regular specialist eye examinations, particularly under wartime conditions where access to healthcare facilities is disrupted. CheckEye enables screening through retinal image analysis, using AI to identify signs of diabetic retinopathy and prioritise patients who require ophthalmological follow-up. At a conceptual level, the platform shifts screening from a scarce specialist-service model towards a scalable preventive-health model: images can be collected through distributed screening points, analysed by AI and used to identify patients needing further care. In Ukraine, CheckEye reports implementation across six regions, including Chernivtsi, Zakarpattia, Vinnytsia and Kyiv regions, in cooperation with the Ukrainian Diabetes Federation under the “Seeing a Colourful World-2” project. The reported results suggest that around 30% of screened patients had diabetic retinopathy without knowing it, while the platform reports 95% sensitivity and 90% specificity. The expected impact is earlier detection, prevention of avoidable vision loss, more efficient use of ophthalmologist capacity and stronger resilience of screening services during crisis. The case is relevant because it applies AI not to one-off diagnosis, but to population-level preventive screening.

title: New cross-government, AI-powered data management asset
source_description: Estonia’s digital-government model already relies on interoperability, secure data exchange and the ability to deliver services across institutional boundaries, but the next challenge is making public-sector data easier to search, connect and use from the citizen’s point of view. The new cross-government AI-powered data management asset addresses this problem by aiming to create a unified, AI-enabled layer for accessing information and resources held by different ministries and agencies. The operational issue is that citizens do not organise their needs according to government structures: a person may need information related to health, education, benefits, family services, taxation or another public function, but may not know which institution holds the relevant data or how to retrieve it. Estonia’s planned tool is intended to reduce this friction by making information from different parts of government searchable and accessible through a more integrated interface. At a conceptual level, the initiative builds on Estonia’s wider approach to proactive and data-driven public services: instead of requiring citizens to navigate administrative silos, AI can help identify relevant information, connect datasets and support more intuitive service access. The expected impact is improved accessibility of public information, reduced administrative complexity, more efficient use of government data and a stronger basis for proactive citizen services. However, the available evidence describes the asset as still being developed, with initial components expected to become operational first and then improved iteratively. It should therefore be framed as an implementation pathway rather than a fully mature, routinely operating national platform
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: ChatGPT Edu into Estonia's education system
source_description: Education systems increasingly need to equip students and teachers with practical AI literacy while ensuring that access to advanced tools is equitable, secure and pedagogically supported. Estonia’s collaboration with OpenAI addresses this challenge by introducing ChatGPT Edu into the national secondary-school system as part of the country’s AI Leap 2025 initiative. The operational problem is that students are already using generative AI for learning, writing, programming and tutoring, but access and responsible-use frameworks are uneven. Schools therefore need structured deployment, teacher support and education-specific safeguards rather than leaving AI use to individual choice. Under the initiative, Estonia planned to provide students and teachers in the secondary school system with access to ChatGPT Edu, starting with 10th and 11th graders by September 2025. The collaboration also includes OpenAI API services, technical support and knowledge-sharing for custom GPTs focused on teaching and learning. Potential use cases include feedback assistance, student support, study assistance and lesson planning, with the aim of reducing administrative burden for teachers and supporting students’ creativity and critical thinking. At a conceptual level, the project treats generative AI as part of national education infrastructure, comparable to earlier waves of school digitalisation. The expected impact is broader AI literacy, more personalised learning support, greater teacher productivity and a more systematic approach to responsible AI adoption in education. The case is significant because OpenAI describes it as the first government initiative to provide nationwide access to ChatGPT Edu across a national education system
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Thinking Machines Lab – Albanian strategic investment in advanced AI
source_description: Albania’s investment in Thinking Machines Lab should be understood as a strategic AI and innovation-policy initiative rather than as the deployment of an AI tool within public administration. The corrected name of the company is Thinking Machines Lab, an artificial-intelligence research and product company founded and led by Mira Murati, the Albanian-American former CTO of OpenAI. The operational and policy rationale is that a smaller economy such as Albania cannot compete with larger technology ecosystems through domestic scale alone, but it can position itself within the global AI landscape by backing high-profile frontier-AI ventures, strengthening links with internationally recognised Albanian talent and signalling long-term commitment to advanced technology. Public reporting indicates that the Albanian government approved an investment of around EUR 8.8 million, equivalent to approximately 1 billion lek or USD 10 million, through the 2025 budget revision. At a conceptual level, the case is less about immediate service automation and more about industrial policy, technology diplomacy and ecosystem positioning: the public sector is using investment as a lever to connect Albania with frontier AI research and potentially attract expertise, visibility and future collaboration opportunities. The expected impact is therefore indirect, including stronger national branding in AI, possible knowledge spillovers, increased investor attention and support for Albania’s ambition to participate in emerging technology markets. The entry should avoid presenting this as a government AI implementation, because there is no evidence that Thinking Machines Lab is currently delivering an AI system for Albanian public services. It is an implemented strategic investment decision in an advanced AI company
source_license: CC BY 4.0

organization: Ministry of Digital Transformation and Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Innovation
title: A new supercomputer and AI factory to boost technological power
source_description: Advanced AI development depends on access to high-performance computing, data, technical expertise and innovation support, but smaller national ecosystems may struggle to compete if they lack shared infrastructure. Slovenia’s AI Factory initiative addresses this challenge by combining a new supercomputer with services intended to support AI research, development and deployment. The operational problem is that companies, researchers, start-ups and public-sector innovators need infrastructure capable of training and testing large AI models, while Europe also seeks to strengthen digital sovereignty and reduce dependence on external computing capacity. The Slovenian initiative forms part of the wider EuroHPC AI Factories network, which is designed to bring together computing power, data and talent around European supercomputers. At a conceptual level, the AI factory is not only a machine room: it is an ecosystem service that gives users access to compute, expertise and support for developing trustworthy and ethical AI models. It is expected to serve researchers and companies, including SMEs and start-ups, and to contribute to national and European AI strategies. The expected impact is stronger Slovenian AI capacity, improved innovation infrastructure, better opportunities for companies to commercialise AI applications and enhanced participation in the pan-European AI ecosystem. The case is significant because it treats AI as a strategic public infrastructure agenda, linking supercomputing investment to industrial competitiveness, scientific research and European technological sovereignty.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Drones and AI to tackle congestion
source_description: Urban mobility around major transport hubs is difficult to manage because cars, trams, buses, bicycles, electric scooters, pedestrians and ferry passengers interact dynamically, particularly during peak arrival and departure periods. Helsinki’s drone- and AI-supported traffic-monitoring initiative addresses this problem by collecting high-resolution mobility data around the West Harbour, one of Europe’s busiest ferry-port areas. The operational challenge is that transport planners need to understand not only aggregate traffic volumes, but also how passengers move between ferries, trams, metro lines, trains, taxis, scooters, bicycles and walking routes. Since 2023, drones have been used above the harbour area to collect bird’s-eye-view video of multimodal traffic. AI systems process the footage to detect and classify vehicles and track movement patterns, including speed, direction and interaction between transport modes. These outputs are then converted into anonymised trajectory data and integrated into AI-powered digital twins, allowing city regulators and engineers to test traffic-management strategies virtually before implementing them in the real world. At a conceptual level, the initiative turns temporary aerial observations into simulation-ready data for urban planning. It also raises important governance questions, since even GDPR-compliant drone monitoring can create public concerns about surveillance, transparency and cybersecurity. The project aims to test soft measures such as route recommendations and incentives to travel at off-peak times, and to trial an app suggesting alternative routes or modes. The wider expected impact is reduced peak congestion, smoother intermodal connections, better planning evidence and support for sustainable urban mobility
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Gemello Digitale Esteso - Milan's Digital Twin
source_description: Milan is developing a comprehensive digital twin of its metropolitan area under a municipal smart‑city initiative. The project, led by the Municipality of Milan with four geoinformation partners, combines high‑resolution aerial imagery, LiDAR point clouds, and terrestrial mobile mapping data to build a detailed dynamic model of the city and surrounding municipalities. This virtual representation supports urban planning, resource management and decision‑making by providing interactive geospatial datasets and software tools for analysis. The digital twin covers about 1,575 km² and includes thousands of urban objects, helping city authorities make better data‑driven choices and improve quality of life for residents and stakeholders.

title: TOURISMO Project - Florence
source_description: Historic city centres face a difficult balance between welcoming visitors and protecting residents’ quality of life, heritage spaces and urban functionality. Florence’s TOURISMO pilot addresses this issue by testing smart technologies to monitor tourism flows in highly visited areas of the city, including Piazza Duomo, Ponte Vecchio and Piazza Pitti. The operational problem is that overtourism is not only a matter of total visitor numbers; it also depends on where people concentrate, how long they stay, how they move and how visitor behaviour affects local liveability. The implementation combines thermal cameras and “sniffer” sensors with AI-based processing to collect anonymised data on pedestrian movement and presence. Thermal cameras installed in Piazza Duomo and additional sensors across strategic points gather information that can help city authorities understand crowding patterns without identifying individuals. The initiative also includes QR-code tools to collect visitor feedback, adding a qualitative layer to quantitative flow monitoring. At a conceptual level, the system creates a real-time evidence base for sustainable tourism management: rather than relying only on periodic surveys or anecdotal complaints, Florence can use data to assess pressure points and plan interventions. The expected impact is improved liveability in the historic centre, better management of tourism flows, stronger support for sustainable urban-tourism policy and a replicable operational manual for other European contexts. The case is relevant because it applies AI and sensor systems to tourism governance in a UNESCO-sensitive urban environment, where public acceptance and privacy safeguards are essential.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: TOURISMO Project - Malta
source_description: Tourism pressure in environmentally sensitive coastal areas creates a difficult management problem for local authorities and protected-area managers: high visitor numbers can damage fragile habitats, reduce visitor experience and make it harder to plan cleaning, enforcement, traffic management and conservation measures. The TOURISMO pilot at Golden Bay, also known as Ir-Ramla tal-Mixquqa, responds to this challenge by introducing a beach-monitoring system designed to provide evidence on visitor flows and behaviour. The site is one of the Mediterranean pilot areas of the TOURISMO project, which focuses on innovative and sustainable management of tourism flows. The operational problem is that overcrowding at Golden Bay affects both the natural environment and the quality of the tourism experience, but without systematic data it is difficult to know when, where and how visitor pressure is developing. The implementation uses GDPR-compliant people-counting CCTV and deep-learning algorithms to monitor pedestrian and vehicular traffic, producing insights on visitor density and movement during peak tourist seasons. At a conceptual level, the system turns the beach into a monitored management environment where real-time or near-real-time data can support decisions on conservation, services and visitor-flow control. The expected impact is better protection of the area’s dune ecosystems and flora and fauna, improved NATURA 2000 management planning, more informed local stakeholder coordination and a stronger basis for balancing tourism with environmental preservation. The case is significant because it applies AI-enabled monitoring to sustainable tourism governance rather than to promotion or visitor marketing.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Open Rights Data Exchange - A Common European data space for copyright
source_description: Copyright markets depend on reliable information about who created a work, who owns or administers rights, what licences apply, and how royalties should be allocated. The Open Rights Data Exchange addresses the persistent problem that rights data are often fragmented, inconsistent, difficult to verify and poorly interoperable across platforms, distributors and collecting systems. This creates friction for creators, rights holders, publishers, online services and licensing intermediaries, increasing transaction costs and weakening monetisation opportunities. ORDE proposes a common European rights-data infrastructure built on the European Blockchain Services Infrastructure. The operational model allows creators and rights holders to register a digital work by linking a content fingerprint with a verified identity and rights metadata. This binding can then be timestamped and stored immutably on the ledger, creating a verifiable reference point for authorship, ownership and licensing information. At a conceptual level, ORDE functions as a trusted rights-data exchange layer: it does not replace copyright law or licensing contracts, but makes rights information more discoverable, machine-readable and verifiable. Platforms, distributors and users could query this information to understand whether a work can be used, under what conditions and who should be compensated. The expected impact is faster licensing, reduced disputes, more transparent royalty allocation, lower administrative burden and stronger interoperability in European cultural and creative markets. The case is significant because it applies blockchain to the governance of digital creative assets, where reliable metadata and identity binding are essential for fair remuneration and lawful reuse.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Digital Ferry Onboarding Experience
source_description: Ferry travel can involve several identity, eligibility, booking and boarding checks, which may be particularly cumbersome for students who need to prove their status to access discounts. The Digital Ferry Onboarding Experience addresses this problem by using EBSI-based digital identity wallets and verifiable credentials to simplify the journey from ticket booking to embarkation. The operational challenge is that passengers may need to manage different paper and digital documents, while ferry companies must verify identity and discount eligibility reliably and prevent misuse of boarding passes. Cyclades Fast Ferries, the University of the Aegean and the European Digital Identity Wallet Consortium are working on a model in which students can store educational identity credentials in a personal digital wallet. During booking, the ferry company verifies the authenticity of these credentials against the EBSI ledger, automatically fills relevant booking information and applies the appropriate student discount. The boarding pass can then be issued as a verifiable credential and stored in the same wallet. At embarkation, the passenger presents the boarding pass from the wallet and the ferry officer verifies it directly. At a conceptual level, the project demonstrates how digital identity infrastructure can streamline cross-border mobility services by replacing manual document checks with trusted, standardised and privacy-preserving verification. The expected impact is faster booking, fewer errors in student-discount validation, stronger security against ticket misuse, reduced paper handling and a smoother passenger experience. The case is relevant because it applies EBSI to a practical mobility scenario linking education credentials, transport services and digital wallets. (ebsi.eu

organization: Italian Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport (MIT)
title: Milan-Cortina 2026: Digital twin applied to construction site safety and transparency
source_description: Large sporting events require complex infrastructure works to be delivered under strict deadlines, intense public scrutiny and high expectations for safety, legacy and accountability. The Milan-Cortina 2026 digital-twin use case applies dynamic virtual modelling to Olympic construction sites so that infrastructure works can be monitored, communicated and experienced in a more transparent way. The operational problem is that Olympic construction projects involve multiple sites, contractors, design inputs, schedules and safety requirements, while citizens and stakeholders may have limited visibility of progress before the venues and infrastructure are completed. The implementation described by the Italian Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport integrates design data, sensors and 3D models into a digital twin of the infrastructure, creating an interactive representation that can be updated in real time. At a conceptual level, the digital twin acts both as a construction-management tool and as a public-transparency interface: technical teams can follow the evolution of works, while the public can access immersive experiences that allow them to “enter” the construction sites virtually. The expected impact is more efficient monitoring of works, improved oversight of construction progress, stronger safety and risk-management capacity, and a clearer public narrative about the Olympic infrastructure legacy. The case is relevant because it connects digital-twin technology not only with engineering control, but also with civic transparency around major public investment.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Utrecht Digital Twin
source_description: Urban planning in dense and climate-exposed cities increasingly requires tools that can connect spatial development, infrastructure constraints, climate adaptation and citizen evidence before decisions are implemented in the physical environment. Utrecht’s digital twin addresses this need by providing an interactive 3D model of the city that brings together buildings, parks, above-ground urban form, underground infrastructure and climate-related data. The operational problem is that planning decisions often require several types of information that climate-related data. The operational problem is that planning decisions often require several types of information that are not naturally visible together: a proposed surface-level intervention may conflict with underground utilities, while green-space choices may need to respond to heat-island patterns or neighbourhood-level climate evidence. Utrecht’s model allows city officials, researchers and residents to visualise planned changes, assess environmental impacts and test urban-design scenarios before implementation. The twin can be described as a “living data platform” used collaboratively by the municipality, knowledge institutions, technology companies and local communities. Also, residents from four neighbourhoods contributed local climate data on temperature variation, humidity and heat hotspots, helping to create a comprehensive heat map and inform climate-adaptation planning. The expected impact is faster and better-informed infrastructure decision-making, stronger integration of above- and below-ground planning, more evidence-based tree planting and cooling measures, and greater citizen participation in shaping climate-resilient urban space
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Digital Twin for Monte Carlo Station
source_description: Railway stations are complex public environments where passenger flows, energy performance, building systems, safety, maintenance and emergency planning need to be managed together. The Monte-Carlo Station digital twin applies AI, simulation and sensor integration to support smarter operation of transport infrastructure. The operational problem is that station managers need to understand how people, heat, airflow, equipment and building systems interact in real time, but traditional facility-management systems often treat these elements separately. SNCF Gares & Connexions partnered with Akila and NVIDIA to deploy a real-time AI and simulation platform at Monte-Carlo train station, using Akila’s digital-twin platform and NVIDIA Omniverse technologies. At a conceptual level, the system merges several computational layers: a 3D digital twin for simulation, AI training based on historical and real-time data, and AI agents that can generate operational insights from cross-system analytics. The platform ingests data such as crowd movement, solar heating, airflow and IoT sensor feeds, allowing operators to visualise and interact with station conditions. The expected impact is better energy management, preventive maintenance, reduced intervention times, lower downtime, improved emergency simulation and new safety, security and crowd-control capabilities. The case is significant because it presents the station as a “physical AI” environment where built infrastructure can be continuously simulated, analysed and optimised rather than managed only through static building information.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: AI-Powered Digital Twin of the Ocean
source_description: Ocean governance requires the ability to understand how climate change, pollution, coastal erosion, biodiversity loss and human activity may affect marine systems over different timescales. The European Digital Twin of the Ocean provides an AI-powered platform for exploring “what-if” scenarios and translating complex marine data into actionable intelligence. The operational problem is that policymakers, environmental agencies, researchers and communities need to anticipate future ocean conditions, but relevant information is spread across satellite observations, in-situ measurements, numerical models and specialised marine services. The EU DTO integrates data from the Copernicus Marine Service, EMODnet and other sources, combining them with artificial intelligence and advanced GPU computing. At a conceptual level, the platform creates a dynamic virtual representation of marine systems that can simulate scenarios such as Sargassum drift, turtle movements and fishing-risk exposure, coastal erosion protection, plastic-pollution drift and local coastal-risk projections. AI models can accelerate forecasting, producing results in seconds rather than hours and improving ocean-current prediction accuracy. The expected impact is more informed marine policy, better coastal and biodiversity planning, stronger pollution response, increased transparency and wider access to ocean intelligence as a public good. The case is significant because it treats digital twins as decision infrastructure for planetary-scale environmental governance, linking scientific modelling with practical policy and community use.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: TWIN4DEM: Strengthening Democratic Resilience Through Digital Twins
source_description: Democratic backsliding is difficult to analyse because it develops through complex interactions between institutions, political actors, citizens, media systems, legal frameworks and informal norms. TWIN4DEM addresses this challenge by using digital twin technology and computational social science to prototype dynamic representations of democratic systems in Czechia, France, Hungary and the Netherlands. The operational problem is that traditional democracy-monitoring tools can identify institutional deterioration, but they often struggle to simulate how different drivers of democratic erosion interact over time or how specific policy interventions might strengthen resilience. TWIN4DEM therefore brings together political scientists, computational social scientists, humanities scholars, technologists and democracy stakeholders to model the pathways leading to executive aggrandisement and threats to rule-of-law institutions. At a conceptual level, the project treats democratic systems as complex adaptive systems that can be represented through data aggregation, natural-language processing, agent-based modelling and dynamic simulation. These digital twins are intended to help researchers and stakeholders test hypotheses, simulate policy scenarios and anticipate democratic risks before they become entrenched. The project also emphasises GDPR-compliant, open and FAIR tools, participatory engagement with policymakers and civil society, and the creation of an open-source community around democracy research. The expected impact is stronger analytical capacity for identifying early warning signs of democratic decline, more evidence-based policy responses, and improved democratic resilience across Europe. The case is significant because it extends digital twin methods beyond physical infrastructure into institutional and political systems.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Dryads - AI-powered platform to manage forest resilience and mitigate climate change impacts
source_description: Wildfires are becoming more frequent and severe in Mediterranean regions, creating urgent pressure for better early warning, prevention and operational response. Dryads addresses this challenge by developing an AI-powered environmental-monitoring platform for forest resilience and wildfire-risk management in Greece. The operational problem is that fire risk is shaped by many interacting factors, including weather, microclimate, vegetation, human activity, terrain, sensor signals and real-time visual information. Traditional monitoring approaches may not combine these data sources quickly enough to detect danger, assess vulnerability or predict how a fire could evolve. Dryads is a cooperation project between the SCAN Laboratory of the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens and the Greek Ministry of Environment and Energy, funded by ICLEI with support from Google.org. The platform uses multimodal sensing and AI to extract microclimate profiles, identify anthropogenic risk factors, monitor fire outbreaks and predict fire evolution. At a conceptual level, the system combines IoT sensors, satellite imagery, weather data, real-time video streams and geospatial modelling into an AI-enabled forest-management environment. The expected impact is earlier wildfire detection, more accurate risk assessment, improved prevention planning, stronger protection for communities and better climate-adaptation capacity for forests. The case is significant because it moves wildfire governance from reactive response towards continuous sensing and predictive forest-resilience management.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Valencia shows how integrated geospatial systems can be used to build AI-empowered cities
source_description: Extreme rainfall and flash floods create urgent information needs for emergency services, especially when roads, infrastructure and affected communities are difficult or dangerous to access. The Valencia case concerns the use of drones, scientific expertise and high-resolution geospatial information after the DANA event that struck the province on 29 October 2024. The operational problem was that emergency responders needed to assess damage rapidly, locate debris and vehicles, identify pollution and infrastructure impacts, and support decision-making in areas where ground access was constrained. CSIC activated its Disaster and Emergency Advisory Group on 30 October 2024, mobilising around 200 professionals from multiple research centres and deploying drones in the Barranco del Poyo and nearby municipalities such as Paiporta, Picanya, Catarroja and Massanassa. The implementation used low-altitude drone flights to collect high-resolution images, which were then used to detect dragged vehicles, contaminating waste and infrastructure damage, as well as to support three-dimensional modelling of affected areas. At a conceptual level, the case illustrates how integrated geospatial systems can turn emergency data into operational intelligence, giving responders and planners a rapid spatial understanding of disaster impacts. The expected impact is faster situational assessment, better prioritisation of emergency action, stronger scientific support for civil protection and improved preparation for future climate-related disasters. The case should be framed as emergency-response geospatial intelligence rather than as a fully institutionalised city digital twin unless stronger municipal evidence is added.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Nottingham shows how integrated geospatial systems can be used to build AI-empowered cities
source_description: Urban regeneration requires planners, developers, elected officials and residents to understand how proposed projects will affect the physical city before construction begins. Nottingham City Council’s digital-twin work uses 3D geospatial modelling to support planning, redevelopment and public engagement. The operational problem is that traditional two-dimensional drawings and isolated planning documents can make it difficult to assess the visual, spatial and cumulative effects of new development, particularly across a city centre undergoing major renewal. Nottingham’s approach combines a 3D object model, real-world scans of buildings and location-specific planning data, using ArcGIS Urban and related GIS technology. At a conceptual level, the digital twin acts as a shared planning environment: it allows planners to visualise existing conditions, test development proposals, discuss schemes more interactively with developers and communicate future scenarios in a way that is easier for non-specialists to understand. The expected impact is a faster planning process, better-quality discussions with applicants, improved transparency, stronger investor confidence and more accessible public consultation. The case is relevant because it shows how a city-wide 3D model can become a practical planning tool rather than a purely visual showcase. It also demonstrates that AI-empowered or digitally enabled cities often depend first on high-quality geospatial data infrastructure, into which more advanced analytics and simulation functions can later be integrated.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Digital Twin for the Reconstruction of Ukraine
source_description: Reconstruction after large-scale destruction requires rapid damage assessment, transparent cost estimation, scenario comparison and coordination between municipalities, citizens, national authorities and international donors. The European Commission’s Digital Twin for the Reconstruction of Ukraine is being developed to support Ukrainian authorities across the full reconstruction cycle. The operational problem is that damage information can come from many sources, including satellite imagery, drone footage and written inspection reports, while planners need reliable and comparable assessments at building, neighbourhood and city scale. The planned platform will generate 3D virtual replicas of Ukrainian cities and use AI models to categorise damage, compare reconstruction strategies and calculate costs. At a conceptual level, the digital twin functions as a reconstruction-planning environment: it brings together spatial imagery, inspection data, AI-based damage analysis, scenario generation and financial estimation so that different rebuilding options can be evaluated against cost and policy objectives. The expected impact is faster and more consistent assessment of damage, more transparent reconstruction planning, improved municipal decision-making and stronger accountability to citizens and donors. The first phase will focus on residential buildings, with potential later extension to infrastructure such as rail, roads, bridges and energy substations. The case is significant because it applies AI-enabled digital twins to post-war reconstruction, where speed, accuracy, public trust and financial accountability are essential.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: CretanPass
source_description: Tourism destinations need to streamline visitor services while maintaining trust, data security and efficient coordination across hotels, activity providers and local experiences. CretanPass is described in the available source as a blockchain-based tourism solution for Crete that provides tamper-proof digital identities and a unified wallet for tourists. The operational problem is that hotel check-in, activity booking and verification of visitor information can create repetitive administrative work, delays at reception desks and errors in manual data handling. In the described model, travellers would use a digital identity and wallet to simplify interactions across the island, allowing hotels and service providers to verify information more efficiently and reduce duplicated paperwork. At a conceptual level, blockchain is used as a trust layer for identity and transaction verification: the visitor’s credentials and booking-related information can be presented in a way that is harder to tamper with and easier to reuse across services. The expected impact is faster check-in, fewer administrative errors, improved guest satisfaction and smoother integration of tourism services. However, the evidence base for this case is weak. The available source is a secondary market article rather than an official public-administration, project or technology-provider source, and I did not find independent confirmation that CretanPass is operated by the Cretan Government or implemented at scale. For catalogue purposes, the case should therefore be treated cautiously and not presented as a confirmed public-sector government deployment unless a stronger source is added.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: Random Red Ltd. - Measurements and Digital Calibration Certificates
source_description: Scientific measurement, calibration and conformity-assessment processes depend on trust in the credentials of laboratories, instruments and certification bodies. Across borders, this trust can be slowed by manual verification, paper certificates, fragmented databases, semantic differences and uncertainty about whether a laboratory or instrument credential is valid. Random Red Ltd.’s EBSI use case addresses these problems by applying blockchain-based verifiable credentials to metrology and calibration. The operational challenge is that traditional certification and accreditation processes can be lengthy, costly and vulnerable to human error or data manipulation, while users often lack an immediate view of certificate or accreditation status. The proposed infrastructure combines digital wallets, verifiable credentials and blockchain verification through the European Blockchain Services Infrastructure. At a conceptual level, national accreditation bodies, laboratories and companies can issue, store, present and verify calibration certificates and laboratory credentials in machine-readable form. For example, a laboratory technician can receive a laboratory-accreditation credential, issue a digital calibration certificate for an instrument, and allow a company or authority in another Member State to verify the certificate against the EBSI ledger. The expected impact is faster cross-border recognition, reduced administrative overhead, stronger transparency, greater resistance to fraud and improved trust in precision-dependent industries. The case is significant because it applies blockchain to a narrow but economically important public-interest function: reliable measurement underpins trade, safety, consumer protection, health and environmental monitoring.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: e-Origin - Building the foundation of a cross-border e-commerce verification services for customs declarations using EBSI
source_description: Cross-border e-commerce creates large volumes of parcels and customs declarations, making it difficult for customs authorities, marketplaces, sellers and brokers to verify transaction data quickly and reliably. e-Origin addresses this problem by using EBSI-based verifiable credentials and digital wallets to strengthen trust in commercial and shipment information used for customs procedures. The operational challenge is that fraud can occur through undervaluation, incorrect origin information, false declarations or misuse of IOSS numbers, while legitimate sellers and brokers also face delays, penalties and administrative friction when data are incomplete or hard to verify. e-Origin proposes a blockchain-based trust framework where relevant actors can issue, hold and verify credentials related to shipments, commercial transactions and compliance data. At a conceptual level, the system turns customs-relevant information into structured credentials that can be checked by authorised parties without relying solely on paper documentation or repeated manual verification. Customs brokers can receive and present trusted data, online sellers and marketplaces can demonstrate compliance more efficiently, and authorities can improve auditability. The expected impact is faster clearance, reduced fraud risk, lower administrative burden, fewer disputes and a more transparent e-commerce import ecosystem. The case is significant because it applies blockchain to a concrete Single Market and customs-control bottleneck: how to verify high-volume parcel data across borders while preserving interoperability and trust. It should be framed as a customs-compliance infrastructure pilot rather than a fully operational EU-wide service.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: TRACE4EU - Building the foundation of traceable seafood supply-chain infrastructure
source_description: Seafood supply chains require reliable traceability because illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, mislabelling and weak documentation can undermine food safety, sustainability and consumer trust. TRACE4EU Seafood Tracing uses the European Blockchain Services Infrastructure to build a traceability model for seafood products, with a focus on Norwegian king crab and related supply-chain actors. The operational problem is that information about catch origin, fisher identity, product handling, customs clearance, packaging, transport and final sale may be stored in separate systems or exchanged through documents that are hard to verify. TRACE4EU uses verifiable credentials, QR codes and blockchain timestamping to create an auditable chain of events for seafood products. At a conceptual level, each step in the product journey can be recorded and linked: a fisher receives an identity credential, catch information is registered, product and sales-order credentials are issued, packaging and customs credentials are added, and downstream buyers or consumers can verify provenance against the ledger. This creates a digital traceability layer that supports authorities, intermediaries, retailers and end customers. The expected impact is stronger detection of illegal fishing, improved confidence in catch certificates, better food-safety oversight, more transparent supply-chain documentation and support for future Digital Product Passport capabilities. The case is relevant because it applies EBSI to supply-chain integrity in a sector where public regulation, market trust and environmental sustainability are closely connected. It should be treated as an EBSI pilot infrastructure case rather than a fully scaled operational system.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: OnePass: SME Financing
context: Executive and legislative organs, financial and fiscal affairs, external affairs.
source_description: Innovative SMEs and start-ups often struggle to access cross-border financing because investors, public funding bodies and support organisations need to verify business credibility, eligibility, documents, due-diligence information and “investability” before committing resources. OnePass SME Financing addresses this problem by proposing a verifiable-credentials framework for start-ups, investors and trusted operators in the European innovation ecosystem. The operational problem is that investment readiness data are often fragmented across incubators, accelerators, public agencies, funders and company documents, creating repeated checks and slow onboarding. OnePass uses EBSI to create a trusted framework in which SMEs can hold and present digital credentials, while investors and funding intermediaries can verify them more efficiently. At a conceptual level, the model turns business credentials into reusable, tamper-resistant digital proofs: rather than repeatedly submitting the same documents to different funding actors, an SME can build a trusted digital profile that demonstrates relevant attributes such as participation in recognised incubators, eligibility for funding, or verification by trusted service operators. The expected impact is lower due-diligence friction, reduced transaction costs, faster cross-border investment, improved trust between investors and SMEs, and more scalable support for European innovation. The case is significant because it applies blockchain-based identity and credentials to financing rather than to token speculation. Its public value lies in strengthening the European start-up support ecosystem, especially where cross-border investment is limited by trust and verification barriers. It should be treated as a pilot or standard-building use case rather than a fully deployed financing marketplace.

title: LUMI AI Supercomputer and High-Performance Computing (HPC)
source_description: AI development increasingly depends on access to computing resources that exceed the capacity of ordinary organisational IT systems, especially when models require large-scale training, simulation, optimisation or processing of sensitive scientific and industrial datasets. The LUMI AI Factory addresses this need by combining one of Europe’s most powerful supercomputing environments with expert support, curated datasets and an innovation ecosystem for companies, researchers and public-sector actors. Hosted by CSC in Kajaani, Finland, LUMI provides AI-optimised computing capacity for users working in sectors such as manufacturing, healthcare, language technologies, digital twins and climate research. The operational problem is that many organisations have promising AI use cases but lack the infrastructure, expertise or data pipelines needed to test and scale them responsibly. The LUMI AI Factory therefore functions as an enabling platform rather than a single AI application: it gives users access to high-performance computing, tailored training, expert services and “Datasets as a Service”, including Finnish and Swedish speech data, pathology imaging and European web content. At a conceptual level, it brings together compute, data and human expertise so that AI models can be trained, evaluated and deployed more effectively. The expected impact is faster experimentation, stronger AI adoption by SMEs and start-ups, improved research capacity, better support for public-sector innovation and stronger European technological sovereignty in AI and high-performance computing.
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: L-AIF - Luxembourg AI Factory
source_description: Advanced AI development requires secure computing capacity, reliable access to data, specialist support and governance conditions that allow companies and public institutions to train, fine-tune and deploy models responsibly. The Luxembourg AI Factory addresses this challenge by creating a trusted national AI infrastructure built around MeluXina-AI, an AI-optimised supercomputer intended to support large-scale model training and AI services. The operational problem is that start-ups, SMEs, researchers and public-sector organisations may lack access to the compute power, datasets, financial instruments and compliance support needed to move from experimentation to production-grade AI. L-AIF is designed to provide end-to-end AI services, tailored support for adopters, secure supercomputing access and high-quality datasets, with a focus on sectors where Luxembourg has strategic strengths, including finance, space, cybersecurity and the green economy. At a conceptual level, the AI Factory acts as a national AI adoption platform: it combines infrastructure, data access, research expertise, business engagement and skills development in one coordinated ecosystem. L-AIF is supported by a consortium of LuxProvide, Luxinnovation, the Luxembourg National Data Service, LIST and the University of Luxembourg, with LuxProvide as coordinator. The expected impact is stronger national digital transformation, more secure and trusted AI adoption, improved access for start-ups and SMEs, and better integration of Luxembourg into the European network of AI Factories. The case is relevant because it treats AI compute, data governance and support services as strategic public-interest infrastructure
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: HammerHAI - New AI-optimised Supercomputer
source_description: Industrial and scientific AI adoption depends on more than access to models: organisations need high-performance computing, suitable datasets, open-source tools, technical expertise and support across the full AI lifecycle. HammerHAI addresses this need by establishing Germany’s AI Factory for manufacturing, engineering and research, coordinated by the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart and operated by a consortium of German academic research centres. The operational problem is that SMEs, start-ups, industrial users and academic researchers may know where AI could create value, but lack the computing infrastructure or specialist support needed to train, scale and deploy robust applications. HammerHAI provides access to hardware, tools, training and personalised consulting, including a “Concierge Service” intended to connect users with resources, knowledge and partners. Its sectoral positioning is particularly relevant for manufacturing and engineering, where AI can support simulation, optimisation, predictive maintenance, product development and research workflows. At a conceptual level, HammerHAI is designed as a one-stop AI adoption environment: it combines high-performance computing systems, data-management capabilities, open-source software, pre-trained models, datasets, training curricula and an expertise network. The initiative also plans to host a cloud-accessible, AI-optimised supercomputer at HLRS, with data handling framed as secure and compliant with the European AI Act. The expected impact is lower barriers to industrial AI adoption, faster development of applied AI services and stronger European capacity for trustworthy, scalable AI in research and industry
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: BRAIN++ New AI-optimised Supercomputer
source_description: Bulgaria’s BRAIN++ initiative is designed to strengthen the country’s position in the European AI ecosystem by combining a new AI-optimised supercomputer with a national AI hub for government, education and private-sector users. The operational problem is that advanced AI development requires infrastructure, talent, domain expertise and support services that individual organisations often cannot assemble alone. BRAIN++ responds by creating a modern GPU-based AI data centre in Sofia, linked to Discoverer++, a next-generation supercomputer tailored for AI workloads, and a broader Bulgarian AI Factory offering one-stop-shop support for responsible AI adoption. The initiative is led by INSAIT in collaboration with Sofia Tech Park and has a reported value of EUR 90 million. At a conceptual level, BRAIN++ acts as both infrastructure and ecosystem: it will provide compute capacity while also supporting Bulgarian-language large language models, robotics AI, space-observation AI, product manufacturing, trustworthy AI compliance tools, federated AI data lakes and collaborative physical and virtual workspaces through the BulgAI Sandbox. The expected impact is to support start-ups and SMEs, develop national AI talent, accelerate responsible AI entrepreneurship and position Bulgaria as a regional AI innovation leader. The case is relevant because it links frontier AI infrastructure to specific national priorities, including language technology and robotics, while also connecting Bulgaria to the wider EuroHPC AI Factory network. It should be framed as an AI Factory under development rather than a mature recurring public service
source_license: CC BY 4.0

title: MIMER New AI-optimised Supercomputer
source_description: Organisations that want to adopt AI often face a gap between strategic ambition and practical implementation: they may lack computing resources, model-development expertise, trusted AI governance, data-management capability or staff training. Mimer, Sweden’s AI Innovation Factory, addresses this gap by providing free access to powerful GPUs and expert support for companies, researchers and public-sector organisations. The operational problem is that advanced AI projects require more than software tools; they need suitable compute allocations, guidance on model optimisation, support for production-scale deployment and compliance with emerging expectations for trustworthy AI. Mimer brings these elements together through a service portfolio covering expert support, access to national and European supercomputing resources, secure data pipelines, training and upskilling, trustworthy AI services and wider ecosystem navigation. At a conceptual level, Mimer acts as an intermediary between AI users and the European high-performance computing ecosystem: it helps users identify the right access pathway, apply for compute resources, structure their projects and move from proof of concept to scalable use. The expected impact is faster AI experimentation, reduced infrastructure barriers for SMEs and researchers, stronger uptake of trustworthy AI practices and improved competitiveness of Sweden’s AI ecosystem. The case is relevant because it frames AI infrastructure as a service layer that combines hardware, expert guidance and governance support, rather than simply as a new supercomputer.

organization: IZUM – the Institute of Information Science
title: SLAIF New AI-optimised Supercomputer
source_description: Slovenia’s AI ecosystem requires shared infrastructure capable of supporting large-scale model development, advanced scientific computing and industrial deployment across sectors where individual organisations may not have sufficient capacity. The Slovenian AI Factory, known as SLAIF, responds to this need by combining an AI-optimised EuroHPC supercomputer with a broader ecosystem for research, industry and public institutions. The operational problem is that AI expertise in Slovenia is distributed across universities, research institutes and companies, while access to advanced computing, data and deployment support remains essential for scaling AI applications. SLAIF is designed as a coordinated hub that bridges academia and industry, providing access to AI infrastructure, expertise, data, pre-trained models and tailored cloud-based AI services. The new supercomputer will be hosted by IZUM in collaboration with the Jožef Stefan Institute and Arnes, with the wider AI Factory involving Slovenian universities, research bodies, industry organisations and innovation actors. At a conceptual level, SLAIF connects hardware, datasets, domain expertise, training programmes and business support into a single national AI-enabling environment. It will support use cases in energy optimisation, environmental monitoring, smart agriculture, healthcare, biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, language technologies, materials science and creative industries. The expected impact is stronger national AI capacity, improved competitiveness, more accessible AI adoption for companies and researchers, and Slovenia’s closer integration into the European network of AI factories.
